title: Aurivan CISA Topic Notes
source: Original Aurivan study notes, organized by the 2024 CISA exam content outline. Not affiliated with or endorsed by ISACA.
description: Plain-language notes for every topic in the CISA exam outline: what each idea means, how ISACA expects you to think about it, and the traps to avoid.

domains.overview: Domain 1 is the method behind every information systems (IS) audit: the professional rules and mandate, risk-based planning, testing and sampling, evidence, data analytics, reporting and quality review. Part A covers planning: standards and ethics, engagement types, risk-based planning and how controls work. Part B carries the plan out, from managing the engagement to reporting and improving audit quality. Principles such as independence and risk-based scope appear in questions across all five domains.
domains.analogy: An IS audit works like an independent home inspection. The inspector works under clear written terms (the charter) and must not be the builder who did the work (independence). With limited time, the inspector focuses on the riskiest areas, such as wiring and the roof (risk-based planning), tests a sample of outlets rather than every one (sampling), and trusts what they measure over what the seller says (evidence reliability). The report rates each defect and recommends fixes, but the owner decides what to repair (management decides). A later visit confirms the repairs were made (follow-up).

topics.topic_name: IS Audit Standards, Guidelines, Functions, and Codes of Ethics
topics.overview: This topic covers the professional ground rules behind every information systems (IS) audit: ISACA's standards and ethics code, the charter that gives audit its authority, and the independence that makes its work credible. It also covers other rulebooks auditors follow and how to rely on other people's work.
can_do: Tell a mandatory ITAF standard from a guideline or a tool in a scenario
Name who approves the audit charter and where the audit function reports
Choose between a safeguard and reassignment for an independence threat
Decide what to check before relying on an expert's or another auditor's work

subtopics.name: ITAF: Standards, Guidelines, and Tools and Techniques
subtopics.definition: ITAF (IT Audit Framework) is ISACA's professional practices framework for information systems (IS) audit and assurance work, in three layers ranked by how binding they are.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It tells the auditor what must happen on every engagement and what can be adapted. Many exam questions turn on which layer a requirement belongs to.
how_it_works: Standards are mandatory minimum requirements for ISACA members and certification holders on every audit and assurance engagement.

Standards come in three groups: general (charter, independence, objectivity, due care, proficiency), performance (risk assessment, planning, supervision, evidence, using experts, irregularities) and reporting (reporting, follow-up).
Guidelines explain how to apply the standards. They are not mandatory, but the auditor considers them and must be able to justify any departure.
Tools and techniques are informational aids, such as sample audit programs and white papers, that the auditor tailors to each engagement.

rows.label: Status
cells: Mandatory
Advisory
Informational

rows.label: Can the auditor depart?
cells: No
Yes, with a documented reason
Yes; adapt freely

rows.label: Example
cells: The requirement for an approved audit charter
Guidance on applying audit sampling
An ISACA audit program for change management

subtopics.example: During a payroll audit, the chief financial officer asks the audit manager to skip documenting evidence to save time. The manager refuses because evidence requirements come from a standard. Separately, the team cannot use an approach a guideline recommends because the payroll system lacks the needed logs, so it uses an alternative procedure and records that reason in the working papers.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Standards are the floor on every engagement; time, cost or a client's request cannot remove them. Guidelines call for judgment: consider them, and document the reason for any departure.

exam_traps.trap: Guidelines are optional, so the auditor can ignore them without explanation.
exam_traps.why: Guidelines are not mandatory, but the auditor is expected to consider them and justify any departure.

exam_traps.trap: A well-documented reason allows the auditor to depart from a standard.
exam_traps.why: A justified departure applies only to guidelines. Standards are minimum requirements and cannot be set aside.

key_terms.definition: A step-by-step list of procedures for auditing a subject; ISACA publishes examples as tools.
Applying the skill, diligence and skepticism expected of a competent auditor.
Applying training and experience to decide what is appropriate when the rules leave room for choice.
An ITAF general standard: accept an engagement only when it can be completed to standards, and disclose any scope limitation.

subtopics.analogy: Learning to drive works the same way: traffic laws are compulsory, the instructor's advice is strongly recommended, and practice routes are samples you adapt.
subtopics.memory_aid: Must, should, could: standards must be followed, guidelines should be considered, tools could be used.

subtopics.name: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics
subtopics.definition: The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics is a set of seven conduct principles that every ISACA member and certification holder agrees to follow in professional work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Boards trust audit results only if auditors are honest, careful and discreet. A breach can lead to an investigation and disciplinary action, up to losing the certification.
how_it_works: Governance: support sound standards, procedures and controls for information systems and technology.
Due care and lawful conduct (two principles): work objectively and diligently to professional standards, and serve stakeholders lawfully and honestly.
Confidentiality: keep information gained at work private unless the law requires disclosure, and never use it for personal gain.
Competence: accept only work you can do well, and keep your skills current through continuing education.
Disclosure: report the results of work to the right parties, including every significant fact that would otherwise distort the picture.
Education: help stakeholders understand governance, risk, control and security, and help the profession grow.
subtopics.example: Kenji, an IS auditor at a shipping line, finds that the vendor running its cargo-tracking system still has unrestricted administrator access. The vendor's account manager then offers him a free resort week. Kenji declines, reports the finding in full, and tells the chief audit executive (CAE) about the offer so it is recorded.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Ethics questions usually turn on honest, complete reporting. Disclose every significant fact to the people entitled to it, protect information from everyone else, and refuse any reward or role that could sway your judgment.

exam_traps.trap: Confidentiality means a sensitive finding should be kept out of the audit report.
exam_traps.why: Confidentiality limits sharing outside proper channels. The audit committee and responsible management are proper channels, and the disclosure duty requires significant facts to reach them.

exam_traps.trap: A finding can be dropped if management promises to fix it quietly.
exam_traps.why: Omitting a significant fact distorts the reported results, whatever the reason. Remediation plans are reported next to the finding, not instead of it.

key_terms.definition: Learning that certification holders must log to stay current; CISA holders need at least 20 hours a year and 120 every three years.
A gift, favor or promise, such as a contract or job offer, that could sway an auditor's judgment.
ISACA's response to a proven breach of the code, which can include losing membership or certification.

subtopics.memory_aid: Good Doctors Can Cure Diseases Early: governance, due care, confidentiality, competence, disclosure, education.

subtopics.name: The Audit Charter
subtopics.definition: The audit charter is a formal document, approved by the board or audit committee, that sets the audit function's purpose, responsibility, authority, accountability and reporting line.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The charter is the source of audit's right to see people, systems and records. Who approves it decides whether the function is independent of the managers it audits.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive (CAE) drafts the charter, and the board or its audit committee approves it.
It grants access to all records, systems, premises and staff that audit work requires.
It sets a functional reporting line to the audit committee and, usually, an administrative line to senior management.
It describes the services audit provides, such as assurance and advisory work, and any limits on them.
It stays high-level and stable; it is reviewed periodically and re-approved when audit's role changes.

rows.label: Purpose
cells: Grants the audit function its authority
Lists the audits chosen for the cycle by risk
Sets the terms of one engagement, often with an outside audit firm

rows.label: Approved by
cells: Board or audit committee
Audit committee
The client and the audit provider

rows.label: How often it changes
cells: Rarely; reviewed periodically
Every cycle, and when risk changes
For each engagement

rows.label: Typical content
cells: Right of access, reporting line, scope of services
Audit subjects, timing and resources
Scope, deliverables, timing and fees

subtopics.example: An energy retailer sets up its first IS audit function. The chief information officer (CIO) offers to sign the new charter, since IT is audit's main subject. The chief audit executive (CAE) thanks him, records his comments, and instead submits the draft, with its access rights and functional reporting line, to the audit committee for approval.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Audit's authority and independence come from the charter, which must be approved above the people being audited. Asked who approves it, choose the board or audit committee (or, without one, the highest level of management), never the chief information officer or another auditee manager.

exam_traps.trap: The chief information officer (CIO) can approve the IS audit charter because the CIO owns IT.
exam_traps.why: Approval by the auditee makes audit answer to the people it reviews. Only the board or audit committee can grant authority that stays independent of management.

exam_traps.trap: The GREATEST concern with a charter the CIO signed off on is its missing reporting line.
exam_traps.why: A missing clause can be added. Approval by the wrong body undermines the charter at its source, so fixing who approves it comes first.

key_terms.definition: The senior person who leads the internal audit function and reports to the audit committee.
The line through which the audit committee oversees audit's plan, budget, findings and leadership.
The line to a senior executive for day-to-day matters such as office space, travel and expense approval.

subtopics.name: The IS Audit Function and the Audit Committee
subtopics.definition: The information systems (IS) audit function is the permanent team that gives independent assurance over information systems; the audit committee is the board group that oversees it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The function needs skilled people, a plan and quality checks to produce reliable work. The audit committee shields it from management pressure and makes sure its findings reach the board.
how_it_works: The audit committee is a board committee of independent, non-executive directors who oversee audit, internal control and financial reporting.
The committee approves the charter and the risk-based audit plan, reviews audit's budget and resources, and receives its reports.
The chief audit executive (CAE) plans the work, assigns staff, supervises engagements and runs a quality program, all scaled to the function's size and risk.
The team as a whole must hold each engagement's skills, closing gaps with training or specialists.
Internal and external auditors coordinate to avoid duplicated work; each keeps its own reporting line.
Urgent, critical findings go to the committee chair between meetings, not at the next scheduled one.

types.meaning: The organization employs all of its own audit staff.
Internal staff work with an outside firm that adds skills or capacity; the internal function keeps responsibility.
An outside firm performs the audit work; the audit committee still oversees it and the organization stays accountable.

subtopics.example: At a regional airline, the chief financial officer asks the chief audit executive (CAE) to drop a planned audit of the maintenance-tracking system to save money. The CAE declines and explains its risk rating. When the request returns twice more, with hints about audit's budget, the CAE raises it with the audit committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The audit committee protects audit independence, so repeated pressure from management to drop or soften findings goes to the committee. Every function, however small, plans, supervises and checks its own quality; size changes how simple those processes are, not whether they exist.

exam_traps.trap: A small audit team can defer quality monitoring until it grows.
exam_traps.why: Planning, supervision and quality monitoring are needed at any size. They can be kept simple, but never skipped.

exam_traps.trap: Coordinating closely with the external auditor weakens internal audit's independence.
exam_traps.why: Coordination avoids duplicated effort and is expected. Independence comes from each function's reporting line, not from isolation.

key_terms.definition: A board member outside management, able to oversee managers objectively.
Having, as a team, the knowledge and skills an engagement needs; a general standard in ISACA's IT Audit Framework (ITAF).
A member with accounting or financial-reporting expertise; US-listed companies must disclose, under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX), whether one serves and, if not, why.

subtopics.name: Independence and Objectivity
subtopics.definition: Independence is the audit function's freedom from control by those it audits; objectivity is each auditor's unbiased state of mind. Both make conclusions credible.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An audit opinion is worthless if readers suspect it was bent. Threats must be spotted and handled before and during every engagement, not after a report is challenged.
how_it_works: Before each engagement, auditors disclose any ties to the area under review to audit management, and update the disclosure if circumstances change.
The audit manager assesses each threat separately and judges how serious it is.
Minor threats are managed with safeguards, such as disclosure, extra supervision or an independent review of the work.
Serious threats are removed, usually by reassigning the auditor, because no safeguard reduces them enough.
Independence must hold in appearance as well as in fact: a reasonable outsider should see no conflict.

rows.label: About
cells: Where the audit function sits
The mindset of each auditor

rows.label: Protected by
cells: Functional reporting to the audit committee and an approved charter
Declaring conflicts, rotation and reassignment

rows.label: Impaired when
cells: Audit reports to an executive who controls its budget or findings
An auditor reviews their own work or gains from the result

rows.label: Typical fix
cells: Change the reporting line
Reassign the auditor or add safeguards

types.meaning: Auditing work you designed, built or ran, such as a system you helped implement; earlier advice that left decisions to management is a lesser, manageable threat.
A personal stake in the result, such as an accepted job offer from the auditee.
Closeness from long tenure or personal ties that dulls skepticism; rotation is the usual safeguard.
Pressure or undue influence, such as management pushing the auditor to narrow the scope or soften findings.

subtopics.example: Before joining internal audit eight months ago, Marcus ran the payroll system's batch jobs for two years. Now an IS auditor assigned to a payroll controls audit, he tells his IS audit manager about his former role before fieldwork starts. The manager judges the self-review threat serious, assigns an auditor with no involvement, and records the threat assessment in the engagement file.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Disclose any threat to audit management before work starts, never afterward. Audit management then judges its severity: reassign an auditor who designed, built or ran the subject or accepted an auditee job; manage minor or unrelated ties with safeguards; rotate after long tenure, even with no visible problem.

exam_traps.trap: A peer review of the conflicted auditor's conclusions fixes a self-review threat.
exam_traps.why: The fieldwork, sampling and judgments still come from the conflicted auditor. Review only reduces the threat; reassignment removes it.

exam_traps.trap: Asked to audit a system they helped design, the auditor should simply decline the assignment.
exam_traps.why: The auditor's duty is to disclose the conflict to audit management before work starts. Audit management weighs its severity and decides on reassignment or safeguards; a silent refusal leaves the threat undocumented.

key_terms.definition: An action that reduces a threat to an acceptable level, such as disclosure, extra review or rotation.
A wait before auditing work you recently ran; internal audit standards presume objectivity is impaired for 12 months.

subtopics.name: Other Professional Standards and Conflicts
subtopics.definition: Multiple professional standards means an auditor is committed to more than one rulebook at once, such as ISACA's IT Audit Framework (ITAF) and the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) standards.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The rulebooks mostly agree but can differ on details, such as documentation or review timing. Without a rule for conflicts, auditors could pick the easiest option and breach a commitment.
how_it_works: The charter or audit manual states which standards the function commits to, such as ITAF, the IIA standards or a public-sector code.
Where two committed standards differ, the auditor applies the more rigorous requirement, which satisfies both.
The difference and the choice made are documented, so quality reviewers can follow the reasoning.
Laws and regulations can add requirements on top of professional standards; those are met as well, not traded off.
If a requirement truly cannot be met, the nonconformance is disclosed to the audit committee.
subtopics.example: Lena, the IS audit manager at a state transport agency, follows both ITAF and the government auditing standards that state law requires. The government standards demand more continuing education hours than ISACA's minimum for her certified staff. She sets the team's training target at the higher figure, which satisfies both, and records the reason in the audit manual.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Meet every standard you have committed to. When two differ, the more rigorous requirement satisfies both, so apply it and document why. Convenience, local habit or the order in which frameworks are listed never decides.

exam_traps.trap: Follow whichever framework the audit charter lists first.
exam_traps.why: List order carries no authority. Following one framework where it is weaker knowingly breaches the other commitment.

exam_traps.trap: Apply the more lenient requirement, since meeting either standard is enough.
exam_traps.why: The function committed to both. Only the stricter requirement meets both at once.

key_terms.definition: The global professional body for internal auditors; it issues the Global Internal Audit Standards, in effect since January 2025.
Failing to meet a requirement of a standard the function has committed to; it must be disclosed to governance.
The audit function's internal handbook of methods and policies, including how it applies its standards.

subtopics.name: Using the Work of Other Experts and Auditors
subtopics.definition: Using the work of others means relying on evidence produced outside the audit team, such as by a specialist or another auditor, to support audit conclusions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: No team has every skill, and repeating sound work wastes effort. But the information systems (IS) auditor stays responsible for the conclusion, so weak work relied on becomes the auditor's own failure.
how_it_works: Decide whether outside work is needed, for example when a subject requires cryptography, legal or actuarial skills the team lacks.
Before relying on it, assess the provider's competence, qualifications and objectivity, including any ties to the auditee.
Agree on the scope, objectives and access in writing, so the work answers the audit's question.
When the work arrives, evaluate it: check the methods, the evidence and whether the conclusions follow from them.
If the work is inadequate, do not rely on it; require correction or perform added procedures.
Document how the work was used and why it was judged reliable.

rows.label: Example
cells: A cryptographer reviewing an encryption design
The external auditor's IT tests or a provider's System and Organization Controls (SOC) report
Control self-assessment results or monitoring reports

rows.label: Independence from the auditee
cells: Must be checked
Usually high, but confirm it
None; management rates itself

rows.label: How the auditor can use it
cells: As evidence, after evaluating the expert and the work
As evidence, after checking scope, period and exceptions
To guide scope; never instead of audit testing

subtopics.example: A power utility's IS auditor engages an operational technology security firm to judge whether the grid-control network is segmented as designed. She first confirms the firm's staff hold relevant credentials and had no part in designing the network. When the report says "segmentation adequate" without listing the firewall rules examined, she withholds reliance and asks for the rule sets and test results.
subtopics.isaca_rule: You can delegate the work but not the responsibility. Check competence and objectivity before relying, evaluate the delivered work itself, and rely only on what holds up. Credentials alone never make a report reliable.

exam_traps.trap: Once a qualified expert is hired, the auditor can accept the report as delivered.
exam_traps.why: Credentials do not prove the delivered work is sound. The auditor evaluates methods, evidence and conclusions, and withholds reliance until gaps are fixed.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor should first reperform a sample of the expert's tests.
exam_traps.why: An auditor without the expertise cannot reperform them meaningfully, and reperformance does not show the expert was qualified or objective. Those are assessed first.

key_terms.definition: Using someone else's work as audit evidence, which reduces the auditor's own testing in that area.
A chart showing which provider gives assurance over each key risk, exposing gaps and overlaps.
An independent auditor's report on a service provider's controls, which customers' auditors can rely on.

topics.topic_name: Types of Audits, Assessments, and Reviews
topics.overview: Not every review gives the same comfort. This topic sorts engagements by their objective and by what the report promises, from full assurance to advice and plain facts. It also covers integrated audits, control self-assessment and the service provider reports auditors rely on when work is outsourced.
can_do: Choose the engagement type that answers a stated objective
Explain why advisory work, maturity ratings and agreed-upon procedures give no assurance
Pick the right SOC report and type, then check its carve-outs and user controls
Use control self-assessment results without letting them replace audit testing

subtopics.name: Audit Types by Objective
subtopics.definition: Audit types are named for the question an engagement answers and the criteria it tests against, such as laws, efficiency goals, accounting rules or information systems (IS) controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The audit type decides the criteria, the evidence and what the report can conclude. The wrong type produces a sound answer to a question nobody asked.
how_it_works: Start from the objective the requester states, such as "Do we meet the new regulation?"
Identify the criteria: laws and contracts, management's performance goals, accounting rules or a control framework.
Match the type to the criteria; in a question stem, the criteria usually give the type away.
Combine types when risks cross boundaries, as an integrated audit does.
Bring in specialists where a type needs skills the team lacks, such as forensic evidence handling.

types.meaning: Tests conformity with laws, regulations, policies or contracts.
Tests whether a process is efficient and effective at meeting management's goals.
Tests whether financial information is fairly presented.
Tests controls over information systems, infrastructure and data.
Gathers evidence of suspected fraud or wrongdoing, handled so it can support legal action.
Covers one defined subject, such as a service provider's controls or a privacy program.

subtopics.example: A hotel group's chief operating officer asks whether its new booking platform handles peak demand without wasted cloud spending. A board member suggests checking the platform against the card-payment security standard instead. The IS auditor explains that the question concerns efficiency against management's goals, so she plans an operational audit, and proposes a separate compliance review for the payment standard.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Read the objective and the criteria first; they name the audit type. Laws, regulations or contracts as criteria mean a compliance audit. Efficiency and effectiveness against management's goals mean an operational audit.

exam_traps.trap: An operational audit showing an efficient, resilient process proves the company meets the regulation.
exam_traps.why: Operational audits judge efficiency against management's goals. A well-run process can still miss a mandatory legal requirement, which only a compliance audit tests.

exam_traps.trap: A forensic audit is simply a more detailed financial audit.
exam_traps.why: Forensic work gathers evidence for possible legal action. It needs specialist skills, strict evidence handling and coordination with legal counsel that a financial audit does not.

key_terms.definition: The benchmarks a subject is measured against, such as a law, policy, contract or framework.
Whether a process achieves its intended result.
Whether a process achieves its result without wasting time, money or other resources.

subtopics.name: Assurance, Advisory, and Agreed-Upon Procedures
subtopics.definition: Engagement types differ by what the report promises: assurance gives a conclusion against criteria, advisory gives advice, and agreed-upon procedures report facts with no opinion.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Readers rely on these reports in very different ways. Agreeing on the type before work starts stops anyone treating advice or facts as assurance, and protects audit's independence later.
how_it_works: In an assurance engagement, the auditor tests the subject against criteria and gives a conclusion others can rely on.
In an advisory (consulting) engagement, the auditor helps management improve something, and management keeps every decision.
In an agreed-upon procedures engagement, the requester picks the steps, and the auditor reports what was done and what was found.
Agree on the type, scope, limits and responsibilities in writing before work starts.
If audit advises on controls it will later audit, disclose the self-review threat and keep the advisers off that later audit.

rows.label: Who sets the procedures
cells: The auditor, based on risk
Agreed with management
The engaging party

rows.label: What the report gives
cells: An opinion or conclusion
Recommendations
Procedures and factual findings only

rows.label: Level of assurance
cells: Reasonable (audit) or limited (review)
None
None

rows.label: Typical use
cells: The board relies on controls working
Control design input before go-live
A regulator checks specific facts

subtopics.example: A fintech's partner bank asks IS audit to confirm three facts: that 25 named loan files hold signed consents, that encryption is switched on for the loan database, and that backups ran every night in March. The IS audit manager agrees in writing that this is an agreed-upon procedures engagement, performs only those steps, and reports the factual results with no opinion on the controls.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the engagement type before work begins. Only assurance work supports a conclusion others can rely on. Advisory work is allowed, but the auditor never makes management's decisions and must manage any self-review threat it creates.

exam_traps.trap: An agreed-upon procedures report confirms that the controls are effective.
exam_traps.why: It reports only the procedures and the facts found. It contains no opinion or assurance, so readers draw their own conclusions.

exam_traps.trap: Audit should refuse all advisory work to keep its independence.
exam_traps.why: Advisory work is allowed when the type, terms and safeguards are agreed up front. Refusing loses useful early input; the safeguards protect independence.

key_terms.definition: A lower level of comfort, often worded negatively: nothing came to the auditor's attention suggesting a problem.
The written agreement on an engagement's type, scope, limits, responsibilities and reporting.
In an attest engagement the auditor reports on management's written assertion about a subject; in a direct engagement, on the subject itself.

subtopics.name: Readiness and Maturity Assessments
subtopics.definition: Readiness and maturity assessments are non-assurance reviews: readiness checks whether controls are designed for a coming audit, and maturity rates a process's capability against a model.
subtopics.why_it_matters: They help management prepare and set improvement targets. They are often mistaken for proof that controls work, which gives boards comfort that was never tested.
how_it_works: A readiness assessment compares current controls with a target standard, such as ISO/IEC 27001, before a formal audit or certification.
It looks mainly at design and documentation, and produces a list of gaps to fix.
A maturity assessment rates how well defined and managed a process is on a numbered scale, such as the 0-to-5 capability levels in ISACA's COBIT 2019 framework.
Neither one tests whether controls operated over a period, so neither gives assurance.
An assurance audit adds tests of operating effectiveness, which is what supports reliance.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: Are we ready for the audit?
How capable is the process?
Do the controls work?

rows.label: Tests operation over a period
cells: No
No
Yes

rows.label: Typical output
cells: A list of gaps
A rating and a target level
An opinion or conclusion

rows.label: Proof that controls work
cells: No
No
Yes

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A readiness assessment checks control design; a formal audit checks design and operating effectiveness'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Readiness review</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Checks control design</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Formal audit</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Design and operation</text></svg>
illustration.caption: A readiness review looks only at control design. A formal audit goes further and tests whether the controls operate.

subtopics.example: A software company's chief executive wants to tell its largest customer that access controls are proven effective, citing an internal readiness review that found no design gaps against ISO/IEC 27001. The IS auditor explains that the review checked design and documentation only. She recommends testing the key access controls over a period before anyone makes that claim.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the work to the question. If someone needs evidence that controls operate, only testing operating effectiveness over a period answers it. Ratings and readiness reviews are useful inputs, never substitutes.

exam_traps.trap: A high maturity score shows the controls are operating effectively.
exam_traps.why: Maturity measures how well a process is defined and managed. A process can score well while its key controls fail.

exam_traps.trap: Reperforming the consultant's scoring turns the maturity rating into assurance.
exam_traps.why: Checked scoring makes the rating more accurate, but it is still a rating. Assurance needs tests of whether the controls actually worked.

key_terms.definition: A comparison of the current state with a target, listing what must change to meet it.
Whether a control, if it works as described, would address the risk.
Whether a control actually worked as designed, consistently, throughout a period.

subtopics.name: Integrated Audits
subtopics.definition: An integrated audit combines IT, financial and operational audit work into one risk-based engagement, with one team and one report.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Business results depend on IT and people-run controls working together. Separate audits can each pass their own piece and miss the weakness where one feeds the other.
how_it_works: Choose integration when processes depend on each other, such as trading algorithms that feed regulatory filings.
Staff a mixed team with IT, financial and operational skills under one accountable engagement leader.
Test IT general controls (ITGCs), such as access and change management, early, because they decide whether automated controls can be relied on.
If ITGCs are weak, reduce reliance on automated controls and increase substantive testing, which checks the data directly.
Report each IT weakness with its business or financial effect in a single report.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Integrated auditing combines IT, financial and operational audit work into one combined report'><rect x='14' y='16' width='150' height='30' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='89' y='35' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>IT audit</text><rect x='14' y='52' width='150' height='30' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='89' y='71' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Financial audit</text><rect x='14' y='88' width='150' height='30' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='89' y='107' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Operational audit</text><line x1='166' y1='67' x2='243' y2='67' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M243,63 L250,67 L243,71 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='252' y='46' width='190' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='347' y='71' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>One combined report</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Integrated auditing. IT, financial and operational work come together in a single engagement and one report.

subtopics.example: In an integrated audit of a wine distributor's order-to-cash process, the IS auditor finds that developers can change the pricing engine in production without approval. Ana, the engagement leader, tells the financial auditors not to rely on the system's automated price checks. The team instead tests invoice prices directly against the approved price list, and the report links the change-control gap to revenue risk.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The reason to integrate is interdependence, not cost. Weak IT general controls cut reliance on automated controls and push the auditor toward more substantive testing. A truly integrated report connects each IT cause to its business effect.

exam_traps.trap: The PRIMARY reason to choose an integrated audit is lower cost and less disruption.
exam_traps.why: Savings are a side benefit. Integration is justified because financial or operational results depend on IT controls, and separate audits leave that boundary untested.

exam_traps.trap: When IT general controls fail, rely more on the application controls instead.
exam_traps.why: Application controls run on top of the general controls. If they could have been changed unnoticed, they cannot be trusted either, so substantive testing must grow.

key_terms.definition: A control performed by a system, such as a calculation or edit check, which works the same way every time unless changed.
The one person accountable for an engagement's plan, staffing, conclusions and report.
When one process or control relies on another, so a failure in one corrupts the other's results.

subtopics.name: Control Self-Assessment (CSA)
subtopics.definition: Control self-assessment (CSA) is a technique in which the people who run a process evaluate their own controls, often in a workshop an auditor facilitates.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Process owners know where controls really break. CSA builds their ownership and stretches scarce audit staff, but self-ratings are not independent, so they cannot carry an audit conclusion alone.
how_it_works: Management owns the CSA program, which shifts some control monitoring to the business; internal audit may design it, train staff and facilitate sessions.
Common formats are facilitated workshops, questionnaires and written reviews prepared by management.
The facilitator asks open questions, records the group's views and any dissent, and avoids steering toward the auditor's opinion.
CSA fits best where sites are spread out, owners are engaged and audit staff are few.
Auditors use CSA results to guide risk assessment and scope, then test high-risk controls themselves.

rows.label: Who evaluates
cells: Process owners and staff
Independent auditors

rows.label: Role of audit
cells: Facilitator and adviser
Tester and reporter

rows.label: Main benefit
cells: Ownership and wide coverage
Independent assurance

rows.label: Main limit
cells: Self-ratings can be optimistic
Limited coverage with limited staff

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 108' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Control self-assessment: staff and management assess their own controls; the IS auditor facilitates'><rect x='14' y='28' width='206' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='117' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Staff assess controls</text><rect x='246' y='28' width='200' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='346' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>IS auditor facilitates</text><text x='117' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>they own the controls</text><text x='346' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>guides the workshop</text></svg>
illustration.caption: In a control self-assessment, process owners judge their own controls and the auditor facilitates. Independent audit testing happens separately.

subtopics.example: A convenience-store chain with 220 stores wants yearly coverage of store system controls from a four-person IS audit team. The chief audit executive (CAE) has store managers complete a facilitated self-assessment, uses the results to rank stores by risk, and personally tests point-of-sale access controls at the highest-risk stores. Where self-ratings and test results disagree, the report shows both.
subtopics.isaca_rule: CSA shifts routine control monitoring to process owners and extends audit's reach, but it complements independent audit work and never replaces it. Use it for coverage, ownership and early warning, and base audit conclusions on the auditor's own testing.

exam_traps.trap: Strong CSA ratings let the auditor cut independent testing.
exam_traps.why: Self-ratings lack independence. If incidents contradict them and audit has stepped back, nobody is giving reliable assurance.

exam_traps.trap: The facilitator should present the auditor's list of weaknesses for the group to confirm.
exam_traps.why: That anchors participants on the auditor's view and turns self-assessment into confirmation. Open questions and recorded dissent capture what only the owners know.

key_terms.definition: A neutral guide who runs a workshop, draws out participants' views and records them without imposing conclusions.
A process manager's accountability for designing, operating and monitoring the controls in their area.

subtopics.name: System and Organization Controls (SOC) Reports
subtopics.definition: System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports are independent auditors' reports on a service provider's controls, which customers' auditors use instead of auditing the provider themselves.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Outsourcing a service does not outsource its risk. The customer's auditor must check that a report fits the objective and know what it leaves out.
how_it_works: An independent service auditor tests the provider's controls under American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) standards or international ISAE 3402 and reports.
Pick SOC 1 for financial reporting, SOC 2 for the Trust Services Criteria such as security, and Type 2 for reliance over a period.
Read the period, systems in scope, test exceptions and opinion; cover any gap before your year end with a bridge letter or other evidence.
Confirm your organization runs the complementary user entity controls (CUECs) that the report lists.
Get separate assurance for any carved-out subservice organization, such as the provider's own data center supplier.

rows.label: Covers
cells: Controls relevant to customers' financial reporting
Trust Services Criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy
The same criteria as SOC 2, in summary

rows.label: Audience
cells: Customers and their financial auditors
Customers and others with a business need (restricted use)
Anyone (general use)

rows.label: Test details
cells: Included in Type 2
Included in Type 2
None

rows.label: Use it when
cells: Outsourced payroll or billing feeds the financial statements
Relying on a cloud provider's security
General comfort only; not enough for reliance

types.meaning: An opinion on the design of controls at a single date; no evidence that they kept working.
An opinion on design and operating effectiveness over a period, often 6 to 12 months, with test results.

subtopics.example: A media company's subscriber portal runs on a cloud provider whose SOC 2 Type 2 report covers the year to March 31; the company's year ends June 30. The IS auditor reviews the exceptions, confirms the company performs the listed user entity controls, and requests a bridge letter and other evidence for April to June.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the report to the objective: SOC 1 for financial reporting, SOC 2 for the Trust Services Criteria, Type 2 for reliance over a period. Then check exceptions, carve-outs, any period gap and your own user controls.

exam_traps.trap: A SOC 2 Type 1 report shows the provider's controls worked all year.
exam_traps.why: Type 1 covers design at a single date. Evidence of operation across the year needs a Type 2 report or the auditor's own testing.

exam_traps.trap: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organization is covered because its services are described.
exam_traps.why: Carve-out excludes the subservice organization's controls, so they were not tested. Get separate assurance, such as that organization's own report.

key_terms.definition: Checks the customer must run itself, such as reviewing payroll reports, so the provider's controls achieve their objectives.
A report approach that excludes a subservice organization's controls from testing; the inclusive method includes and tests them.
A provider's statement covering the gap between a SOC report's period end and the customer's year end, saying whether controls changed.

topics.overview: Audit time is limited, so it goes where risk is highest. This topic moves from the full audit universe to the annual plan, then to the plan for one engagement, using risk assessment, legal requirements, the audit risk model and materiality to decide what to audit and how much to test.
can_do: Build or adjust an audit plan from a complete, risk-ranked audit universe
Pick a risk assessment method that fits the data available
Trace an engagement's scope back to its objectives and risks
Set the amount of testing using detection risk, and judge materiality beyond dollar size

subtopics.name: The Audit Universe and the Annual Plan
subtopics.definition: The audit universe is the full list of areas that could be audited; the risk-based audit plan picks the highest-risk areas from it for each cycle.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Audit hours are scarce, so they must go where risk is highest. Anything missing from the universe can never be selected, so a gap there becomes a permanent blind spot.
how_it_works: List auditable entities at a useful level: processes, systems, locations, vendors, legal obligations and shared services.
Map each entity to its risks and to the organization's strategy and objectives, using management's risk register as one input but not the only one.
Rank entities by current risk, refreshed each cycle, and choose which to audit and how often.
Have the audit committee approve the plan and the resources it needs.
Update the universe and the plan mid-cycle when risk changes, such as after an acquisition, a new regulation or a major incident.
If resources fall, re-prioritize by risk, document the change and inform the audit committee.
subtopics.example: Midway through the year, a regional grocer buys a meal-kit company that has its own ordering app and warehouse systems. The IS audit manager adds the new systems to the audit universe and rates their risk against every existing entity. She then re-ranks the plan and asks the audit committee to approve the revised plan and the resources it needs.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A complete universe comes first, then ranking by current risk. Rotation, habit, last year's findings or the cheapest option never decide the plan on their own. When risk or resources change, re-prioritize, document the change and inform the audit committee.

exam_traps.trap: Keep the fixed three-year rotation so every system gets equal coverage.
exam_traps.why: Rotation ignores where risk is now. High-risk areas can wait years while low-risk ones are audited on schedule.

exam_traps.trap: When staff leave mid-year, finish every planned audit at reduced depth.
exam_traps.why: Thin work on high-risk areas gives assurance the evidence cannot support. Deliver the highest-risk audits in full, defer the rest and brief the audit committee.

key_terms.definition: Any unit the audit function could review, such as a process, system, location, vendor or shared service.
The period a plan covers, usually one year, after which risk is reassessed.
Management's record of identified risks, their ratings, owners and responses.

subtopics.name: Risk Assessment Methods
subtopics.definition: Risk assessment, in audit planning, rates each area by how likely a problem is and how much harm it would cause, allowing for the controls in place.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The ranking decides where audit hours go. An inconsistent or one-sided rating sends auditors to the wrong places and leaves serious risks unexamined.
how_it_works: Rate likelihood and impact together; neither one alone ranks risk correctly.
Use defined scales, so every rater means the same thing by "high" or "medium."
Use numbers where reliable history exists, and qualitative ratings where data is thin.
Estimate intangible harm, such as brand damage, from indirect indicators like customer loss, and state the assumptions.
Combine methods: a structured process such as ISO 31000 for the whole risk list, plus loss modeling such as FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) for the top few.
Refresh ratings when the business changes, not only once a year.

rows.label: Expresses risk as
cells: Ratings such as high, medium and low
Money or probabilities, such as expected annual loss

rows.label: Needs
cells: Defined criteria and experienced judgment
Reliable historical or modeled data

rows.label: Strength
cells: Fast; works with little data
Precise; supports cost-benefit decisions

rows.label: Weakness
cells: Subjective unless scales are defined
False precision when the data is poor

subtopics.example: An insurer's IS auditor ranks risks for next year's plan. Claims-system outages have ten years of reliable loss data, so she expresses that risk as expected annual loss. A new mobile app has no history, so she rates it on the defined high, medium and low scales used across the register. Both feed one ranking, and she records the assumptions behind each.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank on likelihood and impact together, adjusted for existing controls. Fit the method to each area's data: numbers where history is reliable, defined qualitative scales where it is not. Consistency means shared definitions, not one method forced on every area.

exam_traps.trap: Rank first the risk with the worst possible impact.
exam_traps.why: Impact alone misleads. A very high impact with low likelihood can rank below a risk that is both likely and harmful.

exam_traps.trap: Average widely different ratings into one score.
exam_traps.why: Averaging hides the disagreement. Very different scores usually mean raters are using different scales, so define the criteria and rate again.

key_terms.definition: How probable it is that a risk event occurs within a given period.
The harm an event would cause, in money, operations, compliance or reputation.
A grid plotting likelihood against impact, with colored cells that show relative risk.

subtopics.name: Laws, Regulations, and the Audit Plan
subtopics.definition: Legal and regulatory requirements are external obligations, such as privacy or financial reporting laws, that shape what the information systems (IS) audit plan covers and how often.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Breaking a law can bring fines, lost licenses and lawsuits, so legal obligations raise risk ratings. The auditor must know which apply without acting as the organization's lawyer.
how_it_works: Identify the laws, regulations and contracts that apply to each auditable area, with help from legal and compliance staff.
Rely on legal counsel to interpret them; the auditor tests against agreed requirements, not a personal reading of the law.
Weight risk ratings and audit frequency by regulatory exposure and deadlines.
Where several regimes apply, evaluate each one's requirements, including those unique to it.
Where management maps one control set to several frameworks, check the mapping itself for gaps.
Check that management has a process to track new and changing legal requirements and assign owners; plan audit scope before new laws take effect.
subtopics.example: A US university with a campus in Ireland holds student records covered by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Management maps one control set to both. The IS auditor reviews the mapping with the compliance office, finds no control for GDPR's 72-hour breach notice, and audits against each law's own requirements.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Understand legal requirements well enough to plan, and let legal and compliance interpret them. Never assume that compliance with one regime, or one certification, covers another: map the requirements and look for gaps.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor should interpret a new law independently and design tests from that reading.
exam_traps.why: Legal interpretation belongs to counsel and compliance. A misreading would point the whole audit at the wrong criteria.

exam_traps.trap: ISO/IEC 27001 certification proves compliance with every security law that applies.
exam_traps.why: ISO/IEC 27001 is a voluntary standard. Laws carry their own specific obligations, such as notification deadlines, that a certification may not cover.

key_terms.definition: The potential for fines, sanctions or lost licenses if a legal requirement is not met.
A documented mapping between two frameworks' or laws' requirements, showing where they overlap and where they differ.

subtopics.name: Planning an Individual Engagement
subtopics.definition: Engagement planning turns one audit from the annual plan into objectives, scope and an approach, based on the risks of that specific subject.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Good planning aims fieldwork at the risks that matter the first time. Weak planning lets risks surface halfway through fieldwork, forcing rework, missed deadlines or conclusions the evidence cannot support.
how_it_works: Learn the subject: its processes, systems, interfaces, recent incidents and prior audit results.
Do a walkthrough, tracing one transaction from start to finish, to confirm how the process and its controls really work.
Assess this subject's risks, then set objectives that state what the audit must determine.
Set the scope from the objectives: the systems, locations and period covered, and what is excluded.
Plan the approach and assign staff with the right skills; the audit program then lists the detailed steps.
Match the depth of planning to the subject's risk and complexity.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: What must the audit determine?
Which systems, sites and period are covered?
Which steps will the team perform?

rows.label: Comes from
cells: The risks that put the audit in the plan
The objectives
The objectives and scope

rows.label: Example
cells: Does access to the trading system enforce segregation of duties?
Trading system, head office, January to June
Check a sample of access changes for approval

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 584 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Engagement planning: understand the subject, analyze risk, set objectives, set scope, then plan and staff the work'><rect x='8' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='56' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Understand</text><rect x='126' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='174' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Analyze risk</text><rect x='244' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='292' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Set objectives</text><rect x='362' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='410' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Set scope</text><rect x='480' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='528' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Plan and staff</text><line x1='106' y1='46' x2='117' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M117,42 L124,46 L117,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='224' y1='46' x2='235' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M235,42 L242,46 L235,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='342' y1='46' x2='353' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M353,42 L360,46 L353,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='460' y1='46' x2='471' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M471,42 L478,46 L471,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Planning one audit. Understanding the subject and analyzing risk come before objectives are set, and objectives drive the scope.

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at a gas pipeline operator has six weeks to audit a new remote-monitoring system that links field sensors to a vendor cloud. Instead of reusing last year's program, she reviews recent outage reports, follows one pressure alarm from the sensor to the control room, and sets the objectives and scope around the vendor link and alarm handling.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Scope follows risk. Understand the subject, assess its risks, then set objectives and scope. Every procedure should trace to an objective and every objective to a risk. Thorough planning saves fieldwork time rather than wasting it.

exam_traps.trap: A high-priority audit should cover every connected system for maximum coverage.
exam_traps.why: Priority calls for depth, not breadth. Scope comes from the risks that justified the audit; testing everything spreads effort thin.

exam_traps.trap: Under a tight deadline, keep planning brief and start testing early.
exam_traps.why: Rushed planning lets risks surface halfway through fieldwork, forcing rework that a tight deadline cannot absorb.

key_terms.definition: Tracing one transaction through a process, end to end, to confirm the auditor's understanding of the process and its controls.
An area deliberately left out of an engagement, stated in the plan and report so readers know the limits.

subtopics.name: Audit Risk and Its Three Parts
subtopics.definition: Audit risk is the risk that the auditor reaches the wrong conclusion, such as reporting controls as effective when a material problem exists.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It explains why testing must grow as the subject gets riskier. The auditor controls only one part of audit risk, so every adjustment happens there.
how_it_works: Audit risk combines three parts: inherent risk × control risk × detection risk.
Inherent and control risk belong to the subject; the auditor assesses them but cannot change them.
Detection risk comes from the auditor's own procedures, so it is the only part the auditor controls.
When inherent and control risk are high, lower detection risk by testing more, closer to period end, or with stronger procedures.
When both are low, accept higher detection risk and test less, but never skip substantive work entirely.

rows.label: Meaning
cells: Risk of a material error before any controls
Risk that controls fail to prevent or detect it
Risk that audit procedures miss it

rows.label: Driven by
cells: The nature of the business and system
Management's controls
The auditor's testing

rows.label: High when
cells: Activity is complex, high-value or fast-changing
Controls are weak or missing
Tests are too few, too early or unsuited

rows.label: Auditor's response
cells: Assess it and plan accordingly
Assess it, partly by testing controls
Set it through the nature, timing and extent of testing

illustration.caption: The audit risk model. The business and its controls drive the first two factors; the auditor adjusts the third through testing.

subtopics.example: At an online sports-betting operator, the IS auditor rates inherent risk high because of heavy volume and complex odds calculations, and control risk high after finding weak access controls. Instead of testing the weak controls further, she lowers detection risk: she recalculates every payout for the year with data analytics and moves her testing close to year-end.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The auditor manages audit risk only through detection risk. Higher inherent and control risk mean lower acceptable detection risk, so more and stronger testing. Low assessed risk allows less testing, never none.

exam_traps.trap: When control risk is high, do more control testing to bring it down.
exam_traps.why: Control risk reflects how well the controls work. More testing only confirms the weakness; the auditor responds by expanding substantive testing.

exam_traps.trap: With low inherent and control risk, substantive testing can be skipped.
exam_traps.why: Controls give only reasonable assurance, so some substantive work on material areas is always needed.

key_terms.definition: The three levers of testing: what kind of test, when it is done, and how much is tested.
A questioning mind that does not accept evidence or explanations at face value.

subtopics.name: Materiality
subtopics.definition: Materiality is the point at which an error, weakness or omission could change the decisions of the people who rely on the audit.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It tells the auditor what is worth finding and reporting. Judging it by dollar size alone lets small but sensitive problems slip through.
how_it_works: Start with a quantitative guide, such as a percentage of revenue or transaction value, as a planning threshold.
Add qualitative factors: legal or regulatory breach, fraud, sensitive data or harm to customers.
Judge errors in aggregate; many small errors from one cause can add up to a material problem.
Consider reliance: a weak control that other controls depend on can be material even if its direct loss is small.
In information systems (IS) audits, weigh how critical the system is and what it feeds, not just the dollars it processes.
subtopics.example: A pharmacy benefits manager's claims system pays thousands of dispensing fees a day, averaging $4 each. The IS auditor learns that a pricing-table change went live untested and that some fees may breach state reimbursement rules. Although each error is tiny, she treats the pricing module as material, citing volume, aggregation and the possible legal breach, and tests it fully.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Materiality is a judgment about what would change a user's decision, not a fixed dollar line. Weigh size, nature and context, add up related errors, and remember that a small-dollar weakness in a regulatory or critical system can still be material.

exam_traps.trap: A weakness is immaterial because the average amount per item is small.
exam_traps.why: Volume, aggregation and reliance count. Thousands of small errors, or a failing compensating control, can add up to a material problem.

exam_traps.trap: Whether management agrees an issue is significant decides its materiality.
exam_traps.why: Materiality is the auditor's professional judgment about users' decisions. Management's view is useful context but does not decide it.

key_terms.definition: Significance that comes from the nature of an issue, such as fraud or a legal breach, rather than its size.
Adding related errors together to judge whether, combined, they are material.
The people who rely on the audit report, such as the board, regulators or management.

topics.overview: Controls are how management keeps risk within limits it accepts, and judging them is the core of IS audit work. This topic covers what controls can and cannot do, how to classify them by timing, reach and who performs them, and how to judge substitutes, layered defenses, remaining risk and monitoring.
can_do: Classify a control as preventive, detective or corrective, and as general or application
Explain why weak IT general controls cut reliance on automated and report-based controls
Judge whether a compensating control or a layered design truly covers the risk
State who accepts residual risk and when audit can rely on management's monitoring

subtopics.name: Internal Control Basics
subtopics.definition: Internal control is the set of policies, procedures, practices and structures management uses to give reasonable assurance that the organization's objectives are met.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls keep risk within the limits the organization accepts. Knowing their limits stops managers and auditors from expecting a guarantee that no control can give.
how_it_works: Controls support three kinds of objectives: effective operations, reliable reporting and compliance with laws and regulations.
They give reasonable, not absolute, assurance because of limits built into any control system.
Those limits include human error, collusion, management override and the cost of controls compared with their benefit.
Because preventive controls can be defeated, detective controls are layered behind them to catch what gets through.
The COSO (Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission) framework groups internal control into five linked components.

types.meaning: The tone, ethics, structure and accountability that every other control rests on.
Identifying and analyzing what could stop objectives from being met.
Specific actions, such as approvals, reconciliations and access limits, that address risks.
Getting accurate, timely information to the people who need it.
Ongoing and separate evaluations that check whether controls are present and working.

subtopics.example: After a costly data leak, an architecture firm's managing partner asks the IS auditor to confirm that a new data-loss prevention tool means leaks "cannot happen again." The IS auditor explains that controls give reasonable assurance, not a guarantee, because people make mistakes, collude or override controls. She recommends a periodic detective review of the transfers the tool allowed and blocked.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Controls reduce risk to an acceptable level; they never eliminate it. Expect their built-in limits and pair preventive controls with detective ones. An answer claiming that a control guarantees or eliminates a risk is almost always wrong.

exam_traps.trap: A well-designed preventive control removes the need for detective controls.
exam_traps.why: Collusion and override can defeat any preventive control. Detective controls catch what gets through, which is why controls give only reasonable assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Internal control only concerns financial reporting.
exam_traps.why: It covers operations, reporting and compliance objectives, and IS controls support all three.

key_terms.definition: A high, but not absolute, level of confidence that objectives will be met.
A manager deliberately bypassing a control, which no control design can fully stop.
Two or more people secretly working together to defeat a control, such as segregation of duties.

subtopics.name: Control Objectives and Control Measures
subtopics.definition: A control objective is the result a control must achieve, such as "only approved changes reach production"; a control measure is the mechanism that achieves it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Auditors test controls against objectives. If an objective is vague or missing, nobody can tell whether a control works or whether a risk is left uncovered.
how_it_works: Derive each objective from a risk or a requirement, such as a regulation or a contract.
Write objectives that are specific, testable and traceable to that risk or requirement.
Design one or more control measures to meet each objective; different teams may meet the same objective in different ways.
Start from a framework such as COBIT 2019, ISACA's framework for governing and managing IT, and adapt its objectives and practices.
Test whether each measure addresses its objective's risk, not just whether it runs.
Treat any objective with no control behind it as a gap to report.

rows.label: Answers
cells: What must be achieved?
How is it achieved?

rows.label: Example
cells: Ensure batch processing keeps data complete
Reconcile batch totals after each run

rows.label: Changes when
cells: The risk or requirement changes
The technology or process changes

rows.label: Auditor checks
cells: It is complete and tied to a risk
It is designed and operating to meet the objective

subtopics.example: A hospital's policy sets the control objective that only a patient's treating clinicians may open psychiatric records. The IT manager points to the access-control rule in the records system that blocks other users. The IS auditor classifies that rule as a control measure, then tests a sample of record openings to see whether it actually achieves the objective, including emergency access.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Objectives come from risks, not from the controls already in place. Test each measure against the objective it serves. A control that runs perfectly but misses its objective's risk adds little assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Write control objectives from the controls that already exist.
exam_traps.why: Objectives drawn from current controls hide gaps where no control exists yet. Derive them from risks and requirements first.

exam_traps.trap: A control that operates every time must be effective.
exam_traps.why: It must also target the right risk. A daily check against an unverified reference list can run flawlessly and still miss errors in that list.

key_terms.definition: The ability to link each objective to its risk and each control to its objective, in both directions.
A structured set of control objectives and practices, such as COBIT, used as a starting point for design and audit.

subtopics.name: Preventive, Detective, and Corrective Controls
subtopics.definition: Preventive, detective and corrective controls sort controls by timing: stopping a problem before it happens, finding it afterward, or fixing its effects.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When a control acts shows what it can and cannot do. Good design mixes all three, because prevention fails and detection without correction leaves the damage in place.
how_it_works: Classify by function, not technology: ask what the control does and when it acts.
The same tool can play different roles; a log becomes detective only when someone reviews it or an alert fires.
A permanent fix, such as automatic account disablement, is preventive for future events even if an incident prompted it.
Deterrent controls discourage attempts, and compensating controls substitute for a missing one; some frameworks list both separately.
Preventive controls are usually preferred, but detective and corrective controls are still needed because prevention is never perfect.

rows.label: Acts
cells: Before the event
During or after the event
After detection

rows.label: Example
cells: A fraud engine blocks a suspicious card payment
A reviewed report of active accounts belonging to leavers
Disabling those accounts and checking what they did

rows.label: Weakness
cells: Collusion or override can bypass it
Works only if someone acts on it
Some damage has already happened
