illustration.caption: Sorting controls by timing. Most risks are covered by all three types working together.

subtopics.example: A veterinary clinic chain's dispensing system refuses to print a label when a dose exceeds the safe limit for the animal's weight, unless a vet overrides it. The operations manager lists it as detective because it "finds dosing errors." The IS auditor classifies it as preventive, since the error never reaches the animal, and checks whether vet overrides are reviewed afterward.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify a control by what it does and when it acts. Prefer prevention, but expect it to fail: a strong design layers detective and corrective controls behind it.

exam_traps.trap: A control that identifies suspicious activity is always detective.
exam_traps.why: If it stops the transaction before harm occurs, it is preventive. Detective controls report events that have already happened.

exam_traps.trap: An unreviewed log is a detective control.
exam_traps.why: A log only records. Detection happens when a person or an automated alert reviews it and someone acts.

key_terms.definition: A control that discourages an attempt, such as a warning banner or visible camera, without physically stopping it.
A system report listing items that break a rule, for someone to review and act on.

subtopics.name: IT General Controls and Application Controls
subtopics.definition: IT general controls (ITGCs) protect the whole IT environment, while application controls work inside one system to keep its transactions complete, accurate and valid.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Automated application controls can be trusted only if nobody can change or bypass them unnoticed. That trust rests on the general controls underneath.
how_it_works: ITGCs cover access to programs and data, program changes, IT operations, and backup and recovery.
Application controls cover input, processing and output, such as edit checks, batch totals and output reconciliation.
Test ITGCs early: if they fail, any automated control could have been altered, so it cannot be relied on.
When ITGCs are weak, shift to substantive testing of the data the application produced.
Sound change control separates the roles that build, test, approve and move changes into production.
Judge application controls by whether each covers a specific process risk and operates consistently across transactions, not by vendor default settings.

rows.label: Reach
cells: Every system in the environment
One application or business process

rows.label: Examples
cells: User provisioning, change management, job scheduling, backups
Input validation, batch totals, output reconciliation

rows.label: Usual owner
cells: IT functions
Business process owners, with IT support

rows.label: If they fail
cells: Reliance on every automated control in that environment falls
Errors in that process's transactions go unnoticed

subtopics.example: At a cement producer, the IS auditor tests a batching application whose input checks reject invalid ingredient weights. She then finds that two developers can move code into production without a ticket or approval. She reports that the input checks cannot be relied on until change control is fixed, and plans substantive testing of recorded batch weights.
subtopics.isaca_rule: General controls come first. If access or change management fails, automated application controls lose their reliability, however well designed, and the auditor shifts to substantive testing.

exam_traps.trap: A batch reconciliation between two systems is a general control because it spans systems.
exam_traps.why: It checks that specific processing is complete, so it is an application control. General controls apply across the whole environment.

exam_traps.trap: Logging every change in one ticket tool makes change management well designed.
exam_traps.why: Logging gives traceability, but a logged change can still be untested or self-deployed. Approval, testing and separate roles are what stop unauthorized changes.

key_terms.definition: An automated test that rejects input that is missing, out of range or in the wrong format.
The live systems that process real business transactions and data.
A control built into and enforced by an information system, such as role-based access in an application, rather than performed by people.

subtopics.name: Key Controls and IT-Dependent Manual Controls
subtopics.definition: A key control is one the auditor relies on to cover a significant risk; an IT-dependent manual control is a person's check that uses system-produced information.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Auditors cannot test every control, so they focus on key ones. Many key controls are manual reviews of system reports, and a review is only as good as the report behind it.
how_it_works: Identify key controls: those whose failure would leave a significant risk uncovered. Test them first and most thoroughly.
Treat other controls as non-key; they support the key ones but are not relied on alone.
For an IT-dependent manual control, test both the person's review and the completeness and accuracy of the report used.
A report's reliability depends on how it was built and run, and on the IT general controls over its system.
An automated control may be tested with a small sample, even one item, when IT general controls are effective; manual controls need larger samples.

types.meaning: A person performs the check without relying on system output, such as counting physical stock.
A person performs the check using system output, such as reviewing an overdue-payments report.
The system performs the check every time, such as blocking invoices that do not match an order.

subtopics.example: Each month, a retailer's finance manager reviews a system report of credit notes over $5,000 and signs it off. The IS auditor sees every signature, then checks how the report is produced and finds its filter skips one region's entries. She reports that the review cannot be relied on until the report is complete.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Focus testing on key controls. For any manual review that uses system output, test the report as well as the reviewer: a careful review of an incomplete report gives false comfort.

exam_traps.trap: The manager's monthly sign-off proves the review control works.
exam_traps.why: A signature shows the review happened, not that the report was complete and accurate. The auditor must also test the information the reviewer relied on.

exam_traps.trap: Every control in a process deserves the same amount of testing.
exam_traps.why: Testing is risk-based. Key controls carry the weight of the conclusion; non-key controls get less attention or none.

key_terms.definition: Reports, queries and data extracts from the organization's own systems that are used in controls or as evidence.
Assurance that a report includes every relevant record and that each value in it is correct.

subtopics.name: Compensating Controls and Defense in Depth
subtopics.definition: A compensating control reduces a risk when the preferred control is impractical; defense in depth layers several controls so one failure does not expose the asset.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Small teams and old systems often cannot have the ideal control. Knowing what makes a substitute or a layered design truly work prevents false comfort from controls that only look reassuring.
how_it_works: Identify the gap: which preferred control is missing and which risk it leaves open.
Choose a substitute that addresses the same risk, often an independent review after the fact.
Confirm independence: the reviewer must not be the person whose work is reviewed.
Test the compensating control as rigorously as the control it replaces.
For layered defenses, list each way the asset could be exposed and check that at least one layer covers it.
If a compensating control fails, residual risk rises and the audit scope must grow.
subtopics.example: At a small charity, one clerk both records donations and deposits them. As a compensating control, the treasurer reviews monthly bank statements against the donation log. The IS auditor finds that for three months the clerk prepared the review pack and the treasurer only signed it. She reports that the control relies on the clerk's own work and recommends the treasurer get statements directly from the bank.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A compensating control works only if it covers the same risk and, where it is a review, the reviewer is independent of the work. Judge layered controls by whether, together, they cover every way things can fail, not by how many layers exist.

exam_traps.trap: A review done by the person who did the work counts as a compensating control.
exam_traps.why: Self-review removes the independence the control depends on. It looks complete in metrics but gives no assurance.

exam_traps.trap: More layers of control always mean stronger protection.
exam_traps.why: Five layers that share the same blind spot still leave it open. The auditor maps layers to failure modes and looks for gaps.

key_terms.definition: Splitting the steps of a sensitive task so no one person can complete and conceal it alone.
A specific way a control can fail or an asset can be exposed.
A check of someone's work by a person who did not do it and has no stake in the result.

subtopics.name: Controls, Inherent Risk, and Residual Risk
subtopics.definition: Residual risk is the risk that remains after controls are applied to inherent risk, which is the risk that would exist with no controls at all.
subtopics.why_it_matters: No set of controls removes all risk, so someone must decide whether what remains is acceptable. That decision belongs to management, and auditors must not take it on.
how_it_works: Start from inherent risk: the exposure if no controls existed.
Judge how much the controls in place reduce likelihood or impact, based on testing rather than descriptions.
Compare the remaining risk with the organization's risk appetite, the amount of risk it is willing to take.
Management responds to residual risk above appetite: mitigate it further, transfer (share) it, avoid the activity, or formally accept it.
The auditor evaluates and reports residual risk and recommends action; management decides and owns the risk.
Untested or failing controls mean residual risk is closer to inherent risk than management may think.
