illustration.caption: Controls bring inherent risk down to residual risk. Some risk remains, and management decides whether to accept it.

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at an insurer finds that weak password settings on the claims system leave residual risk above the stated appetite. The IT director asks the auditor to sign off that the risk is acceptable so the project can close. The auditor declines, reports the residual risk and recommends that the claims business owner take the acceptance decision to senior management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Residual risk never reaches zero, and accepting it is a documented management decision by someone with authority. The auditor evaluates, reports and recommends; the auditor never accepts risk on the organization's behalf.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor can accept residual risk on behalf of the business.
exam_traps.why: Accepting risk is a management decision. An auditor who accepts it takes on a management role and impairs independence.

exam_traps.trap: Residual risk can be removed if enough controls are added.
exam_traps.why: Every control has limits and a cost. The goal is residual risk within appetite, not zero.

key_terms.definition: A documented decision by an authorized manager to live with a residual risk, with reasons and a review date.
The manager accountable for a risk and for deciding how to respond to it.

subtopics.name: Control Monitoring and the Control Environment
subtopics.definition: Control monitoring is checking, over time, that controls still work, through management's ongoing reviews and periodic separate evaluations, all resting on the control environment.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls decay as people, systems and risks change. Monitoring catches the decay early, but only in a culture where staff feel safe reporting problems.
how_it_works: Management monitors its own controls as part of daily work, such as supervisors reviewing exception reports and tracking fixes.
Separate evaluations step back from daily work periodically, such as internal audits, annual self-assessments or consultant reviews.
The culture, including tone at the top and protection for people who raise concerns, decides whether monitoring results are honest.
The auditor tests management's monitoring before relying on it, then adjusts other testing.
If management's monitoring missed failures the auditor found, that gap is reported as a separate finding.

rows.label: When
cells: Continuously, as part of normal work
Periodically, as a standalone exercise

rows.label: Who
cells: Line managers and supervisors
Internal audit, consultants, or owners in an annual self-assessment

rows.label: Example
cells: A supervisor reviews daily access exceptions
An annual internal audit of access controls

rows.label: Strength
cells: Finds problems quickly
Gives a deeper, more objective look

subtopics.example: At a telecom carrier, network managers review a weekly report of firewall rule changes and sign that every change was approved. Before relying on these reviews, the IS auditor reperforms four weeks of them and finds two unapproved changes the managers had signed off on. She reports the unapproved changes and, as a separate finding, the failed monitoring, and expands her own testing.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Management monitoring and independent audit complement each other; neither replaces the other. Audit may rely on management's monitoring only after testing it. A weak control environment undermines every control, however well documented.

exam_traps.trap: Management's monthly monitoring makes independent audit testing unnecessary.
exam_traps.why: Audit also tests whether the monitoring itself works. Letting management's unverified results set audit scope removes independent assurance.

exam_traps.trap: An annual control self-assessment by process owners is an ongoing evaluation.
exam_traps.why: It is periodic and standalone, so it is a separate evaluation, even though the owners perform it.

key_terms.definition: The attitude toward ethics and control that leaders show through their words, decisions and behavior.
A protected route for staff to raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

topics.overview: An audit is a project with objectives, a team, a budget and a deadline. This topic covers how an engagement moves from kickoff to follow-up, how the audit program and work papers keep the work controlled, and how teams adapt when skills, budgets or key facts change.
can_do: Put the audit phases in order and name what each one produces
Explain why an audit program is tailored, and updated only with approval
Choose the right response when skills, budget or key facts change mid-engagement
Judge whether work papers let a reviewer trace every conclusion to evidence

subtopics.name: Audit Engagement Phases
subtopics.definition: Audit engagement phases are the stages every audit moves through: planning, fieldwork, reporting and follow-up, each with its own job and outputs.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each phase depends on the one before it. Thin planning causes rework in fieldwork, and weak fieldwork leaves the report unsupported.
how_it_works: Planning sets the objectives, scope and criteria from a risk assessment; the more risky and complex the subject, the deeper the planning.
An engagement letter or notice confirms the objectives, scope, timing, access needs and report recipients before work begins.
An opening meeting walks the auditee through the plan, names contacts and agrees on how requests and progress updates will flow.
During fieldwork, supervisors direct staff, review evidence as it arrives and document any approved change to the planned procedures.
Reporting confirms facts with management and finalizes conclusions; the auditor reopens work only if new facts emerge and never hands the wording to the auditee.
Follow-up later verifies that management carried out the actions it agreed to.
subtopics.example: Two weeks into fieldwork on a port authority's cargo-billing audit, the team learns that billing moved to a new cloud platform last month, which the plan never covered. The chief audit executive (CAE) pauses fieldwork, documents what changed, and briefs the audit committee chair on the options: rescope now, or finish the original scope and disclose the limitation.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match planning depth to risk, supervise evidence as it is gathered, and keep each phase to its own job. When new facts undermine an engagement's basis, pause, document the change and brief the audit committee on options; do not quietly carry on.

exam_traps.trap: With a tight deadline, cut planning short to leave more time for fieldwork.
exam_traps.why: Thin planning misses risks that surface during fieldwork and force rework. Careful risk-based planning is what makes a short fieldwork window workable.

exam_traps.trap: During reporting, keep gathering evidence in case findings are challenged.
exam_traps.why: Evidence should already support each finding when fieldwork ends. Reporting validates facts with management; further work is justified only when management supplies new facts that could change a finding.

key_terms.definition: The kickoff meeting, also called the entrance conference, where the auditor explains the plan and agrees contacts and timing.
The phase in which the team performs the planned procedures and gathers evidence.

subtopics.memory_aid: Plan, Do, Tell, Check: planning, fieldwork, reporting, follow-up.

subtopics.name: Audit Programs
subtopics.definition: An audit program is the written, step-by-step list of procedures the team will perform to meet each objective of an engagement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It keeps fieldwork consistent, gives supervisors a standard to review against and records what was done. A program that misses the real risks produces tidy work papers and the wrong conclusions.
how_it_works: Engagement planning sets the objectives and scope first; the program then sets out how each objective will be tested.
Each procedure links to an objective and states what to test, how to test it and what evidence to collect.
Templates, such as audit programs published by ISACA, give structure, but each step is tailored to the subject's actual risks and controls.
When fieldwork reveals a significant risk the program misses, the manager updates the program, with approval, and documents the change.
Supervisors check completed steps against the program and confirm that the evidence supports each conclusion.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 458 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='An audit program links audit objectives to procedures, the evidence they gather, and the conclusion'><rect x='8' y='24' width='110' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='63' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Audit objective</text><rect x='140' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='186' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Procedures</text><rect x='254' y='24' width='82' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='295' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Evidence</text><rect x='358' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='404' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Conclusion</text><line x1='120' y1='46' x2='131' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M131,42 L138,46 L131,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='234' y1='46' x2='245' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M245,42 L252,46 L245,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='338' y1='46' x2='349' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M349,42 L356,46 L349,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: An audit program connects each objective to the procedures that gather evidence for a conclusion.

subtopics.example: An IS audit manager at a ski resort operator starts from a published audit program for point-of-sale systems. She keeps its objectives, rewrites the steps for the resort's lift-pass scanners, and drops steps for a loyalty module the resort does not use. When fieldwork shows rental staff can issue refunds offline, she adds procedures with the chief audit executive's approval and records why.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Every procedure serves an objective. Tailor templates to the engagement's risks and document each change. A program is a controlled plan, not a fixed contract: update it with approval when significant new risks appear, rather than deferring them or changing steps off the record.

exam_traps.trap: Use the standard template as-is and add a few steps for anything new.
exam_traps.why: The untailored steps test controls that may not exist, while real risks stay under-tested. Tailor every step to the subject and document why.

exam_traps.trap: A high-risk area found outside the program should wait for next year's audit.
exam_traps.why: Leaving a known significant risk untested weakens this engagement's conclusions. Update the program, with approval, and test the area now.

key_terms.definition: One specific test step, such as inspecting, reperforming or analyzing, that gathers evidence for an objective.
A reusable set of procedures for a common subject, which the auditor tailors before use.

subtopics.name: Work Papers and Documentation
subtopics.definition: Work papers are the audit's documented record of what was planned, what was done, what evidence was found and how each conclusion was reached.
subtopics.why_it_matters: They are the proof behind the report. When a committee member, regulator or quality reviewer challenges a conclusion, the auditor answers from the work papers, not from memory or management's agreement.
how_it_works: Each work paper records the objective, the procedure performed, the evidence obtained, who did and reviewed the work, and the conclusion.
Cross-references link each finding to its procedures and evidence, and each piece of evidence to the findings it supports.
The test is whether an experienced auditor new to the engagement could follow the trail and reach the same conclusion.
Retention periods come from law, regulation and policy, and the file is protected from unauthorized access, change or deletion.
A legal hold suspends routine destruction of relevant files until legal counsel releases it.
subtopics.example: An audit committee member challenges a finding that former employees kept access to the trading system. The audit senior does not point to management's agreement at the exit meeting. She opens the cross-referenced work paper, showing the leavers list, the access extract, the matched accounts and the reviewer's sign-off, and walks the member through the trail.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Documentation must let a reviewer trace every conclusion back to sufficient, appropriate evidence. Keep it for the required period, protect its integrity, and let legal holds override routine deletion. Management's agreement never substitutes for documented evidence.

exam_traps.trap: Ticked-off program steps show the work papers are complete.
exam_traps.why: A step can be marked done while its evidence still fails to support the conclusion. Reviewers check that the evidence actually supports each conclusion.

exam_traps.trap: Under a legal hold, hand all audit files to legal counsel and stop managing them.
exam_traps.why: The audit function stays the custodian. It suspends destruction, preserves relevant files under access control and agrees on the scope of the hold with counsel.

key_terms.definition: A link that lets a reviewer move between a finding, the procedure performed and the evidence behind it.
A legal instruction, also called a litigation hold, to preserve records that may relate to a lawsuit or investigation, overriding normal deletion schedules.
How long records must be kept, as set by law, regulation and organizational policy.

subtopics.name: Audit Resources, Skills and Budgets
subtopics.definition: Audit resource management means having enough people, with the right skills and budget, available at the time each engagement runs.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A team that does not understand the subject cannot gather appropriate evidence. Budget or staff cuts handled badly leave the riskiest conclusions thinly supported, often without anyone being told.
how_it_works: Before fieldwork, the manager compares the skills the engagement needs with the team's current skills and names the specific gaps.
Gaps are closed with targeted training, an outside expert, or co-sourcing with a specialist firm that works alongside staff.
When an engagement's budget is cut, the remaining effort moves to the highest-risk areas and the scope reduction is disclosed in the report.
When the function loses staff mid-year, the audit plan is re-prioritized by risk and the audit committee is briefed on the revised coverage.
Whoever performs the work, the auditor keeps responsibility for the conclusions.
subtopics.example: A retailer's audit plan includes a review of warehouse robotics controls in four months, and no one on the audit team understands industrial control systems. The chief audit executive (CAE) engages an outside specialist to work beside two staff auditors, agrees on the specialist's scope in writing, evaluates the specialist's work before relying on it, and keeps sign-off of the conclusions in-house.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Proficiency must be in place for the engagement at hand. Close specific gaps with training, experts or co-sourcing, and keep responsibility for the conclusions. When resources shrink, cut by risk and say so: disclosed reduced scope is better than thin coverage presented as full assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Absorb a budget cut by trimming every sample by the same percentage.
exam_traps.why: An even cut spreads the shortfall across high- and low-risk areas alike. Protect the high-risk work, cut lower-risk procedures and disclose the reduced scope.

exam_traps.trap: Hire permanent specialists to fix a skill gap for an audit due in three months.
exam_traps.why: New hires need time to become effective. Co-sourcing or an outside expert covers the engagement now; hiring serves the longer-term goal.

key_terms.definition: Using an outside firm's specialists alongside in-house auditors, often with skills transferred to the staff.
A record of each auditor's skills and certifications, used to staff engagements and spot gaps.
The difference between the skills an engagement requires and the skills the assigned team has.

subtopics.name: Agile Auditing
subtopics.definition: Agile auditing runs an engagement in short, fixed cycles called sprints, each delivering results and adjusting the next cycle's plan from what was learned.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When a subject changes monthly, one report delivered months later describes a system that no longer exists. Sprints give stakeholders earlier and more current assurance.
how_it_works: The team turns the engagement into a backlog of audit questions ranked by risk.
Each sprint, often two to four weeks long, takes the top items, tests them and delivers a result to stakeholders.
Short daily check-ins surface blockers early, and stakeholders give feedback at the end of each sprint.
A team retrospective closes every sprint, and its lessons feed directly into the next sprint's plan.
Evidence, documentation, supervision and independence standards apply in every sprint, exactly as in a traditional audit.

rows.label: Delivery
cells: One report at the end
Results after each sprint

rows.label: Planning
cells: Fixed at the start; changes need approval
Re-prioritized every sprint by risk

rows.label: Best for
cells: Stable subjects with a set reporting date
Fast-changing subjects and frequent assurance needs

rows.label: Audit standards
cells: Apply in full
Apply in full, in every sprint

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A traditional audit runs as one long linear pass; an agile audit runs in short iterative cycles'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Traditional audit</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>One long linear pass</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Agile audit</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Short iterative cycles</text></svg>
illustration.caption: A traditional audit is one long pass. An agile audit runs short cycles and adjusts as it learns.

subtopics.example: A streaming service changes its billing and recommendation features every two weeks, and the audit committee wants assurance before each quarterly board meeting. The IS audit manager builds a risk-ranked backlog and runs three-week sprints, starting with subscription-billing accuracy, reporting results to the product owner after each one. When a retrospective shows data requests are slow, the next sprint opens with an agreed data feed.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Agile changes how audit work is organized and delivered, not the standards it must meet. Choose it for fast-changing subjects or stakeholders who need frequent assurance, and let each sprint's lessons steer the next one.

exam_traps.trap: Agile audits can lighten documentation because results are delivered quickly.
exam_traps.why: Speed does not lower the bar. Each sprint's conclusions still need sufficient, appropriate, documented evidence and independent judgment.

exam_traps.trap: Hold one retrospective at the end of the engagement to capture lessons.
exam_traps.why: Lessons that arrive at the end cannot improve this audit. Agile depends on a retrospective after every sprint that feeds the next plan.

key_terms.definition: The ranked list of audit questions or tasks still to be done, re-prioritized as the team learns.
A short team meeting at the end of a sprint to agree what to keep doing and what to change.

topics.overview: Auditors rarely test everything, so they choose the kind of test that answers the objective and a sample that supports a defensible conclusion. This topic covers compliance and substantive tests, sampling methods, the settings that drive sample size, and what to do when results are unclear.
can_do: Tell a compliance test from a substantive test in a scenario
Pick attribute, variable or discovery sampling to match an objective
Predict how confidence, precision and the expected and tolerable rates change sample size
Decide the next step when a sample's deviation rate is near or above the tolerable rate

subtopics.name: Compliance Testing versus Substantive Testing
subtopics.definition: Compliance testing checks whether a control operated as designed over a period; substantive testing checks whether the transactions, balances or data themselves are correct.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The two tests answer different questions, and the first shapes the second: controls that test well allow less substantive work, and weak controls demand more.
how_it_works: Compliance tests sample instances of a control, such as change tickets, and check each one for evidence the control operated, such as an approval.
Substantive tests examine the data directly, such as recomputing interest or confirming balances, to find and measure misstatement.
Compliance results set the amount of substantive testing: weak controls mean more, strong controls mean less, but never none for material areas.
Inspecting a configuration shows how a control is designed today, not that it operated throughout the period.
Controls tested at an interim date need roll-forward evidence for the remaining months before the auditor relies on them for the whole period.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: Did the control operate?
Is the data right?

rows.label: Typical evidence
cells: Approvals, logs, reperforming the control
Recalculation, confirmation, data analysis

rows.label: Usual sampling method
cells: Attribute sampling (a rate)
Variable sampling (an amount)

rows.label: Result used for
cells: Deciding how far to rely on controls
Measuring misstatement

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Compliance testing checks whether a control operates; substantive testing checks whether the data is accurate'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Compliance</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Does the control operate?</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Substantive</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Is the data accurate?</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Compliance testing asks whether the control works. Substantive testing asks whether the data is right.

subtopics.example: At a toll-road operator, the IS auditor tests the toll-rate change control in September and finds it effective. Before relying on it for the fiscal year ending in December, she tests rate changes made from October to December. Separately, she recalculates a sample of customer tolls against the approved rates to measure any overcharging directly.
subtopics.isaca_rule: If the objective is whether a control works, perform compliance testing; if it is whether the data is right, perform substantive testing. Compliance results set how much substantive work is needed, and reliance needs evidence for the whole period.

exam_traps.trap: Recomputing loan interest is a compliance test of the interest calculation control.
exam_traps.why: Recomputation examines recorded amounts directly to detect misstatement, so it is substantive, even if it hints at how the control performed.

exam_traps.trap: A control found effective at an interim date can be relied on for the whole year.
exam_traps.why: The interim test covers only the months tested; roll-forward evidence is needed for the rest of the period.

key_terms.definition: Testing done before the period ends; it covers only the dates tested.
Extra testing that extends an interim control conclusion to the rest of the period.
A difference between a recorded amount and the correct amount, caused by error or fraud.
One test on one sample that checks both whether the control operated and whether the amount is correct.

subtopics.name: Statistical and Non-Statistical Sampling
subtopics.definition: Statistical sampling selects items randomly and uses probability to project results with stated confidence; non-statistical, or judgmental, sampling relies on the auditor's choice.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When a committee or regulator wants a stated confidence level, only a statistical sample can provide it. Either kind of sample is useless if the population it was drawn from is incomplete.
how_it_works: Define the population against the objective, then confirm it is complete, for example by reconciling an extract's record count to the source system.
Statistical samples use random selection and a planned sample size, so the result can be projected to the population with measured confidence.
Judgmental samples target items the auditor considers risky; they give useful insight but cannot be projected statistically.
Where no error is acceptable, such as approvals for shipping hazardous materials, test the whole population instead of sampling.
Data analytics often make testing every item practical, which removes sampling risk for that test.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Statistical sampling projects to the population with quantifiable confidence; judgmental sampling cannot be projected statistically'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Statistical</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Projects to the population</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Judgmental</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>No statistical projection</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Only a statistical sample can be projected to the whole population with measurable confidence.

subtopics.example: A regulator asks a pension fund to show, at a stated confidence level, that its benefit-calculation review control works. The IS auditor first reconciles the extract of benefit payments to the payment system's totals and finds a month missing, which she obtains. She then draws a random statistical sample sized for 95 percent confidence, rather than picking cases that look risky.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Use statistical sampling when the conclusion must carry a stated confidence level. A sample speaks only for the population it was drawn from, so define that population and prove it is complete before sizing anything.

exam_traps.trap: Picking the riskiest items by judgment gives the strongest evidence about the whole population.
exam_traps.why: Targeted items are useful leads, but a judgmental sample cannot be projected statistically, so it cannot support a population conclusion at a stated confidence.

exam_traps.trap: Size the sample first, then check whether the extract is complete.
exam_traps.why: A precisely sized sample from an incomplete extract gives a precise answer about the wrong population. Confirm completeness first.

key_terms.definition: The full set of items a conclusion will cover, such as every access change made during the year.
The single item selected and tested, such as one change ticket, one invoice or one dollar.

subtopics.name: Sampling Design Terms: Confidence, Precision and Error Rates
subtopics.definition: Sampling design terms are the settings an auditor chooses before sampling: how confident to be, how precise, and how many errors to expect and accept.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These settings drive the sample size and decide what a result means. Exam questions name them directly and ask which change makes a sample larger or smaller.
how_it_works: The confidence coefficient is the chance that the sample truly reflects the population, such as 95 percent; the level of risk is the remainder.
Strong, tested controls may justify a lower confidence level; weak controls or high risk call for a higher one.
Precision is how close the sample result must be to the true value, such as within 2 percentage points; the tighter the precision, the larger the sample.
For tests of amounts, tolerable error is set at or below materiality, the size of misstatement that would change users' decisions.
Population size barely affects sample size once it passes a few thousand items; in variable sampling, greater spread in values needs a larger sample.

rows.label: What it is
cells: How sure the auditor wants to be that the sample reflects the population
The error rate the auditor predicts before testing
The highest error rate that still allows reliance on the control

rows.label: Set from
cells: Risk and the strength of related controls
Prior audits or a small pilot sample
Auditor judgment about how important the control is

rows.label: Raise it and the sample
cells: Grows
Grows
Shrinks

subtopics.example: A cruise line's IS auditor plans an attribute test of refund approvals at 90 percent confidence, a 2 percent expected deviation rate and a 6 percent tolerable rate. After refund frauds at rival lines, the audit committee asks for 95 percent confidence and a 4 percent tolerable rate. She explains that both changes enlarge the sample, agrees on the added cost and resizes it.
subtopics.isaca_rule: More confidence, more expected errors, tighter precision, a lower tolerable rate or wider variation in values each mean a larger sample. Set tolerable error from materiality, not from a wish for zero.

exam_traps.trap: Doubling a large population roughly doubles the sample size needed.
exam_traps.why: Beyond a few thousand items, population size barely changes the sample size. Confidence, precision and the expected and tolerable rates drive it.

exam_traps.trap: Set tolerable error near zero to be safe.
exam_traps.why: A near-zero tolerance ignores what matters to users and drives impractical sample sizes. Derive it from materiality.

key_terms.definition: One minus the confidence coefficient: the chance the sample misleads, such as 5 percent at 95 percent confidence.
The largest misstatement in an amount the auditor can accept, set from materiality.
How widely item values vary around their average; in variable sampling, a larger standard deviation requires a larger sample.

subtopics.memory_aid: More sure, more errors expected, tighter precision or tolerance: each means a bigger sample.

subtopics.name: Attribute, Variable and Discovery Sampling
subtopics.definition: Sampling methods differ by what they measure: attribute sampling estimates how often something happens, variable sampling estimates an amount, and discovery sampling seeks at least one case.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Matching the method to the objective is the most tested sampling skill. The wrong method answers a different question, however carefully it is run.
how_it_works: Ask whether the objective is a rate, an amount, or the presence of even one case.
Control tests produce a yes-or-no result per item, so they use attribute sampling to estimate a deviation rate.
Substantive tests of value use variable sampling to project how much money is misstated, for example mean-per-unit estimation.
Discovery sampling suits suspected fraud or critical errors: it gives stated confidence of finding at least one case if the rate exceeds a set level.
One engagement may need several designs; never stretch one sample to serve objectives it was not built for.

types.meaning: Estimates the rate of yes-or-no deviations, such as missing approvals; used for compliance tests.
Estimates an amount, such as total overbilling in dollars; used for substantive tests.
A form of attribute sampling sized to find at least one deviation if deviations exceed a set rate.
A form of attribute sampling that lets the auditor stop early when few or no deviations appear.

subtopics.example: At a city parking authority, the IS auditor has three objectives: how often fine refunds lack supervisor approval, how many dollars of meter revenue were misposted, and whether even one fine was voided by an officer for a relative. She uses attribute sampling for the approvals, variable sampling for the revenue, and a discovery sample sized to find at least one such void if they exceed 1 percent.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Let the objective choose the method: a rate calls for attribute sampling, an amount for variable sampling, and the question of whether even one exists for discovery sampling. Separate objectives need separate designs.

exam_traps.trap: To test how often a control fails, sample by dollar value.
exam_traps.why: Dollar-based methods estimate amounts. A control failure rate is a yes-or-no rate, so attribute sampling fits.

exam_traps.trap: Use an attribute sample that estimates the overall rate to detect suspected fictitious vendors.
exam_traps.why: An estimating attribute sample measures how often something occurs. When the goal is to find even one case of suspected fraud, discovery sampling, a form of attribute sampling, is designed for it.

key_terms.definition: An instance where a control did not operate as designed, such as a change made without approval.
A variable method that projects a population total from the average value of the sampled items.

subtopics.name: Sample Selection Methods
subtopics.definition: Sample selection methods decide which items enter a sample, from giving every item an equal chance to weighting larger dollar amounts or sampling subgroups separately.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A poor selection method can bias the sample or waste effort on items that rarely contain errors. The right method lets a smaller sample give a more precise answer.
how_it_works: Use random selection when every item should have an equal chance and no subgroup needs special attention.
Use stratification when known subgroups have different error rates or values, sizing each subgroup's sample to its variability.
Use monetary-unit sampling (MUS) to estimate dollar overstatement when item values vary widely.
MUS projects each error: if a sampled item is 10 percent overstated, it assumes 10 percent error across its whole sampling interval, then adds a margin for sampling risk.
MUS rarely selects small or zero-value items, so it is weak at finding understatements.
Avoid systematic selection when the list has a repeating pattern that could line up with the interval.

types.meaning: Every item has an equal chance of selection, usually picked by a random number generator.
Every nth item after a random start; simple, but biased if the list follows a repeating pattern.
The population is split into subgroups that are sampled separately; supports conclusions for each subgroup.
Whole groups, such as every transaction from randomly chosen days or branches, are selected and tested.
Each dollar is a sampling unit, so larger items are more likely to be picked; projects dollar misstatement.
Items picked without a conscious pattern; non-statistical, so results cannot be projected statistically.

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at a wholesale distributor must test whether customer credit balances are understated. A colleague proposes monetary-unit sampling. She explains that it favors large balances and rarely picks small or zero ones, where understatement hides. She stratifies the accounts by balance size instead, including zero balances, sizes each stratum's sample to its risk, and reports conclusions for each stratum and overall.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the method that fits the population's structure and the objective. Stratify when subgroups behave differently, use monetary-unit sampling to estimate dollar overstatement, and never let the selection method skip the place where errors cluster.

exam_traps.trap: Monetary-unit sampling is always the best choice when amounts vary widely.
exam_traps.why: MUS favors large items. If errors cluster in small items, or understatement is the concern, stratified sampling serves the objective better.

exam_traps.trap: Taking every 50th invoice always gives an unbiased sample.
exam_traps.why: If the list repeats in a pattern, such as weekly batches, a fixed interval can line up with it. Check for patterns or use random selection.

key_terms.definition: One subgroup of a stratified population, such as all invoices over $10,000.
In systematic or monetary-unit sampling, the fixed gap between selected items or dollars.

subtopics.name: Sampling Risk and Evaluating Results
subtopics.definition: Sampling risk is the chance that a conclusion drawn from a sample differs from the conclusion that testing the whole population would have reached.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every sample can mislead. The dangerous direction is false comfort: concluding a control works or a balance is right when it is not, and passing that assurance to the board.
how_it_works: Each kind of test has two sampling risks (see the table): false comfort hurts audit effectiveness, while the other only wastes effort.
If the sample deviation rate clearly exceeds the tolerable rate, conclude the control is not effective, find out why it failed and expand substantive work.
If the rate falls between the expected and tolerable rates, extend or redesign the sample, keeping deviations already found and documenting why.
A risky area with weak controls leaves less room for false comfort, so accept less risk of passing a misstated balance and use a larger sample.
Evaluate the cause of each deviation, not just the count; one deliberate override can matter more than several clerical slips.

rows.label: False comfort: beta or Type II risk (more dangerous)
cells: Overreliance: trusting a control that is failing
Incorrect acceptance: passing a balance that is misstated

rows.label: Extra work: alpha or Type I risk (less dangerous)
cells: Underreliance: distrusting a control that works
Incorrect rejection: flagging a balance that is correct

subtopics.example: At a community college, the IS auditor tests 120 grade changes for registrar approval, expecting 1 percent deviations and tolerating 4 percent. She finds three, or 2.5 percent. One is a clerical slip, but two were made by one staff member for the same student. She extends the sample, keeps all three deviations and refers the pattern to the chief audit executive.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Guard hardest against false comfort. A clear breach of the tolerable rate ends reliance on the control; a borderline result calls for more evidence. Judge why deviations happened, not just how many, and adjust other testing to match.

exam_traps.trap: A deviation rate well above the tolerable rate calls for a larger sample before concluding.
exam_traps.why: Extending suits borderline results. Far above the tolerable rate, a larger sample would almost certainly not change the conclusion that the control failed.

exam_traps.trap: Underreliance is the more serious sampling risk because it wastes audit effort.
exam_traps.why: Wasted effort is only an efficiency cost. Overreliance gives the board unwarranted assurance about a failing control, which is the more dangerous error.

key_terms.definition: Error unrelated to sample size, such as using the wrong procedure or misreading the evidence.
The highest deviation rate likely in the population, given the sample result and the confidence level.

topics.overview: Audit conclusions are only as strong as the evidence behind them. This topic covers the two tests every piece of evidence must pass, which techniques give strong or weak evidence, how to rely on system-generated data, and how to handle signs of fraud without damaging the case.
can_do: Tell whether evidence fails on sufficiency, relevance or reliability
Rank evidence sources by reliability in a scenario
Explain how to show that a system report or extract can be trusted
Choose the IS auditor's FIRST action when fraud indicators appear

subtopics.name: Sufficient and Appropriate Evidence
subtopics.definition: Audit evidence must be sufficient, meaning there is enough of it, and appropriate, meaning it is relevant to the objective and reliable.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A conclusion built on too little evidence, or on evidence that is off-topic or untrustworthy, can mislead the board. A larger pile cannot rescue poor-quality evidence.
how_it_works: Sufficiency is about quantity: enough items, covering enough of the period, to support the conclusion.
Relevance asks whether the evidence actually relates to the control or claim being tested.
Reliability asks whether the evidence can be trusted, given its source, how it was obtained and how it was protected.
Check relevance first: evidence that does not address the objective is worthless, however reliable or plentiful it is.
The amount needed rises with risk and materiality, and falls as the quality of the evidence rises.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Audit evidence must be sufficient, meaning enough of it, and appropriate, meaning relevant and reliable'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='119' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Sufficient</text><text x='119' y='51' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>enough of it (quantity)</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='341' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Appropriate</text><text x='341' y='51' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>good enough (quality)</text><line x1='341' y1='60' x2='290' y2='88' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='341' y1='60' x2='392' y2='88' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='236' y='88' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='286' y='114' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Relevant</text><rect x='346' y='88' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='396' y='114' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Reliable</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The two tests of audit evidence. Sufficiency is about quantity; appropriateness is about quality, which means relevant and reliable.

subtopics.example: To test whether a clinic network's backups can be restored, the IS auditor receives 200 nightly backup-success logs. Her manager points out that the logs show copies were made, not that data can be restored, so the evidence is plentiful but not relevant. She obtains records of quarterly restore tests and observes one restore herself before concluding.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Evidence must clear both bars: enough of it, and the right kind. Quality comes before quantity. Read the scenario for which test is failing, then fix that test rather than collecting more of the same.

exam_traps.trap: A large volume of evidence means the auditor is ready to conclude.
exam_traps.why: Volume answers only sufficiency. The auditor must first confirm the evidence is relevant to the objective and reliable.

exam_traps.trap: Collecting more evidence from the same source fixes a reliability concern.
exam_traps.why: More of the same improves quantity only. If the source is weak, the auditor needs a better one, such as independent or auditor-obtained evidence.

key_terms.definition: Whether there is enough evidence to support the conclusion.
The quality of evidence: whether it is both relevant and reliable.
A claim built into management's records, such as that all transactions are recorded or that amounts are accurate.

subtopics.memory_aid: Enough, on-topic, trustworthy: sufficient, relevant, reliable.

subtopics.name: Evidence Techniques and Their Reliability
subtopics.definition: Evidence techniques are the ways auditors gather proof, such as inquiry, observation, inspection, confirmation and reperformance, and they differ in how far they can be trusted.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam questions often ask which evidence is MOST reliable. Knowing the ranking rules lets the auditor choose the strongest source and avoid resting a conclusion on someone's word.
how_it_works: Evidence from independent outside sources is more reliable than evidence produced inside the organization being audited.
Evidence the auditor obtains directly, by observing or reperforming, is more reliable than evidence described or handed over by the auditee.
Documents and system records are more reliable than verbal statements, and originals more than copies.
For a specific past event, records made at the time are more reliable than reperformance, which shows only how the process works today.
Inquiry alone is never enough; it shows where to look and must be backed by other evidence.
A qualified, objective provider gives more reliable evidence than an unqualified or interested one, and objective facts outweigh personal opinions.

types.meaning: Asking staff or management questions, in writing or in person; the weakest technique on its own.
Watching a process or control as it is performed.
Examining documents, records, configurations or physical assets.
Getting a direct answer from an independent third party, such as a customer, supplier or bank.
The auditor independently redoes a control or calculation to see whether it gives the right result.
Comparing recorded data with an expectation; as substantive evidence, the expectation must be precise and built from reliable data.

subtopics.example: An IS auditor must show that a minimum password length rule works in production. The security administrator offers a screenshot of the setting. The auditor instead tries a password shorter than the minimum, records the system's rejection, and checks for exception settings that could exempt some accounts.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank evidence by independence and directness: what the auditor sees or redoes, or what an outsider confirms, is more reliable than what the auditee says or supplies. Match the technique to the question; past events need records made at the time.

exam_traps.trap: Reperforming a process today is the best evidence of how a specific past incident was handled.
exam_traps.why: Reperformance shows how the process works now. For what happened then, time-stamped records made at the time are more reliable.

exam_traps.trap: Inspecting a correctly configured setting proves the control operates.
exam_traps.why: Inspection shows the design at one moment, and overrides can defeat it. Reperformance shows the control working; reliance over a period also needs evidence across that period.

key_terms.definition: A request the third party must answer either way; preferred when risk is high or balances are large.
A request the third party answers only if it disagrees; weaker, suited to many small, low-risk balances.
A statement from management about facts or controls; useful, but weak evidence alone.

subtopics.name: Interviews and Observation
subtopics.definition: Interviews and observation are evidence techniques that show how people actually run a process, by asking them about it and by watching it happen.
subtopics.why_it_matters: They reveal workarounds and gaps that policies and documents hide. They are also easy to over-trust, because people describe the ideal and behave better while watched.
how_it_works: Prepare by reviewing policies, prior findings and process documents, so questions are informed.
Ask open-ended questions, such as asking someone to walk through a recent case, and listen actively before narrowing in.
Interview the people who do the work, not only their managers, and record answers as they are given.
Observe the control in operation, noting the date, the time and who performed it.
Back up what was heard or seen with documents, data or reperformance before concluding.
subtopics.example: Before reviewing a car-rental company's vehicle-return process, the IS auditor reads the procedures and the prior audit report. At the counter, she asks an agent to walk her through yesterday's damage claim and learns that agents waive fees using a manager's saved login. She notes who said it and when, then pulls the waiver log to see how often that login was used, and from which terminals.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Interviews and observation build understanding and find leads; they rarely prove a control on their own. Prepare, ask open questions, then corroborate with stronger evidence before drawing a conclusion.

exam_traps.trap: A yes-or-no checklist makes interviews consistent, so it is the most effective approach.
exam_traps.why: Closed questions invite the expected answer and miss how controls really work. Open questions, asked after preparation, surface workarounds.

exam_traps.trap: Watching a control work once proves it operated all year.
exam_traps.why: Observation shows only what happened while the auditor watched, and people often act differently when observed. Test records across the period too.

key_terms.definition: A question that cannot be answered yes or no, inviting people to describe the process in their own words.
Confirming information from one source with evidence from another, independent source.
The tendency of people to follow procedures more carefully while they know they are being watched.

subtopics.name: Electronic and System-Generated Evidence
subtopics.definition: System-generated evidence is any report, log, extract or file produced by the auditee's systems, which the auditor must show is complete, accurate and unaltered before relying on it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most evidence now comes from systems. A report can look official yet leave out records or contain logic errors, and a file can change after capture, quietly corrupting every conclusion built on it.
how_it_works: Before relying on a system report, known as information produced by the entity (IPE), test the controls that produce it or reproduce it independently.
Trace in two directions: from report lines back to source records to check accuracy, and from source records forward into the report to check completeness.
Capture extracts in a controlled way, ideally by running or watching the query yourself, and record the parameters used.
Calculate a hash value when data is captured and check it again at use, to show the file has not changed.
Document the trail from source system to work paper, and store evidence on read-only media under access control.
subtopics.example: An IS auditor at a ride-share company plans to rely on a system report of driver background-check dates. The operations analyst offers to email a spreadsheet version. The IS auditor instead runs the report herself with documented parameters, traces sample drivers from the driver database into the report and back, and records a hash of the exported file before filing it.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Never rely on a system report because it looks official. Prove completeness and accuracy first, then protect integrity from capture to work paper. Controlled capture plus verification gives stronger assurance than restricting access to the files.

exam_traps.trap: Tracing a sample of report lines back to source records proves the report is reliable.
exam_traps.why: That checks the accuracy of what is listed but cannot reveal items the report left out. Completeness needs separate testing.

exam_traps.trap: Restricting access to the evidence folder proves the extracts are unaltered.
exam_traps.why: Access control protects files but cannot show they were unchanged before storage. A hash taken at capture and checked again gives tamper-evident proof.

key_terms.definition: A check that every relevant source record appears in a report or extract, done by tracing from source to report.
A short fingerprint calculated from a file; any change to the file produces a different value.

subtopics.name: Handling Suspected Fraud
subtopics.definition: Handling suspected fraud means recognizing warning signs during an audit, documenting them and escalating through proper channels, without investigating alone or alerting the suspect.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A mishandled lead can destroy evidence, tip off a suspect or miss a regulatory deadline. Management must prevent and detect fraud; the IS auditor watches for red flags and reports them.
how_it_works: On finding red flags, record the facts objectively and escalate through the fraud-response procedure, usually via the chief audit executive (CAE).
Where regulators are involved, escalate promptly to the audit committee and legal counsel, going above management if it may be implicated.
Preserve evidence that may reach court with a documented chain of custody for each original item.
Any authorized interview of a suspect needs a second interviewer and notes taken as answers are given.
Once forensic specialists take over, the auditor supports them and runs no parallel analysis.
A whistleblower claim about an in-scope area gets targeted, confidential procedures; only evidence-backed findings are reported.

types.meaning: A financial or personal need, such as debt or unrealistic targets, that pushes someone toward fraud.
A weakness that lets fraud happen and stay hidden, such as sole control of a process; the element auditors can observe and test.
The story a person tells to justify the act, such as feeling underpaid or planning to pay the money back.

subtopics.example: Testing vendor payments at a construction firm, the IS auditor sees that one buyer created three vendors sharing a staff member's home address and approved their invoices herself. Without questioning the buyer or widening the sample, she records the facts, secures the vendor-master change logs and reports to the CAE under the fraud procedure.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Management owns fraud prevention and detection. The IS auditor stays skeptical, then documents, preserves and escalates red flags; authorized investigators and counsel investigate. Act promptly, keep it confidential, and never confront a suspect or expand testing before escalating.

exam_traps.trap: Expand the sample first to confirm the fraud before telling anyone.
exam_traps.why: Acting alone lacks authority, can alert suspects and can miss legal deadlines. Escalate first; investigators decide what follows.

exam_traps.trap: File fraud evidence in the secure work-paper archive.
exam_traps.why: Routine filing does not record who handled each item and when; evidence for court needs a chain of custody.

key_terms.definition: A model in which fraud usually needs pressure, opportunity and rationalization together.
A warning sign of possible fraud, such as unexplained overrides or staff who never take leave.
A record of who held each piece of evidence, and when, so it holds up in court.
ITAF's fraud standard: management prevents and detects fraud; the IS auditor stays alert and reports indicators.

topics.overview: Technology lets auditors test entire populations, watch transactions as they happen and spot patterns no person could. This topic covers computer-assisted audit techniques, continuous and online auditing, and both using artificial intelligence (AI) in the audit and auditing the organization's own AI systems.
can_do: Choose the right computer-assisted or online audit technique for a scenario
Tell continuous auditing from continuous monitoring by who owns it
Explain why an auditor must understand and validate an automated tool's output
Identify the key risks to test at each stage of an AI model's life cycle

subtopics.name: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques (CAATs)
subtopics.definition: Computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) are software tools and methods auditors use to test data and program logic directly, often across a whole population.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Manual sampling cannot keep up with millions of transactions or spot patterns such as duplicates and gaps. CAATs make full-population testing possible, but only if the data and the procedure stay under the auditor's control.
how_it_works: Choose CAATs when the objective needs full-population tests, pattern detection or high volumes; lower cost is a side benefit, not the reason.
Agree on data needs with the data owner, then obtain a read-only copy or extract rather than querying the production system live.
Confirm the extract is complete, for example by reconciling record counts and totals to the source system.
Run the auditor's own queries, such as duplicate, gap and threshold tests, and keep the scripts and results in the work papers.
To analyze data that already exists, use audit software. To check how a program processes data, use test data, an integrated test facility or parallel simulation.

rows.label: What it tests
cells: Existing data, such as last year's transactions
Program logic, using auditor-made inputs
Live program logic, alongside real transactions
Program logic, by rerunning real data through the auditor's own program

rows.label: Where it runs
cells: The auditor's tool, on an extract
Usually a test copy of the application
The live system, using a dummy entity
The auditor's own software, outside production

rows.label: Main caution
cells: The extract must be complete and protected
The test copy may differ from production code
Test entries must be isolated and reversed
Tests the auditor's replica, not the live program

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Manual testing covers a sample of transactions; CAATs can test the entire population'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Manual testing</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>A sample of transactions</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>CAATs</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Can test every transaction</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Manual testing looks at a sample. CAATs can test every transaction in the population.

subtopics.example: A cinema chain's IS auditor must check a full year of loyalty-point redemptions for points used on closed accounts and points issued twice. The loyalty team offers to run the queries on the live system. She instead obtains a read-only extract, reconciles its record count and point totals to the loyalty ledger, and runs her own queries in audit software.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Use CAATs when the objective demands them, run them on protected copies the auditor controls, and match the technique to the question: existing data or processing logic. Auditee staff can supply data but should not run the auditor's tests.

exam_traps.trap: Have the database administrator run the audit queries to save time and protect production.
exam_traps.why: Production is protected, but the auditor then relies on the auditee to perform the test, weakening independence and evidence integrity. Run your own queries on a read-only copy.

exam_traps.trap: The PRIMARY reason to use CAATs is a lower audit cost.
exam_traps.why: Efficiency is a by-product, and CAATs sometimes cost more. The decision rests on what the objective needs, such as testing every transaction.

key_terms.definition: A copy of selected records pulled from a system for analysis, which must be shown to be complete.
Testing every item rather than a sample, which removes sampling risk for that test.

subtopics.name: Continuous Auditing and Continuous Monitoring
subtopics.definition: Continuous monitoring is management's automated, ongoing check of its own processes; continuous auditing is the audit function's automated testing for independent assurance, often in near real time.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The technology can be identical, so people mislabel one as the other. The difference decides who acts on alerts and how far the auditor can rely on the results.
how_it_works: Ownership decides the label: if operations designs the rules and handles the alerts, it is continuous monitoring, even if auditors can read the dashboard.
Continuous auditing is designed and run by the audit function to give independent assurance.
Management's monitoring is a control: the auditor tests whether it works, then adjusts the nature and extent of other testing.
When a continuous-auditing alert fires, the auditor investigates, escalates to those with authority and preserves the evidence.
Operational responses, such as freezing an account or blocking a payment, belong to management, not to audit.

rows.label: Owner
cells: Management, such as operations or compliance
The audit function

rows.label: Purpose
cells: Keep processes in control day to day
Independent assurance on controls and data

rows.label: When an alert fires
cells: Management acts on it
The auditor investigates and escalates

rows.label: How the other side uses it
cells: Audit tests it, then may rely on it
Management receives findings and decides

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 490 126' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Periodic audits leave gaps between checkpoints; continuous auditing covers every transaction'><rect x='14' y='20' width='148' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='88' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Periodic</text><rect x='186' y='20' width='80' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='226' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Q1</text><rect x='290' y='20' width='80' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='330' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Q2</text><rect x='394' y='20' width='80' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='434' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Q3</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='148' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='88' y='99' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Continuous</text><rect x='186' y='74' width='288' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='330' y='99' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Every transaction, in near real time</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Periodic audits leave gaps between checkpoints. Continuous auditing looks at transactions as they occur.

subtopics.example: A casino group's continuous-auditing routine flags a cashier issuing $9,000 in voids within ten minutes on a Sunday night. The IS auditor does not lock the cashier's account herself. She calls the on-duty surveillance manager, who has authority to act, and preserves the transaction data and alert details for the investigation.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Ownership and purpose, not technology, separate the two. Audit may test and rely on management's monitoring but never accepts it untested, and audit alerts lead to escalation, not to auditors running operations.

exam_traps.trap: Monitoring alerts that go to information technology (IT) operations count as continuous auditing if auditors can view them.
exam_traps.why: Read access does not change ownership. Operations owns the response, so it is continuous monitoring, a management control.

exam_traps.trap: Clean continuous-monitoring reports can replace the auditor's own testing.
exam_traps.why: That lets management's unverified output set audit conclusions. Test the monitoring control first, then decide how much other testing to reduce.

key_terms.definition: Processing within seconds or minutes of a transaction, rather than at the end of a period.
A transaction or event that breaks a rule the routine checks, flagged for review.

subtopics.name: Online Audit Techniques: EAM, SCARF, Snapshots, Audit Hooks and CIS
subtopics.definition: Online audit techniques are audit tools built into or running alongside a live application that examine transactions while they are processed, not afterward.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some systems process too fast, or leave too little trail, for periodic review. These techniques catch problems as they happen, but each trades coverage against cost and load on production.
how_it_works: Embedded audit modules (EAM) are audit code inside the application that screens every transaction against auditor-set rules and writes exceptions to an audit file.
SCARF (systems control audit review file) is the file the embedded modules write exceptions to; the auditor reviews it regularly.
Snapshots record a transaction's data at chosen points in processing, building a trail that shows how it was handled.
Audit hooks are small embedded triggers that flag selected suspicious transactions for immediate attention, before errors grow.
Continuous and intermittent simulation (CIS) passes transactions meeting set criteria to an audit routine that processes them in parallel and logs any differences.
The integrated test facility (ITF), covered with computer-assisted audit techniques, also works online; choose it when running separate test data is impractical.

rows.label: What it watches
cells: Every transaction, against rules the auditor sets
Chosen transactions, at set steps in processing
Only transactions that trip a trigger
Transactions that match the auditor's selection rules

rows.label: What the auditor receives
cells: A running log of exceptions to review on a schedule
A step-by-step picture of how each chosen transaction was handled
An early alert to look into one item before the problem spreads
Results recomputed by the audit routine, with any mismatch logged

rows.label: Where it falls short
cells: Costly to build, and it adds load to live processing
Blind to whatever happens between capture points
Blind to anything no trigger covers
Only as reliable as the auditor's copy of the program logic

rows.label: Audit must keep control of
cells: The screening rules and the exception file
The capture points and the captured records
The trigger list
The simulation routine and its selection rules

rows.label: Exam cue
cells: Live processing must run without pauses; the most complex to build
A step-by-step audit trail of processing is needed
Early warning on a few selected risky items; the simplest to build
Only transactions that meet set criteria need checking

subtopics.example: A payments processor wants every card authorization screened for anomalies as it posts, with no gaps, and accepts some extra processing load. The IS auditor chooses embedded audit modules writing exceptions to a review file, rather than snapshots, which would miss transactions between capture points. Before relying on the module, she tests its rules and confirms the audit file is protected.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the technique to the need: full screening calls for embedded modules, a processing trail for snapshots, a few risky items for audit hooks. Weigh coverage against cost and production load, and keep the rules and audit file under audit's control.

exam_traps.trap: Snapshots give full near-real-time coverage of every transaction.
exam_traps.why: Snapshots capture selected transactions at chosen points, so anomalies between captures go undetected. Embedded audit modules screen every transaction.

exam_traps.trap: Embedded modules that block suspicious transactions are the best audit design.
exam_traps.why: Blocking is a preventive operational control owned by management, and inline blocking slows critical systems. Audit modules flag and report; management decides what to stop.

key_terms.definition: A record of the steps, data and people involved in processing a transaction, from start to finish.
A system that processes each transaction as it is entered, rather than in later batches.

subtopics.memory_aid: EAM sees everything; snapshots photograph; hooks catch a few; CIS reruns the chosen ones.

subtopics.name: Implementing Continuous Auditing
subtopics.definition: Implementing continuous auditing means securing reliable data access, choosing an architecture, deciding where to deploy first and planning how alerts are handled.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Continuous auditing is only as good as the data it reads and the follow-up its alerts get. Programs that skip these basics produce noisy, untrusted results or stall before delivering any assurance.
how_it_works: First confirm reliable, read-only access to complete source data; dashboards and rules come after.
Deploy where risk and transaction volume justify the build and running costs; audit hours saved are a secondary benefit.
Start with a pilot where data feeds are already reliable, prove the value, then expand in order of risk.
Tune alert thresholds to what the team can handle, so real issues are not buried in noise.
Investigate small but consistent anomalies; a pattern that persists usually signals a systematic cause such as a misconfiguration.

rows.label: Detection speed
cells: Instant
Within minutes
Days or weeks later

rows.label: Load on production
cells: Some; the system owner must accept it
None
None

rows.label: Fits when
cells: Every transaction must be screened the moment it posts
Fast coverage is needed with zero production impact
Speed matters less than cost

subtopics.example: A food-delivery platform's IS audit team switches on continuous-auditing rules for courier payouts. The first month brings 4,000 alerts, far more than two auditors can review, and a small overpayment repeats every night in one city. The IS auditor tunes the thresholds to the team's capacity, keeps a rule for repeating patterns, and investigates the nightly overpayment, which traces to a misconfigured distance rate.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Data access comes first, risk and volume justify the cost, and the design must not degrade production. Start where data is ready, expand by risk, and treat persistent small anomalies as signals worth testing, not noise.

exam_traps.trap: Begin continuous auditing with the highest-risk system, whatever the state of its data.
exam_traps.why: With unreliable feeds, the team spends months fixing data feeds before producing any assurance. Pilot where data is ready, then expand by risk.

exam_traps.trap: A small deviation that repeats for weeks can wait for more monitoring.
exam_traps.why: A consistent pattern points to a systematic cause, and small amounts add up. Investigate likely causes now with targeted tests.

key_terms.definition: The trigger level at which a routine flags a transaction, tuned to balance missed issues against false alarms.
A small first deployment used to prove a method works before a wider rollout.

subtopics.name: Using Artificial Intelligence in the Audit
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) in the audit means using machine-learning tools to scan large datasets and flag unusual items, while the auditor interprets the results and owns the conclusions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI can find patterns no sample would catch. But output the auditor cannot explain, reproduce or validate cannot support a conclusion, and accountability for the opinion never passes to a tool.
how_it_works: Define the audit question first; the tool supports the objective rather than setting it.
Understand how the tool reaches its outputs, including its data inputs and limits, well enough to judge their reliability.
Validate the tool before relying on it, for example by testing it on data with known outcomes.
Treat flags as leads, and follow each one up with evidence the auditor can explain and document.
Use only approved tools for confidential audit data, and record the tool, version and settings so results can be reproduced.
