illustration.caption: AI analyzes the data and flags anomalies. The auditor investigates and makes the call.

subtopics.example: An energy retailer's audit team adopts a machine-learning tool that scores journal entries for unusual patterns. Before relying on it, the IS auditor runs it on last year's entries, where the team already knows which were improper, and finds it misses entries posted at month-end. She records the tool's version and settings, treats its scores as leads only, and adds a manual month-end test.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Automated output is only as reliable as the auditor's understanding of it. Use AI to point where to look, validate it before relying on it, and keep professional judgment and accountability with the human auditor.

exam_traps.trap: A high accuracy rating makes an AI tool's output reliable audit evidence.
exam_traps.why: The auditor must be able to explain and defend each conclusion. Output that cannot be explained cannot be validated, however accurate the vendor claims it is.

exam_traps.trap: Validate an AI tool once at purchase, then rely on its output on every later engagement.
exam_traps.why: Models, data and settings change over time. Revalidate when the tool, its version or the data changes, and record the version and settings so results can be reproduced.

key_terms.definition: A type of AI that learns patterns from historical data instead of following hand-written rules.
An item a tool flags as a problem that turns out to be normal.

subtopics.name: Auditing AI Systems
subtopics.definition: Auditing AI systems means assessing the risks of an organization's own artificial intelligence (AI) models across their life cycle, from training data through production use to retirement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI models can drift, carry bias from their training data and make decisions nobody can explain. Standard change and access tests miss these risks.
how_it_works: Give each life-cycle stage its own procedures, then combine the results into one conclusion.
Check that training data is representative, free of harmful bias and labeled through a documented, reliable process.
Confirm the model is reproducible and can be explained at a depth that fits the risk of its decisions.
In production, look for drift monitoring, tracking of human overrides and, for high-stakes models, an independent challenger model.
For generative AI that uses tools or data, check controls on inputs, outputs and which tools it may call, to resist prompt injection.
At retirement, preserve the model version, data lineage (where data came from) and decision logs so past decisions can be explained.
subtopics.example: A bank's AI model approves small-business loans. After a regional downturn, loan officers there override it twice as often, yet the launch validation report still shows strong accuracy. The IS auditor compares recent applications with the training data, finds the input mix has shifted, and recommends drift monitoring and retraining triggers; the credit risk officer decides.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Audit an AI model across its whole life, starting with its training data. Expect reproducibility and explainability, independent challenge for high-stakes models, and preserved records. Frozen test results and vendor reports are inputs, not the full answer.

exam_traps.trap: Stable accuracy on the original test set shows the model is not drifting.
exam_traps.why: A frozen test set reflects old data. Drift shows in production signals, such as more frequent human overrides.

exam_traps.trap: A vendor's System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 report is enough assurance for a vendor-hosted AI model.
exam_traps.why: A SOC 2 report covers general controls, not the model's behavior. Combine it with testing outputs on the organization's own data.

key_terms.definition: A decline in a model's accuracy as real-world data moves away from its training data.
An independently built model run on the same inputs to expose the production model's errors.
An attack that hides instructions in input so a language model ignores its rules or misuses its tools.

topics.overview: An audit creates value only when the right people understand its results and act on them. This topic covers writing findings, the exit meeting, report structure and distribution, audit opinions, and how the auditor escalates urgent issues and follows up.
can_do: Build a finding from its criteria, condition, cause and effect
Handle management disagreement or pressure without weakening a finding
Choose the right opinion type from a scenario's facts
Plan risk-based follow-up and know when to escalate to the audit committee

subtopics.name: Writing Findings and Recommendations
subtopics.definition: An audit finding is a documented gap between what should happen and what does happen, with its cause and risk, plus a recommendation to fix it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A finding that is vague, overstated or missing its cause gets disputed, or fixed only on the surface. A clear finding helps management act on the real problem.
how_it_works: Criteria: state what should happen, drawn from a policy, standard, regulation or contract.
Condition: state what the auditor actually found, supported by evidence.
Cause: explain why the gap exists, digging past the symptom to the root cause.
Effect, or consequence: describe the risk or impact if nothing changes, in business terms.
Recommendation: propose a fix aimed at the root cause; management decides how to carry it out.
Write every finding in the same neutral, factual tone, whatever the seniority of the people involved.
subtopics.example: An IS auditor finds that 14 of 40 leavers kept network access for over 30 days. Tracing the cause, she learns that human resources emails leaver notices to one administrator, who was on extended leave. She recommends an automatic feed from the human resources system with a named backup owner, rather than just a one-off cleanup of the 14 accounts.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Findings rest on evidence and target root causes. The auditor recommends; management decides and implements. If management's own monitoring missed a failure the auditor found, report that as a separate finding, because the process meant to catch it did not work.

exam_traps.trap: Recommending removal of the specific exceptions found is enough.
exam_traps.why: Cleaning up the exceptions treats the symptom. Unless the root cause is fixed, the same gap reappears next quarter.

exam_traps.trap: Drop a finding from the report because management fixed it before fieldwork ended.
exam_traps.why: The weakness existed during the period audited, so governance needs to know. Report it, note the corrective action already taken, and verify the fix in follow-up.

key_terms.definition: The underlying reason a problem occurred; fixing it stops the problem from recurring.
The auditor's judgment of a finding's importance, such as high, medium or low, based on facts and risk.

subtopics.memory_aid: Criteria, condition, cause, effect, then recommendation: what should be, what is, why, so what, fix.

subtopics.name: The Exit Meeting and Management Responses
subtopics.definition: The exit meeting, or closing conference, is where the auditor reviews draft findings with management to confirm the facts and collect action plans before the report is issued.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It catches factual errors before they reach the board and turns findings into owned, dated commitments. It is also where pressure to soften or delay the report usually appears.
how_it_works: Management confirms the facts are accurate and adds context the auditor may have lacked.
Management gives its response to each finding: the planned action, the owner and the target date.
Findings and ratings change only when new facts or evidence justify it, never on request alone.
If management still disagrees, the report shows the finding at the auditor's rating with management's view alongside it.
The report is issued on time with action plans; remediation in progress is no reason to delay it, and a weakness fixed during fieldwork is still reported.
subtopics.example: At the exit meeting for an access audit, the IT director disputes a high-rated finding, saying the stale accounts belonged to contractors who never logged in. The IS auditor checks the login records he supplies and confirms that three accounts were used after the contracts ended. She keeps the rating and records his view and action plan beside the finding.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The exit meeting validates facts; it does not negotiate conclusions. Change a finding only for new evidence, record disagreement instead of deleting the finding, and issue the report on time.

exam_traps.trap: Get management's sign-off on every finding before issuing the report.
exam_traps.why: The auditor does not need management's agreement to report a finding. Disagreement is recorded in the report, not settled by signature.

exam_traps.trap: Delay the report until remediation is complete so findings appear closed.
exam_traps.why: Delay keeps known risks from governance and lets management control the timing. Issue on time and include the planned actions and dates.

key_terms.definition: Management's written reply to a finding, stating agreement or disagreement, the planned action, the owner and the date.
The version shared with management before issue so facts can be checked; conclusions remain the auditor's.

subtopics.name: Report Structure, Audience and Distribution
subtopics.definition: The audit report communicates findings, conclusions and recommendations so readers can make informed decisions; its structure and distribution depend on who must act on it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A report the board cannot digest, or one that reaches the wrong people, fails even when every finding is right. Sensitive detail sent too widely can itself create risk.
how_it_works: Address the formal report to the governance body the audit function reports to, usually the audit committee, with copies to managers who must fix issues.
Use one layered report: an executive summary for leaders, then detailed findings, ratings, recommendations and management responses.
State the objectives, scope, period covered, any scope limitations and the overall conclusion.
Limit distribution of exploitable detail to those who need it, under restricted-use terms, but never hide findings from governance.
When a user such as a regulator needs its own criteria, date or wording, plan a separate engagement rather than rewording an existing report.

illustration.caption: Findings are checked at the exit meeting, the final report includes management's responses, and the auditor then follows up.

subtopics.example: An IS audit report on a water utility's control systems lists remote-access weaknesses an attacker could use. The chief executive wants the full report read out at the city council's public session. The IS auditor issues one layered report to the audit committee, gives the operations director a copy under restricted-use terms, and agrees that only the executive summary goes to the public session.
subtopics.isaca_rule: One report, one set of conclusions, layered for different readers. It goes to governance and to the people who must act. Restrict sensitive detail on a need-to-know basis, but never use restriction or delay to keep findings from oversight.

exam_traps.trap: Write separate reports for each audience, each with its own conclusions.
exam_traps.why: Separate conclusions can conflict and split the record governance oversees. One report with one set of conclusions, layered with a summary and details, serves every reader.

exam_traps.trap: Address the report to the chief information security officer, who will fix the finding.
exam_traps.why: That officer is part of the management being reported on. The report goes to the audit committee, with copies to accountable executives.

key_terms.definition: A short opening section giving leaders the overall conclusion and the most important findings.
A report whose distribution is limited to named recipients because its detail is sensitive.
A report built for one user's criteria, date or wording, backed by work designed for that purpose.

subtopics.name: Audit Opinions
subtopics.definition: An audit opinion is the auditor's formal overall conclusion on a subject, graded by how significant and how widespread any problems or evidence gaps are.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The opinion is often the only part of the report a reader remembers. The wrong type either overstates assurance or alarms the board without cause.
how_it_works: First ask whether the auditor obtained enough evidence; if not, the issue is a scope limitation, not a control failure.
Then ask whether the problems found are significant and, if so, whether they are contained or pervasive.
Pervasive means the problem affects the subject as a whole, not just one or two areas.
A scope limitation confined to one area is disclosed, while the overall conclusion still covers the rest of the work.
Management's disputed responses are reported alongside the opinion; they do not change it unless new evidence does.

rows.label: When used
cells: No significant exceptions or limits
A significant but contained exception or limitation
Significant and pervasive exceptions
A pervasive scope limitation with no alternative evidence

rows.label: Message to readers
cells: Controls are effective
Effective except for the named issues
Controls are not effective
No opinion can be formed

rows.label: Underlying cause
cells: None
An exception or a limitation
Controls tested and failed
Evidence missing

subtopics.example: An IS auditor tests change management across all six core platforms of a payroll bureau. On every platform, developers move their own code into production without approval, and no detective review exists. Management argues that no outage has occurred. The IS auditor issues an adverse opinion because the failures are significant and pervasive, and reports management's view alongside it.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Separate missing evidence from failed controls, then weigh significance and pervasiveness. Contained problems lead to a qualified opinion, pervasive failures to an adverse one, and a pervasive lack of evidence to a disclaimer. Never claim more assurance than the evidence gives.

exam_traps.trap: When most of the scope cannot be tested, issue an adverse opinion.
exam_traps.why: Adverse means controls were tested and found to fail. When evidence is missing across most of the scope, the auditor cannot conclude at all, so a disclaimer fits.

exam_traps.trap: Two significant but contained weaknesses call for an adverse opinion.
exam_traps.why: Adverse is for pervasive failure. Contained significant issues lead to a qualified opinion: effective except for the named weaknesses.

key_terms.definition: Affecting the subject as a whole, or many parts of it, rather than one contained area.
A restriction, imposed or practical, that stops the auditor from obtaining the evidence needed.

subtopics.name: Escalation and Follow-Up
subtopics.definition: Escalation takes urgent or unresolved risks to the audit committee without waiting for the normal cycle; follow-up verifies that management's agreed actions were actually carried out.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A report changes nothing if actions stall or a critical issue waits weeks for a meeting. Escalation and follow-up turn findings into reduced risk, with governance holding management accountable.
how_it_works: Take critical issues with legal or regulatory deadlines to the audit committee chair at once, between meetings if needed, with legal counsel.
Escalate repeated pressure to drop or soften a finding to the audit committee; decline a single request first and offer to review the facts.
Plan follow-up by risk: verify critical findings early and report their status to the committee; give lower ratings lighter, later checks.
Follow-up independently tests that each agreed action was implemented and works; it neither relies on management's word nor repeats the whole audit.
If management accepts a risk instead of fixing it, confirm the right level of management approved it and report it to the committee.
Treat findings that recur year after year as failed remediation: analyze the root cause and escalate for accountability.
subtopics.example: During follow-up, an IS auditor finds that a high-rated backup finding the IT manager marked closed was fixed on only two of five servers, after being reported in each of the two previous years. The chief audit executive reopens it, analyzes why remediation keeps failing, and reports the repeat finding and its root cause to the audit committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Severity sets the timing: urgent risks go to governance now, not at the next meeting. Follow-up is independent verification scaled to risk. Management may accept a risk, but the audit committee must know, and repeated failure to fix is itself a finding to escalate.

exam_traps.trap: Accept management's statement that all findings are fixed and close them.
exam_traps.why: A self-report is not evidence. Follow-up independently verifies each agreed action, scaled to the finding's severity.

exam_traps.trap: Reissue a finding repeated for three years with a firmer deadline.
exam_traps.why: That repeats a failed approach. Find the root cause of the failed remediation and escalate to the audit committee for accountability.

key_terms.definition: An agreed corrective action past its target date, tracked by audit and reported to the audit committee.
A finding reported again because earlier agreed actions did not fix it.

topics.topic_name: Quality Assurance and Improvement of Audit Process
topics.overview: Auditors are audited too. A quality assurance and improvement program checks that audit work meets standards, through supervision on every engagement, periodic internal reviews and independent external assessments, then feeds the lessons back into the function. Control self-assessment and integrated audits, often grouped with process improvement, are covered in topic 1A2.
can_do: Tell ongoing monitoring, periodic internal assessment and external assessment apart
Judge whether a quality reviewer is independent enough for the review
State how often an external assessment is expected and who may perform it
Link quality results and skill gaps to targeted improvements

subtopics.name: Supervision and Ongoing Monitoring
subtopics.definition: Ongoing monitoring is the quality control built into every engagement, mainly supervisors reviewing work papers and conclusions while the work is happening.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is the only quality check that catches defects before a report is issued. Later reviews find problems only after flawed conclusions have reached the audit committee.
how_it_works: Supervisors assign work to match skills, direct staff and review work papers as evidence comes in.
Reviewers check that each conclusion follows from sufficient, appropriate evidence, not just that steps are signed off.
Standard checklists and templates keep reviews consistent across engagements.
Automated work-paper tools can check form, such as sign-offs, cross-references and attachments.
Review notes and how they were resolved are documented, so the file shows that supervision actually happened.
subtopics.example: To meet a tight deadline, an audit manager proposes signing off work papers after checking only that sign-offs and attachments are present. The chief audit executive (CAE) rejects the shortcut and has the manager review each key work paper as evidence comes in, so that unsupported conclusions are caught before the draft report reaches management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Quality is built in, not inspected in afterward. Ongoing monitoring is part of routine supervision on every engagement, and it is judged by whether it stops unsupported conclusions from reaching a report.

exam_traps.trap: An automated checker can replace supervisory review of work papers.
exam_traps.why: Tools confirm form, not substance. Only a human reviewer can judge whether evidence is sufficient and conclusions are supported.

exam_traps.trap: An annual deep review of a sample of engagements is enough ongoing monitoring.
exam_traps.why: That is a periodic assessment. It adds to, but cannot replace, supervision built into every engagement, and it leaves most work unreviewed.

key_terms.definition: A supervisor's written question or challenge on a work paper, which the auditor must resolve and document.
A conclusion the evidence in the work papers does not back; the most serious quality defect.

subtopics.name: Periodic Internal Assessments
subtopics.definition: A periodic internal assessment is a structured review, run inside the audit function, of completed engagements and practices by people who did not do the work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Supervisors can share the blind spots of their own teams. A periodic review by uninvolved reviewers tests whether standards are met across engagements and over time.
how_it_works: Reviewers sample completed engagements and check conformance with standards, the audit methodology and the audit charter.
Reviewers must not have worked on the engagements they review; teams reviewing their own files weaken objectivity.
Engagement-level reviews check one audit's file; program-level reviews check the quality system, methodology and supervision across engagements.
Results and action plans go to the chief audit executive and are summarized for the audit committee.
Internal assessments continue between external assessments; they do not replace them.
subtopics.example: A chief audit executive (CAE) is designing the internal assessment part of her quality program. A team lead suggests each team review its own files because they know them best. The CAE instead assigns reviewers from other teams to sample completed engagements twice a year, and adds a yearly program-level review of methodology and supervision.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal assessment combines ongoing monitoring with periodic reviews by people independent of the work under review. Engagement-level and program-level reviews answer different questions, so a mature program uses both.

exam_traps.trap: Once a program-level review exists, reviews of individual engagement files are unnecessary.
exam_traps.why: Program reviewers sample only a few files and focus on the system. Engagement reviews test individual audits; each answers a different question.

exam_traps.trap: The team that did the work is best placed to review it.
exam_traps.why: Knowledge is not objectivity. People who did the work cannot judge it impartially, so reviewers must be uninvolved.

key_terms.definition: A review of one audit's file to check that its work met standards.
A review of the whole quality system, methodology and supervision across many engagements.
Meeting the requirements of the applicable professional standards and the function's own methodology.

subtopics.name: External Quality Assessments
subtopics.definition: An external quality assessment is an independent review of the whole audit function's conformance with standards, carried out by a qualified assessor from outside the organization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Self-assessment alone gives the audit committee unverified, possibly false, assurance. An outside view tests the function against standards and good practice and catches blind spots the whole team shares.
how_it_works: The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) standards require an external assessment at least once every five years.
The assessor or team must be qualified and independent of the organization, not just of the audit function.
It can be a full external assessment, or a self-assessment checked and confirmed by a qualified outside assessor.
The chief audit executive agrees on the scope and the assessor's independence with the audit committee, and reports the results and action plan to it.

rows.label: Who does it
cells: Supervisors on each engagement
Audit staff not involved in the work
A qualified assessor independent of the organization

rows.label: How often
cells: Continuously, on every engagement
Periodically, such as once a year
At least once every five years

rows.label: Main value
cells: Catches defects before reports are issued
Checks conformance across engagements
Independent assurance for the audit committee

subtopics.example: A credit union's three-person audit function has never had an external quality assessment. To save money, the board chair suggests that the credit union's compliance officer review the audit files. The chief audit executive (CAE) tells the audit committee that the compliance officer is not independent of the organization and recommends a self-assessment validated by a qualified outside assessor.
subtopics.isaca_rule: External means independent of the organization. Self-assessment, however thorough, needs periodic independent validation. A missing or overdue external assessment is a significant quality-program weakness to report to the audit committee.

exam_traps.trap: A review by another division of the same company counts as external.
exam_traps.why: Reviewers inside the organization are not independent of it, even if they sit outside the audit function.

exam_traps.trap: Strong yearly self-assessments remove the need for an external review.
exam_traps.why: Self-assessment by the people being assessed gives unverified assurance. The IIA standards still require an independent external assessment at least every five years.

key_terms.definition: The audit function's full quality system: ongoing monitoring, internal and external assessments, and improvement actions.
An internal self-assessment whose results a qualified outside assessor checks and confirms.

subtopics.name: Continuous Improvement
subtopics.definition: Continuous improvement is the part of the quality program that turns review results, feedback and performance data into better audit methods, skills and tools.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Finding quality problems is pointless if the same ones keep coming back. Improvement keeps the function's skills and methods in step with the risks it must audit.
how_it_works: Collect inputs: quality review results, stakeholder surveys, lessons learned from engagements and performance measures.
Track measures such as audit plan completion, time from fieldwork to report and the share of findings closed on time.
Base training on gaps between the team's current skills and the skills the approved audit plan requires.
Update methodology, templates and tools when reviews show a weakness that keeps recurring.
Report quality results and improvement actions to the audit committee, and track them to completion.
subtopics.example: Quality reviews of an audit function find the same defect three years running: work papers do not record why each sample size was chosen. The audit manager adds a required sampling-rationale section to the work-paper template, runs a short session for the staff whose files showed the gap, tracks the defect rate in the next review cycle, and reports the trend to the audit committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Improvement is targeted, not generic. Tie training to the skill needs of the approved audit plan, fix methods where reviews show recurring weaknesses, and report quality results and actions to the audit committee.

exam_traps.trap: Focus training on emerging technology, because that is where the risk is.
exam_traps.why: Training should close actual gaps against the approved plan, which may include older technology. A generic focus misses skills the plan needs.

key_terms.definition: A measure that shows how well the audit function meets a goal, such as the share of reports issued on time.
A short review at the end of an engagement recording what worked and what to change next time.
A feedback form sent to auditees and audit committee members about the value and conduct of audits.

key_terminologies.ITAF (IT Audit Framework): ISACA's professional practices framework for IS audit and assurance: mandatory standards, advisory guidelines, and informational tools and techniques.
key_terminologies.Audit committee: A board committee of independent directors that oversees audit, internal control and financial reporting.
key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The senior person who leads the internal audit function and reports functionally to the audit committee.
key_terminologies.Independence: Freedom, in structure and in mindset, from influences that could bias the auditor's conclusions.
key_terminologies.Self-review threat: The risk to objectivity when auditors evaluate work they designed, built or ran; earlier advice that left decisions to management is a lesser threat.
key_terminologies.Due professional care: The diligence, skill and skepticism a reasonable, competent auditor would apply, including proper review before sign-off.
key_terminologies.Proficiency: Holding, as a team, the knowledge and skills each engagement needs; gaps are closed with training, specialists or co-sourcing.
key_terminologies.Audit universe: The complete, risk-mapped list of everything in the organization that could be audited.
key_terminologies.Risk-based audit plan: The set of audits for a cycle, chosen and ordered by current risk and approved by the audit committee.
key_terminologies.Audit risk: The risk of reaching the wrong conclusion; it combines inherent, control and detection risk.
key_terminologies.Materiality: The point at which an issue could change the decisions of those relying on the audit, judged on size and nature.
key_terminologies.Walkthrough: Tracing one transaction from start to finish to confirm how a process and its controls really work.
key_terminologies.Reasonable assurance: A high but not absolute level of confidence, reflecting the limits of any control system.
key_terminologies.Key control: A control whose failure would leave a significant risk uncovered, so the auditor relies on it and tests it first.
key_terminologies.Compensating control: An alternative control that reduces the same risk when the preferred control is impractical; a review-type substitute works only if the reviewer is independent.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The risk left after controls are applied, which management, not the auditor, decides whether to accept.
key_terminologies.SOC report: A System and Organization Controls report: a service auditor's report on a service provider's controls.
key_terminologies.Integrated audit: One engagement that combines IT, financial and operational audit work, linking IT weaknesses to business impact.
key_terminologies.Sufficient and appropriate evidence: Enough evidence (sufficient) that is relevant and reliable (appropriate) to support a conclusion.
key_terminologies.Sampling risk: The risk that a conclusion drawn from a sample differs from the conclusion a test of the whole population would give.
key_terminologies.CAATs: Computer-assisted audit techniques: using software to test data and systems, often across full populations.
key_terminologies.Integrated test facility (ITF): A dummy entity in a live system used to compare actual processing with expected results.
key_terminologies.Work papers: The record of procedures performed, evidence obtained and conclusions reached, supporting the audit report.
key_terminologies.Chain of custody: A documented record of who held evidence and when, preserving its integrity for possible legal use.
key_terminologies.Follow-up: Audit work that verifies whether management implemented the agreed corrective actions, scaled to each finding's severity.
key_terminologies.Quality assurance and improvement progra: The audit function's ongoing supervision, periodic internal reviews and independent external assessments of its own work.

domains.overview: This domain is about making sure IT serves the business. Governance sets direction, decides who is accountable and checks results; management plans, builds and runs IT within that direction. Part A covers laws and frameworks, structures, policies, enterprise architecture, risk, privacy and data governance. Part B covers the day-to-day management of IT people, money, vendors, performance and quality.
domains.analogy: Think of a hospital. The board of trustees does not perform surgery, but it sets the hospital's mission, approves its budget and policies, decides how much risk is acceptable and checks that patients are safe. The medical director and department heads run daily operations within those rules, and an independent inspector reports to the trustees on whether things really work. IT governance is the trustees' role, IT management is the director's, and the IS auditor is the inspector, who reports and recommends but does not run the wards.

topics.overview: Every enterprise works inside outside rules: laws and regulations it must obey, and industry standards and frameworks it adopts by choice or by contract. Governance must know which rules apply, choose frameworks that fit, and turn each obligation into an owned, tested control.
can_do: Tell a mandatory legal obligation from a voluntary framework or a contract-based standard
Match COBIT 2019, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, NIST CSF 2.0, ITIL, COSO and ISO/IEC 38500 to the question each one answers
Recommend mapping many regulations to one owned control set that is tested once
Recognize when a legal conflict belongs with counsel, not with the IS auditor

subtopics.name: How Outside Rules Shape IT Governance
subtopics.definition: Legal and regulatory compliance means meeting the mandatory duties that laws, regulators and binding contracts place on how an organization uses and protects information.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Outside rules decide what data may be kept, for how long, who may see it and what must be reported. Breaking them brings fines, lost licenses and lost trust.
how_it_works: Laws and regulations apply based on where the organization operates, its sector and whose data it holds.
Industry standards, such as the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), often bind through contracts rather than law.
Regulators can inspect, demand evidence and penalize, so each obligation needs proof of compliance.
Mandatory obligations are funded before optional improvements when budgets are ranked.
The board stays accountable for compliance even when legal, compliance or IT teams do the work.
When a regulator investigates, counsel coordinates: preserve evidence, review what is produced, and meet the requested scope and deadline.
subtopics.example: A retailer takes card payments online and plans to store card numbers for one-click checkout. Its merchant agreement requires PCI DSS, though no law names that standard, and the chief information officer treated it as optional. The IS auditor reports that the contract makes the standard binding and recommends that management add it to the compliance plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Mandatory obligations are not open to a cost trade-off. Management decides how to comply, not whether to comply, and the board stays accountable. The IS auditor verifies that every applicable obligation is identified and treated, and reports gaps without ruling on legal questions.

exam_traps.trap: The fine is smaller than the cost of compliance, so accepting the risk is reasonable.
exam_traps.why: Mandatory law is not a risk to buy out with a fine. It ranks ahead of discretionary spending, and penalties often bring reputation damage too.

exam_traps.trap: When a regulator opens an investigation, hand over every record at once to show full cooperation.
exam_traps.why: Unreviewed material can be wrong or widen the inquiry. Preserve evidence, let counsel review it and cooperate within the requested scope and deadline.

key_terms.definition: A binding rule issued by a government agency under a law's authority and enforced through inspections and penalties.

key_terms.term: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS)
key_terms.definition: The card brands' security standard for anyone handling card data; it binds through merchant and service contracts.

subtopics.name: Selecting Industry Standards and Frameworks
subtopics.definition: A good-practice framework is a published, ready-made structure of principles, processes and controls that an organization adapts instead of designing governance from scratch.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks save time and make practice comparable and auditable. Choosing the wrong one, or copying one without tailoring it, produces paperwork that does not fit the business.
how_it_works: Each framework answers a different question, so mature organizations combine several and map them to one control set.
Adoption is usually voluntary, unless a regulator, contract or major customer makes a specific framework mandatory.
Management tailors the chosen frameworks to the enterprise's size, goals, risk profile and legal duties.
Certification against a standard proves a management system operates within a stated scope, not that everything in the company is sound.
Governance reviews framework use from time to time, keeping what adds value and dropping ritual that does not.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: How do we govern and manage enterprise IT?
How do we run an information security management system (ISMS)?
What security outcomes should we reach?
How do we deliver IT services that create value?

rows.label: Published by
cells: ISACA
International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), as its Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
PeopleCert, which absorbed the former AXELOS brand

rows.label: Certifiable?
cells: No; used to design and assess governance
Yes, by accredited certification bodies
No; voluntary
Individuals are certified; organizations are not

rows.label: Main parts
cells: Five domains: one governance domain (Evaluate, Direct and Monitor) and four management domains
Mandatory ISMS requirements (clauses 4 to 10), plus Annex A reference controls selected through risk treatment
Six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Four dimensions (from ITIL 4): organizations and people; information and technology; partners and suppliers; value streams and processes

subtopics.example: A software company's board wants one framework for everything. The chief information officer proposes adopting all 40 COBIT 2019 governance and management objectives at once, while sales needs ISO/IEC 27001 certification for enterprise customers. The IS auditor recommends tailoring COBIT to the company's priorities, using ISO/IEC 27001 for the security management system, and mapping both to one control set. Management chooses the approach.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A framework is a tool for meeting enterprise objectives, not an objective in itself. Choose frameworks by the question they answer, tailor them to the business, and link them through shared goals and metrics rather than forcing one method on everyone.

exam_traps.trap: Forcing every team onto one framework is the most mature approach.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks are complementary. Mixed environments work best when the frameworks that fit each area are linked by shared goals and metrics, not replaced by a single method.

exam_traps.trap: COBIT and ITIL do the same job, so either answers a board-level governance question.
exam_traps.why: COBIT covers governing and managing enterprise IT; ITIL focuses on service management. For board direction and oversight, COBIT or ISO/IEC 38500 fits better.

key_terms.definition: The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission's model of five components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, monitoring.
An international standard giving boards principles for overseeing IT use, including conformance with laws and internal policies.
Adapting a framework's scope and depth to the enterprise's needs instead of adopting every element.

subtopics.memory_aid: COBIT governs, 27001 secures, CSF sets outcomes, ITIL serves, COSO controls.

subtopics.name: Mapping Obligations to Controls
subtopics.definition: A compliance obligations register lists every law, regulation and contract duty that applies, and maps each requirement to the internal control that satisfies it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many rules ask for the same thing, such as access reviews or logging. Mapping exposes overlaps and gaps, so each control is tested once and relied on everywhere instead of being audited separately for every rule.
how_it_works: Legal and compliance staff list each applicable obligation and break it into specific, testable requirements.
Each requirement links to a control in one unified control library, with a named control owner.
Shared controls are tested once, and the result is reused as evidence for every rule that relies on them.
Named staff scan for proposed and new rules, and the mappings are updated before deadlines arrive.
Genuine conflicts between laws go to legal counsel and management; the IS auditor reports them but does not resolve them.
subtopics.example: A cruise line must meet maritime security rules, card-payment requirements and two national privacy laws. Its compliance, security and privacy teams each run their own control tests, so crew access reviews are tested four times a year while nobody checks shipboard backup encryption. The IS auditor recommends one owned control library mapped to every obligation, with tests planned from the map.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Map first, then test. One owned control set, mapped to every obligation, shows overlaps and gaps. Keeping the map current is a management duty, and resolving conflicts between laws belongs to counsel, not to the auditor.

exam_traps.trap: Run a separate compliance audit for each regulation.
exam_traps.why: Separate audits duplicate work, burden control owners and hide gaps between rules. Mapping requirements to common controls is the efficient and complete first step.

exam_traps.trap: Wait for the regulator's letter before updating controls for a new rule.
exam_traps.why: Compliance is proactive. Owned horizon scanning feeds new rules into the control map before they take effect, not after a finding or breach.

key_terms.definition: One library of internal controls mapped to many outside requirements, so each control serves several obligations.
Watching for proposed and new laws, rules and guidance so the organization can prepare before they apply.
Running governance, risk and compliance work on one platform, with one list of risk categories and one set of reports, while each function stays distinct.

topics.topic_name: Organizational Structure, IT Governance, and IT Strategy
topics.overview: This topic covers who decides, who does the work and who checks it. It separates governance from management, names the committees and the three lines around IT, shows how IT strategy flows from business strategy, explains why no one person should control a sensitive process from end to end, and covers governing artificial intelligence (AI).
can_do: Tell board-level governance from management work in a scenario, including oversight of AI
Match a decision to the right body: board, IT strategy committee, IT steering committee or audit committee
Place functions in the Three Lines Model and protect internal audit's independence
Recommend a compensating control when segregation of duties is not practical

subtopics.name: Governance Versus Management
subtopics.definition: Enterprise governance of information and technology (EGIT) is the board's direction and oversight of IT, so that technology supports strategy, creates value and stays within risk limits.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When the board does management's job, or management sets its own direction unchecked, accountability blurs. A clear split lets the board hold executives to account for results.
how_it_works: The board evaluates options and stakeholder needs, directs through strategy, policy and priorities, and monitors performance and compliance.
Executives plan, build, run and monitor IT within the direction the board sets.
COBIT 2019 keeps governance objectives separate from management objectives, so each role stays distinct.
EGIT is part of enterprise governance and applies to every organization that depends on IT, not only regulated firms.
The board can delegate execution, but it keeps accountability for how IT serves the enterprise.

rows.label: Who
cells: The board of directors and its committees
The chief executive officer, chief information officer and other executives

rows.label: Core activities
cells: Evaluate, direct and monitor
Plan, build, run and monitor

rows.label: Main question
cells: Are we doing the right things?
Are we doing things right?

rows.label: COBIT 2019 objectives
cells: Evaluate, Direct and Monitor (EDM)
Align, Plan and Organize; Build, Acquire and Implement; Deliver, Service and Support; Monitor, Evaluate and Assess
