illustration.caption: The board sets direction and checks results; management plans, builds and runs IT, then reports back.

subtopics.example: At a logistics firm, board members have started approving server designs and vendor quotes, yet nobody at board level has set IT priorities for the year. The IS auditor reports that the board is doing management's work while its own governance role sits empty. The auditor recommends that the board set direction and risk limits and leave design decisions to the chief information officer.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The board sets direction and holds accountability; management executes and reports back. When a question asks about the scope of governance, choose the board-level answer about direction, value and risk, not a process the chief information officer runs.

exam_traps.trap: The chief information officer's IT planning process is IT governance.
exam_traps.why: Planning, building and running IT is management. Governance is the board-level direction and oversight that management's plans must serve.

exam_traps.trap: A board that approves technical designs shows strong governance.
exam_traps.why: That is management work done by the wrong body. Strong governance sets direction, approves priorities and risk limits, and monitors outcomes.

key_terms.definition: Realizing benefits while optimizing risk and resources, which COBIT names as the core aim of governance.
What owners, customers, regulators and staff require from the enterprise; governance weighs them when setting direction.
The system by which the whole enterprise is directed and controlled; IT governance is one part of it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Board: Evaluate, Direct, Monitor. Management: Plan, Build, Run, Monitor.

subtopics.name: Boards, Committees and Roles
subtopics.definition: An IT governance structure is the set of boards, committees and roles that hold IT decision rights, each defined by a charter with a clear escalation path.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When two bodies think they own a decision, or neither does, priorities stall and risks go unowned. Charters and decision rights make clear who decides, who advises and who checks.
how_it_works: Each committee has a charter stating its purpose, members, decision rights, meeting cadence and reporting line.
Senior business and IT leaders sit together on the IT steering committee, so priorities reflect business strategy rather than IT preference.
Every committee can escalate unresolved issues and enforce its decisions; review without authority lets problems recur.
A project management office (PMO) applies common stage gates, the approval checkpoints between project phases, and consolidated reporting across concurrent projects.
The audit committee oversees internal and external audit, approves the audit charter and receives audit findings; it oversees risk and control but does not own them.

rows.label: Level
cells: Board
Senior management
Board

rows.label: Main job
cells: Advises the board on IT direction, emerging technology and strategic risk
Prioritizes projects, allocates resources and tracks delivery
Oversees internal and external audit and the reliability of reporting

rows.label: Members
cells: Board members plus expert advisers
Senior business and IT managers
Independent directors, at least one with financial expertise

rows.label: Exam cue
cells: Long-term direction, advice to the board
Project ranking, resource conflicts
Audit independence, reporting assurance

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 222' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Board level: the IT strategy committee advises on long-term direction and the audit committee oversees audit. Management level: the IT steering committee ranks projects and allocates resources'><text x='20' y='18' text-anchor='start' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text2)'>BOARD LEVEL</text><rect x='20' y='26' width='300' height='46' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>IT strategy committee</text><text x='170' y='63' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>Advises on long-term direction</text><rect x='20' y='80' width='300' height='46' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='99' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Audit committee</text><text x='170' y='117' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>Oversees internal and external audit</text><line x1='20' y1='140' x2='320' y2='140' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='20' y='160' text-anchor='start' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text2)'>MANAGEMENT LEVEL</text><rect x='20' y='168' width='300' height='46' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='187' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>IT steering committee</text><text x='170' y='205' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text)'>Ranks projects, allocates resources</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Two committees sit at board level: the IT strategy committee advises on direction, and the audit committee oversees audit. The IT steering committee belongs to management and ranks projects.

subtopics.example: A hospital network's steering committee charter says the committee reviews project status, but it has no power to stop or reorder projects, and the same overruns repeat every quarter. The IS auditor recommends adding decision rights and an escalation path to the executive team, and reports the finding to the audit committee. The chief executive amends the charter.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Each decision belongs to one chartered body with clear decision rights and an escalation path, and each outcome has one Accountable role. A committee that only reviews, without authority to act, gives the look of governance without its effect.

exam_traps.trap: The IT strategy committee prioritizes projects and allocates resources.
exam_traps.why: That is the IT steering committee, a management body. The IT strategy committee works at board level and advises on long-term direction.

exam_traps.trap: Naming two Accountable roles for an outcome makes ownership stronger.
exam_traps.why: Shared accountability lets decisions fall between owners. A RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) chart allows many Responsible roles but one Accountable role per outcome.

key_terms.definition: A table naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity or outcome.
The formal authority to make a specific decision, assigned to one role or body.
An approved document setting a committee's purpose, authority, membership and reporting line.

subtopics.name: The Three Lines Model and Audit's Place
subtopics.definition: The Three Lines Model, from the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA), assigns risk roles: management owns risk, specialist functions support and challenge, and internal audit provides independent assurance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Clear lines prevent gaps and overlaps in managing risk. They also protect internal audit's independence, which is what makes its assurance worth relying on.
how_it_works: The governing body sets direction and receives reports from both management and internal audit.
First-line operational managers own risks and run the controls in their daily work.
Second-line risk, compliance and security functions set frameworks, give expertise, monitor and challenge the first line.
Internal audit, the third line, reports functionally to the governing body, usually the audit committee, and administratively to a senior executive outside the areas it audits.
Audit can advise on control design, but it must not run, own or approve the controls it will later assure.

rows.label: Who
cells: Operational and IT management
Risk management, compliance and security functions
Internal audit

rows.label: Role
cells: Owns and manages risk
Supports, monitors and challenges
Gives independent assurance and advice

rows.label: Independent of management?
cells: No
No; part of management, though some roles also report directly to the board
Yes; it reports to the governing body

subtopics.example: A university's chief information officer asks internal audit to design and run the new user-access review process, because audit knows the controls best. The chief audit executive (CAE) sees that audit would later be assuring its own work. The CAE offers advice on control design only, recommends that the identity team run the reviews, and reports the request to the audit committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Management owns risk; internal audit provides independent assurance. Audit recommends and management decides. Audit must not design, operate or approve the controls it will later evaluate, because that creates a self-review threat.

exam_traps.trap: The compliance function gives the board independent assurance.
exam_traps.why: The second line reports to management and helps run risk management. Only internal audit, independent of management, provides independent assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Audit can run risk management for a while or join the IT steering committee as a voting member.
exam_traps.why: Either role means audit later reviews its own work or decisions. Audit reports its findings to governance bodies, but it should not hold a seat on them or run what it assures.

key_terms.definition: The risk to objectivity when auditors evaluate work they designed, performed or approved.
The board or equivalent group that is accountable for the organization and oversees management.
An objective opinion on risk and control from a party free of management's influence.

subtopics.analogy: A building works the same way: the people who use it keep it safe day to day, a safety office sets rules and checks on them, and an independent inspector reports to the owners.

subtopics.name: IT Strategy and Strategic Planning
subtopics.definition: An IT strategic plan sets out how technology will help the business meet its goals over several years, with a target state and a prioritized roadmap.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a plan derived from business goals, IT spends on whatever is loudest or newest. A traceable plan lets leaders fund what matters and stop what does not.
how_it_works: The plan starts from the business strategy and describes the IT target state needed to support it.
A gap analysis compares today's capabilities with the target, and a prioritized roadmap closes the gaps.
Tactical plans turn the roadmap into this year's projects, budgets and milestones.
Each major investment traces to a business objective with a measure of success.
Material change mid-cycle, such as a merger, new law or major breach, triggers a focused update endorsed by the board.
New technologies are trialed in controlled pilots and pass stage gates before joining normal delivery.

rows.label: Time horizon
cells: Three to five years
Usually one year

rows.label: Content
cells: Direction, target state and priorities
Projects, budgets, milestones and staffing

rows.label: Endorsed by
cells: The board, advised by the IT strategy committee
The IT steering committee and IT management

rows.label: Changes when
cells: Business strategy or the environment changes materially
Each planning cycle, or when priorities shift

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 174' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Business strategy drives IT strategy, which delivers business value'><rect x='20' y='8' width='300' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='32' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Business strategy</text><line x1='170' y1='48' x2='170' y2='59' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M166,59 L170,66 L174,59 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='20' y='68' width='300' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>IT strategy</text><line x1='170' y1='108' x2='170' y2='119' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M166,119 L170,126 L174,119 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='20' y='128' width='300' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='152' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Business value delivered</text></svg>
illustration.caption: IT strategy is derived from business strategy, and IT adds value only when it delivers outcomes the business can see.

subtopics.example: Two years into a four-year IT strategy, a regional airline buys a smaller carrier, and a new cyber law requires incident reporting within 72 hours. The chief digital officer wants to fund the work as side projects and leave the strategy untouched. The IS auditor recommends a focused, board-endorsed strategy update that re-ranks priorities and funding.
subtopics.isaca_rule: IT strategy is derived from business strategy, never the reverse. Alignment is proven by tracing each major investment to a business objective with a measure of success, not by IT efficiency figures. Material change calls for a governed update, not a fresh start.

exam_traps.trap: On-time projects and high uptime prove IT is aligned with the business.
exam_traps.why: Those figures measure IT activity and efficiency. Alignment shows in the share of investment linked to approved business objectives and in the outcomes delivered.

exam_traps.trap: After a major breach, approve the security team's emergency funding request at once.
exam_traps.why: Unplanned spending should first rest on finding the root cause and the risk that remains, so money targets the real gaps and fits the strategy.

key_terms.definition: How directly IT goals, investments and services support the enterprise's business objectives.
Testing new technology in controlled pilots, then moving proven ideas into normal governance through defined gates.
COBIT's chain that turns stakeholder needs into enterprise goals, then alignment goals, then the governance and management objectives that deliver them.

subtopics.name: Information Security Governance
subtopics.definition: Information security governance is the board's direction and oversight that keeps information protected in line with business goals, legal duties and risk appetite.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security run as a technical silo buys tools that may not match business risk. Board ownership ties protection to what the business values most and keeps senior management accountable for breaches.
how_it_works: The board approves the security strategy and policy and sets how much information risk is acceptable.
The chief information security officer (CISO) designs and runs the program and reports regularly to senior management.
The strategy maps security capabilities to each business goal, such as expansion or acquisitions, with measurable targets.
Executive security metrics show control effectiveness and risk trends, with thresholds that trigger escalation.
Awareness is measured by behavior, such as phishing-simulation results, not by course completion.
The CISO reports to senior management outside IT operations, so security concerns are not filtered or overruled by the people who run IT.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Information security governance sits inside IT governance, which sits inside enterprise governance'><rect x='10' y='8' width='320' height='134' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent-fill)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><text x='170' y='28' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Enterprise governance</text><rect x='30' y='40' width='280' height='94' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent-fill)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><text x='170' y='60' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>IT governance</text><rect x='48' y='72' width='244' height='52' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='103' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Information security governance</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Security governance lives inside IT governance, which lives inside enterprise governance. It is part of the whole, not a separate silo.

subtopics.example: A logistics company plans to launch drone deliveries and to sell to government agencies within two years. Its new security strategy lists tools and staffing but links none of them to these goals, and no executive outside IT has reviewed it. The IS auditor recommends tying each security capability to a business goal with measurable targets, and securing senior management sponsorship before the strategy goes to the board.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Senior management commitment is the MOST important success factor for security governance. The board can delegate running security to the CISO, but not accountability. Security strategy must serve business objectives, and security policy needs board or top-management approval.

exam_traps.trap: The CISO is ultimately accountable for information security.
exam_traps.why: The CISO is responsible for running the program. Ultimate accountability stays with the board and senior management, who cannot delegate it away.

exam_traps.trap: High training completion rates prove the awareness program works.
exam_traps.why: Completion shows attendance, not behavior. Simulation results, incident reports and fewer risky actions show whether staff actually act more securely.

key_terms.definition: A multi-year plan linking security capabilities and spending to business objectives and risk appetite.
A measure of what people actually do, such as phishing report rates, rather than which training they finished.
Handing a task and the authority to do it to someone else, while the delegator stays accountable.

subtopics.name: Segregation of Duties in IT
subtopics.definition: Segregation of duties (SoD) splits a sensitive task among different people, so no one person can start, approve, carry out and hide a transaction or change.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If one person controls every step, an error or fraud can go unnoticed. Splitting duties means a wrongdoer needs a partner, which makes fraud harder to commit and easier to detect.
how_it_works: Keep four functions apart: authorizing a transaction, holding the asset, recording it, and reconciling or reviewing it.
In IT, keep development, production operations, database administration and security administration apart, so no one can change code or data and also grant access or clear logs.
Watch for toxic combinations, where one account can change data or code and also alter the logs that would reveal it.
Where a small team cannot split duties, add compensating controls: usually an independent person reviews activity afterward to detect problems.
Review role assignments regularly, because access tends to build up as people change jobs.

rows.label: When used
cells: Enough staff and system support to split conflicting duties
Team too small, or the system cannot enforce the split

rows.label: Type
cells: Mainly preventive: stops problems before they happen
Mainly detective: finds problems afterward

rows.label: Example
cells: Developers cannot move their own code to production
Independent review of production logs against approved change tickets

rows.label: Main limit
cells: Can be costly in small teams
Finds problems after they happen

subtopics.example: A family-owned winery has two IT staff. The database administrator also manages user accounts and can clear the audit log, and the owners will not hire more staff. The IS auditor recommends sending logs to a service the administrator cannot alter, with the finance controller reviewing account changes monthly against signed requests.
subtopics.isaca_rule: SoD fails most dangerously when one person can change data or code and also alter the evidence. Where full separation is impossible, management adds independent detective controls; small size does not remove the need for control.

exam_traps.trap: The team is too small, so segregation of duties does not apply.
exam_traps.why: The risk does not shrink with headcount. When duties cannot be split, independent compensating controls, such as log review against approved changes, must cover the gap.

exam_traps.trap: The greatest SoD concern is a user with read access to many systems.
exam_traps.why: Broad read access is a confidentiality issue. The greatest SoD concern is the power to change data or code and also conceal it, for example by editing logs.

key_terms.definition: Two or more access rights that, held together, let one person commit and hide an error or fraud.
Two or more people working together to get around a control that segregation of duties put in place.
A periodic check by managers that each person's access still matches their current job.

subtopics.memory_aid: Split the four hands: authorize, hold, record, review.

subtopics.name: Governing Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) governance is the board-approved policy, ownership, inventory and monitoring that keep an organization's AI use lawful, fair, explainable and within risk appetite.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI models can make biased, opaque or wrong decisions at scale, and the organization answers for them even when a vendor built the model.
how_it_works: The board approves an AI policy and risk appetite, and each model or AI service has a named business owner.
An inventory lists every AI use, including vendor and embedded AI, ranked by impact on people and the business.
Higher-impact uses get an impact assessment before deployment, covering data sources, bias, explainability and human oversight.
Deployed models are monitored for drift and for outcomes by population group, with thresholds that trigger review.
Frameworks such as ISO/IEC 42001 and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework structure the program.
Laws such as the European Union (EU) AI Act add duties, such as human oversight, for high-risk uses.
subtopics.example: A staffing agency uses a vendor's AI tool to rank job applicants. Older applicants rarely reach interviews, yet no one owns the tool, it appears in no inventory, and results were never checked by age. The IS auditor recommends an independent review of the rankings, a named business owner, an inventory entry and outcome monitoring under a board-approved AI policy.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Govern AI like any high-impact process: business ownership, an inventory, assessment before use and outcome monitoring after. The organization stays accountable for AI decisions, even with a vendor's model. Fix governance gaps FIRST, before technical tuning.

exam_traps.trap: Retrain the model immediately when biased outcomes are found.
exam_traps.why: Retraining before diagnosing the cause may repeat the bias and leaves ownership and monitoring gaps open. Assess the harm independently and fix governance first.

exam_traps.trap: A vendor-supplied AI model makes the vendor accountable for its decisions.
exam_traps.why: The organization using the model answers to customers and regulators. Contracts can require transparency and testing, but accountability stays with the user.

key_terms.definition: A decline in a model's accuracy as real-world data drifts away from its training data.
The ability to show, in terms people can understand, why a model produced a given result.
A maintained register of every AI model and AI-enabled service, with owner, purpose and risk rating.

topics.topic_name: IT Policies, Standards, Procedures, and Guidelines
topics.overview: Written rules turn governance intent into daily behavior. This topic covers the four document types and how they rank, how policies are developed and approved, and how they stay current, handle exceptions and are proven to work in practice.
can_do: Classify a document as a policy, standard, procedure or guideline from its wording
Identify who must approve a policy and why a functional head is not enough
Recommend controls for policy review, version control and exceptions
Choose evidence that shows a policy operates, not just that it exists

subtopics.name: The Four Document Types
subtopics.definition: The policy document hierarchy ranks four kinds of written rules, from broad intent down to detailed advice, and each lower document must conform to those above it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: IS auditors evaluate compliance against the right document. Treating advice as a rule creates false findings, and a policy without standards is too vague to enforce. Security policy is covered in 5A1.1.
how_it_works: The board or senior management approves policies, which state intent and direction in short, stable language.
Senior management, or a function it delegates such as IT or security leadership, approves standards that make a policy measurable and mandatory.
Process owners approve and maintain procedures, the step-by-step actions people follow to meet a standard.
The issuing function publishes guidelines, which recommend good practice and stay advisory.
Each document has a named owner and review date; a lower document weaker than the one above is a compliance gap.

rows.label: Answers
cells: Why, and what in principle
What exactly, in measurable terms
How, step by step
Suggested ways to do it well

rows.label: Mandatory?
cells: Yes
Yes
Yes
No; advisory

rows.label: Approved by
cells: Board or senior management
Senior management or a delegated function
The process owner
The issuing function, which keeps them consistent with standards

rows.label: Example
cells: Customer data must be protected wherever it is stored
Laptops use full-disk encryption with the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES-256)
Steps to turn on and verify encryption on a new laptop
Tips for choosing a memorable passphrase

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 184' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The document hierarchy: policy sets intent, standards make it mandatory and specific, procedures give step-by-step instructions, guidelines are recommended'><rect x='10' y='8' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='31' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Policy: what management intends</text><rect x='10' y='52' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Standards: mandatory specifics</text><rect x='10' y='96' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='119' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Procedures: step by step</text><rect x='10' y='140' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='163' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Guidelines: recommended</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Each layer gets more specific and changes more often. Only the bottom layer, guidelines, is optional.

subtopics.example: A hospital's security standard requires screens to lock after 10 minutes of inactivity. The emergency department's local procedure sets 60 minutes, and its nursing director says local procedures are the department's own choice. The IS auditor reports a finding, because a procedure must conform to the standard above it, and recommends aligning the procedure or seeking an approved exception. Management decides which.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Policies, standards and procedures are mandatory; guidelines are advisory. Authority flows down: top management approves policy, each lower document has an owner and must conform to the one above, and technical specifics sit in standards so the policy stays short and stable.

exam_traps.trap: Developers skipped a checklist suggested in the secure-coding guideline, so the IS auditor reports a finding.
exam_traps.why: Guidelines are advisory. If the mandatory standard is still met, there is no compliance finding, though the auditor may note an improvement opportunity.

exam_traps.trap: A good security policy lists password lengths, algorithms and firewall port numbers.
exam_traps.why: Those details change often and belong in standards the policy refers to. Putting them in the policy forces frequent re-approval at the top and dates it quickly.

key_terms.definition: A lower document meeting or going beyond the requirements of the documents above it.
How work is actually done day to day; auditors compare it with what the documents require.
A standard listing the approved minimum settings for a type of system, such as a server build.

subtopics.memory_aid: Why, What exactly, How, Hint: Policy, Standard, Procedure, Guideline.

subtopics.name: Developing and Approving Policy
subtopics.definition: Policy development is how an organization drafts, consults on and approves its policies, either top-down from business objectives or bottom-up from risks and operations.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A policy without top-level approval lacks authority, and one written without the people who must apply it gets bypassed. Either way, staff do not follow it in practice.
how_it_works: Top-down policies start from enterprise objectives and strategy, so they stay aligned with what the business needs.
Bottom-up policies grow from risk assessments and operating practice; they are practical but may lock in local habits.
Drafts are reviewed by the functions that must apply them, such as human resources, legal and business units.
Top management or the board approves policies, which gives them authority across the enterprise.
A group sets one policy baseline, and subsidiaries add approved local addenda where local law differs.

rows.label: Starting point
cells: Business objectives and strategy
Risk assessments and current operations

rows.label: Strength
cells: Aligned with enterprise goals
Practical and quick to apply

rows.label: Main risk
cells: Hard to apply if users were not consulted
May lock in local habits and miss enterprise goals

subtopics.example: A city government's IT security manager drafts a remote-work policy alone, adapts a template from another city, and signs it into force. Department heads first hear of it by email. The IS auditor reports that the policy lacks top-level authority and was written without the departments that must apply it, and recommends consultation followed by approval from the city manager's executive team.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Policies get their authority from top management or the board, and their workability from consulting the people who must follow them. Approval by a functional head, such as the chief information security officer (CISO) or an IT manager, gives neither enterprise authority nor business alignment.

exam_traps.trap: The chief information security officer wrote and approved the security policy, so it is properly authorized.
exam_traps.why: A functional head cannot give a policy enterprise-wide authority or confirm business alignment. Policies need approval from top management or the board.

exam_traps.trap: Each subsidiary should write its own full policy set to respect local law.
exam_traps.why: Separate sets fragment control and drift apart. A group baseline with approved local addenda handles legal differences while keeping one framework.

key_terms.definition: The senior role accountable for a policy's content, review and communication.
An approved supplement that adapts a group policy to one country's law without replacing it.
Asking the functions affected by a policy for input before approval, so its rules are workable.

subtopics.name: Policy Maintenance, Exceptions and Compliance
subtopics.definition: Policy maintenance keeps policies, standards and procedures current and enforced through scheduled reviews, version control, an exception process and tests of real practice.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A policy that is never reviewed drifts away from reality, and staff following old versions break rules without knowing it. Uncontrolled exceptions quietly become the real policy.
how_it_works: Policies are reviewed at planned intervals and whenever something significant changes, such as a new law, major incident or reorganization.
One authoritative, version-controlled source holds the current documents, and old versions are withdrawn.
Each procedure has a named owner who keeps it accurate and reviews it on a schedule.
Exceptions need risk-owner approval, an expiry date, an entry in a register and periodic review.
Proof that a policy operates comes from observing or testing practice, not from documents or signed acknowledgments.
subtopics.example: At a construction firm, site offices print their own copies of the mobile-device policy, and two sites still follow a version withdrawn last year. Site managers also let crews skip device encryption for now, with no record or end date. The IS auditor reports both issues and recommends one controlled policy portal, plus an exception register with approval at the right level, expiry dates and periodic review.
subtopics.isaca_rule: An exception is accepted risk, so the risk owner approves it at the level the risk requires, with an expiry date and tracking. Reviews run on a schedule and after significant change. Evidence that a policy works comes from testing what people actually do.

exam_traps.trap: Signed staff acknowledgments prove the clean-desk policy is operating.
exam_traps.why: Acknowledgments show awareness only. Unannounced spot checks, or other observation of actual practice, show whether the policy operates.

exam_traps.trap: A fixed annual review cycle is enough on its own.
exam_traps.why: Fixed schedules miss sudden change. Reviews must also be triggered by events such as new regulation, major incidents or new technology.

key_terms.definition: Approved, time-limited permission to depart from a policy, recorded as accepted risk.
Managing document versions so one current, approved copy exists and old copies are withdrawn.
An event, such as a new law or major incident, that requires a review before the scheduled date.
A user's signed or recorded statement that they received and read a policy.

topics.overview: Enterprise architecture (EA) is the master plan for how an organization's processes, data, applications and technology fit together and should change. It keeps individual projects from building disconnected, duplicate or unsupported systems, and it gives IS auditors a map of where controls belong.
can_do: Explain why EA exists and name its four layers
Tell the Zachman Framework from TOGAF and say what each is used for
Put architecture planning in the right order: current state, target state, gap analysis, roadmap
Judge whether architecture governance works by testing projects, waivers and purchasing

subtopics.name: What Enterprise Architecture Is
subtopics.definition: Enterprise architecture (EA) is a structured description of how business processes, information, applications and technology fit together today and should evolve to support strategy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without EA, each project picks its own tools and data stores, creating duplicates, fragile integrations and support gaps. EA lets leaders trace every system back to a business need.
how_it_works: EA starts from the business layer: the capabilities and processes the strategy needs.
The data, application and technology layers are then designed to serve those business needs.
Architecture principles and standards guide project and purchase decisions across the enterprise.
Models and views are kept current, so leaders can see the impact of a change before approving it.

types.meaning: Capabilities, processes, roles and how the organization is structured.
What information exists, where it is stored and how it flows between systems.
The business systems, what each one does and how they interact.
The infrastructure, platforms and networks that host and connect everything.

subtopics.example: A national parks agency's architecture repository holds detailed network diagrams and an application list, but no model of the agency's services, such as permits and campsite bookings. When the finance committee asks why three booking systems are funded, IT cannot say which service each supports. The IS auditor reports the missing business layer and recommends capability and process models that the other layers trace to.
subtopics.isaca_rule: EA exists to align IT with business strategy. Cost savings, standardization and simpler support are benefits that follow from alignment, not its purpose. A sound EA starts with the business layer.

exam_traps.trap: The PRIMARY purpose of EA is to cut IT costs or standardize vendors.
exam_traps.why: Those are side benefits. The primary purpose is aligning processes, data, applications and technology with business strategy.

exam_traps.trap: Detailed documentation of servers and networks is a complete EA.
exam_traps.why: Technology-only architecture cannot show why systems exist. Without the business layer, IT cannot be traced to business needs.

key_terms.definition: Something the business must be able to do, such as onboarding customers, whoever or whatever does it.
A lasting rule that guides design choices, such as reuse before buying and buying before building.
A picture of the architecture drawn for one audience's concerns, such as a data-flow view for auditors.

subtopics.name: Enterprise Architecture Frameworks: Zachman and TOGAF
subtopics.definition: An enterprise architecture (EA) framework is a published scheme or method that tells architects what to describe and how to develop the architecture consistently.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks give architects a common language and a repeatable approach, so different teams produce comparable models. IS auditors use them as criteria for judging completeness and process.
how_it_works: The Zachman Framework is a grid that sorts architecture descriptions by six questions (what, how, where, who, when, why) and six audience perspectives.
Zachman tells you what to document, but not the steps for building the architecture.
TOGAF (The Open Group Architecture Framework) supplies a step-by-step cycle, the Architecture Development Method (ADM), plus guidance on content.
The ADM is a repeating cycle: set a vision, design the business, data, application and technology layers, choose solutions and plan the move, then govern the build and manage change.
Many organizations combine them, using a Zachman-style grid to check completeness and TOGAF to run the work, tailored to their size.

rows.label: What it is
cells: A classification grid (a taxonomy) for architecture descriptions
A method and content framework for developing architecture

rows.label: Structure
cells: Six questions across six stakeholder perspectives
Development method phases around central requirements management

rows.label: Best for
cells: Checking that nothing important is left undescribed
Running architecture work from vision to governance

rows.label: Limit
cells: No process for creating or governing the architecture
Heavy if adopted whole; needs tailoring

subtopics.example: A university's architecture team has hundreds of diagrams but no agreed way to produce or update them. The chief information officer asks whether adopting TOGAF in full will fix this. The IS auditor recommends tailoring the TOGAF development cycle to the team's size, using a Zachman-style grid to spot missing views, and tying both to the project approval process.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A framework is a means to aligned architecture, not proof of it. Tailor it to the organization and judge EA by whether decisions follow it. Zachman classifies what to describe; TOGAF guides how to develop and govern it.

exam_traps.trap: Zachman gives a step-by-step method for building an architecture.
exam_traps.why: Zachman is a classification grid that organizes descriptions. A development method, such as the TOGAF ADM, is needed to produce and govern them.

exam_traps.trap: Adopting a recognized framework proves the EA program is effective.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks shape the work but do not prove outcomes. Effectiveness shows when projects conform to standards and deviations are tracked.

key_terms.definition: TOGAF's repeatable cycle of phases for creating, moving to and governing an enterprise architecture.
One audience's view of the enterprise, such as owner, designer or builder; these form Zachman's rows.
A scheme that sorts things into defined categories; Zachman is a taxonomy for architecture descriptions, not a method.

subtopics.memory_aid: Zachman is the filing cabinet; TOGAF is the recipe.

subtopics.name: Current State, Target State and the Roadmap
subtopics.definition: Architecture planning documents the current state, defines the target state, analyzes the gaps between them and sequences the work into a transition roadmap.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a baseline, nobody can measure the gaps or the migration effort. Without a roadmap, an approved target stays a drawing while projects launch ad hoc.
how_it_works: Document the current architecture first, including systems, data flows, interfaces and known pain points.
Define the target architecture from the business capabilities the strategy requires.
Compare the two to list what must be added, changed or retired.
Sequence the work into transition projects, with dependencies, costs and interim states.
Use the roadmap to approve, reject or reorder projects, and update it as strategy changes.
subtopics.example: A telecom operator's architects finished a target design for billing eighteen months ago. Since then, product teams have started five billing changes, none planned against it, and nobody has documented how today's four billing platforms connect. The IS auditor recommends documenting the current state, running a gap analysis, and sequencing transition projects into a roadmap that the project approval board uses.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Know where you are before planning the move. A target architecture changes nothing until a gap analysis and sequenced roadmap guide which projects are approved. When rationalizing systems, business capabilities decide, and cost is one factor.

exam_traps.trap: Design the target architecture and launch migration projects immediately.
exam_traps.why: Without a documented baseline, the gaps, effort and risk cannot be measured. Document the current state first.

exam_traps.trap: After a merger, keep the cheapest of the overlapping systems.
exam_traps.why: Cost is one input. The right choice maps required business capabilities to each platform, then weighs cost, risk and migration effort.

key_terms.definition: The documented current state of processes, data, applications and technology; also called the as-is state.
The desired future state that supports the business strategy; also called the to-be state.
A structured comparison of baseline and target that lists what must be added, changed or removed.
A sequenced plan of projects and interim states that moves the enterprise from baseline to target.

subtopics.name: Governing and Auditing Architecture
subtopics.definition: Architecture governance makes projects and purchases follow enterprise architecture (EA) standards, through a review board, approved time-bound waivers and regular updates to the standards.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Architecture matters only if decisions follow it. Bypassed reviews leave fragmented, unsupported technology that raises integration, support and security risk for years.
how_it_works: An architecture review board (ARB) checks project designs and technology purchases against the standards.
Architecture review is built into procurement, so business units cannot buy technology around it.
Approved deviations are logged as waivers with an owner, a remediation plan and a sunset date.
A growing waiver rate signals outdated standards, which should be reviewed rather than routinely waived.
IS auditors use EA data-flow and interface views to find control points where data enters, moves and changes.
subtopics.example: An IS auditor at a regional health insurer finds 45 open architecture waivers with no owner or end date, and half cite the same database standard written before the move to cloud. Marketing also signs software subscriptions on corporate cards. The auditor recommends reviewing that standard, adding owners and sunset dates to waivers, and requiring architecture review before any technology purchase is approved.
subtopics.isaca_rule: EA effectiveness shows in projects that conform to standards and in tracked, time-bound waivers, not in attractive models or executive endorsement. Many waivers point to stale standards; bypassed reviews point to weak governance.

exam_traps.trap: Business units buying SaaS tools directly is acceptable when it saves time.
exam_traps.why: Bypassing architecture review creates duplicate data stores, unmanaged integrations and long-term support and security risk. Review belongs inside procurement.

exam_traps.trap: Approved waivers can stay open indefinitely.
exam_traps.why: A waiver is technical debt. Without an owner, a remediation plan and a sunset date, deviations pile up and the architecture loses meaning.

key_terms.definition: An approved, time-bound deviation from an architecture standard, tracked with an owner and a remediation date.
The future cost of shortcuts or outdated technology that must eventually be fixed or replaced.
A place in a process or data flow where a control can check, block or record what passes.

topics.overview: Enterprise risk management (ERM) is how the whole organization decides which risks to take, which to reduce and who answers for each. IT risk is managed against the risk appetite the board sets, through a continuous cycle of identifying, assessing, responding and monitoring. The same discipline applies when the organization buys another company.
can_do: Tell risk appetite, tolerance and capacity apart, and know who may accept a risk
Choose a qualitative, semi-quantitative or quantitative method and calculate annualized loss expectancy
Select the right risk response for a scenario
Judge a risk program's maturity by whether risk information changes decisions

subtopics.name: Building a Risk Management Program
subtopics.definition: A risk management program is the continuous cycle of identifying, assessing, responding to and monitoring risk, run against a board-approved risk appetite with named owners.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One-off risk exercises age quickly. A living program lets leaders see emerging risks in time and spend on the ones that matter.
how_it_works: A board-approved risk policy sets the appetite, roles and accountability for the program.
Identification starts from critical business processes and their assets, then the threats and vulnerabilities facing each; risks are rated for likelihood and impact before and after controls.
Each risk has a named owner who chooses a response and tracks it to completion.
The register records ratings, owners, responses, status and an audit trail of decisions.
Monitoring repeats the cycle; a serious new risk is registered and treated when it appears, not at the next annual review.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 354 88' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Risk management program: identify, assess, respond, monitor, then repeat'><rect x='4' y='8' width='70' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='39' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Identify</text><line x1='76' y1='28' x2='87' y2='28' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M87,24 L94,28 L87,32 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='96' y='8' width='70' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='131' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Assess</text><line x1='168' y1='28' x2='179' y2='28' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M179,24 L186,28 L179,32 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='188' y='8' width='70' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='223' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Respond</text><line x1='260' y1='28' x2='271' y2='28' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M271,24 L278,28 L271,32 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='280' y='8' width='70' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='315' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Monitor</text><path d='M315,48 L315,64 L39,64 L39,55' fill='none' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M35,55 L39,48 L43,55 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><text x='177' y='80' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>repeat</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The core cycle: find the risk, size it, decide what to do, then keep watching. The loop repeats because risk keeps moving.

subtopics.example: A port authority paid consultants to build an IT risk register that rates 85 risks. A year later, no risk has a treatment plan, no manager updates the register, and the board approved a crane-control system without consulting it. The IS auditor reports that the register gives false assurance and recommends an internal program owner and a response for each risk.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Risk management adds value only when risks are treated and monitored and risk information shapes business decisions. Expertise can be bought in; accountability for the program cannot be outsourced.

exam_traps.trap: A full register of rated risks shows a mature program.
exam_traps.why: Ratings without responses or monitoring give false assurance. Maturity shows when risk results visibly shape investment and project decisions.

exam_traps.trap: A serious new risk can wait for the next annual assessment.
exam_traps.why: Risk management is continuous. A high-impact emerging risk is registered, owned and treated as soon as it is known.

key_terms.definition: The working record of each risk with its owner, rating, response, status and decision history.
Risk before any controls or other responses are applied.
The risk left after responses; it must fit within appetite, or be treated further unless the board approves an exception.
The manager accountable for a risk and for deciding and tracking its response.
The international standard giving principles and a process for managing any risk; it is guidance and is not certifiable.

subtopics.name: Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Ownership
subtopics.definition: Risk appetite is the board's overall stance on how much risk to take for the enterprise's objectives; tolerances set measurable limits within it, below risk capacity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without agreed limits, each manager decides alone what risk is acceptable. Clear limits tell staff when to proceed and when to escalate.
how_it_works: The board states appetite broadly, linked to strategy, such as moderate risk to grow online sales.
Senior management or the board sets tolerances within appetite: measurable limits for specific risks, such as maximum yearly outage hours.
Risk capacity is the most loss the organization can absorb; appetite must sit well below it.
Risk within appetite can be accepted by the risk owner or senior management under delegated authority; tolerance breaches go to senior management.
Risk above appetite must be treated until it fits; senior management cannot accept it alone, and keeping it needs a board-approved exception.

rows.label: What it is
cells: The broad stance on how much risk to take
The allowed deviation for one specific risk
The most loss the organization can survive

rows.label: Set by
cells: The board
Senior management or the board, within the appetite
Finances and obligations; a fact, not a choice

rows.label: Example
cells: We accept moderate IT risk to grow online sales
No more than four hours of unplanned outage a year
Losses beyond the capital reserve would threaten survival

rows.label: Form
cells: Qualitative statement
Measurable limit
Financial ceiling

rows.label: When exceeded
cells: Treat the risk; only the board can approve an exception
Escalate to senior management to decide
Survival is at stake; the board acts at once

subtopics.example: A hospital group's board has set a low appetite for patient-data exposure. The head of radiology wants to keep an unvetted overseas scan-reading service and offers to sign off the risk. The IS auditor reports that the exposure exceeds appetite and the department head lacks authority, and recommends escalation to senior management for treatment.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Authority to accept rises with the risk: owners accept within tolerance, senior management decides tolerance breaches within appetite, and risk above appetite is treated until it fits or the board approves an exception. The IS auditor never accepts risk.

exam_traps.trap: A four-hour yearly outage limit is the board's risk appetite.
exam_traps.why: A measurable limit for one specific risk is a tolerance. Appetite is the broad statement of how much risk to take.

exam_traps.trap: The CIO, or senior management alone, can sign off risk above appetite to keep a project moving.
exam_traps.why: Above appetite, the risk must be treated until it fits. Only the board, which set the appetite, can approve keeping the excess as an exception.

key_terms.definition: A documented decision, by someone with authority for that risk level, to keep a risk, with reasons and a review date.
Exposure from heavy dependence on one provider, location, technology or customer.
A documented board decision to keep a specific risk above appetite for a set time, with a plan to bring it within limits.

subtopics.name: Risk Analysis Methods
subtopics.definition: Risk analysis sizes each risk by likelihood and impact, using descriptive ratings (qualitative), calibrated scores (semi-quantitative) or money values (quantitative).
subtopics.why_it_matters: The method shapes how decision makers see risk. False precision from weak data misleads them as badly as vague labels do when solid data exists.
how_it_works: Qualitative analysis rates likelihood and impact with words such as high, medium and low; it is fast and suits sparse data.
Semi-quantitative analysis uses calibrated numeric scales with defined ranges, so loss data and expert judgment compare consistently.
Quantitative analysis estimates loss in money: single loss expectancy (SLE), annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) and annualized loss expectancy (ALE).
The Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR) model is a quantitative method: it estimates how often losses happen and how big they are as ranges, not single numbers.

rows.label: Output
cells: Ratings such as high, medium, low
Scores on calibrated scales
Money values, such as expected yearly loss

rows.label: Data needed
cells: Little; mostly expert judgment
Mixed: some data, some judgment
Reliable loss and frequency data

rows.label: Strength
cells: Fast and easy to understand
Consistent across mixed evidence
Supports cost-benefit decisions

rows.label: Weakness
cells: Subjective and hard to compare
Scores can look more precise than they are
Misleading when inputs are weak
