subtopics.example: A university's risk committee wants every IT risk priced in dollars, but loss history exists only for laptop theft. A $2,000 laptop loses 80% of its value per theft, so SLE is $1,600; about 25 thefts a year (ARO 25) give an ALE of $40,000. The IS auditor recommends money values only where data like this exists and calibrated scores elsewhere; management chooses the method.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the method that fits the available data and the decision it must support. Quantitative analysis helps only when its inputs are reliable; otherwise it gives false precision.

exam_traps.trap: Quantitative analysis is always the best method.
exam_traps.why: With sparse or unreliable data, money figures look precise but mislead. Qualitative or semi-quantitative methods serve better until good data exists.

exam_traps.trap: An analysis follows FAIR because it multiplies likelihood by impact on a 1-to-5 scale.
exam_traps.why: FAIR splits risk into how often losses happen (loss event frequency) and how big they are (loss magnitude), estimated as ranges. A simple 1-to-5 score is not FAIR.

key_terms.definition: The percentage of an asset's value lost in one occurrence of a threat.
The expected loss from one occurrence: asset value times exposure factor.
How many times a year the event is expected to happen.
The expected yearly loss: SLE times ARO.

subtopics.memory_aid: ALE = SLE x ARO: one loss times how often per year equals the yearly loss.

subtopics.name: Choosing a Risk Response
subtopics.definition: Risk response, also called risk treatment, is management's choice to accept, mitigate (reduce), transfer (share) or avoid a risk so the residual risk fits within risk appetite.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The wrong response wastes money or leaves the enterprise exposed. A clear, owned choice for each significant risk is what turns analysis into protection.
how_it_works: Accept the risk when it is within appetite, with the owner's decision recorded; risk above appetite needs another response or a board-approved exception.
Mitigate (reduce) it by adding or improving controls that lower likelihood or impact.
Transfer (share) financial impact through insurance or contracts; accountability and reputational harm stay with the organization.
Avoid it by stopping or redesigning the activity when no other response brings the risk within appetite.
Under budget limits, fund mandatory obligations first, rank the rest by expected loss reduced per dollar, and escalate unfunded risk above tolerance to senior management.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 344 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The four risk responses: accept, avoid, transfer, mitigate'><rect x='8' y='8' width='160' height='48' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='88' y='29' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Accept</text><text x='88' y='47' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Within appetite</text><rect x='176' y='8' width='160' height='48' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='256' y='29' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Avoid</text><text x='256' y='47' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Stop the activity</text><rect x='8' y='64' width='160' height='48' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='88' y='85' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Transfer</text><text x='88' y='103' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Insure or contract</text><rect x='176' y='64' width='160' height='48' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='256' y='85' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Mitigate</text><text x='256' y='103' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Add controls</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The four responses. Mitigate is also called reduce. Whatever is left after the choice is residual risk.

subtopics.example: A water utility plans to let a contractor run pumping stations remotely through a tool that supports neither multifactor authentication nor logging. No available control brings the risk within the board's appetite, and the operations director proposes insurance and accepting the rest. The IS auditor recommends presenting avoidance options to senior management, because insurance would not prevent the harm.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the response to the risk. When no control or insurance brings a risk within appetite, avoid it rather than accept it. Transfer moves money, not accountability. Under budget limits, treat mandatory obligations first and escalate unfunded risk above tolerance for a documented senior management decision.

exam_traps.trap: Outsourcing or insuring a risk transfers it completely.
exam_traps.why: Insurance and contracts shift some financial impact. The organization keeps accountability, regulatory duties and the damage to its reputation.

exam_traps.trap: Accept a high-likelihood, high-impact risk because the fix is expensive.
exam_traps.why: Acceptance suits risks within appetite. Mitigate a severe risk when a fix exists; when no control or insurance brings it within appetite, avoid it. Only the board could approve keeping it as an exception.

key_terms.definition: The documented actions, owner, budget and deadline for carrying out a chosen risk response.
A policy covering some financial losses from cyber incidents; its limits should match the quantified exposure.
Comparing a control's full cost with the expected loss it prevents, to decide whether to fund it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Four Ts: tolerate (accept), treat (mitigate), transfer, terminate (avoid).

subtopics.name: IT Due Diligence in Mergers and Acquisitions
subtopics.definition: IT due diligence is a risk-based review of an acquisition target's systems, security, data and contracts before a deal, so leaders can price, condition or stop it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Buying a company also buys its breaches, unsupported systems, license gaps and regulatory problems. Issues missed before closing become the buyer's cost and liability.
how_it_works: Agree the review scope and deal-breaker criteria with the deal sponsor before work starts.
Focus depth on critical and regulated systems, known incidents and their root causes, and key-person and vendor dependencies.
Check software licenses, privacy compliance, open audit findings and contracts that may end when ownership changes.
Use the seller's data room and advisers' reports as inputs, but test key claims, because advisers serve the deal.
Feed findings into the price, deal conditions and the integration plan that enterprise change management will carry out.

rows.label: Main question
cells: What IT risk are we buying, and is it a deal-breaker?
How do we combine systems, people and controls safely?

rows.label: Typical output
cells: Findings that shape price, conditions or a no-go decision
A phased integration plan with go/no-go gates

rows.label: Leverage
cells: High: terms can still change
Low: problems are now the buyer's

subtopics.example: A hotel group has four weeks to review a boutique booking-platform company it wants to buy. The seller's data room is thin, and the platform runs on an operating system that lost vendor support last year. The IS auditor recommends concentrating on the booking platform, payment-card compliance and license transfers, and agreeing deal-breaker criteria with the board's deal committee before it votes.
subtopics.isaca_rule: IT due diligence is risk-based: go deep where critical systems, regulated data and known incidents sit, agree deal-breakers up front, and verify rather than rely on the seller's or adviser's claims. The buyer stays accountable for the IT risk it acquires.

exam_traps.trap: Rely on the transaction adviser's IT due diligence report.
exam_traps.why: Advisers work for the deal and may have a narrow scope. The buyer stays accountable, so it tests critical claims itself or through independent experts.

exam_traps.trap: Review every system at the same depth, or leave the deep review until after closing.
exam_traps.why: Time is short, and issues found after closing can no longer change the price or terms. Depth goes where risk is highest.

key_terms.definition: Conditions agreed before the review that, if found, would stop the deal or force new terms.
A controlled repository where the seller shares documents for buyers to review.
A contract term that lets the other party end or renegotiate the contract when the company is sold.

topics.overview: Privacy is the fair and lawful use of information about people. Security protects the data; privacy decides whether it should be collected and used at all, for what purpose and for how long. This topic covers how a privacy program is built, documented, designed into systems and run for individual rights and cross-border transfers.
can_do: Tell privacy from security and name the core privacy principles
Match a privacy policy, privacy notice, record of processing and impact assessment to its purpose
Tell privacy by design from privacy by default in a scenario
Judge how a rights request or a cross-border transfer should be handled and evidenced

subtopics.name: Foundations of a Privacy Program
subtopics.definition: A privacy program is the governance, policies, roles and processes that make an organization's use of personal data lawful, fair, limited to stated purposes and accountable.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Mishandled personal data brings regulator fines, lawsuits and lost trust. Strong security does not help if the data should never have been collected or used that way.
how_it_works: An accountable privacy lead, such as a chief privacy officer, owns the program with board support.
An inventory records what personal data exists, why it is processed and on what lawful basis.
Core principles guide every use: lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, security and accountability.
Named privacy stewards in each business unit build privacy steps into normal processes.
Organizations under many privacy laws set one global baseline, plus a mapped layer for local differences; no single law, even GDPR, covers every local duty.

rows.label: Core question
cells: Should we collect and use this data, and how?
Is the data protected from unauthorized access, change and loss?

rows.label: Protects
cells: The rights and expectations of individuals
The confidentiality, integrity and availability of information

rows.label: Typical controls
cells: Purpose limits, consent records, retention limits
Encryption, access control, monitoring

rows.label: Can fail while the other succeeds?
cells: Yes: well-secured data can still be used unlawfully
Yes: lawful processing can still suffer a breach

subtopics.example: A fitness-app company with users in Brazil and California plans to start its privacy program by buying a data-masking tool. Nobody owns privacy, and no one can say what personal data the app collects or on what lawful basis. The IS auditor recommends first naming an accountable privacy lead and building an inventory of personal data, purposes and lawful bases. The chief executive approves.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Privacy starts with accountable governance and knowing what personal data you hold, why and on what lawful basis. Security controls support privacy, but they cannot make unlawful processing lawful.

exam_traps.trap: Encrypting all personal data makes the processing compliant.
exam_traps.why: Encryption protects data but does not create a lawful basis, limit purpose or honor rights. Fully encrypted processing can still be unlawful.

exam_traps.trap: Customers bought from us, so we can use their purchase history for personalized marketing.
exam_traps.why: The sale gives a lawful basis to deliver the order, not to reuse the data for marketing. Marketing usually needs its own basis, such as consent or a documented legitimate interest.

key_terms.definition: The legal ground for processing personal data, such as consent, contract, legal obligation or legitimate interests.
Using personal data only for the specific purposes stated when it was collected.
Collecting and keeping only the personal data needed for the stated purpose.
A named person in a business unit who builds privacy tasks into that unit's normal work.

subtopics.name: Privacy Documentation and Impact Assessments
subtopics.definition: Privacy documentation is the set of records showing how personal data is handled: the internal policy, the external notice, processing records and impact assessments.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Regulators and individuals judge an organization by what it can show. Missing records, or an assessment done too late, turn good intentions into findings.
how_it_works: The internal privacy policy tells staff how the organization must handle personal data.
The external privacy notice tells individuals what is collected, why, who receives it and what rights they have.
The record of processing activities (RoPA) lists purposes, data categories, recipients, transfers, retention and safeguards, ready for regulators.

A privacy impact assessment (PIA), called a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), comes before new or changed processing; high-risk uses require one.
The PIA checks that processing is necessary and proportionate (really needed and no more intrusive than required), weighs risks to individuals, and shapes the design.

rows.label: Audience
cells: Individuals whose data is used
Regulators and internal governance
Decision makers, and the regulator if high risk remains

rows.label: Purpose
cells: Tell people what happens to their data
Show all processing in one register
Assess and reduce the risks of one planned activity

rows.label: When
cells: At collection, and kept current
Ongoing, updated as processing changes
Before new or high-risk processing starts

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 104' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A privacy policy tells staff how to handle data; a privacy notice tells individuals what is collected and why'><rect x='10' y='10' width='152' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='86' y='35' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Privacy policy</text><rect x='178' y='10' width='152' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='254' y='35' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Privacy notice</text><text x='86' y='74' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>For staff:</text><text x='86' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>how to handle data</text><text x='254' y='74' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>For individuals:</text><text x='254' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>what is collected, why</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Two documents with two audiences: the policy guides the organization's own people, the notice informs the individuals whose data is used.

subtopics.example: A European city transit agency plans to add voice recording and emotion analysis to its customer-service chatbot next quarter. The vendor contract is signed, but no privacy assessment exists. The IS auditor recommends a privacy impact assessment, in its GDPR form as a DPIA, before any processing starts, and reports that launch should wait for the result. Management decides on timing.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A PIA (a DPIA under the GDPR) comes before new or high-risk processing, while its findings can still change the design. The RoPA is the main evidence of what an organization processes. Policies speak to staff; notices speak to individuals.

exam_traps.trap: Run the PIA after go-live, once the system is stable.
exam_traps.why: By then design choices are fixed and individuals may already be harmed. The assessment must shape the decision, so it comes first.

exam_traps.trap: The privacy notice shows a regulator what processing takes place.
exam_traps.why: A notice is a public summary for individuals. The record of processing activities is the detailed register that regulators request.

key_terms.definition: The organization that decides why and how personal data is processed, and carries primary accountability.
An organization that processes personal data on the controller's instructions, such as a payroll provider.
An independent role, required in some cases, that advises on and monitors privacy compliance.

subtopics.name: Privacy by Design and by Default
subtopics.definition: Privacy by design builds privacy requirements into systems from the start; privacy by default sets them to use only the personal data needed unless users choose more.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Privacy added at the end is costly and often impossible to retrofit. Building it in early prevents harm and avoids redesign after launch.
how_it_works: Privacy requirements are written alongside business requirements at the start of the system development life cycle (SDLC).
Each SDLC stage has privacy checks and gate criteria, such as design reviews and testing with masked data.
Techniques such as pseudonymization, aggregation and short retention reduce the personal data exposed.
Out-of-the-box settings collect, share and keep only what the stated purpose needs.
More intrusive features are switched on deliberately, for a defined purpose, never by default.

rows.label: Focus
cells: How the system is built
How the system is set up when delivered

rows.label: When it applies
cells: Every life-cycle stage, from requirements to retirement
At configuration and with each new feature

rows.label: Example
cells: Privacy requirements and gates in every development phase
Analytics show team averages unless an individual view is enabled for a purpose

subtopics.example: A smart-thermostat maker is adding a feature that shares room-by-room occupancy data with utility partners for energy rebates. The product team wants sharing switched on for every new customer. The IS auditor recommends that sharing stay off until a customer opts in for a stated purpose, that partners receive only aggregated data, and that privacy checks gate each development stage. The product owner adopts the design.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Build privacy in from requirements onward, with checks at each stage; do not inspect it in at the end. Defaults must favor the individual: collect and share the least, and make anything more a deliberate choice.

exam_traps.trap: Privacy by default means privacy requirements in every development phase.
exam_traps.why: That is privacy by design. By default is about the out-of-the-box settings: the least data, unless more is deliberately enabled.

exam_traps.trap: A privacy review just before launch is enough.
exam_traps.why: Late reviews find problems when the design is fixed. Privacy by design needs checks from requirements through testing.

key_terms.definition: Replacing direct identifiers with codes, so data cannot be linked to a person without separately protected information.
A setting that stays off until the user actively chooses to turn it on.
Combining records into group totals or averages, so individuals are not shown.

subtopics.name: Individual Rights and Cross-Border Transfers
subtopics.definition: Data subject rights let people see, correct, erase or move their personal data; transborder data flow rules control when that data may leave a country.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Mishandled requests and unlawful transfers are highly visible privacy failures. Releasing data to an impostor turns a rights request into a breach.
how_it_works: Log each request, verify the requester's identity, and answer within the legal deadline.
When two laws apply, meet both sets of duties and the shorter deadline, and document the basis.
Erasure has limits: data a law requires keeping is retained, restricted, and erased when the duty ends.
Transfers out of the European Union (EU) need a valid mechanism, such as an adequacy decision (including EU-US Data Privacy Framework for certified US firms) or standard contractual clauses (SCCs).
With SCCs, the organization sending the data documents a transfer impact assessment of the destination country's laws.
IS auditors test sampled real data flows against the documented mechanisms, not just the paperwork.

types.meaning: Get a copy of one's personal data and learn how it is used.
Have inaccurate data corrected.
Have data deleted when no legal reason to keep it remains.
Limit processing, for example while a dispute is settled.
Receive data in a reusable format to move it to another provider.
Object to processing, such as direct marketing.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 174' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Handling a data subject request: log it, verify the requester identity, respond by the legal deadline'><rect x='20' y='8' width='300' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='32' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Log the request</text><line x1='170' y1='48' x2='170' y2='59' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M166,59 L170,66 L174,59 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='20' y='68' width='300' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Verify identity</text><line x1='170' y1='108' x2='170' y2='119' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M166,119 L170,126 L174,119 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='20' y='128' width='300' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='152' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Respond by the deadline</text></svg>
illustration.caption: A rights request in three steps: log it, confirm the requester's identity, and answer within the legal time limit.

subtopics.example: A German car-rental company sends customer records to a call center in India under SCCs. India has no EU adequacy decision, and nobody has assessed whether local law lets authorities reach the data. The IS auditor traces sampled transfers and reports the missing transfer impact assessment (TIA) as a gap for the privacy officer to fix.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Verify identity before releasing personal data, meet every applicable law's duties, and respect legal retention limits on erasure. For transfers, the mechanism must be valid and proven by tracing actual data flows.

exam_traps.trap: Release the data quickly; the deadline matters more than identity checks.
exam_traps.why: Sending personal data to the wrong person is a breach. Verification comes first, scaled to the data's sensitivity, within the deadline.

exam_traps.trap: Erase everything when a customer asks for erasure.
exam_traps.why: Records a law requires keeping, such as accounting data, are retained and restricted. Only the rest is erased.

key_terms.definition: A European Commission ruling that a country or certified scheme protects personal data adequately, allowing free transfer.
Pre-approved contract terms that bind a data importer to protect transferred personal data.
A documented review of whether the destination's laws undermine the safeguards on transferred data.
A requirement that data be stored and processed within a named country or region.

topics.overview: Data governance answers who is accountable for each kind of data, where it is, how sensitive it is and how long it is kept. Classification is the foundation: it tells every other control, from access to data loss prevention to disposal, how strongly to protect what. The same discipline makes published sustainability figures reliable.
can_do: Identify the data owner, custodian, steward and user in a scenario
Recommend how to keep a data inventory current and catch drift
Judge whether a classification scheme has workable levels and handling rules
Evaluate whether retention is set per data category without keeping personal data too long

subtopics.name: Data Ownership and Custodianship
subtopics.definition: Data ownership makes a senior business role accountable for a data set's classification, access and use; custodians and stewards act under the owner's decisions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When no one is accountable for data, access creeps, quality decays and nobody signs off on risk. Clear decision rights let governance hold a named person to account.
how_it_works: A data governance committee sets data policies, approves owners and settles disputes between business units.
Owners come from the business that relies on the data, such as the head of claims for claim files.
Ownership follows business accountability, not storage location, so moving data to a vendor or the cloud does not move it.
Providers that store the data act as custodians under contract, following the owner's rules.
Stewards maintain quality, definitions and lineage, so reports built on the data can be trusted.

rows.label: Typical role
cells: Senior business manager
IT operations or a service provider
Business data specialist
Any authorized staff member

rows.label: Main duty
cells: Accountable for classification, access approval and acceptable use
Storing and protecting data as the owner directs
Maintaining quality, definitions and inventory entries
Using data only for approved work

rows.label: Example decision
cells: Who may view loan applications
How backups of loan files are run
What counts as an active customer
Following handling rules when sharing a report

subtopics.example: A school district shifts student records to a hosted learning service. The IT director says the vendor now owns the records, while principals say IT does. The IS auditor recommends naming the assistant superintendent for student services as owner, with the vendor acting as custodian under contract and IT as internal custodian. The superintendent's cabinet approves.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Ownership follows business accountability. Owners decide classification and access; custodians carry out their decisions. Outsourcing storage creates a custodian, never a new owner, and accountability stays inside the enterprise.

exam_traps.trap: The cloud provider owns the data because it stores it.
exam_traps.why: Holding data is custody. The business owner keeps accountability, and the provider acts under the contract and the owner's rules.

exam_traps.trap: IT should own all data because it runs the systems.
exam_traps.why: IT lacks the business context to judge sensitivity and who needs access. It is a custodian; a business manager is the owner.

key_terms.definition: The decision rights, policies and accountability that control how data is defined, used, protected and kept.
A cross-functional body that sets data policy, appoints owners and resolves data disputes.
A record of where data came from and how it changed on its way into a report.

subtopics.name: Data Inventory
subtopics.definition: A data inventory is a maintained list of an organization's data assets, recording where each lives, what it contains, who owns it and how sensitive it is.
subtopics.why_it_matters: You cannot protect, classify or delete data you do not know you have. Privacy rights, breach response and retention all depend on an accurate inventory.
how_it_works: Stewards record each new data asset as part of normal change and project processes.
Entries capture location, owner, content categories, classification, retention period and data flows.
Automated discovery scans search systems for data, including personal data in unexpected places.
Scan results are reconciled to the inventory on a schedule, and stewards follow up every difference.
The same discipline covers interfaces: an inventory of application programming interfaces (APIs) reveals undocumented shadow APIs.
subtopics.example: A sports-betting operator built its data inventory during a licensing review three years ago. Since then, marketing has added a dozen analytics tools, and a discovery scan finds customer identity documents in two file shares the inventory does not list. The IS auditor reports the gaps to the data owners and recommends recording new data assets through change management, with scan results reconciled each quarter.
subtopics.isaca_rule: An inventory stays current only when updating it is part of normal change, and drift is caught by independent, recurring reconciliation against discovery results. A one-time project starts to decay at once.

exam_traps.trap: A thorough one-time inventory project is enough.
exam_traps.why: Data changes daily. Without capture in change processes and recurring reconciliation, the inventory is out of date when the next system goes live.

exam_traps.trap: System owners' self-reported lists prove the inventory is complete.
exam_traps.why: Self-reports miss what owners do not know about. Independent discovery scans reconciled to the inventory find hidden data.

key_terms.definition: Automated scanning of systems to find data stores and sensitive content, such as personal or card data.
A searchable inventory that adds business definitions, owners and lineage to each data asset.
The growing gap between what the inventory records and the data that actually exists.
An application programming interface that is in use but not documented or governed.

subtopics.name: Data Classification
subtopics.definition: Data classification groups data by the harm its disclosure, alteration or loss would cause, and attaches handling rules to each level.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without classification, controls are too weak for sensitive data or too costly for routine data. Every downstream control needs to know what deserves protection.
how_it_works: The data owner assigns each data set a level; IT and security do not classify business data on their own.
A few clear levels, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, work better than many fine ones.
Each level carries handling rules for access, encryption, sharing, labeling, retention and disposal.
Regulated categories, such as health or card data, are mapped onto the levels rather than run as separate schemes.
Data loss prevention (DLP) rules, access policies and retention all depend on the classification.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 184' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Data classification levels from public, least sensitive, up to restricted, most sensitive'><rect x='10' y='8' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='31' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Public: no harm if disclosed</text><rect x='10' y='52' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Internal use only</text><rect x='10' y='96' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='119' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Confidential</text><rect x='10' y='140' width='320' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='163' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Restricted: highest protection</text></svg>
illustration.caption: An example scheme. Labels and number of levels vary by organization; what matters is that each level carries its own handling rules.

subtopics.example: A law firm's partners want every client file marked Highly Confidential and handled the same way, down to printed office newsletters. Staff now ignore the label, and encryption slows routine work. The IS auditor reports that blanket labels weaken protection where it matters and recommends a few levels set by the data owners, each with its own handling rules. The managing partner approves the scheme.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Classification comes first: it drives proportionate protection, DLP rules and retention. The owner assigns the level by business impact. Labels that do not change handling add no protection.

exam_traps.trap: Deploy data loss prevention first and classify the data later.
exam_traps.why: DLP needs classification to tell sensitive data from routine data. Without it, rules either block normal work or miss what matters.

exam_traps.trap: More classification levels give finer protection.
exam_traps.why: Many levels confuse users and are applied inconsistently. A few levels, each tied to clear handling rules, work better.

key_terms.definition: The required controls for each classification level, such as who may access, how to send and how to destroy.
Marking data or documents with their classification, so people and tools apply the right handling.
Rating data as more sensitive than it is, which wastes money and teaches users to ignore labels.

subtopics.name: Retention and Disposal
subtopics.definition: A records retention schedule sets how long each category of data is kept, based on legal and business needs, and how it is securely destroyed afterward.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Keeping data too briefly breaks legal duties; keeping it too long adds breach exposure, storage cost and privacy violations. Both are compliance failures.
how_it_works: Each data category gets a retention period with a documented basis, such as tax law or a contract.
Where several laws apply, the period meets each law's minimum without keeping personal data longer than needed.
A legal hold suspends disposal of data linked to litigation or an investigation until counsel releases it.
When retention ends, data is destroyed by a method matched to its classification, and evidence is kept.
Retention rules cover every copy, including backups, archives and data held by vendors.

rows.label: What happens
cells: Data is destroyed before its legal or business period ends
Data is kept after its purpose and legal period have ended

rows.label: Typical cause
cells: Aggressive cleanup or short backup cycles
Fear of losing something, or no disposal process

rows.label: Consequence
cells: Fines, lost legal evidence, unanswerable audits
Bigger breaches, higher cost, privacy-law violations

subtopics.example: An online travel agency keeps every booking, chat transcript and call recording forever in case of disputes. Tax law requires seven years for invoices, while call recordings serve no purpose after 90 days. The IS auditor recommends a retention schedule by data category, each with a documented basis, legal holds that pause disposal, and verified deletion at expiry, including backups. The general counsel approves.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Set retention per data category with a documented basis. Meet each law's minimum, keep personal data no longer than needed, honor legal holds, and destroy data securely when the period ends, including copies held elsewhere.

exam_traps.trap: Keep everything forever to be safe.
exam_traps.why: Over-retention raises breach impact and storage cost, and it can break privacy laws that limit how long personal data is kept.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting files from the live system completes disposal.
exam_traps.why: Copies in backups, archives and vendor systems remain. Disposal covers every copy, using methods suited to the data's classification.

key_terms.definition: An instruction to preserve specified data for litigation or an investigation, overriding normal disposal.
Destroying data so it cannot be recovered, by overwriting, cryptographic erasure or physical destruction, with evidence kept.
The privacy principle that personal data is kept no longer than its purpose requires.

subtopics.name: ESG and Climate Disclosure Data
subtopics.definition: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) data governance applies ownership, quality controls and audit trails to published sustainability figures, such as data-center energy use and emissions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Climate and sustainability disclosures are now required in several jurisdictions and checked by assurance providers and investors. Figures pulled from IT systems without controls can be wrong, inconsistent and impossible to defend.
how_it_works: Each published metric, such as data-center electricity or cloud emissions, has a named data owner and a documented calculation method.
Source data comes from systems of record, such as meters, cloud provider reports and asset inventories, under change and access controls.
The same data-quality checks, reconciliations and audit trails used for financial reporting apply, so figures are ready for external assurance.
One controlled data set feeds every disclosure regime, with differences mapped, instead of separate filings built by hand.
The audit committee oversees disclosures, while the sustainability, IT and finance teams hold defined roles.
subtopics.example: A regional bank must report the emissions of its data centers and cloud services in its annual sustainability report. Analysts copy figures from utility bills and provider dashboards into spreadsheets, and last year's total was restated twice. The IS auditor recommends named owners, documented calculation methods and reconciliation controls like those over financial data, and reports the weakness to the audit committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat ESG figures drawn from IT like financial data: owned, defined once, controlled at the source and traceable, so they can be assured. Management is responsible for the disclosures under board oversight; the IS auditor evaluates the controls and reports gaps.

exam_traps.trap: Sustainability disclosures belong to the sustainability team, so IT data controls are not needed.
exam_traps.why: Many key figures come from IT systems. Without owners, source controls and audit trails, the disclosed numbers cannot be relied on or assured.

exam_traps.trap: Hire consultants to collect the IT figures and prepare each filing.
exam_traps.why: Consultants can help, but management stays accountable for disclosures, and repeatable internal controls are needed every reporting period.

key_terms.definition: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or cooling, such as the power an owned data center uses.
Other indirect emissions in the value chain, including those from cloud services and purchased equipment.
A lower level of external assurance, common for sustainability reports, stating that nothing suggests a material misstatement.

topics.overview: IT runs on people, money, capacity and the organization's ability to change. This topic covers how those resources are hired, developed, funded, planned and steered so they serve strategy, and how they stay protected when people leave or plans change.
can_do: Recommend people controls that expose fraud and reduce key-person risk
Spot hiring and termination gaps, especially late removal of access
Judge IT investment by business value, using business cases, portfolios and cost allocation
Tell enterprise change management from IT change management

subtopics.name: Managing IT People
subtopics.definition: IT human resource management is how an organization hires, develops, deploys and keeps IT staff, so the right skills are available and people risks stay controlled.
subtopics.why_it_matters: People are IT's greatest asset and a source of risk. Skill gaps slow delivery, one-person dependencies stall operations, and unchecked insiders can hide fraud for years.
how_it_works: Controls follow the employee's journey: screening when joining, development and oversight while working, and prompt removal when leaving.
Role-based competency frameworks set the skills each job needs; staff are assessed, trained on gaps and reassessed.
Mandatory vacations and job rotation put someone else in the role, which can reveal concealed fraud or errors.
Cross-training and succession plans reduce dependence on a single expert.
Performance goals for IT staff link to business and IT objectives and are reviewed regularly.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 344 56' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='HR security controls across the employee lifecycle: joining, during employment, leaving'><rect x='4' y='8' width='74' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='41' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Joining</text><line x1='80' y1='28' x2='87' y2='28' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M87,24 L94,28 L87,32 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='96' y='8' width='150' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='171' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>During employment</text><line x1='248' y1='28' x2='255' y2='28' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M255,24 L262,28 L255,32 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='264' y='8' width='74' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='301' y='33' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Leaving</text></svg>
illustration.caption: People controls across the employee journey. The leaving stage is where access is most often left behind.

subtopics.example: At a commodity trading firm, the engineer who maintains the trade-settlement interfaces has not taken a week off in four years and keeps the configuration notes on a personal drive. The IS auditor rates this the highest people risk, recommends enforced leave with a trained substitute running the interfaces, and reports the finding to the heads of IT and human resources.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Mandatory leave, rotation and cross-training are detective and resilience controls, not perks. A privileged user who avoids them is a red flag. Competence comes from role-based skills assessment and reassessment, not from training hours alone.

exam_traps.trap: An expert who never takes vacation shows commitment, not risk.
exam_traps.why: Someone who must always be present may be hiding activity that a substitute would notice. It is also a key-person dependency.

exam_traps.trap: Measure training effectiveness by courses completed per employee.
exam_traps.why: Course counts show activity, not competence. Role-based skill-gap assessments with reassessment show whether skills actually improved.

key_terms.definition: Required consecutive leave during which another person performs the role, exposing irregularities.
Moving staff between roles from time to time, which spreads skills and can surface concealed fraud.
Reliance on one individual whose absence would stop a critical process.
A defined set of skills and levels required for each role, used to assess and develop staff.

subtopics.name: Hiring and Termination Controls
subtopics.definition: Hiring and termination controls screen people before they get access, and promptly remove that access and company assets when they leave or change roles.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Much insider damage happens at the edges of employment: a poorly screened hire, or a former employee whose account still works. These gaps are common and easy to exploit.
how_it_works: Before hiring, background checks are scaled to the role's sensitivity and done within the law.
New staff, contractors and temporary workers sign confidentiality and acceptable use agreements before getting access, and their manager approves that access by role.
When people change roles, access tied to the old job is removed, not just added to.
Human resources (HR) notifies IT of every departure through a timely, ideally automated, feed from the HR system.
For involuntary terminations, access is disabled at or before the moment the person is told.
Leavers return devices, badges and tokens; shared passwords they knew are changed, and their knowledge is handed over.

rows.label: When to remove access
cells: By the end of the last working day
Immediately, at or before notice
On the transfer date, for old-role access

rows.label: Main risk
cells: Forgotten accounts left active
Sabotage or data theft by a disgruntled employee
Access piling up across jobs

rows.label: Key extra step
cells: Knowledge transfer and asset return
Disable remote access first; collect assets at the meeting
Manager recertifies the new set of access

subtopics.example: An IS auditor compares a manufacturer's HR leaver list with active network accounts. Fourteen former staff still have working accounts, including a dismissed engineer with remote access, because HR emails IT a leaver list once a month. The auditor reports the gap, recommends an automated HR-to-IT feed with same-day disabling, and recommends that management review the engineer's account for activity after departure.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Access ends when employment or the role ends, not when paperwork catches up. Involuntary terminations need access removed at or before notice. The IS auditor tests by matching HR records to active accounts.

exam_traps.trap: Removing a leaver's access is an HR paperwork task that can follow the monthly cycle.
exam_traps.why: Late revocation is one of the most common real control failures. Access must end on departure, through a timely HR-to-IT trigger.

exam_traps.trap: Background checks should be identical, and as deep as possible, for everyone.
exam_traps.why: Screening is scaled to the role's sensitivity and limited by privacy and employment law. Privileged roles get deeper checks.

key_terms.definition: Checking identity, references, qualifications and, where lawful, criminal or credit history before hiring.
A signed promise to protect confidential information that continues after employment ends.
The build-up of access rights as people move between roles without old rights being removed.

subtopics.name: IT Financial Management and Investment
subtopics.definition: IT financial management plans, funds, allocates and tracks IT spending, so money goes where it creates the most business value at an acceptable risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Spending can rise while value falls. Without business cases, portfolio discipline and cost transparency, IT funds the loudest request instead of the most valuable one.
how_it_works: Each business case states life-cycle costs (total cost of ownership), quantified benefits, risks, alternatives and success measures, modeling each outcome when a known uncertainty drives value.
Portfolio management ranks investments as a set, often in three tiers, each with a funding range: run (keep services going), grow (expand the business) and transform (create new business).
Material mid-year changes go back to the body that approved the portfolio, with items re-ranked by risk and value.
Mandated cuts follow risk and value, protecting regulatory and critical services and documenting the risks accepted.
Cost allocation shows business units what they consume, and FinOps (cloud financial operations) applies the same discipline to cloud spending.
Value is reported as realized business benefits, not money spent or projects delivered.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Reports each unit's IT costs without billing them
Bills each unit for the IT it uses

rows.label: Effect
cells: Builds awareness of consumption
Makes units budget for and own their consumption

rows.label: Must be
cells: Accurate and easy to understand
Traceable to actual cost, usage-driven and reproducible

subtopics.example: Halfway through the year, a public university's council orders an 8% cut to IT spending, while a new accessibility law requires portal updates by spring. The chief information officer plans equal cuts to every project. The IS auditor recommends re-ranking the portfolio by risk and value, protecting the mandated work, and returning it to the council for approval.
subtopics.isaca_rule: IT value shows in business outcomes realized from investment. Rank spending by risk and value, fund mandatory obligations first, and take material changes back to the body that approved the portfolio.

exam_traps.trap: Cut IT costs evenly across all areas.
exam_traps.why: Even cuts starve critical and regulatory services while protecting low-value work. Cuts should follow risk and value, with accepted risks documented.

exam_traps.trap: Money spent and projects delivered show the value IT creates.
exam_traps.why: Those are inputs and activity. Value is realized business benefit traced to approved investments.

key_terms.definition: The justification for an investment: costs, quantified benefits, risks, alternatives and success measures.
Managing IT investments as one set, balancing value, risk and strategy across them.
A cloud cost practice that tags spending, allocates it to the teams that use it and makes them accountable for it.
Tracking whether the benefits promised in a business case are actually delivered.

subtopics.name: Capacity and Resource Planning
subtopics.definition: Capacity and resource planning forecasts the computing, storage, network and staff capacity the business will need, and arranges it before demand arrives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Running out of capacity hurts the business as much as an outage, while overbuying wastes money. Planning keeps service steady at a sensible cost.
how_it_works: Planning starts from validated business demand forecasts, not from last year's usage alone.
Headroom thresholds trigger action early enough to cover the time needed to buy or provision more.
Resilience and capacity spending match each service's business value and service commitments.
Funding is released in stages as validated forecasts change, rather than fixed a year ahead.
When teams dispute a shared resource, a governance forum with defined decision rights settles it.
subtopics.example: At an online grocery chain, the storage team plans next year's capacity by extending last year's growth line, while marketing prepares to launch in three new cities. Two teams also dispute who gets a spare database cluster. The IS auditor recommends planning from business-validated demand forecasts and giving a cross-team forum clear decision rights over shared capacity. The chief technology officer agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Capacity follows business demand and value. Plan from validated forecasts, act on thresholds before limits are hit, and settle contested resources in an accountable forum, not by whoever escalates loudest.

exam_traps.trap: Plan next year's capacity by extending this year's usage trend.
exam_traps.why: Past usage misses launches, mergers and new channels. Capacity plans start from business-validated demand forecasts, with headroom thresholds set to cover procurement lead time.

exam_traps.trap: Every service needs the same top-tier resilience.
exam_traps.why: Investment should match each service's commitments and revenue. A uniform top-tier design overspends on low-value services.

key_terms.definition: Spare capacity kept above expected peak demand to absorb growth and surges.
A business-validated estimate of future workload, such as users or transactions.
The time needed to buy, deliver and set up new capacity.

subtopics.name: Enterprise Change Management
subtopics.definition: Enterprise change management, also called organizational change management, is the people side of change: preparing, supporting and reinforcing staff so they adopt new ways of working.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A system can pass every technical test and still fail because people keep working the old way. Benefits arrive only when behavior changes.
how_it_works: Stakeholder analysis identifies each affected group, its concerns and its influence.
Engagement, communication and training are planned for each group, with two-way feedback channels.
Go/no-go gates judge readiness on business outcomes, not only on IT deadlines.
Reinforcement, such as coaching and updated performance measures, keeps new habits from slipping.
Status reporting to governance must be honest, because misleading reports prevent course correction.

rows.label: Controls
cells: Technical changes to production systems
How people adopt new processes and tools

rows.label: Main steps
cells: Request, test, approve, release
Analyze stakeholders, engage, train, reinforce

rows.label: Success measure
cells: Changes released without unplanned outages
New ways of working adopted and benefits realized

rows.label: Owner
cells: IT change manager and change advisory board
Business sponsor with change leads

subtopics.example: A hospital network's new electronic health record went live a year ago. Clinicians still keep paper notes, overtime has doubled, and the steering group's monthly report still shows every milestone green. The IS auditor rates the inaccurate status reporting as the most serious finding, because it blocks correction, and recommends business-set adoption measures, clinician engagement and go/no-go gates for the remaining sites.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Major initiatives need both IT change management and enterprise change management, with business-set go/no-go criteria. Inaccurate status reporting to governance is among the most serious failures, because it stops leaders from correcting course.

exam_traps.trap: The technical change process also covers user adoption.
exam_traps.why: IT change management controls releases, not behavior. Adoption needs stakeholder engagement, training and reinforcement.

exam_traps.trap: Run a merger integration to the IT deadline.
exam_traps.why: An integration is business change. Business leaders should set go/no-go criteria based on business outcomes, and switch over in stages rather than all at once.

key_terms.definition: Mapping each affected group's interests, influence and likely reaction, to plan how to engage it.
A decision point where agreed readiness criteria must be met before the next phase starts.
The point at which people routinely use the new process or system as intended.

topics.overview: Much of IT is now delivered by outside providers. Vendor management covers deciding what to source, choosing and contracting carefully, monitoring performance and risk, governing cloud services, and leaving cleanly. Throughout, the customer keeps accountability for its data and its results.
can_do: Weigh sourcing options beyond cost, including onshore, near-shore and offshore delivery
Recommend due diligence and contract terms that match a vendor's risk
Choose reliable evidence of vendor performance and controls, such as a System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 Type 2 report
Explain what the customer still owns under infrastructure, platform and software cloud services

subtopics.name: Sourcing Decisions
subtopics.definition: A sourcing strategy decides which IT functions the organization keeps in-house and which it buys from providers, and where the bought services are delivered from.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Outsourcing the wrong function can lose knowledge and control that are hard to rebuild. Choosing on price alone ignores risks that cost more later.
how_it_works: Keep a function in-house when it is strategic, differentiating or knowledge-intensive, or when losing control would be unacceptable.
Weigh data residency, knowledge loss, flexibility, lock-in and regulation alongside cost.
Choose the delivery location by trading cost against time-zone overlap, culture and ease of oversight.
Phase transitions by risk, running old and new services side by side and passing go/no-go checkpoints, rather than one fast cutover.
When a business unit is sold, a transition services agreement (TSA) has the seller keep running the unit's IT for a fixed period, with clear exit dates.

rows.label: Location
cells: Same country
Nearby country in a similar time zone
Distant country

rows.label: Cost
cells: Highest
Moderate
Lowest

rows.label: Collaboration
cells: Easiest
Real-time overlap, small cultural gap
Little overlap, more coordination

rows.label: Oversight
cells: Simplest; same laws
Moderate
Hardest; more data and legal issues

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Work is outsourced to a vendor under an SLA and right to audit, but accountability for the data stays with your organization'><rect x='20' y='8' width='300' height='50' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='170' y='29' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Your organization</text><text x='170' y='48' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>Keeps accountability for data and results</text><line x1='170' y1='62' x2='170' y2='93' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M166,93 L170,100 L174,93 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><text x='182' y='85' text-anchor='start' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>SLA, right to audit</text><rect x='20' y='102' width='300' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='170' y='127' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Vendor does the work</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Outsourcing moves the work to a vendor under contract. Accountability for the data and the result stays with the organization.

subtopics.example: A state pension fund's managers propose outsourcing development of the member-benefits system to a near-shore provider, citing a 30% cost cut. Their analysis ignores where member data would be stored, how much system knowledge would leave with retiring staff, and how hard it would be to bring the work back. The IS auditor recommends adding these risks to the analysis and leaves the sourcing decision to management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsourcing transfers the work, never the accountability. The IS auditor verifies that management weighed every material risk beyond cost; management makes the sourcing decision.

exam_traps.trap: Choose the provider with the lowest price.
exam_traps.why: Cost advantages shift over time, while lost capability, lock-in and data risks persist. Price is one factor among many.

exam_traps.trap: A 90-day cutover with strong contract penalties limits transition risk.
exam_traps.why: Penalties compensate for failures but do not prevent them. A phased, risk-based transition with parallel running and gates limits disruption.

key_terms.definition: Performing a function with the organization's own staff and resources.
Dependence on one provider that makes switching costly or slow; a credible, maintained exit option and market benchmarks keep leverage at renewal.
A time-limited contract under which a former parent keeps providing services to a divested unit.

subtopics.name: Due Diligence, Contracts and SLAs
subtopics.definition: Vendor due diligence checks a provider before signing, scaled to its risk; the contract and its service level agreement (SLA) then set out the customer's protections.
subtopics.why_it_matters: After signing, the customer's leverage drops sharply. Weak checks or vague contracts leave it unable to measure service, audit controls or leave cleanly.
how_it_works: Vendors are tiered by the sensitivity of data they handle, the criticality of the service and regulatory impact, using documented thresholds.
Due diligence depth follows the tier: critical providers get financial, resilience, security, compliance and contract review.
The SLA sets measurable targets backed by consequences such as service credits and exit rights.
Contracts include audit rights, security and breach-notice duties, limits on subcontracting, and data return and deletion.
Exit terms are agreed at signing, when the customer's leverage is greatest.
A central vendor management office keeps the vendor inventory and tiers, working with business owners.
subtopics.example: A blood-donation charity plans to move its donor-matching service to a small software provider. The procurement officer proposes accepting the provider's completed security questionnaire as due diligence. Because the service is critical, the IS auditor recommends checking finances, resilience, compliance and contract terms, plus an SLA with measurable targets, service credits and exit terms agreed before signing. The executive director approves.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Due diligence depth matches vendor risk. An SLA protects the customer only when its targets are measurable and backed by consequences. Negotiate audit rights and the exit strategy before signing, while leverage is highest.

exam_traps.trap: One certificate or questionnaire is enough due diligence for a critical provider.
exam_traps.why: A single artifact covers a narrow scope. Critical providers need review of finances, resilience, compliance, security and contract terms.

exam_traps.trap: An SLA with high availability targets protects the customer.
exam_traps.why: Targets without clear measurement, service credits and exit rights cannot be enforced, so they offer little protection.

key_terms.definition: A contract clause letting the customer or its auditors examine the vendor's controls and records.
A financial remedy, usually a fee reduction, owed when the vendor misses a service level.
Grouping vendors by inherent risk so oversight effort matches the risk each one brings.
Contract terms for data return, verified deletion, transition help and knowledge transfer when the relationship ends.

subtopics.name: Monitoring, Assurance and Offboarding
subtopics.definition: Third-party oversight is the customer's ongoing checking of a vendor's performance, controls and risk after signing, through to a controlled exit.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Vendor risk changes after the contract starts: finances weaken, staff turn over, breaches happen. Oversight that stops at signing misses warning signs.
how_it_works: The customer measures service itself against the service level agreement (SLA) rather than relying on vendor reports.
System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports from an independent auditor show vendor controls; check scope, period, exceptions and the customer-side controls they assume.
Independent signals, such as security ratings and financial monitoring, trigger reassessment between scheduled reviews.
Repeated incidents prompt full risk re-tiering and escalating responses, up to exit readiness.
After a vendor breach, the customer invokes the contract's notice and cooperation terms while starting its own response.
Offboarding keeps service running, enforces data return and verified deletion, and removes vendor access.

rows.label: What it shows
cells: The vendor's own view of performance
Control design at a single date
Control design and operation over a period, with test results
The service the customer actually received

rows.label: Independent?
cells: No
Yes, a service auditor
Yes, a service auditor
Independent of the vendor, when the customer measures it

rows.label: Best use
cells: Starting point only
Initial assurance on control design
Relying on vendor controls
Proving SLA results and claiming credits

subtopics.example: A university's student-information provider has missed SLA targets for nine months, suffered ransomware and lost two senior engineers. The registrar, IT security and procurement each tracked one issue. The IS auditor recommends one combined risk reassessment of the provider and escalating responses, from a remediation plan to tested exit readiness, owned by the vendor management office.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Verify vendor performance with customer-side measurement and independent assurance, not self-reporting. A SOC report covers vendor controls for one scope and period, not how its service or model performs on your data. Accountability never leaves the customer.

exam_traps.trap: Request the vendor's SOC 3 report to rely on its controls.
exam_traps.why: A SOC 3 report is a general-use summary with no test details. Reliance needs a Type 2 report: SOC 1 for financial-reporting controls, SOC 2 for security, availability or confidentiality.

exam_traps.trap: The vendor's monthly SLA dashboard proves the targets were met.
exam_traps.why: Self-reported figures need independent checking. Customer-side measurement, reconciled to the SLA definitions, is the reliable evidence.

key_terms.definition: A service organization's management letter covering the gap between a SOC report's end date and the date the customer needs.
The controlled end of a vendor relationship: service transition, data return, verified deletion and access removal.
A vendor's own subcontractor, whose risks reach the customer indirectly.
Controls a SOC report assumes the customer runs itself so the provider's controls work as intended.

subtopics.name: Cloud Governance
subtopics.definition: Cloud governance sets how an organization chooses, controls and pays for cloud services, based on the shared responsibility model that splits duties with the provider.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Cloud makes it easy to deploy fast and misconfigure fast. Without governance, customers assume the provider handles security it does not, and costs and evidence scatter.
how_it_works: The split of duties moves with the service model, but the customer always keeps its data, identities and configuration choices.
Approved configuration baselines are enforced and checked continuously, not just at deployment.
Organizations using several clouds apply one control layer across them: common identity, cost tags on every resource and policy as code.
A cloud center of excellence (CCoE) sets standards and guardrails, meaning preset limits, while teams manage their own use within them.
Migration is decided per application by value and risk: retire, retain, rehost (move as is), replatform (adjust slightly), refactor (rebuild for the cloud) or repurchase (replace with SaaS).
Data residency needs are enforced per region, backed by transfer safeguards and a ready exit option.

rows.label: Full name
cells: Infrastructure as a service
Platform as a service
Software as a service

rows.label: Provider manages
cells: Facilities, hardware and virtualization
Also the operating system, runtime and middleware
Nearly the whole application stack

rows.label: Customer still manages
cells: Operating system, applications, data, identities, settings
Applications, data, identities, settings
Data, user access, configuration and use

rows.label: Example
cells: Rented virtual servers
A managed database or app platform
Hosted email or customer relationship software
