illustration.caption: Moving from IaaS to SaaS, the provider manages more of the stack. The customer's share shrinks but never disappears.

subtopics.example: An engineering consultancy runs teams on two public clouds. Each team has its own identity setup, a third of resources lack cost tags, and a storage bucket stayed public for weeks. The IS auditor recommends common identity, mandatory tags and policy-as-code guardrails across both clouds, checked continuously against an approved baseline, which the cloud center of excellence implements.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The customer stays accountable for its data, access and configuration in every service model, and must continuously show that configurations stay within an approved baseline, using one control layer across providers.

exam_traps.trap: In software as a service, the provider is responsible for who can access the customer's data.
exam_traps.why: The provider secures the platform; the customer still decides and reviews user access, configuration and data use.

exam_traps.trap: Documenting the shared responsibility split is enough cloud risk management.
exam_traps.why: The split only assigns duties. Continuous monitoring of the customer's own configurations against a baseline shows those duties are met.

key_terms.definition: The division of security and operating duties between cloud provider and customer, which varies by service model.
A cross-functional team that sets cloud standards, guardrails and good practice.
Writing configuration and security rules as machine-checkable code, so they are applied and tested automatically.

topics.overview: What gets measured gets managed, but only if the right things are measured honestly. This topic covers the three kinds of key indicator, how to design metrics that reflect real outcomes, and how to report them to the board in a way that supports decisions.
can_do: Classify a metric as a key performance, risk or control indicator from a scenario
Spot metrics that stay green while the objective fails
Recommend concise, goal-linked reporting for the board
Test the reliability of a management report before relying on it

subtopics.name: KPIs, KRIs and KCIs
subtopics.definition: Key performance, risk and control indicators (KPIs, KRIs and KCIs) are chosen measures showing whether goals are met, risk is growing or a control works.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each indicator answers a different question. Using the wrong one means leaders miss early warnings or act on the wrong problem.
how_it_works: A KPI measures progress toward a stated goal, such as the share of orders processed without error.
A KRI is a leading signal for a specific risk, warning that exposure is growing before an event happens.
A KCI shows whether a control operates as designed, such as the share of changes with documented approval.
Each indicator has a target or threshold, an owner, a data source and a reporting frequency.
A threshold breach triggers defined escalation and response; an indicator whose breach triggers nothing is not working.

rows.label: Question
cells: Are we reaching our goal?
Is this risk getting worse?
Is this control working?

rows.label: Timing
cells: Mostly looks back at results
Looks ahead as an early warning
Shows a control's current state

rows.label: Example
cells: User satisfaction with the service desk
Trend in unpatched critical flaws on internet-facing systems
Share of privileged-access reviews completed on time

rows.label: Exam cue
cells: Goal achievement, performance
Before the event, early warning
Operating as designed

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='KPIs measure performance, KRIs warn of rising risk, KCIs measure control effectiveness'><rect x='10' y='8' width='72' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='46' y='31' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='14' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>KPI</text><text x='94' y='31' text-anchor='start' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text)'>Performance: how are we doing?</text><rect x='10' y='52' width='72' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='46' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='14' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>KRI</text><text x='94' y='75' text-anchor='start' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text)'>Early warning: is risk rising?</text><rect x='10' y='96' width='72' height='36' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='46' y='119' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='14' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>KCI</text><text x='94' y='119' text-anchor='start' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text)'>Control: is it working?</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Three different questions: how well are we doing, is risk rising, and is the control doing its job.

subtopics.example: A ride-hailing company tracks the share of drivers with expired background checks as a key risk indicator. It has stayed above its 2% threshold since spring, and the chart turns red each month, yet no one is assigned to act. The IS auditor recommends naming an owner for each threshold, with a defined escalation path and response deadline. The chief risk officer assigns owners.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A KPI measures goal achievement, a KRI warns of growing exposure for a specific risk, and a KCI shows whether a control operates as designed. Every threshold needs an owner and an escalation path.

exam_traps.trap: Pick a KPI when the board wants early warning that cyber exposure is growing.
exam_traps.why: Early warning before an event points to a KRI, such as a climbing count of unpatched critical flaws.

exam_traps.trap: The number of tickets closed per day shows whether user satisfaction has improved.
exam_traps.why: That is an activity count. If the goal is satisfaction, the KPI should measure satisfaction directly.

key_terms.definition: A measure that changes before an outcome, giving time to act.
A measure that records an outcome after it has happened.
The value of an indicator that triggers escalation or action when crossed.

subtopics.name: Designing Reliable Performance Metrics
subtopics.definition: Metric design defines each measure from an objective's critical success factors, with one agreed calculation, a measured baseline and independently approved targets.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A metric can stay green while the strategy fails. Badly designed or self-reported measures give governance confidence it has not earned.
how_it_works: Identify the critical success factors (CSFs) of each objective, then choose key performance indicators (KPIs) that measure them.
Agree one enterprise definition and calculation before comparing or adding up results across units.
Measure a baseline from current data before setting improvement targets.
Have targets approved by someone outside the team being measured, and never lower them just to stay green.
Draw data from systems of record and validate it independently of the team reporting it.
Benchmark only against peers whose cost definitions, scope and service levels are comparable.
subtopics.example: A hotel chain's IT team meets all its targets for server uptime, ticket closure and project delivery, yet the goal of faster guest check-in keeps slipping. IT also sets its own targets and lowered two of them this year. The IS auditor reports that the metrics miss the check-in goal's critical success factors and recommends targets approved outside IT. Management redesigns the metrics.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Derive KPIs from critical success factors, define them once, start from a measured baseline, and keep target-setting and data validation independent of the team being measured. A green dashboard proves nothing if the metric or its data is weak.

exam_traps.trap: All targets are green, so performance is fine.
exam_traps.why: Targets may be lowered, self-calculated or unrelated to the objective. Check that metrics trace to success factors and that data and targets are independently validated.

exam_traps.trap: Cost per user 20% below a published peer benchmark proves IT is efficient.
exam_traps.why: The comparison is valid only if the peers define cost, scope and service levels the same way.

key_terms.definition: One of the few things that must go right for an objective to be achieved.
Measured current performance, used as the starting point for targets.
The authoritative source system for a given piece of data.
Comparing performance with peers or published standards to set targets or find gaps.

subtopics.name: Reporting to Governance
subtopics.definition: Performance reporting to governance gives the board a concise, goal-linked view of IT, showing targets, trends and exceptions rather than raw operating detail.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Boards can oversee only what they can understand. Too much detail hides problems, and unverified figures can lead directors to wrong decisions.
how_it_works: Reports show a short set of measures linked to enterprise goals, each with its target, trend and exception notes.
An IT balanced scorecard keeps the view balanced across four perspectives rather than cost alone.
Investment reports show business outcomes and benefits realized, by portfolio category.
Exceptions and threshold breaches are flagged with owners and planned actions.
Before relying on a management report, the IS auditor tests its figures back to source records.

types.meaning: The cost of IT and the value it returns to the business.
Satisfaction and service quality as the business sees them.
The efficiency and quality of IT processes.
Skills, innovation and readiness for future needs.

subtopics.example: A shipping company's board receives a 60-page IT pack each quarter, mostly server and ticket statistics, and directors cannot see whether the new booking platform is delivering. The IS auditor recommends about a dozen measures tied to enterprise goals, with targets, trends and exceptions, across all four scorecard perspectives. Before citing the figures in the audit report, the auditor traces a sample to source systems.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Board reporting is concise, focused on outcomes and linked to enterprise goals. A management report is not audit evidence until its data has been tested back to the source.

exam_traps.trap: Give the board every operational statistic so nothing is hidden.
exam_traps.why: Volume hides the message. Governance needs goal-linked trends and exceptions it can act on.

exam_traps.trap: Management's monthly key performance indicator (KPI) report is reliable evidence as delivered.
exam_traps.why: The IS auditor must first test its figures for accuracy and completeness against source records.

key_terms.definition: A reporting tool that measures IT across corporate contribution, user orientation, operational excellence and future orientation, adapting the financial, customer, process and learning views.
Highlighting only results that miss targets or breach thresholds, so attention goes where action is needed.
The direction a measure moves over several periods, showing the board whether things are improving or getting worse.

topics.topic_name: Quality Assurance and Quality Management of IT
topics.overview: Quality means IT products and services are fit for the business purpose they serve. Quality management builds that in through documented standards, independent assurance, measured process capability and continual improvement, rather than relying on inspection at the end.
can_do: Tell quality assurance from quality control in a scenario
Match ISO 9001, Six Sigma and COBIT 2019 APO11 (Managed Quality) to the problems they suit
Read capability and maturity levels and set targets by business need
Recommend independent QA and root cause analysis for recurring defects

subtopics.name: Quality Assurance Versus Quality Control
subtopics.definition: Quality assurance (QA) builds quality into each process step to prevent defects; quality control (QC) inspects finished outputs to find the defects that remain.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Defects found late cost far more to fix than defects prevented. A program that only tests at the end catches problems when they are most expensive.
how_it_works: QA defines standards, reviews and checks for every stage, from requirements to release.
QC inspects and tests products against acceptance criteria before they are released.
Quality criteria trace to business and user requirements, not only to technical specifications.
Both are needed, but prevention through QA lowers the total cost of quality.

rows.label: Focus
cells: The process
The product

rows.label: Timing
cells: Throughout, before defects occur
After the output is built

rows.label: Goal
cells: Prevent defects
Detect defects

rows.label: Example
cells: Design reviews and coding standards at each stage
Final release testing

subtopics.example: A game studio's only quality activity is a two-week test sprint before each launch, and the producer plans to hire more testers to improve quality assurance. Most defects found trace back to unclear requirements. The IS auditor reports that more end testing strengthens quality control, not assurance, and recommends reviews at the requirements and design stages. The studio head approves a pilot.
subtopics.isaca_rule: QA prevents defects by building quality into each stage; QC detects them in finished products. Faster or automated end-of-line testing improves QC, not QA. Quality is judged against business and user requirements.

exam_traps.trap: Automating the final tests strengthens quality assurance.
exam_traps.why: It speeds inspection, but defects are still found late. Assurance means process controls at each stage.

exam_traps.trap: Releases that match the technical specifications are high quality.
exam_traps.why: If they fail user acceptance, the quality criteria do not trace to business needs. Fitness for purpose is the test.

key_terms.definition: How well a product or service meets the business need it was built for.
Agreed conditions a deliverable must meet before the business accepts it.
Any failure of a product to meet its requirements or standards.

subtopics.memory_aid: Assurance = process, before. Control = product, after.

subtopics.name: Quality Management Systems and Methods
subtopics.definition: A quality management system (QMS) is the organization's documented way of achieving quality: its standards, roles, reviews, measures and improvement routines.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without documented standards, quality depends on individuals and reviews turn into arguments. A QMS makes quality repeatable and checkable.
how_it_works: Documented standards for coding, documentation and testing give reviewers objective criteria to judge work against.
Methods complement each other, so choose by the problem, such as statistical methods for high-volume variation.
Certification shows a QMS exists and is followed within its scope; it does not guarantee every product.
Cost of quality analysis shows where spending on prevention lowers total cost.
Global programs standardize objectives and metrics, and let regions adapt how they meet them.

types.meaning: The certifiable international standard for a quality management system.
A statistical method that cuts variation and defects in high-volume processes, using the define, measure, analyze, improve, control cycle.
The COBIT objective that builds quality into IT processes through standards, assurance, measurement and improvement.

subtopics.example: At a logistics software house, two senior reviewers disagree on what counts as acceptable code, so the same change passes with one and fails with the other. The IS auditor recommends written coding and documentation standards as review criteria. When a supplier later claims its ISO 9001 certificate proves its modules are defect-free, the auditor reports that the certificate covers a managed process, not product quality.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Quality reviews need documented standards to judge against. Match the improvement method to the problem, and treat certification as evidence of a managed process within its scope, not as a guarantee of product quality.

exam_traps.trap: A vendor's ISO 9001 certificate guarantees defect-free software.
exam_traps.why: ISO 9001 certifies a quality management system within its scope. Product quality still needs acceptance criteria and testing.

exam_traps.trap: Six Sigma is the best fix for every quality problem.
exam_traps.why: Six Sigma suits high-volume processes where variation drives defects. Other problems may need documented standards, reviews or lighter methods.

key_terms.definition: Quality spending split into prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs.
A documented rule, such as a coding standard, that reviewers measure work against.
The specific sites, services and processes that a certificate covers.

subtopics.name: Capability and Maturity Models
subtopics.definition: A capability or maturity model rates how well processes are performed and managed on a defined scale, usually 0 to 5, to guide improvement targets.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Leaders need to know not only whether a process exists, but how reliable and repeatable it is. Ratings show where to invest and how far to go.
how_it_works: An assessor rates a process against each level's criteria, using evidence such as documents, interviews and records.
Capability levels rate one process; maturity levels rate a group of processes or the whole organization.
COBIT 2019 rates process capability and focus-area maturity from 0 to 5, using level definitions adapted from Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI).
Management sets a target level for each process from business need and cost-benefit, not the highest level everywhere.
The gap between current and target levels becomes an improvement roadmap, reassessed from time to time.
Older material uses COBIT 4.1 maturity names: nonexistent, initial, repeatable, defined, managed and measurable, optimized; the levels still climb the same way.

rows.label: What is rated
cells: One process, such as change management
A set of processes, or the whole organization

rows.label: In COBIT 2019
cells: The processes within each objective, rated 0 to 5
Focus areas made up of several objectives, rated 0 to 5

rows.label: Question
cells: How well is this process performed?
How mature is our practice overall?

types.meaning: The process is missing or does not achieve its purpose.
The purpose is partly achieved through ad hoc, person-dependent work.
Planned, basic activities achieve the purpose.
A standard, documented process is used across the organization.
Performance is measured and controlled with data.
The process is continually improved, based on measurement and goals.

subtopics.example: A state lottery's IT director wants to know how well the problem and release management processes are run, and suggests comparing ticket statistics with other lotteries. The IS auditor recommends an evidence-based capability assessment using a model such as COBIT 2019, with targets set by business risk. Release management rates 1 against a target of 3, and the auditor reports the gap for management to plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A capability assessment shows how well processes are performed and managed, and where to improve. Targets come from business need and cost-benefit, so not every process needs level 5. Ratings must rest on evidence, not on self-assessment alone.

exam_traps.trap: Every process should reach level 5.
exam_traps.why: Higher levels cost more. The target should fit the process's business importance and risk, and a defined, measured process is often enough.

exam_traps.trap: A peer benchmark tells us how mature our processes are.
exam_traps.why: Benchmarks compare results with others. A capability assessment examines how each process is actually performed and managed against defined criteria.

key_terms.definition: A widely used model that rates process capability and organizational maturity on defined levels.
The level management decides a process should reach, based on business need.
An evidence-based evaluation of a process against a capability model's criteria.

subtopics.memory_aid: 0 Incomplete, 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitative, 5 Optimizing: from missing, to repeatable, to self-improving.

subtopics.name: Independence and Continual Improvement
subtopics.definition: Quality assurance (QA) independence means reviewers report outside the team they check; continual improvement means fixing the root causes of recurring defects.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A reviewer who reports to the person under review cannot easily say no. Fixing the same defect again and again wastes money while the process that creates it stays broken.
how_it_works: QA reports to a manager independent of development, so it can reject a release without pressure.
Defects are logged, grouped by type and analyzed for their root causes.
Process changes address those causes, and later results confirm that the fix worked.
The plan-do-check-act (PDCA) cycle repeats this improvement loop over time.
For outsourced development, quality criteria go into the contract and are checked at staged acceptance reviews.
QA's own effectiveness is judged by outcomes, such as production defects, and reported honestly to governance.
subtopics.example: At an airline's digital team, the same type of seat-selection defect has reached production in four of the last six app releases. The QA lead reports to the delivery manager whose deadlines the releases serve, and each defect is patched and closed. The IS auditor recommends a QA reporting line outside delivery and root cause analysis of defect patterns. The chief digital officer agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: QA must be independent of the work it reviews. Recurring defects call for root cause analysis and process correction, not repeated one-off fixes. Judge QA by outcomes, and report them honestly to governance.

exam_traps.trap: Fix each recurring defect quickly as it appears.
exam_traps.why: One-off fixes leave the cause in place. Root cause analysis and process change stop that type of defect from returning.

exam_traps.trap: A high count of defects fixed before release proves QA is effective.
exam_traps.why: One favorable internal metric can hide decline. If production defects are climbing, QA is weakening, whatever the internal count says.

key_terms.definition: Tracing a problem back to the underlying reason it happened, so the fix prevents it from recurring.
A four-step improvement cycle: plan a change, try it, check the results, then adopt or adjust it.
A checkpoint where a vendor's deliverable is tested against contract quality criteria before work continues.

key_terminologies.Enterprise governance of information and: The board's direction and oversight of information and technology, so IT supports strategy, creates value and stays within risk limits. Older ISACA materials call it governance of enterprise IT (GEIT).
key_terminologies.Evaluate, Direct and Monitor (EDM): The three governance activities of the board: weigh options, set direction and check results.
key_terminologies.Three Lines Model: The Institute of Internal Auditors' model: management owns risk, specialist functions support and challenge, internal audit gives independent assurance.
key_terminologies.RACI chart: A table showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, with one Accountable role per outcome.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties (SoD): Splitting a sensitive process so no one person can start, approve, complete and conceal it.
key_terminologies.COSO Internal Control framework: A widely used internal control model with five components, from control environment to monitoring activities.
key_terminologies.Enterprise architecture (EA): A structured description of how business processes, data, applications and technology fit together and should change.
key_terminologies.Architecture waiver: An approved, time-limited exception to an architecture standard, tracked as technical debt.
key_terminologies.Enterprise risk management (ERM): An organization-wide approach to identifying, assessing, responding to and monitoring risk against the board-set risk appetite.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The broad amount of risk the board will take on for its objectives; tolerances set measurable limits within it.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The risk that remains after responses are applied; it must fit within risk appetite, or be treated further unless the board approves an exception.
key_terminologies.Risk treatment: The chosen response to a risk, also called risk response: accept, mitigate (reduce), transfer (share) or avoid.
key_terminologies.Annualized loss expectancy (ALE): Expected yearly loss from a risk: single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence.
key_terminologies.Lawful basis: The legal ground that permits processing personal data, such as consent or a legal obligation.
key_terminologies.Data minimization: Collecting and keeping only the personal data a stated purpose needs.
key_terminologies.Data classification: Grouping data by the harm its exposure or misuse would cause, with handling rules for each level.
key_terminologies.Retention schedule: A list of data categories with how long each is kept, why, and how it is disposed of.
key_terminologies.Business case: The justification for an investment, stating costs, measurable benefits, risks and success criteria.
key_terminologies.IT portfolio management: Ranking and funding IT investments as one set so the mix reflects strategy, value and risk.
key_terminologies.Service level agreement (SLA): Measurable service targets agreed with a provider, with consequences when they are missed.
key_terminologies.Right to audit: A contract clause that lets the customer or its auditors examine a provider's controls and records.
key_terminologies.Shared responsibility model: The split of security and operating duties between a cloud provider and its customer, which changes by service model.
key_terminologies.Critical success factor (CSF): One of the few things that must go right for an objective to succeed; good key performance indicators measure them.
key_terminologies.Key risk indicator (KRI): A measure that warns early that exposure to a specific risk is growing, before a loss event occurs.
key_terminologies.IT balanced scorecard: A reporting tool that measures IT across corporate contribution, user orientation, operational excellence and future orientation, adapting the financial, customer, process and learning views.
key_terminologies.Quality management system (QMS): An organization's documented standards, roles, reviews and measures for achieving quality.
key_terminologies.Root cause analysis: Tracing a problem to its underlying cause so the fix stops it from coming back.

domains.domain_name: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation
domains.overview: This domain follows a system from idea to everyday use. Part A covers deciding whether a system is worth it, running the project, choosing how to build or buy it, and designing controls in from the start. Part B covers testing, controlled release, moving data and users across, and checking afterward that the promised benefits arrived. Throughout, the IS auditor gives independent advice and assurance while management makes the decisions.
domains.analogy: Getting a new system is like renovating a home and moving in. First you decide whether it is worth the money, including the option of staying put. You agree on plans and a budget with a builder, and any extra work needs a signed change order. Before moving in, you walk through and fix anything serious. The movers count boxes when packing and again when unloading. Months later, you check whether the bills and comfort match what was promised. The IS auditor is the independent inspector: they check and report, while you, the owner, decide.

topics.overview: Every new system starts life as a project. This topic covers who governs a project, what authorizes it, how its schedule and costs are tracked, and how it is closed. The IS auditor checks that the business stays in control of the decisions, while staying independent of the work.
can_do: Identify who authorizes, funds, runs and governs a project, and why the IS auditor does none of these
Find the critical path and judge which delays move the end date
Read cost and schedule performance indexes (CPI and SPI) and decide when a variance needs escalation
Tell a proper project closure from a project that simply stopped

subtopics.name: Project Roles and Accountability
subtopics.definition: Project roles divide accountability: the sponsor funds the project and owns the benefits, the project manager delivers it, and the steering committee decides escalated issues.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When roles are vague, nobody decides, nobody owns the benefits and problems surface late. Exam scenarios often ask who should approve, fund or be accountable.
how_it_works: The sponsor owns the business case, secures its approval through investment governance, signs the charter and appoints a project manager.
The project manager runs the project day to day within delegated limits and reports progress, issues and risks upward.
Issues beyond those limits go to the steering committee, whose members must be able to commit money and people.
The project management office (PMO) supplies common methods and templates, supports project managers and combines reporting across projects.
Stakeholder analysis by influence and interest sets what each group is told, and how often.
The IS auditor joins early, from requirements and design, to advise on controls and review at key points, but never designs, builds or approves the system.

rows.label: Main job
cells: Funds the project and owns its benefits
Sets direction and resolves escalated issues
Sets methods and supports project managers

rows.label: Decides
cells: Whether to invest, and whether to re-approve after major change
Scope, budget and priority changes beyond the project manager's limits
No funding or priority decisions; it recommends and reports

rows.label: Common mix-up
cells: Handing benefit ownership to IT
Treating it as an audience for status updates
Thinking it approves funding

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Project roles: sponsor, project manager, steering committee, and IS auditor'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Project sponsor</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Project manager</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Steering committee</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>IS auditor</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Four roles, four jobs. The sponsor pays and owns the benefits, the project manager delivers, the steering committee decides the big questions, and the IS auditor looks on independently.

subtopics.example: At a hospital, the chief financial officer sponsors a billing system and chairs a steering committee of department heads. When the vendor asks for six more weeks, the project manager, who lacks authority to extend the timeline, escalates. The IS auditor confirms the minutes record a decision and recommends adding a clinical lead who can commit nursing staff.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Accountability sits with the business: the sponsor owns the investment and its benefits, and the steering committee decides what exceeds the project manager's limits. The IS auditor advises and reviews from the start but never runs the project or approves its design.

exam_traps.trap: The steering committee is mainly there to receive status reports.
exam_traps.why: It exists to decide. If its members cannot commit money or people, escalated issues stall.

exam_traps.trap: The IS auditor should stay out of a project until it is built, so involvement cannot impair independence.
exam_traps.why: Controls are cheapest to add at requirements and design. Advisory involvement is expected; independence comes from not designing, building or approving, not from staying away.

key_terms.definition: Business managers who own the resulting system, supply staff for requirements and testing, and accept the delivered system.
A group independent of developers that reviews deliverables against standards at each phase; it checks quality but does not build.

subtopics.name: Charter, Scope and Project Structure
subtopics.definition: A project charter is the sponsor-approved document that formally authorizes a project, states its objectives and scope, and gives the project manager authority over resources.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a charter, nobody has clear authority to spend money or assign people. Without a protected scope, small additions pile up until the budget and schedule break.
how_it_works: The business case justifies the investment; once it is approved, the sponsor signs a charter that authorizes the project.
The charter names the sponsor and project manager, sets objectives and high-level scope, and delegates authority over resources.
Planning breaks the scope into deliverables, and the approved result becomes the scope baseline.
Each proposed addition goes through a change request with an impact analysis; management decides, and the plan is rebaselined.
The five process groups (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing) are not phases: they repeat within each phase, and monitoring and controlling runs throughout.
How much real authority the project manager has also depends on the organization's structure, shown below.

types.meaning: Staff stay in their departments and report to line managers; the project manager has little authority.
Staff report to both a line manager and the project manager, so authority is shared.
The team reports to the project manager, who has full authority over project resources.

subtopics.example: A retailer's online store project has an approved charter and scope baseline. In week ten, the marketing director asks developers to 'just add' a loyalty-points feature, and the project manager logs it as a change request. The IS auditor checks that the steering committee saw the cost and schedule impact before approving it, and that the plan was rebaselined.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The business case justifies a project; the sponsor-approved charter authorizes it. After that, the scope baseline is protected by change control: every addition is assessed for impact and decided by management, not absorbed informally by the team.

exam_traps.trap: The approved business case is what authorizes the project and its manager.
exam_traps.why: The business case justifies the spending. The charter formally authorizes the project and delegates authority to a named project manager.

exam_traps.trap: A small scope addition can be absorbed without formal change control.
exam_traps.why: Small additions add up to scope creep. Each needs an impact analysis so management, not the team, decides whether the cost and delay are worth it.

key_terms.definition: A breakdown of the project scope into smaller deliverables and work packages, made after the project is authorized.
Uncontrolled growth in project scope through additions that skip impact analysis and approval.
Formally replacing the approved scope, schedule or cost baseline after management approves a change.

subtopics.name: Scheduling and the Critical Path
subtopics.definition: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks through a project; its total duration sets the earliest date the project can finish.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Delays on the critical path delay the whole project, while other tasks can slip a little without harm. Knowing which is which tells managers where to focus people and attention.
how_it_works: List the tasks, estimate each duration and record which tasks must finish before others can start.
Add up the durations along every chain of dependent tasks, from start to finish.
The chain with the longest total time is the critical path, and its tasks have zero slack.
Tasks off the critical path can slip by their slack without moving the end date.
If a task uses up all its slack, its chain becomes critical and the critical path can change.
Adding resources or overlapping tasks shortens the project only when applied to critical-path tasks.

types.meaning: A bar chart of tasks against a calendar, good for showing timing and progress.
Estimates each task from optimistic, most likely and pessimistic guesses, weighted as (O + 4M + P) / 6, to handle uncertainty.
Finds the longest chain of dependent tasks, which fixes the shortest possible project duration.
A fixed period with a fixed end date; scope shrinks or grows to fit the time.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The critical path is the longest path through a project and sets its duration; other paths are shorter and have slack'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Critical path</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>The longest path — sets duration</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Other paths</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Shorter — have slack</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Only the longest chain of dependent tasks decides when the project finishes. Shorter chains have slack and can absorb some delay.

subtopics.example: A bank's mobile app project has two chains: building the app (30 days) and setting up servers (18 days), so the server chain has 12 days of slack. The servers slip 10 days, and the project manager warns the sponsor that launch will be late. The IS auditor points out that 2 days of slack remain, so the end date holds, and recommends reporting focused on the critical path.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Protect the critical path. Its tasks have zero slack, so schedule risk, monitoring and extra resources belong there first. A delay elsewhere matters only once it uses up that task's slack.

exam_traps.trap: The critical path is the chain with the most tasks.
exam_traps.why: It is the chain with the longest total duration. Three long tasks can outlast ten short ones.

exam_traps.trap: Any late task makes the whole project late.
exam_traps.why: Only critical-path tasks have zero slack. A non-critical task can slip up to its slack without moving the end date.

key_terms.definition: How long a task can be delayed without delaying the project's end date; zero on the critical path.
A link between tasks where one cannot start, or finish, until another does.
A zero-length checkpoint marking a key event, such as design sign-off.

subtopics.name: Estimating, Tracking Cost and Escalating Risk
subtopics.definition: Project cost control means sizing the work fairly, comparing what was achieved with what was spent and planned, and escalating risks beyond the project manager's limits.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Estimates set the budget, and honest tracking shows trouble while there is time to act. Hopeful reporting turns overruns into failed projects.
how_it_works: Function point analysis sizes software by what it delivers to users, so estimates can be made early and compared across programming languages.
Earned value management (EVM) compares three dollar figures: planned value (work scheduled by now), earned value (work actually done) and actual cost (money spent so far).
The cost performance index (CPI) is earned value divided by actual cost; below 1.0 means over budget.
The schedule performance index (SPI) is earned value divided by planned value; below 1.0 means behind schedule.
A risk is escalated when its residual exposure exceeds the project manager's delegated risk tolerance, or the response needs more authority.
A troubled project gets an independent review and a rebaselined plan before more funding is released.

rows.label: Covers
cells: Identified risks with planned responses
Unforeseen risks nobody could list in advance

rows.label: Where it sits
cells: Inside the cost baseline
Outside the cost baseline

rows.label: Who releases it
cells: The project manager, within the plan
The sponsor or steering committee, with the reason recorded

subtopics.example: A transit agency's fare-system project reports it is 'on budget' because actual cost matches planned value: $2 million each. Earned value, the work actually finished, is only $1.5 million, so CPI and SPI are both 0.75. The IS auditor explains that matching spend to plan hid the shortfall and recommends earned value reporting to the steering committee, with a corrective action plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A material variance rarely fixes itself, so it calls for corrective action and escalation, not patience. Management reserve sits outside the cost baseline, so every drawdown needs sponsor or steering committee approval with the reason recorded.

exam_traps.trap: A mid-project CPI of 0.8 will probably even out by the end.
exam_traps.why: Cumulative variances that far below 1.0 rarely self-correct, and rebaselining only resets the yardstick. Report the variance and escalate it to the sponsor.

exam_traps.trap: Lines of code are a fair way to compare productivity across teams using different languages.
exam_traps.why: Code counts depend on language and style and are known only late. Function points measure delivered functionality, so they work early and across languages.

key_terms.definition: The budgeted cost of the work actually completed so far.
Sizing software by the inputs, outputs, inquiries, files and interfaces it provides, independent of the programming language.

subtopics.memory_aid: Earned value goes on top: CPI is EV over cost, SPI is EV over plan.

subtopics.name: Closing a Project and Lessons Learned
subtopics.definition: Project closure is the formal end of a project after the business accepts the result: resources are released, accounts closed, records archived and lessons recorded.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A project that just fades out leaves budgets open, people half-assigned and no proof the business accepted what it received. Lessons that are not captured get repeated on the next project.
how_it_works: The business owner formally accepts the deliverables against the agreed acceptance criteria.
The project manager releases staff, equipment and remaining budget back to the organization.
Finance completes the financial closeout, settling final costs, vendor invoices and contracts.
Project records, decisions and approvals are archived where support teams and auditors can find them.
The team records what worked and what did not, without blame, in a searchable repository.
New projects review relevant lessons during start-up, so the knowledge changes how they are planned.
subtopics.example: A university's learning platform goes live in May, and the project manager closes the project that week, releasing the team. In July, the registrar says she never signed acceptance, two vendor invoices are unpaid and the project budget is still open to new charges. The IS auditor reports that closure skipped formal acceptance and financial closeout, and recommends a closure checklist that the sponsor must sign.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Closure follows formal acceptance by the business, not the last line of code. Lessons learned add value only when they are stored where future projects can find them and are reviewed when new projects start.

exam_traps.trap: Filing a lessons-learned report with the project documents completes the job.
exam_traps.why: A report nobody reads changes nothing. The control is a searchable repository that new projects must review during planning.

exam_traps.trap: The project can close as soon as the system is deployed.
exam_traps.why: Deployment is not acceptance. Closure needs the business owner's formal sign-off, followed by release of resources and financial closeout.

key_terms.definition: The business owner's documented sign-off that deliverables meet the agreed criteria.
Settling final project costs, invoices and contracts and closing the project's accounts.
A searchable store of past project experience that new projects consult during planning.

rows.label: When
cells: At handover, once the business formally accepts
After a period of stable operation, often months later

rows.label: Main question
cells: How well was the project run?
Did the system deliver its benefits, and do its controls work?

rows.label: Led by
cells: The project manager and team
A reviewer independent of the delivery team

rows.label: Main output
cells: Closed accounts, archived records and lessons learned
A benefits verdict, control findings and owned actions

topics.overview: Before money is committed, the organization must show that a system is worth having and that it can work. This topic covers the business case, the feasibility study, the financial measures used to compare options, and buying software from vendors. The IS auditor verifies that these decisions rest on evidence, not enthusiasm.
can_do: Spot a business case whose benefits cannot be measured or owned
Judge whether a feasibility study covers every angle before a go or no-go decision
Choose the right financial measure for a question and reject sunk-cost reasoning
Explain what makes source code escrow give real protection

subtopics.name: Building a Sound Business Case
subtopics.definition: A business case is the documented argument for an investment: the options considered, their costs, measurable benefits and risks, and who will deliver each benefit.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Approvers use it to choose the best use of limited funds. Later, the post-implementation review measures results against it, so vague or unowned benefits can never be proven.
how_it_works: Compare realistic alternatives, including doing nothing, so approvers can see the best use of the money.
State each benefit as a measurable target with a pre-project baseline; express intangible benefits through proxy measures, such as complaint counts.
Name a business owner for each benefit who will answer for delivering it.
Run sensitivity analysis on key assumptions, such as adoption rate, to show how results change if they fall short.
For legally required projects, the obligation is the justification; the case picks the lowest-cost, lowest-risk way to comply.
Update the case and have sponsors re-approve it when costs, benefits or risks change materially.
subtopics.example: A shipping company approves a $1.2 million business case for a customs-filing tool. Midway, the vendor raises its price 35% and a key benefit slips a year, but the project continues under the original approval. The IS auditor recommends that the sponsor update the case, compare it again with keeping the current process, and return it to the investment committee for re-approval.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A benefit with no number, no baseline and no owner cannot be managed or proven. The business case is a living document: when costs, benefits or risks change materially, it goes back to the sponsors for re-approval.

exam_traps.trap: 'Improved efficiency' is an acceptable benefit if the sponsor supports the project.
exam_traps.why: Without a measured baseline, a target and an owner, the benefit cannot be tracked or proven in the post-implementation review.

exam_traps.trap: A legally required project does not need a business case.
exam_traps.why: The law justifies doing it, but a business case still compares ways to comply and chooses the one with the lowest cost and risk.

key_terms.definition: The measured starting value of a benefit metric, taken before the project, so later improvement can be proven.
Testing how a result changes when a key assumption, such as adoption rate or cost, is made less favorable.
The alternative of keeping the current situation, used as the reference point for comparing other options.

subtopics.name: Feasibility Study and Build, Buy or Subscribe
subtopics.definition: A feasibility study tests whether a proposed system can work from every relevant angle before the organization commits, and informs whether to build, buy or subscribe.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A system can be technically possible yet unaffordable, unlawful, unusable or late. Checking only one angle is how organizations commit to systems that fail for reasons nobody examined.
how_it_works: Define the problem and the requirements before looking at any product or vendor.
Assess each feasibility angle with evidence, and record assumptions so approvers can challenge them.
Compare building, buying a package and subscribing to software as a service (SaaS) on total cost over several years.
Weigh requirements fit, vendor lock-in and risk alongside cost; a cheap option that misses key requirements is not cheap.
For legacy modernization, capture knowledge held by retiring staff before comparing options.
Present the results in the business case for management's go or no-go decision.

types.meaning: Can it be built and run with available or obtainable technology and skills?
Do the benefits justify the costs over the system's life?
Does it meet laws, regulations, contracts and privacy rules?
Will people and processes actually use and support it?
Can it be delivered when the business needs it?

rows.label: Fit to needs
cells: Exact fit, if delivered
Close fit, with configuration
Standard features, little tailoring

rows.label: Who controls changes
cells: The organization
The vendor controls the product roadmap
The vendor controls code, hosting and upgrades

rows.label: Main risk
cells: Cost overrun, delay and key-person dependence
Customizations that break on upgrade
Lock-in, data location and exit terms

rows.label: Key control
cells: Full development life cycle and testing
Contract terms and source code escrow
Service levels, assurance reports and an exit plan

subtopics.example: A regional airport authority compares a subscription maintenance-management service with an on-premises package. The comparison counts only first-year fees, so the subscription looks 40% cheaper. The IS auditor notes that the subscription price rises each year, exporting data at exit costs extra and the package meets more of the engineers' requirements. She recommends a seven-year total cost of ownership comparison, including exit costs and requirements fit, before the steering committee decides.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A complete feasibility study covers technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule angles before the go or no-go decision. Sourcing choices follow evidence on lifetime cost, requirements fit, lock-in and risk, not team preference or an impressive demo.

exam_traps.trap: The technology works, so the project is feasible.
exam_traps.why: Technical feasibility is one angle of five. The system must also be affordable, lawful, usable by staff and ready when the business needs it.

exam_traps.trap: Choose the option with the lowest purchase price.
exam_traps.why: Purchase price ignores running, support, upgrade and exit costs. Compare total cost of ownership over several years, along with fit and risk.

key_terms.definition: Every cost of an option over its life: purchase or build, running, support, upgrades and exit.
Dependence on one supplier that makes switching costly or slow, weakening the buyer's position.

subtopics.memory_aid: TELOS: technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility.

subtopics.name: Financial Measures and Investment Decisions
subtopics.definition: Investment measures, such as net present value (NPV), payback period, return on investment (ROI) and internal rate of return (IRR), express an investment's financial worth in different ways.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each measure answers a different question, so the wrong one can make a good project look bad. Continue-or-stop decisions also go wrong when past spending clouds judgment.
how_it_works: Discounting turns future cash flows into today's money, because a dollar received later is worth less than one today.
Match the measure to the question: lasting value suits NPV, while tight cash and quick recovery suit payback.
Compare the IRR with the organization's hurdle rate; if it is higher, the investment clears the bar.
For a continue-or-stop decision, compare only the future costs and benefits of each option, including stopping.
Leave out sunk cost, the money already spent, because it is gone whichever option is chosen.
When considering cancellation, weigh the disruption to live processes that already rely on delivered parts, not just contract penalties.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: What is the whole investment worth in today's money?
How fast do we get our money back?
What is the net gain as a percentage of cost?
What rate of return does the project earn?

rows.label: Time value of money
cells: Yes, every cash flow is discounted
Usually not, in simple payback
Usually not
Yes; it is the discount rate at which discounted gains exactly equal the costs

rows.label: Best used when
cells: Benefits are large and arrive in later years
Cash is tight and quick recovery matters
Comparing options of similar size quickly
Comparing with a required rate of return

rows.label: Blind spot
cells: Depends on the chosen discount rate
Ignores everything after payback
Ignores when returns arrive
Can mislead when options differ greatly in size

subtopics.example: A manufacturer has spent $4 million on a half-built supplier portal. Finishing it will cost $3 million more for benefits worth $2.5 million, while a subscription service would cost $1 million for similar benefits. The chief information officer argues they cannot walk away from $4 million. The IS auditor advises the steering committee to compare only remaining costs and benefits, which favor the subscription.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Decide on what lies ahead. Compare the future costs and benefits of each option, including stopping, and ignore money already spent. Choose the financial measure that fits the question being asked.

exam_traps.trap: We have spent too much to stop now.
exam_traps.why: Money already spent is gone whichever way the decision goes. Only the future costs and benefits of each option should count.

exam_traps.trap: Payback is the best measure for a ten-year platform whose benefits arrive late.
exam_traps.why: Payback ignores everything after the money is recovered, so it undervalues late benefits. NPV captures the whole life in today's money.

key_terms.definition: The rate used to convert future cash flows into today's value, reflecting the cost of money and risk.
The minimum return the organization requires before it will approve an investment.

subtopics.memory_aid: NPV values the whole journey; payback only asks when you break even.

subtopics.name: Acquiring Software from Vendors
subtopics.definition: Software acquisition is the controlled process of choosing a supplier and contracting for software, from written requirements through scored proposals to a contract that protects the buyer.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A weak selection locks the organization into a poor fit, and a weak contract leaves no remedy or exit if the vendor fails. Critical custom software also needs a plan for vendor collapse.
how_it_works: Document requirements first, then issue a request for proposal (RFP) to suitable vendors.
Score responses against weighted criteria fixed before proposals arrive, such as fit, cost, financial stability, support and security.
Check references and run demonstrations using your own business scenarios.
Build the contract around service levels, right to audit, data ownership, security duties and exit terms.
Protect critical custom software with source code escrow, released to the buyer under defined conditions such as vendor bankruptcy.
Have the escrow agent verify regularly that the deposit is complete, current and builds the production version.
subtopics.example: A hospital group's evaluation team for a pharmacy system makes 'modern interface' the top-weighted criterion after the demonstrations, favoring the vendor that presented best. The IS auditor notes that the weights changed after proposals arrived and the demonstrations used vendor-scripted data. She recommends rescoring against the original criteria and a second demonstration using the hospital's own dispensing scenarios.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Select vendors against requirements and criteria fixed in advance, and contract for the right to audit and a clean exit. Escrow protects continuity only when an independent party regularly verifies that the deposit is complete and builds the production version.

exam_traps.trap: A signed escrow agreement means the organization can maintain the software if the vendor fails.
exam_traps.why: An untested deposit may be incomplete, outdated or impossible to build. Assurance comes from independent, periodic verification that it builds the live version.

exam_traps.trap: Choose the lowest bid once vendors meet the minimum requirements.
exam_traps.why: Bids should be scored against weighted criteria set in advance. The cheapest bid may score poorly on fit, support or vendor stability.

key_terms.definition: A formal invitation asking vendors to propose how they would meet stated requirements, and at what cost.
A contract term that lets the buyer, or its auditors, examine the vendor's controls and records.
The events, such as vendor insolvency, that entitle the buyer to receive the deposited source code.

topics.overview: How a system is built shapes how it is controlled and audited. This topic covers traditional models, agile methods, DevOps pipelines, reuse-based approaches and reverse engineering, the requirements discipline under all of them, and machine learning systems. No method removes the need for approved requirements, testing and evidence.
can_do: Choose a development model to fit stable, uncertain or high-risk requirements
Explain what evidence an agile or DevOps team must still produce for an audit
Tell continuous delivery from continuous deployment in a scenario
Use a traceability matrix to show every requirement was built and tested

subtopics.name: Traditional Models: Waterfall, Spiral, Prototyping and RAD
subtopics.definition: Traditional development models structure system building into phases with sign-offs: waterfall runs them once in order, while spiral, prototyping and rapid application development (RAD) repeat cycles deliberately.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The model decides when requirements are fixed, when users first see results and where control evidence is produced. A poor fit causes costly late changes or a system users reject.
how_it_works: Waterfall runs the system development life cycle (SDLC) once, in order: feasibility, requirements, design, build, test, implementation and post-implementation review, with a sign-off before each phase.
Approved requirements are the baseline for every later phase; skipping them risks a system that misses business needs.
Each gate needs evidence: approved deliverables, test results and a documented decision to proceed.
Spiral, prototyping and RAD repeat cycles, so evidence is produced for each cycle rather than once per phase.

rows.label: Best fit
cells: Stable, well-understood requirements
Large, high-risk developments
Uncertain requirements users cannot state in advance
Business systems needed fast, with users free to join workshops

rows.label: How each cycle starts
cells: One pass only; each phase starts after sign-off
By finding and resolving the biggest risks
By letting users try a working model
With joint workshops that refine prototypes inside fixed timeboxes

rows.label: Main risk
cells: Late changes are expensive
Complex and costly to manage
The prototype is pushed into production without controls
Speed squeezes out controls, documentation and quality checks

subtopics.example: A pension fund must replace its benefits calculator, and the rules are fixed by law and fully documented. The vendor proposes prototyping to 'discover requirements with users'. The IS auditor notes that the requirements are already stable, so a waterfall approach with signed gates fits better, and recommends that the steering committee confirm the method before approving the project plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Pick the model that fits the requirements and the risk: stable needs suit waterfall, uncertain needs suit prototyping or iterative methods, and large high-risk work suits spiral. No model removes the need for approved requirements, testing evidence and sign-offs.

exam_traps.trap: A prototype that users like can go straight into production.
exam_traps.why: Prototypes and proofs of concept, including machine learning models, are built for speed. They must pass the same security, testing, monitoring and readiness checks before production use.

exam_traps.trap: Prototyping suits a project with stable, fully documented requirements.
exam_traps.why: Prototyping helps when users cannot state their needs in advance. With stable requirements, a planned sequential approach is more efficient and easier to control.

key_terms.definition: A checkpoint between phases where deliverables are reviewed and an owner formally approves moving on.
One pass through a repeated cycle of work, producing a usable or reviewable result.
A waterfall variant pairing each design phase with a matching test level, such as requirements with acceptance testing and design with integration testing.
Structured workshops where users and developers define requirements and design together, often used to speed up RAD.

subtopics.name: Agile, Scrum and Kanban
subtopics.definition: Agile development delivers working software in short, repeated cycles and adjusts to feedback; Scrum and Kanban are two common ways to organize that work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Agile reduces the risk of building the wrong thing, but its speed can erode documentation and control checks. The IS auditor must know what evidence an agile team should still produce.
how_it_works: The product owner keeps a prioritized product backlog of user stories describing what users need.
Scrum runs fixed-length sprints, and each sprint contains four events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.
Kanban pulls work continuously across a board and caps work in progress (WIP) at each stage.
Teams size stories relative to each other; velocity supports forecasts only after it stabilizes over several sprints.
Documentation is lean but sufficient: design and control decisions are recorded well enough to maintain and audit the system.
Security and privacy requirements are checked at sprint planning and verified within the sprint, not left to a final review.

rows.label: Rhythm
cells: Fixed-length sprints
Continuous flow

rows.label: Roles
cells: Product owner, Scrum Master and developers
No required roles

rows.label: Limits work by
cells: Committing to a sprint goal
WIP limits at each stage

rows.label: Best fit
cells: Iterative product development
Support or operations work with shifting priorities

illustration.caption: Waterfall moves through each stage once, in order. Agile repeats a short plan, build and review loop, so requirements can change between loops.

subtopics.example: A media company's Scrum team marks a story done once the product owner accepts its demo. In ten sampled stories touching subscriber payment data, the IS auditor finds no record of security testing or code review for six. She recommends adding security tests, peer review and updated design notes to the team's Definition of Done, so every increment carries that evidence.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Agile changes how evidence is produced, not whether it exists. Just-enough documentation must still record design and control decisions, and regulated projects can stay agile when stage gates, signed baselines and traceability provide the evidence the IS auditor needs.

exam_traps.trap: Agile teams do not need documentation.
exam_traps.why: Agile favors working software over heavy documents, not over all records. Design and control decisions must be recorded for maintenance, support and audit.

exam_traps.trap: One sprint's velocity is a sound basis for a delivery date.
exam_traps.why: Velocity varies until a team settles. Forecasts become reliable only after velocity stabilizes over several sprints.

key_terms.definition: A short description of a feature from the user's point of view, with criteria for when it is done.
The amount of work, usually in story points, a team completes per sprint.
The team's shared checklist every increment must meet, a natural place to embed testing, security and documentation controls.

subtopics.memory_aid: Scrum boxes the time; Kanban limits the work.

subtopics.name: DevOps, CI/CD and DevSecOps
subtopics.definition: DevOps joins development and operations and automates the path from code change to production; DevSecOps builds security checks into that same pipeline.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Automation applies the same checks to every change. Done well, it produces stronger change evidence than manual releases; done badly, it ships defects faster.
how_it_works: Continuous integration (CI) merges every change into the shared main line at least daily, then builds and tests it automatically.
Quality gates stop the pipeline when tests or scans fail, so a failing build cannot deploy.

Security checks shift left, earlier in development: static application security testing (SAST) scans every pull request, and software composition analysis (SCA) checks open-source parts on every build.
Scan findings go to the delivery team's backlog, with fix deadlines set by severity.
The pipeline keeps tamper-evident records linking each deployment to its approval, tests and scans.
Track delivery with DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) metrics: deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time and, since 2024, deployment rework rate.

rows.label: Release to production
cells: A person decides when
Automatic once every check passes

rows.label: Manual approval step
cells: Yes, before release
No

rows.label: Where the IS auditor looks
cells: Evidence of the release approval
Strength and coverage of the automated gates

subtopics.example: At an online insurer, developers can merge their own pull requests and edit the pipeline file that runs security scans; one recently switched off a failing scan to meet a deadline. The IS auditor recommends independent peer approval of every merge, pipeline changes limited to a platform team, and an alert whenever a quality gate is disabled.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Automated gates that block deployment on failed tests or scans give consistent, preventive assurance. In DevOps, segregation of duties moves into the pipeline: an independent peer approves each merge, only the pipeline deploys, and pipeline settings and logs are protected from the developers they govern.

exam_traps.trap: Continuous delivery means every passing build goes to production automatically.
exam_traps.why: That is continuous deployment. Continuous delivery keeps builds ready to release, but a person decides when each goes live.

exam_traps.trap: Frequent releases cannot be audited, so change control must slow them.
exam_traps.why: A well-built pipeline records approvals, tests and scans for every deployment, which can be stronger evidence than manual change tickets.

key_terms.definition: An automated pipeline check that stops a build moving forward unless set criteria are met.
Merging short-lived branches into the main line at least daily, after automated checks.
Review of a change by a peer other than its author before merge; small, focused changes get real scrutiny.

subtopics.memory_aid: The 'CD' in CI/CD means delivery or deployment; the difference is a human release decision.

subtopics.name: Object-Oriented, Component-Based and Reverse Engineering Approaches
subtopics.definition: Object-oriented and component-based development build systems from self-contained, reusable parts, while reverse engineering works backward from existing software to recover its design.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Reuse speeds delivery but spreads one flaw to every system sharing a part. Reverse engineering helps replace undocumented legacy systems but can breach license terms. Both need specific controls.
how_it_works: Object-oriented development bundles data with the procedures that act on it into objects that hide their internal details.
Component-based development assembles systems from tested, ready-made components that communicate through defined interfaces.

Service-oriented and microservice designs move risk into service interactions, so interface contracts and end-to-end monitoring are key; split or merge services case by case on value, coupling and cost.
Reused components need an inventory, version control and a plan to patch every system that uses them.
Reverse engineering analyzes compiled software to recover its design, often to document or replace a legacy system.
Many software licenses forbid decompiling, so reverse engineering vendor code needs legal review first.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Works backward from existing software to understand its design
Rebuilds or restructures a system, often using what reverse engineering recovered

rows.label: Result
cells: Recovered design, documentation or business rules
An improved or modernized system

rows.label: Key risk
cells: License breach or intellectual property claims
Business rules lost or changed in the rebuild

subtopics.example: A retailer must replace a 20-year-old inventory system whose vendor no longer exists and whose design was never documented. The architect proposes decompiling the code to recover its business rules. The IS auditor asks for legal confirmation that the license allows this, and recommends that the inventory manager validate the recovered rules before re-engineering begins.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Reuse and reverse engineering change the risks, not the need for control. Shared components need inventory, testing and patching across every system that uses them, and reverse engineering needs legal clearance and business validation of what it recovers.

exam_traps.trap: A reused component that passed testing once needs no more testing in a new system.
exam_traps.why: The new system may use it differently or send it different data. Integration testing must confirm it works in its new setting.

exam_traps.trap: The organization may reverse engineer any software it has paid for.
exam_traps.why: A license grants use, not ownership of the code. Many licenses forbid decompiling, so legal review comes before any reverse engineering.

key_terms.definition: Hiding an object's internal data so other code can reach it only through defined methods.
Letting a new class of object reuse and extend the behavior of an existing one.
Converting compiled machine code back into a form people can read, to study how it works.

subtopics.name: Requirements, Traceability and Development Tools
subtopics.definition: Requirements management records what the business needs, gets it approved, and traces each requirement through design, code and tests so nothing is missed or added unapproved.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every later phase builds on the approved requirements. Without traceability, nobody can prove each need was built and tested, or see what a proposed change will affect.
how_it_works: Business owners approve the requirements, which become the baseline for design, build and testing.
A requirements traceability matrix (RTM) links each requirement to its design element, code and test results.
The matrix shows gaps both ways: requirements with no test, and code with no approved requirement.
In behavior-driven development (BDD), business representatives, developers and testers agree on scenarios before coding, and the scenarios become automated tests.
Code from generators and artificial intelligence (AI) coding assistants is source code, so it gets the same review, testing and version control.
AI assistant use also needs license scanning of output, rules on what data may enter prompts, and user training.
subtopics.example: A bank's loan system is ready for user testing, but the business analyst cannot say whether the new affordability checks were tested. The IS auditor asks for the traceability matrix and finds three regulatory requirements with no linked test case. She reports the gap, and the project manager adds the missing tests before the go-live decision.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Approved requirements are the baseline every later phase builds on, and traceability proves each one was built and tested. Code from tools, including AI assistants, is still source code and follows the same review, testing and configuration management.

exam_traps.trap: Code produced by a generator or AI assistant is reliable enough to skip peer review.
exam_traps.why: Generated code needs the same review and testing as any code. Review cannot catch copied licensed code or secrets already sent in prompts; those need scanning and prompt rules.

exam_traps.trap: Design can start before the business approves the requirements, to save time.
exam_traps.why: Without approved requirements there is no baseline to design or test against, and the system may miss business needs.

key_terms.definition: The approved, version-controlled set of requirements that later work is measured against.
Software that automates parts of analysis, design, documentation and code generation.
A tool for building applications by configuring visual components; its output still needs review, testing and change control.

subtopics.name: Developing and Releasing Machine Learning Systems
subtopics.definition: Machine learning (ML) system development builds software that learns its behavior from training data, so the data, the trained model and its monitoring need life-cycle controls like code.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A model can pass testing and still make biased or worsening decisions as real-world data changes. Without an owner, validation and monitoring, nobody notices until customers or regulators do.
how_it_works: Name a business owner for each model, accountable for its decisions, performance targets and retirement.
Record the training data's source, quality checks and permitted use, and version it together with the model and code.
Validate the model independently before release for accuracy, unfair bias and explainability suited to its use.
Release models through normal change and release control, with a tested way back to the previous version.
Monitor live performance for drift, with alert thresholds and agreed retraining triggers.
Keep human review for high-impact decisions, and record which model version made each decision.
subtopics.example: A lender's data science team retrains its credit-scoring model monthly and pushes each version straight to production from a notebook. The chief risk officer cannot say which version scored any declined applicant. The IS auditor recommends independent validation before each release, deployment through the change pipeline, and a record of the model version used for every decision.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat a model, its training data and its monitoring as controlled system components. Each model needs a business owner, independent validation before release, normal change control and live drift monitoring. The IS auditor gives assurance on these controls; management owns the model and its outcomes.

exam_traps.trap: A model that passed validation at launch needs no further checks.
exam_traps.why: Real-world data shifts over time, so accuracy and fairness can decay. Drift monitoring with agreed retraining triggers keeps the model within its approved limits.

exam_traps.trap: Data scientists can push retrained models to production because retraining is not a code change.
exam_traps.why: A retrained model changes system behavior just as code does. It needs validation, approval and deployment through change control, with a way back.

key_terms.definition: A decline in a model's accuracy as live data moves away from the data it was trained on.
Independent testing of a model's accuracy, fairness and limits before it is used for decisions.
The historical data a model learns from; its quality and permitted use shape the model's behavior.

subtopics.memory_aid: Own it, validate it, change-control it, watch it drift.

topics.overview: Controls are cheapest and strongest when they are designed into a system from the start. This topic covers how control requirements are identified, the application controls that protect data as it flows, design choices that favor automated prevention, and the audit trails that make actions traceable. The IS auditor advises; management designs and owns the controls.
can_do: Explain why control requirements come from risk assessment and data classification
Classify a control as input, processing or output from its description
Identify an automated preventive control as the BEST design for a high-volume, well-defined risk
Describe what makes a log usable as evidence

subtopics.name: Identifying Control Requirements
subtopics.definition: Control requirements are the controls a new system must include, identified early from a risk assessment of its data, users and threats, and written into its requirements.
