subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls added after go-live cost more, fit worse and are easier to bypass. Written into the requirements, they become part of what is built and tested.
how_it_works: Classify the system's data, because its sensitivity drives how strong the controls must be.
Assess the risks to the system and its data, including legal, privacy and fraud risks.
Use threat modeling, such as STRIDE (named from the six threat types below), to find how the design could be attacked.
Turn the results into security and privacy requirements, such as phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), which fake login pages cannot capture, and collecting only necessary data.
Choose controls from catalogs, such as ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, after risk shows the need.
Management designs, builds and owns the controls; the IS auditor advises whether the requirements are adequate.

types.meaning: Pretending to be another user or system; countered by strong authentication.
Changing data or code without authorization; countered by integrity checks.
Denying an action was taken; countered by tamper-evident logs tied to authenticated identities.
Exposing data to people who should not see it; countered by encryption and access control.
Making the system unavailable; countered by capacity limits and resilience.
Gaining rights beyond those granted; countered by least privilege and authorization checks.

subtopics.example: A city transport department is designing a parking-payment app. The draft requirements collect drivers' full birth dates and home addresses 'in case they are useful later', and nobody has threat-modeled payments. At the design review, the IS auditor recommends collecting only needed data and a STRIDE review of the payment flow, for the product owner to decide.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Control requirements come from a risk assessment informed by data classification; frameworks help choose controls but do not decide what is needed. During development the IS auditor advises on control requirements, while management designs, implements and owns them.

exam_traps.trap: The IS auditor should design the controls, given audit expertise in effective controls.
exam_traps.why: Designing controls the IS auditor will later audit creates a self-review threat. The auditor advises; management designs and owns the controls.

exam_traps.trap: Applying a recognized framework checklist decides which controls a system needs.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks are menus of controls. The system's own risks and data classification decide which are needed and how strong they must be.

key_terms.definition: A structured review of a design to find how it could be attacked and which controls would stop it.
Building security requirements into a system from the start instead of adding them later.
Building privacy protections, such as data minimization and privacy-friendly defaults, into a system's design from the start.

subtopics.name: Application Controls: Input, Processing, Output
subtopics.definition: Application controls are checks built into a business application that keep its data complete, accurate, valid and authorized as it is entered, processed and reported.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most business errors and many frauds pass through applications. Controls at each stage of the data flow stop or catch problems before they reach financial records or customers.
how_it_works: Input controls check data before it is accepted, using edit checks like those below and authorization of each transaction.
Batch totals and record counts confirm every item in a batch was entered once, and only once.
Processing controls confirm data is handled correctly, using run-to-run totals, reasonableness checks and rules for handling errors.
Output controls confirm results are complete and reach the right people, by reconciling output to input and controlling report distribution.
Together the three stages protect data integrity from entry to output.

types.meaning: The value falls between set lower and upper limits.
The value matches an allowed list, such as a real department code.
The data has the right type and pattern, such as digits only in an amount field.
An extra digit calculated from the others, which catches typing and transposition errors.
A referenced record, such as a customer or vendor, already exists.
The value does not pass one set limit, such as more than 80 hours worked in a week; a range check uses two limits.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 430 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Application controls: input controls, processing controls, output controls'><rect x='8' y='24' width='112' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='64' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Input controls</text><rect x='142' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='212' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Processing controls</text><rect x='304' y='24' width='118' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='363' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Output controls</text><line x1='122' y1='46' x2='133' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M133,42 L140,46 L133,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='284' y1='46' x2='295' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M295,42 L302,46 L295,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Data enters, gets processed and comes out. Each stage has its own controls, and together they protect data integrity end to end.

subtopics.example: At a distributor, a clerk types a credit memo of 15,000 instead of 150.00, and the application accepts it. The sales manager relies on a monthly report to catch such errors. The IS auditor recommends a range check on memo amounts and supervisor approval for memos above a set value, so errors are stopped before they post.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Validate data at the point of entry. Input controls that reject invalid data before processing are cheaper and more effective than finding errors in output. Match each control to the stage it protects.

exam_traps.trap: Password protection on the entry screen is all the input control a system needs.
exam_traps.why: Restricting who can enter transactions supports input authorization, but it does not check the data. Edit checks are still needed to catch invalid, incomplete or inaccurate entries.

exam_traps.trap: Reviewing output reports is enough to catch data entry errors.
exam_traps.why: Output review finds errors after they have been processed and perhaps paid. An edit check at input blocks them before any harm.

key_terms.definition: A total of a field across a group of transactions, compared before and after entry to catch omissions.
A total carried from one processing step to the next to prove nothing was lost or added.
Data staying complete, accurate, valid and unaltered from input through processing to output.
An input check that transaction numbers run in order, flagging gaps and duplicates such as missing or repeated invoice numbers.

subtopics.name: Preventive, Automated and Built-In Controls
subtopics.definition: Built-in controls are checks an application performs automatically, ideally preventing an error or misuse before it happens rather than detecting it afterward.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A rule enforced by the system works on every transaction, every time. A person reviewing exception reports gets tired, falls behind and acts only after the damage is done.
how_it_works: Prefer preventive over detective controls for high-volume, well-defined risks, such as duplicate payments.
Prefer automated over manual controls where the rule can be stated precisely, because automation is consistent.
Build segregation of duties (SoD) into role design, so the system stops one user from both creating and approving a payment.
Treat configurable parameters, such as rates, limits and thresholds, like code: restrict who changes them, require approval and log every change.
Keep manual and detective controls for judgment calls, and as a backup where prevention is impractical.
When business process reengineering (BPR) redesigns a workflow, map each old key control to the new design so none silently disappears with a removed step.

rows.label: When it acts
cells: Before the transaction completes
After the fact, on a report or log

rows.label: Consistency
cells: Same result on every transaction
Depends on the reviewer's time and attention

rows.label: Best for
cells: High-volume, well-defined rules
Judgment calls and unusual patterns

rows.label: Example
cells: The system blocks a duplicate invoice
A monthly review of a duplicate-payment report

subtopics.example: At a utility, accounts payable clerks can both set up vendors and approve payments, and an internal team reviews a monthly conflicts report. The IS auditor finds two fictitious vendors were paid before the review caught them. She recommends roles that block the conflicting combination, and restricted, logged changes to the payment approval limit table.
subtopics.isaca_rule: For high-volume, well-defined risks, prefer automated preventive controls built into the application over manual or detective ones. Design segregation of duties into roles so conflicts are blocked, not found later, and control configuration tables as tightly as code.

exam_traps.trap: A monthly review of conflicting access is as good as preventing the conflict.
exam_traps.why: A review finds misuse only after it happens and depends on a busy reviewer. A role design that blocks the conflict stops it every time.

exam_traps.trap: Changing an approval limit is a setting, not a change, so it needs no approval.
exam_traps.why: Parameters change system behavior just as code does. They need restricted access, approval and a change log.

key_terms.definition: A table value, such as a rate or approval limit, that changes how the system behaves without new code.
A system-produced list of transactions that break a rule, for a person to review.

subtopics.name: Audit Trails, Logging and Data Lineage
subtopics.definition: An audit trail is a reliable, time-ordered record of who did what, when and to which data, designed into a system so actions can be traced and proven.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without trustworthy records, nobody can investigate fraud, prove compliance or hold users accountable. Logs added as an afterthought are often incomplete, editable or impossible to link to a person.
how_it_works: Decide during design which security-relevant events to log, such as logins, approvals, privilege changes and changes to key data.
Send logs to a central store outside the system they describe, so its own administrators cannot alter them.
Synchronize system clocks to one time source, so events from different systems line up.
Tie every logged action to an individual, authenticated identity; shared accounts break that link.
Assign who reviews which events and how often, so logs are used, not just kept.
Capture data lineage automatically as data pipelines run, recording where each item came from and how it changed.
subtopics.example: A drug maker's lab system logs result changes locally, and lab administrators can delete log entries. After a disputed test result, nobody can prove who changed it. The IS auditor recommends sending logs in real time to a central, write-protected store, synchronizing clocks and removing the shared 'labadmin' account so every change is tied to a named person.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Logs are evidence only if they are complete, centrally collected, time-synchronized, protected from alteration and tied to individual identities. Design them in with the application, and capture lineage automatically instead of documenting it by hand.

exam_traps.trap: Detailed logs kept on the application server are sufficient and reliable audit evidence.
exam_traps.why: The administrators of that server can alter or delete them. Evidence needs central storage that the people being logged cannot change.

exam_traps.trap: Hand-maintained lineage documents are enough to trace data.
exam_traps.why: Manual records drift out of date as pipelines change. Lineage captured automatically at run time and stored centrally stays accurate.

key_terms.definition: Proof strong enough that a user cannot credibly deny having performed an action.
A record of where data came from and every transformation it went through.
A log protected so any change or deletion can be detected.

topics.overview: Testing proves a system is ready before the business relies on it. This topic covers the levels of testing, test types and techniques, performance and specialized testing, test environments and data, and the go-live decision. Each test answers a different question, and go-live rests on evidence that agreed criteria were met.
can_do: Name the test level or type that fits a scenario, such as an interface fault or business acceptance
Tell load, stress, volume and soak testing apart
Explain why production data must be masked before it reaches a test environment
Judge whether a go-live decision rests on signed-off criteria and formal risk acceptance

subtopics.name: Levels of Testing
subtopics.definition: Testing levels build confidence step by step: unit, integration and system tests check the software, then user acceptance testing confirms it meets business needs.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each level catches different defects. Skipping one, or letting the wrong people run it, lets defects reach production, where fixes cost more.
how_it_works: Testing moves from small to large; each level starts only when the one before has met its exit criteria.
User acceptance testing (UAT) follows successful system testing and comes before cutover, in a production-like environment.
The business owner, not the development team, approves the UAT result against criteria agreed in advance.
The test pyramid keeps many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and the fewest slow end-to-end tests.
Integration runs top-down, with stubs for unfinished lower modules, finding interface errors early; or bottom-up, with drivers, so testing starts before upper modules exist.

rows.label: Scope
cells: One module or function
Interfaces and data passed between components
The complete system, including non-functional needs
Business processes, end to end

rows.label: Usually run by
cells: Developers
Developers or testers
An independent test team
Business users

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: Does this piece work alone?
Do the pieces work together?
Does the system meet its requirements?
Does it meet business needs?

rows.label: Mainly checks
cells: Verification: the module matches its specification
Verification: interfaces match the design
Verification: the system meets documented requirements
Validation: it is the right system for the business

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 408 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Testing levels: unit, integration, system, then user acceptance testing'><rect x='8' y='24' width='80' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='48' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Unit</text><rect x='110' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='156' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Integration</text><rect x='224' y='24' width='82' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='265' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>System</text><rect x='328' y='24' width='72' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='364' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>UAT</text><line x1='90' y1='46' x2='101' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M101,42 L108,46 L101,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='204' y1='46' x2='215' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M215,42 L222,46 L215,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='308' y1='46' x2='319' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M319,42 L326,46 L319,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Testing grows in scope: one unit, then units working together, then the whole system, then the business users' acceptance.

subtopics.example: A county court's e-filing system passes system testing against every documented requirement. In UAT, clerks find it rejects filings that combine two case types, a daily event never captured in the requirements. The IS auditor explains that system testing verified the specification while UAT validates business fit, and recommends the court administrator withhold acceptance until change control resolves the gap.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Each test level has its own purpose and owner. UAT is the business's acceptance: it follows successful system testing, runs in a production-like environment, and is approved by business users against criteria agreed before testing began.

exam_traps.trap: The development team can run and sign off UAT to save time.
exam_traps.why: UAT is the business confirming the system meets its needs. A developer sign-off removes the independent business judgment UAT exists to provide.

exam_traps.trap: A fault in data passed between two modules calls for more unit testing.
exam_traps.why: Unit tests check pieces alone. Faults in the data passed between components are found by integration testing.

key_terms.definition: Stand-in code imitating an unfinished lower module, used in top-down integration testing.
Stand-in code calling a module in place of an unfinished upper module, used in bottom-up integration testing.
Acceptance testing by IT or quality staff against documented technical specifications; UAT covers business needs.
Checking a product against its specifications and design: did we build the system right?
Checking that a product meets real business needs in use: did we build the right system?

subtopics.name: Test Types and Techniques
subtopics.definition: Test types and techniques describe what a test is trying to find and how its test cases are chosen, from regression checks to boundary values and security probes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Test time is always limited. The right types and techniques find the most serious defects for the effort, and show whether a passing test suite really proves anything.
how_it_works: Regression testing reruns existing tests after any change to confirm that what worked before still works.
Choose a test design approach by how much of the code testers can see: black-box, white-box or gray-box, as listed below.
Boundary-value analysis tests values on and either side of each limit, where off-by-one errors cluster.
Risk-based testing concentrates effort where failure would have the greatest impact and is most likely.
Code coverage shows which code ran; mutation testing injects small faults to show whether the tests catch them.
Dynamic (DAST) and interactive (IAST) application security testing probe running applications; runtime application self-protection (RASP) guards them live in production.

rows.label: How it works
cells: Probes the running application from outside, like an attacker
Adds sensors inside the application that watch its code while tests run
An agent inside the live application detects and blocks attacks

rows.label: When it is used
cells: Testing
Testing
Production

rows.label: Kind of control
cells: Detective: finds flaws
Detective: finds flaws with code-level detail
Preventive: stops attacks as they happen

subtopics.example: A water utility changes one rounding rule in its billing engine, and the team lead wants to release it without regression testing because 'only one line changed'. Rounding feeds tax, late fees and payment plans. The IS auditor recommends rerunning the billing regression suite, and asks that test effort be weighted toward the calculations where an error would hit the most customers.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Test effort follows risk: concentrate it where failure impact and likelihood are highest. Every change gets regression testing, and coverage alone proves only which code ran, not whether the tests would catch a defect.

exam_traps.trap: High code coverage proves the test suite is effective.
exam_traps.why: Coverage shows which lines ran, not whether tests check the results. Mutation testing shows whether the suite catches injected faults.

exam_traps.trap: A small change does not need regression testing.
exam_traps.why: Small changes often break things elsewhere. Regression testing is how teams confirm existing functions still work.

key_terms.definition: The share of code lines or paths executed by a test suite.
Deliberately planting small faults in code to check whether the tests detect them.
Grouping inputs the system should treat the same way, then testing one value from each group.

types.meaning: Tests behavior through inputs and outputs, designed from requirements without seeing the code; typical of system and acceptance testing.
Tests internal logic and paths, designed from the code itself; typical of unit testing and code review.
Uses partial knowledge of internals, such as the database design, to aim outside-in tests more precisely.

subtopics.name: Performance and Specialized Testing
subtopics.definition: Performance and specialized tests check how a system behaves in real conditions: under heavy or long load, with large data volumes, beside other systems, and with real users.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A system can pass every functional test and still collapse on payday or slow down after a week. These tests expose failures that appear only at scale or over time.
how_it_works: Set performance targets from business needs, such as response time at peak volume, before testing starts.
Run performance tests in an environment that matches production in data volume, infrastructure tier and load pattern.
Sociability testing confirms the new system can share the production environment without harming existing systems or being harmed by them.
Alpha testing uses internal users at the developer's site; beta testing gives a near-final version to selected real users.
Recovery testing deliberately causes failures, such as stopping a server, to confirm the system fails safely and restores as designed.
Record results against targets; each miss becomes a defect to fix or a risk for management to accept.

types.meaning: Checks behavior at the expected peak number of users or transactions.
Pushes beyond expected limits to find the breaking point and see how the system fails.
Loads large amounts of data, such as years of records, to check processing and storage.
Holds expected load for a long period to expose memory leaks and slow decline.

subtopics.example: An online tax-filing service passes its load test at expected peak traffic. Two days into filing season, response times climb until the site fails. The IS auditor finds no soak test was run and that test servers held a tenth of production's data. She recommends a soak test on production-scale data before next season.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Performance results count only when targets come from business needs and tests run in a production-like environment. Match the test to the risk: peak load, breaking point, data volume, endurance or coexistence with other systems.

exam_traps.trap: A load test at expected peak proves the system will cope through a whole busy week.
exam_traps.why: Load tests are short. Leaks and slow decline appear only over time, which soak testing is designed to expose.

exam_traps.trap: Results from a small test server can be scaled up to predict production.
exam_traps.why: Performance does not scale in a straight line. Tests are valid evidence only on production-like data volumes, tiers and load.

key_terms.definition: Testing that a new system works alongside existing systems without conflict.
Early testing of a near-complete system by internal users, usually at the developer's site.
Testing of a near-final release by selected real users in their own setting, before general release.

subtopics.name: Test Environments and Test Data
subtopics.definition: Test environments and test data are the separate systems and data sets used for testing; they should resemble production closely without exposing real production data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Tests in an unrealistic environment give false confidence. Copies of live personal data in loosely controlled test systems are a common cause of data breaches.
how_it_works: Keep development, test and production environments separate, with different access rights and no developer write access to production.
Make the test environment production-like in configuration and software versions, and in data volume for performance work.
Mask or pseudonymize personal data before it is extracted from production, not after it lands in test.
Use synthetic data where real patterns are not needed.
Control test data like any sensitive data set: owner approval, restricted access and deletion when testing ends.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Replaces sensitive values with realistic fakes
Swaps identifiers for tokens that a separately held key can re-link
Generates artificial records with no link to real people

rows.label: Still personal data?
cells: No, but only if no one can re-identify people from it
Yes, because people can be re-identified
No

rows.label: Best for
cells: Realistic tests using production patterns
Tests needing consistent identities across systems
Early testing and unusual edge cases

subtopics.example: An airline's analytics vendor finished testing a loyalty upgrade three months ago, but its test environment still holds a pseudonymized copy of 2 million member records, with the re-linking key on the same server. The IS auditor notes that pseudonymized data is still personal data. She recommends moving the key under the data owner's separate control and deleting the test copy, as the test data procedure requires.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Non-production environments should not hold directly identifiable personal data, so mask or pseudonymize it before it leaves production. Test environments must be separate from production but similar enough that test results are reliable.

exam_traps.trap: Copy production data to test, then mask it there.
exam_traps.why: Once copied, real data sits unprotected in a less controlled environment. Masking must happen before or during extraction, inside production.

exam_traps.trap: Testing directly in production is the most realistic option.
exam_traps.why: It puts live data and service at risk and mixes test activity with real transactions. Testing belongs in a separate, production-like environment.

key_terms.definition: Keeping development, test and production separate, with different access rights for each.
A test setup that mirrors production in configuration, versions and, where it matters, scale.

subtopics.name: Go-Live Readiness and Acceptance
subtopics.definition: Go-live readiness is the evidence-based decision that a system may enter production, made by accountable owners against acceptance criteria agreed before testing started.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Deadline pressure pushes teams to launch untested or broken systems. Signed criteria and visible risks keep the decision with the people who own the consequences.
how_it_works: Agree on measurable acceptance criteria, tied to business requirements, with the business owner before testing.
Rehearse the cutover in stages, covering technical and business steps, and confirm users are trained and support teams are ready before go-live.
Collect sign-offs on a readiness checklist: testers certify that controls meet requirements, and a senior official accredits the system, accepting residual risk and exceptions.
Fix high-risk findings before go-live, or have the accountable risk owner formally accept them.
If user acceptance testing (UAT) misses its exit criteria, defer go-live; any deviation is decided and documented by the steering committee.
Under a fixed deadline, release a fully tested smaller scope and defer the rest with documented risk acceptance.

rows.label: What it is
cells: A technical assessment of whether controls meet requirements
A management decision to accept the residual risk and approve operation

rows.label: Who does it
cells: Assessors or testers
An authorized senior official

rows.label: Output
cells: Evidence and a list of weaknesses
Authority to operate the system

subtopics.example: A home-care provider plans to launch a visit-scheduling system on Monday. UAT is signed, but the readiness checklist shows only 40% of coordinators trained and no help desk scripts. The project director wants to train after launch. The IS auditor reports the gap against the agreed readiness criteria to the steering committee, which decides to delay or formally accept the risk.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Go-live rests on readiness criteria signed off by accountable owners, with exceptions visible. High-risk issues are fixed first or formally accepted by the risk owner. The IS auditor recommends and reports; management makes the go-live decision.

exam_traps.trap: The IS auditor should block go-live when serious issues remain.
exam_traps.why: The IS auditor reports the risk and recommends; management decides and owns the outcome. Approving or blocking go-live would impair the auditor's independence.

exam_traps.trap: To meet a fixed deadline, shorten testing across the whole release.
exam_traps.why: Quietly cutting testing hides risk. Ship a fully tested smaller scope and defer the rest with documented risk acceptance.

key_terms.definition: Measurable conditions, agreed with the business owner before testing, that a system must meet to be accepted.
A documented decision by the accountable owner to retain a known risk rather than mitigate it first.
A practice run of the switch-over steps, used to find and fix problems before the real event.

topics.overview: Once a system is built, every component must be known, every change approved and every release reversible. This topic covers configuration baselines, change and release control for a new system, deployment strategies with rollback, and the integrity of the software supply chain. The IS auditor looks for evidence that what runs in production is exactly what was approved.
can_do: Decide whether an item, such as a schema change or feature flag, belongs under configuration management
Explain why developers must not move their own code into production
Choose between canary and blue-green releases and judge a rollback plan
Explain what an SBOM and signed builds prove, and what they do not

subtopics.name: Configuration Management and Baselines
subtopics.definition: Configuration management identifies and controls every component that makes up a system, so the exact approved version of each one is always known.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If nobody knows exactly which versions make up the working system, changes cannot be assessed, failures cannot be traced and the system cannot be rebuilt reliably.
how_it_works: Identify every configuration item: code, requirements, designs, scripts, configuration files, builds and environment definitions.
Freeze an approved set as the baseline, and measure every later change against it.
Keep every configuration item in version control, so any approved build can be rebuilt exactly; production drift checks are in 4A8.2.
Write database schema changes as versioned migration scripts that are reviewed, tested and deployed through change management.
Define servers and networks as infrastructure as code (IaC), scanned for misconfigurations before use; with GitOps, an agent keeps live systems matching approved state.
Give feature flags named owners, versioned definitions, retirement dates and logged, authorized changes.
subtopics.example: A software firm versions its code, but requirement documents and build scripts sit on laptops. When a client disputes what release 4.2 was meant to do, nobody can rebuild it or show which requirements it delivered. The IS auditor recommends putting requirements, build scripts and environment definitions under version control as configuration items in each release baseline.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Everything that defines the system is a configuration item under formal change control, not just source code. Requirements, schema changes, environment definitions and feature flags all belong in the baseline; direct production edits bypass it.

exam_traps.trap: Only source code needs to be a configuration item.
exam_traps.why: Requirements, designs, scripts, settings and builds also define the system. Leaving them out makes the baseline incomplete and changes untraceable.

exam_traps.trap: A quick manual edit in production is acceptable if it solves the problem.
exam_traps.why: Manual edits skip review and leave production different from the baseline, so the next release can fail and nobody can trace why.

key_terms.definition: Any component that must be controlled to keep a system working, such as code, a design or a build script.
An approved, frozen set of configuration items that later changes are measured against.
Using a Git repository as the single source of approved system state, with an agent correcting any drift.
A setting that switches a feature on or off without new code.

subtopics.name: Change and Release Control in the Delivery Pipeline
subtopics.definition: Change and release control in development makes sure every change moving from code to production is requested, tested, approved on evidence and deployed by someone other than its author.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most production failures follow a change. A developer who can approve or deploy their own code can slip in errors or fraud unnoticed.
how_it_works: Log each change as a request linked to its requirement, stating purpose, impact and a rollback plan.
Build the change once in the pipeline after an independent peer review, with automated tests and security scans as gates that block a failing build.
The change advisory board (CAB) assesses risk and readiness of significant changes and advises the change authority, who approves on attached evidence.
Deploy through the pipeline or by operations staff, never by the code's author.
Coordinate releases across teams by risk tier, using interface contracts to catch cross-team breaks before release.
Once live, changes follow operational change control (4A8.1), with its standard, normal and emergency routes.
subtopics.example: At an online retailer, a developer marks a pricing change as tested, and the change authority approves it on that note alone. The pipeline deploys it on Friday, and prices for 2,000 items drop to zero for an hour. The IS auditor finds no test results attached and recommends that the pipeline block deployment until test evidence is attached and an independent reviewer approves.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Apply segregation of duties: those who write code do not approve or deploy it. A change moves forward only on evidence, such as attached test and scan results, never on its author's word. The CAB advises; the change authority decides.

exam_traps.trap: The CAB plans and carries out significant changes.
exam_traps.why: The CAB assesses risk, impact and readiness and advises whoever authorizes the change. Planning and doing the change stay with the change owner and implementers.

exam_traps.trap: Approve the change because the developer confirms it was tested.
exam_traps.why: The requester's word is not evidence. The change authority approves only on attached test results, and someone other than the author deploys the release.

key_terms.definition: The person or body empowered to approve a given type of change.
A tested, approved bundle of one or more changes deployed to production together.
An agreed definition of the data and behavior one component offers another, checked by automated tests.

subtopics.name: Deployment Strategies and Rollback
subtopics.definition: Deployment strategies control how a new release reaches users, limiting the harm of a bad release and keeping a tested way back to a working state.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Even well-tested releases fail in production. Staged rollouts limit how many users are affected, and a rehearsed rollback decides whether an outage lasts minutes or days.
how_it_works: Release to a small share of users or regions first, and widen only while error rates and response times stay within agreed limits.
If a staged rollout starts failing, halt it and follow the rollback playbook first; investigate the cause afterward.
A sound rollback plan is tested and time-bound, and restores data and configuration, not just the old code.
If rolling back would destroy data the new release has already written, preserve that data first, then apply a quick fix (hotfix) or roll forward.
Some teams agree on an error budget, an allowed amount of failure; once it is used up, non-essential releases pause until reliability recovers.

rows.label: How it works
cells: Sends a small share of live traffic to the new version
Runs two identical environments and switches all traffic to the new one

rows.label: Limits harm by
cells: Exposing only a few users at first
Allowing an instant switch back

rows.label: Cost
cells: Little extra infrastructure, but needs good monitoring
Two full environments during the release

rows.label: Watch for
cells: Expanding before health signals are clear
Database changes the old version cannot read

subtopics.example: A ride-hailing app's reliability target allows 40 minutes of failed requests a month. By mid-month, three faulty releases have used 55 minutes, yet the product team plans two more feature releases that week. The IS auditor notes that the agreed error-budget policy pauses non-essential releases once the budget is spent, and recommends that the release manager enforce it and put reliability fixes first.
subtopics.isaca_rule: When a release starts failing, stop the spread and restore service first, following the tested playbook; root cause comes after. A rollback plan counts only if it is tested, time-bound and restores data and configuration while preserving valid new data.

exam_traps.trap: Find the root cause before stopping a failing rollout.
exam_traps.why: Every minute of investigation lets the bad release reach more users. Halt and roll back first, then investigate.

exam_traps.trap: Roll back at once, whatever data the new release has written.
exam_traps.why: A blind rollback can destroy valid new transactions. Preserve that data first, then restore service by hotfix or roll forward.

key_terms.definition: Fixing a failed release by deploying a corrected version instead of returning to the old one.
The amount of unreliability a service may have in a period before releases must slow down.
Pre-agreed, tested steps and decision points for reversing a release.

subtopics.name: Software Supply Chain Integrity
subtopics.definition: Software supply chain integrity is assurance that every component and build is known, comes from a trusted source and was not altered on its way to production.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most software is assembled from outside parts. One poisoned library or tampered build can compromise every system using it, and teams that do not know their parts cannot respond quickly.
how_it_works: Keep a software bill of materials (SBOM) listing each product's components, versions and dependencies.
Run software composition analysis (SCA) on every build to flag components with known vulnerabilities.
Sign each build artifact, such as a container image, when it is built, and record its provenance: where, how and from which sources it was built.
Verify the signature before deployment, and block anything unsigned or altered.
Scan open-source licenses before merge and isolate strong copyleft code, which can force publishing linked code on distribution or, under the GNU Affero GPL (AGPL), for hosted services.
Match supplier checks to risk: contract basics for all suppliers, deeper checks for critical ones.
subtopics.example: A serious flaw is announced in a popular logging library. A financial technology firm's security lead asks which of 60 applications use it, and teams spend a week searching code by hand. The IS auditor recommends an SBOM for every build. She also finds that images are signed but never checked before deployment, and recommends enforcing signature verification.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Know your components and prove your builds: keep an SBOM for every product, sign artifacts at build time and verify signatures before deployment. A control that is created but never checked, such as an unverified signature, gives no assurance.

exam_traps.trap: An SBOM fixes vulnerable components.
exam_traps.why: An SBOM is an inventory. It shows where a vulnerable component sits, but someone still has to patch it.

exam_traps.trap: Signing images at build time is enough.
exam_traps.why: A signature proves nothing unless it is checked. Verification before deployment is what blocks altered or unknown images.

key_terms.definition: An open-source license, such as the GNU GPL, that requires releasing linked code on distribution; the AGPL extends this to hosted services.
A statement alongside an SBOM saying whether a listed component's known flaw actually affects the product.
Graded build-integrity levels; meet the level a contract requires first, then raise levels where risk justifies the cost.

topics.topic_name: System Migration, Infrastructure Deployment, and Data Conversion
topics.overview: Moving from an old system to a new one is where data quietly goes missing and services break. This topic covers how to switch users over, how to prove converted data is complete and accurate, and how to prepare the new platform and retire the old one safely. Each step needs controls, evidence and a way back.
can_do: Choose parallel, pilot, phased or direct cutover to fit the risk
Explain what record counts, control totals and hash totals each prove in a conversion
Identify who approves data mapping and cleansing decisions
Name the checks needed before production data is loaded or a legacy system is switched off

subtopics.name: Cutover Strategies
subtopics.definition: A cutover strategy is the plan for switching users and work from an old system to a new one: in parallel, by pilot, in phases or all at once.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Cutover is when the business first depends on the new system. The method decides how much harm a hidden defect can do and whether a way back still exists.
how_it_works: Choose the method by risk, complexity and how well the business could tolerate a failure.
Set go/no-go checkpoints during cutover, each with reconciliation results and named decision makers.
For a parallel run, set tolerances for differences per data category by materiality (how much a difference would matter), with rules for investigating each one.
Keep a tested fallback plan, and keep the legacy system able to run until the new one is accepted.
If checks show an unexplained material variance, stop at the checkpoint so management can proceed or fall back on the evidence.

rows.label: How it works
cells: Old and new run side by side and results are reconciled
One site or group goes first
Rolled out in stages by module or business unit
Everyone switches at once

rows.label: Safety
cells: Strongest evidence and easy fallback
Real use, on a limited scale
Each wave limits damage and allows correction
Weakest; hard to go back

rows.label: Cost and speed
cells: Highest cost and staff effort
Moderate
Longer overall; may need temporary interfaces
Fastest and cheapest

rows.label: Best for
cells: High-impact financial systems
Proving a system before wide rollout
Large, multi-unit replacements
Simple, low-risk systems

subtopics.example: A national retailer plans to switch all 300 stores to a new point-of-sale system on one Sunday. The vendor has never run it at this scale, and stores cannot trade without it. The IS auditor notes that a big-bang cutover leaves no easy way back, and recommends a pilot in five stores, followed by regional waves, each with a go/no-go checkpoint and a tested fallback to the old tills.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the cutover method to risk and complexity, and always keep a tested way back. An unexplained material variance at a checkpoint means stop: management decides to proceed or fall back based on evidence, never on schedule pressure.

exam_traps.trap: Big-bang cutover suits a complex, high-impact system because it completes the transition fastest.
exam_traps.why: Switching everything at once leaves no easy way back. High-impact systems suit a parallel run or pilot, and large multi-unit replacements suit phased waves, so problems surface while fallback exists.

exam_traps.trap: Proceed with go-live despite an unexplained material variance, and correct it afterward.
exam_traps.why: Once customers transact on bad data, errors spread and are hard to unwind. Stop at the checkpoint and decide on evidence.

key_terms.definition: Tested steps for returning to the legacy system if the cutover fails.
A planned decision point where named managers proceed or stop based on agreed evidence.
The largest difference between old and new results that is accepted without investigation.

subtopics.name: Data Conversion Controls
subtopics.definition: Data conversion controls make sure data moved from an old system into a new one arrives complete and accurate with its meaning unchanged, and that this can be proven.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Conversion is where records silently disappear, duplicate or change meaning. Errors loaded into a live system spread into every report and decision that relies on the data.
how_it_works: The data owner approves the mapping rules that say how each old field becomes a new one.
Data is cleansed before loading, with the data owner authorizing each correction.
Every record extracted, loaded and rejected is counted; rejected records are fixed and reloaded or formally written off.
Source and target are reconciled using the totals compared below, and every difference is investigated and explained.
A cross-reference from each legacy key to its new key is kept with the conversion logs, so any record can be traced.
The data owner reviews the reconciliation results and signs off acceptance of the converted data before go-live.

rows.label: What is added up
cells: The number of records
A meaningful amount field, such as balances
A field that is meaningless to add, such as account numbers

rows.label: What a match shows
cells: No records were lost or duplicated
Money values were not changed
Key identifiers were not altered

rows.label: What it can miss
cells: Changed values inside a complete set
Errors that cancel out, and non-amount fields
Which record is wrong

subtopics.example: A health insurer migrates 4 million member records. IT writes the mapping rules alone and decides that a blank coverage end date means coverage is active. The IS auditor finds the claims director never approved this, and that only 50 records were spot-checked. She recommends owner approval of all mapping rules and full reconciliation of counts and totals before go-live.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Prove a conversion with full source-to-target reconciliation of counts and totals, with every variance explained, not with spot checks. Mapping and cleansing decisions change what data means, so the data owner approves them, not IT alone.

exam_traps.trap: Spot-checking a sample of converted records proves the conversion was complete.
exam_traps.why: A sample can miss lost or duplicated records. Full reconciliation of record counts and totals proves completeness for the whole population.

exam_traps.trap: IT should set the mapping rules because it knows both systems.
exam_traps.why: Mapping decides what converted data means to the business. The data owner is accountable for that meaning and must approve the rules.

key_terms.definition: Rules stating how each field in the old system translates into a field in the new one.
Correcting or removing inaccurate, duplicate or incomplete records before they are loaded.
A retained table linking each legacy record key to its new key, so converted records can be traced back.

subtopics.name: Infrastructure Deployment and Migration Planning
subtopics.definition: Infrastructure deployment and migration planning prepares the new platform, moves systems in a safe order and retires the old environment without losing required data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Data loaded onto an unhardened platform is exposed from day one. Moving systems without knowing their dependencies breaks interfaces, and switching off the old system too soon can destroy records the law requires.
how_it_works: Build the target platform and verify it against its approved security baseline before any production data is loaded.
Discover systems, data flows and interfaces first, especially after a merger or acquisition.
Map dependencies, then group tightly coupled systems into the same migration wave.
Choose each application's migration path by its business value, not one rule for the whole portfolio.
Confirm legal, regulatory and contractual retention needs are met, for example by archiving, before any irreversible step.
Decommission the legacy system only after final reconciliation is signed off and its records are archived in a readable form.

types.meaning: Move the application as it is to new infrastructure, such as the cloud.
Move with small changes, such as switching to a managed database service.
Redesign and rebuild the application to use the new platform fully.
Replace the application with a commercial product or subscription service.
Switch the application off because it is no longer needed.
Keep the application where it is for now, and revisit the decision later.

subtopics.example: After buying a competitor, a logistics firm plans to move its 40 applications to the cloud in alphabetical order. The IS auditor notes that nobody has mapped which applications share databases, and the old warehouse system holds shipping records that must be kept for seven years. She recommends dependency mapping to set the waves and an archive plan approved by legal counsel before decommissioning.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Secure the destination before moving data, map dependencies before planning waves, and protect required records before anything irreversible. Decommissioning is the last step, after reconciliation sign-off and archiving, never a cost-saving shortcut the day after go-live.

exam_traps.trap: Harden the new servers after the migration, once the data is there.
exam_traps.why: Production data would sit on an unverified platform. Check the target against its approved security baseline before any data loads.

exam_traps.trap: Switch off the legacy system right after go-live to save costs.
exam_traps.why: Without final reconciliation sign-off and archived records, there is no fallback, and records required by law may be lost.

key_terms.definition: The approved minimum security configuration a platform must meet before it is used.
Identifying which applications, databases and interfaces rely on each other.
A group of related systems moved together in one planned step.

topics.overview: After a new system settles in, the organization checks whether it delivered the promised benefits and whether its controls work in real use. This topic covers when to hold the review, what the IS auditor examines and how results are acted on. The business owns the benefits; the IS auditor gives independent assurance.
can_do: State the primary purpose of a post-implementation review and when it should happen
Choose objective, measured evidence of benefits over opinions and assertions
Treat low adoption and user workarounds as symptoms to investigate
Name who owns a benefit shortfall and how recommendations are followed up

subtopics.name: Purpose and Timing of the Review
subtopics.definition: A post-implementation review (PIR) checks, once a system has run stably for a while, whether it delivered the business case benefits and works as designed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Projects are approved on promised benefits. Without a review, nobody learns whether the money was well spent, and benefit shortfalls and weak controls go unnoticed.
how_it_works: Schedule the review after a period of stable operation, often a few months, so the data reflects normal use.
Compare realized benefits with the targets and baselines in the approved business case.
Check that the system meets its requirements and that its designed controls operate.
Scale the depth of the review to the significance and risk of the change, as set out in policy.
Capture lessons that improve future projects and business cases.

rows.label: What the data shows
cells: Start-up problems and the learning curve
Normal use and real benefit results
Changed processes and lost context

rows.label: Can findings be acted on?
cells: Too early to judge benefits
Yes, while fixes are still practical
Too late to correct cheaply

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 476 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Post-implementation review happens after the system goes live and settles in'><rect x='8' y='24' width='120' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='68' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>System goes live</text><rect x='150' y='24' width='120' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='210' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Settle-in period</text><rect x='292' y='24' width='176' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='380' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Post-implementation review</text><line x1='130' y1='46' x2='141' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M141,42 L148,46 L141,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='272' y1='46' x2='283' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M283,42 L290,46 L283,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Go live, let the system settle, then review. Waiting for stable operation means benefits and controls are judged on real data.

subtopics.example: A port authority's cargo-tracking system launches on time and under budget, so the chief operating officer proposes canceling the post-implementation review planned for month six. The business case promised a 30% cut in container dwell time. The IS auditor recommends keeping the review, because on-time delivery says nothing about dwell time, and confirms that a pre-launch dwell-time baseline was recorded.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The primary purpose of a post-implementation review is to confirm that the business case benefits were realized, alongside whether controls work. Hold it once the system has run stably long enough to measure, and scale its depth to the risk of the change.

exam_traps.trap: A project delivered on time and on budget needs no post-implementation review, or only a technical bug check.
exam_traps.why: On time and on budget shows the project ran well, not that the investment paid off. The review's primary purpose is to confirm business case benefits and working controls.

exam_traps.trap: Hold the review right after go-live, while the project team is still together.
exam_traps.why: Early results show start-up issues and the learning curve, not normal performance. Wait for stable operation so benefits can be measured.

key_terms.definition: Confirming that the business outcomes promised in the business case were actually achieved.
The time after go-live when start-up issues are fixed and users settle into normal work.
A review held at project closure of how the project itself was run; unlike a PIR, it does not measure realized benefits.

subtopics.name: Review Scope: Controls, Benefits and Evidence
subtopics.definition: In a post-implementation review, the IS auditor gives assurance on whether designed controls work in live operation and whether benefit claims rest on objective evidence.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Project teams naturally report success. An objective check of controls and evidence shows whether the system is really safe and delivering, before problems become part of daily work.
how_it_works: Test whether input, processing, output and access controls work in production as designed and meet their objectives.
Judge benefit claims on measured data compared with the pre-project baseline, not on assertions or opinion.
Report a missing benefit baseline as a finding, because benefits cannot be proven without one.
Treat user workarounds as signs of a missing or broken control, and rate the resulting risk.
Find out why adoption is low before recommending fixes such as training.
Make sure the reviewer is independent: not on the delivery team and not an IS auditor who designed the controls; advisory input alone does not impair independence.
subtopics.example: A rail operator plans to have the IS auditor who designed its rostering system's approval controls lead their post-implementation review. The chief audit executive (CAE) assigns an IS auditor who had no part in the project. Testing approvals on live rosters, the new reviewer finds two supervisor override paths that skip approval entirely and reports them to the operations director for remediation.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The IS auditor's distinct contribution is assurance that controls work in real use and that benefits rest on objective evidence. Workarounds and low adoption are symptoms whose causes come first, and no reviewer judges their own work.

exam_traps.trap: The project manager's statement that benefits were achieved is enough evidence.
exam_traps.why: It is an assertion from an interested party. Measured results compared with a pre-project baseline are objective evidence.

exam_traps.trap: Low adoption means users need more training.
exam_traps.why: Low adoption is a symptom. Users may avoid a slow, incomplete or badly designed system, so find the cause first.

key_terms.definition: The result a control is meant to achieve, such as only authorized payments being made.
Measured, verifiable data that does not depend on the opinion of the person supplying it.
The risk to objectivity when someone reviews work they produced or were responsible for.
An informal way users get a task done outside the designed process, often bypassing a control.

subtopics.name: Acting on the Results
subtopics.definition: Acting on review results means turning each finding into an owned, dated action tracked to closure, with the business sponsor owning any benefit shortfall.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A review that ends in a report changes nothing. Owned, tracked actions are how missing benefits are recovered and control gaps are closed.
how_it_works: Discuss each recommendation with management, which decides the response and agrees on the corrective action.
Give each action a named owner, a due date and a status tracked until it is closed.
Assign a benefit shortfall to the business sponsor who committed to the benefit, not to IT or the closed project team.
If management accepts a risk that seems beyond appetite, or actions stall, the chief audit executive (CAE) escalates to senior management or the audit committee.
Feed lessons, such as recording baselines, into future business cases and project methods.
Follow up to confirm that actions were taken and worked.
subtopics.example: Nine months after a post-implementation review of a property tax system, four of six agreed actions are overdue, and the revenue director now calls the missing refund-approval control 'not worth fixing'. The IS auditor confirms each action's status and reports the overdue items. Because the accepted risk exceeds the stated risk appetite, the chief audit executive (CAE) raises it with senior management and then the audit committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Benefits realization is a business responsibility: the sponsor who promised the benefits owns the plan to close a shortfall. The IS auditor recommends and follows up; management decides, acts, and accepts any residual risk it chooses not to mitigate.

exam_traps.trap: IT should own the plan to close a benefit shortfall.
exam_traps.why: IT delivers the system, but benefits come from the business using it. The sponsor who committed to them owns the recovery plan.

exam_traps.trap: The IS auditor's job ends when the review report is issued.
exam_traps.why: Recommendations need follow-up. The IS auditor confirms that owned, dated actions were completed and effective, and escalates if they stall.

key_terms.definition: Recording each agreed action's owner, due date and status until it is closed.
The gap between the benefits promised in the business case and those actually achieved.
A later check by the IS auditor that agreed actions were completed and are working.

key_terminologies.Project charter: The sponsor-approved document that formally authorizes a project and gives the project manager authority over its resources.
key_terminologies.Critical path: The longest chain of dependent tasks; it sets the shortest possible project duration and has no slack.
key_terminologies.Earned value management (EVM): Tracking cost and schedule by comparing the value of work done with the planned value and the actual cost.
key_terminologies.Business case: The justification for an investment, comparing options and stating measurable benefits, each with an owner.
key_terminologies.Feasibility study: An assessment, made before funds are committed, of whether a proposal is workable on technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule grounds.
key_terminologies.Sunk cost: Money already spent that cannot be recovered and should not drive a continue-or-stop decision.
key_terminologies.Source code escrow: An arrangement where a neutral party holds a vendor's source code for release to the buyer if the vendor fails.
key_terminologies.System development life cycle (SDLC): The phases a system passes through, from feasibility and requirements through design, build, testing and implementation to post-implementation review and maintenance.
key_terminologies.Agile: An iterative approach that delivers working software in short cycles with lean but sufficient documentation.
key_terminologies.Continuous integration (CI): Merging and building every code change frequently, with automated tests run each time.
key_terminologies.DevSecOps: Building security checks into the automated delivery pipeline, with findings owned by the delivery team.
key_terminologies.Requirements traceability matrix (RTM): A table linking each requirement to its design, code and tests.
key_terminologies.Application controls: Checks inside a business application that keep data complete, accurate, valid and authorized from input to output.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties (SoD): Splitting conflicting tasks between people or roles so no one can commit and hide an error or fraud alone.
key_terminologies.Audit trail: A protected, time-ordered record of who did what, when and to which data.
key_terminologies.Regression testing: Re-running existing tests to confirm a change did not break functions that already worked.
key_terminologies.Configuration management: Identifying and controlling every component of a system so the approved version of each is always known.
key_terminologies.Change advisory board (CAB): A group that assesses the risk, impact and readiness of significant changes and advises the change authority.
key_terminologies.Rollback plan: Tested, time-bound steps, also called a back-out plan, to return to a working state, including data and configuration, if a release fails.
key_terminologies.Software bill of materials (SBOM): An inventory of the components, versions and dependencies inside a piece of software.
key_terminologies.Cutover: The switch of users and work from an old system to a new one.
key_terminologies.Data conversion: Moving and transforming data from an old system's format into a new system's format.
key_terminologies.Reconciliation: Comparing source and target figures, such as counts and totals, and explaining every difference.
key_terminologies.Go-live decision: Management's evidence-based approval that a system may enter production.
key_terminologies.Post-implementation review (PIR): A review after stable operation that compares realized benefits with the business case and checks that controls work.
key_terminologies.Lessons learned: Recorded experience from a project, stored so future projects can find and apply it.

domains.domain_name: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience
domains.overview: Domain 4 is about keeping IT services running day to day and restoring them after a serious disruption. Part A, operations, covers the components and assets that services run on, the jobs, interfaces and user-built tools that move data, and the processes that manage availability, incidents, changes, logs, service levels and databases. Part B, resilience, covers the business impact analysis (BIA) that sets recovery priorities, systems designed to tolerate failure, and the backups, business continuity plan (BCP) and disaster recovery plan (DRP) that restore the business.
domains.analogy: Think of running a busy airport. Day to day, ground crews follow a timetable, every repair is logged, nothing moves on the airfield without clearance, and the control tower keeps a record of every instruction. That is IT operations. The airport also plans for the day a runway closes: it knows which flights matter most, how long passengers can wait before real harm is done, which nearby airport takes the diverted flights, and it rehearses the switch before it is ever needed. That is business resilience.

topics.overview: IT components are the networks, storage, operating systems, utilities and hardware that every business service runs on. The IS auditor asks the same questions of each one: is it configured to an approved standard, changed under control, supported by its vendor, and free of single points of failure?
can_do: Tell a switch, a router and a firewall apart, and say which one enforces security policy
Map a control to the OSI or TCP/IP layer where it works
Spot single points of failure in storage and network designs
Recommend the right response when hardware reaches end of support

subtopics.name: Network Building Blocks
subtopics.definition: Network infrastructure is the devices and services, such as switches, routers, firewalls and the domain name system (DNS), that carry traffic between systems and control where it goes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every application depends on the network, so one misconfigured device can cut service or expose sensitive data. Network devices are production systems and need the same control as servers.
how_it_works: A local area network (LAN) links devices on one site; a wide area network (WAN) links distant sites.
Switches connect devices inside one network segment, and routers forward traffic between segments or networks.
Firewalls apply a rule set that permits or denies each flow, so they, not routers, enforce security policy between zones.
Network address translation (NAT) swaps private internal addresses for a public one at the boundary; DNS turns names into addresses.
Load balancers spread requests across servers, so one faulty change can stop every application behind them.
Firewall, router and DNS changes are approved, peer-reviewed and tested before they go live, then verified against the approved baseline.

rows.label: Main job
cells: Connects devices within one segment
Moves traffic between networks
Permits or denies traffic by rule

rows.label: Usual OSI layer (explained in the next subtopic)
cells: Data link (layer 2)
Network (layer 3)
Network up to application (layers 3 to 7)

rows.label: Enforces security policy?
cells: No, though virtual LANs separate traffic
Only through basic access lists
Yes; that is its purpose

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 364 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='DNS translates a domain name into the IP address a computer connects to'><rect x='8' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='60' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>example.com</text><rect x='134' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='184' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>DNS lookup</text><rect x='256' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='306' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>IP address</text><line x1='114' y1='46' x2='125' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M125,42 L132,46 L125,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='236' y1='46' x2='247' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M247,42 L254,46 L247,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Name to number. A DNS lookup turns the name a person types into the IP address the network actually routes to. If DNS fails, working systems look unreachable; if it is tampered with, users can be sent somewhere else.

subtopics.example: A dental clinic group's internal DNS server is run by one contractor who edits entries directly, with no request or review. A wrong entry sends staff to a look-alike login page. The IS auditor recommends approving and peer-reviewing DNS changes before they go live, and comparing records with an approved copy. The IT manager owns the fix.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Forwarding traffic is not enforcing policy. Look for a firewall rule set between zones of different trust, and treat every network device as production infrastructure: changes approved and tested first, running settings compared with an approved baseline.

exam_traps.trap: A router or switch placed between two networks secures the traffic between them.
exam_traps.why: Routers and switches move traffic. Only a firewall or similar rule-based filter permits or denies flows by policy.

exam_traps.trap: Firewalls that filter only Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) traffic also protect servers running IPv6 by default.
exam_traps.why: Version 6 (IPv6) left on but uninspected opens a parallel, unfiltered path. A network running both versions needs equal rules for each.

key_terms.definition: Running IPv4 and IPv6 side by side on the same devices, so both must be filtered.
Central planning of Internet Protocol address ranges, so joined networks do not overlap.
A device that connects networks using different protocols and translates between them.

subtopics.name: OSI and TCP/IP Reference Models
subtopics.definition: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) and TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) models are layered maps of network communication, where each layer serves the one above.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Layers give IS auditors and engineers a shared map. Placing a control at its layer shows what it can and cannot stop, and which layers have no control at all.
how_it_works: OSI layers 1 to 4 (physical, data link, network and transport) move data between devices and networks.
OSI layers 5 to 7 (session, presentation and application) manage conversations, data formats and the services users touch.
TCP/IP, the model the internet runs on, has four layers and merges OSI layers 5 to 7 into one application layer.
Transport is its own layer in both models: TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery, and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) gives fast delivery without guarantees.
A control at a lower layer cannot read the content handled by the layers above it.

rows.label: OSI layers covered
cells: 1 Physical and 2 Data link
3 Network
4 Transport
5 Session, 6 Presentation and 7 Application

rows.label: Main job
cells: Moves data across one physical link
Addresses and routes data between networks
Delivers data between programs on two hosts
Provides services to users and programs

rows.label: Examples
cells: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, switches
IP, routers
TCP, UDP, port numbers
Web (HTTP), name lookup (DNS), email

rows.label: Controls that work here
cells: Port security (only known devices may connect), virtual LANs
Router access lists, encrypted tunnels (IPsec)
Firewall rules on ports and connections
Proxies and web application firewalls (read content)

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='OSI model seven-layer pyramid from Physical at the base to Application at the peak'><rect x='135' y='10' width='130' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='32' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>7 · Application</text><rect x='115' y='50' width='170' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='72' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>6 · Presentation</text><rect x='95' y='90' width='210' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='112' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>5 · Session</text><rect x='75' y='130' width='250' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='152' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>4 · Transport</text><rect x='55' y='170' width='290' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='192' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>3 · Network</text><rect x='35' y='210' width='330' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='232' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>2 · Data Link</text><rect x='15' y='250' width='370' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='272' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>1 · Physical</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The seven OSI layers, from Physical at the base to Application at the top. Layers 1 to 4 move data across the network; layers 5 to 7 prepare it for the application.

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at an insurer maps a network control list to the TCP/IP layers. Firewall port rules sit at transport and the web application firewall at application, but remote offices have no link-layer control: any device plugged into a wall port joins the network. She reports the gap to the network manager, who decides on a fix.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Map each control to the layer where it acts, then look for layers with no control at all. A control can judge only what its own layer can see, so match each control to the threat's layer; content threats need application-layer controls.

exam_traps.trap: The TCP/IP application layer covers the OSI transport, session, presentation and application layers.
exam_traps.why: Transport is a separate layer in both models. TCP and UDP sit in the TCP/IP transport layer, so the application layer covers only OSI layers 5 to 7.

exam_traps.trap: A firewall that filters ports also stops attacks hidden inside allowed web requests.
exam_traps.why: Port filtering works at the transport layer and cannot read a request's content. Attacks inside allowed traffic need an application-layer control.

key_terms.definition: An agreed set of rules for how two systems format and exchange data.
Each layer wrapping the data with its own header before passing it down to the next layer.
A number that tells the transport layer which program on a host should receive the data.

subtopics.memory_aid: Bottom to top: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" for Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

subtopics.name: Storage Architecture and Network Topologies
subtopics.definition: Storage architecture is how disks connect to the servers that use them: attached directly, shared as files over the network, or reached through a dedicated storage network.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Shared storage puts many systems' data on a few devices and links. One fault can stop dozens of applications at once, and broad storage administrator rights expose all of that data.
how_it_works: Direct-attached storage (DAS) sits inside or is cabled to one server, and only that server uses it.
Network-attached storage (NAS) is a file server on the ordinary network that shares folders with many users.
A storage area network (SAN) is a separate high-speed network giving many servers disk access as if the disks were local.
Converged networks carry storage, voice and data over one Ethernet core, which saves cost but concentrates risk.
The topology, the layout of links between devices, decides how many paths survive a failed link or device.
The IS auditor checks for redundant paths, reviews who can assign storage to which servers, and identifies any single point of failure.

rows.label: Connected through
cells: A direct cable or internal bus
The normal office network
A dedicated storage network

rows.label: Provides
cells: Raw disk space to one server
Ready-made files and folders to many users
Raw disk space to many servers

rows.label: Typical use
cells: A single server or small office
Shared team folders
Databases and virtual server farms

rows.label: Main risk
cells: The server's failure takes its data offline
Overly broad share permissions
One storage network fault hits many systems

types.meaning: Every device links to a central switch. Simple to manage, but the center is a single point of failure unless it is duplicated.
Devices have several links to one another. Most resilient and most costly; a partial mesh is common in network cores.
All devices share one cable, so a single break disrupts the segment. Mostly found in older networks.
Each device links to two neighbors. A single ring fails at one break; a dual ring survives it.

subtopics.example: At a media company, storage administrators can present any storage area network (SAN) volume to any server. The IS auditor finds a test server that can read the payroll database's disk volume because LUN masking was never set for it. She recommends assigning volumes only through approved requests, enforcing masking and reviewing assignments quarterly, and reports the exposure to the infrastructure manager.
