subtopics.isaca_rule: Consolidation trades cost for concentration. When many systems share one storage network, switch or path, look for redundancy, controlled admin rights and tested failover, and report any single point of failure with its business impact.

exam_traps.trap: Running storage and voice over one network is efficient, so it lowers risk.
exam_traps.why: Convergence lowers cost, not risk. One shared core becomes a single point of failure for storage, phones and data together unless the design adds redundancy.

exam_traps.trap: A star network is resilient because every device has its own link.
exam_traps.why: Every link meets at one central switch. If that switch fails, the whole star fails unless the center is duplicated.

key_terms.definition: One component whose failure stops a whole service because nothing else can take over its work.
A SAN setting that controls which servers can see which disk volumes (logical unit numbers, or LUNs).

subtopics.name: Operating Systems and Utility Programs
subtopics.definition: An operating system (OS) is the base software that runs the hardware and every application; utility programs are powerful admin tools that work on it directly.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A weak OS weakens everything above it. Utilities can read or change data directly, skipping application checks, so misuse may leave no trace in application records.
how_it_works: Vendor default settings favor ease of use, with extra services and known accounts left on.
A hardened baseline, often based on a Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmark, sets secure values for services, accounts, logging and privileges.
Configuration scans compare each server with its baseline and flag drift for follow-up.
File integrity monitoring (FIM) alerts on any change to system files compared with a known-good copy.
Utilities such as disk editors and data loaders are limited to named administrators, used through approved requests and logged.
Where a server class cannot meet the baseline, management approves a documented, expiring exception with compensating controls.

rows.label: What it detects
cells: Any change to the files it watches
Known malicious code and suspicious behavior

rows.label: Compares against
cells: A trusted baseline of each file's fingerprint
The vendor's signatures and behavior rules

rows.label: Misses
cells: Malware that changes no watched file
Unauthorized changes that are not malicious code

rows.label: Answers the question
cells: Was a system file changed?
Is malware present?

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Operating system controls: access control, audit logging, patch management, privileged accounts'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Access control</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Audit logging</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Patch management</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Privileged accounts</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Four core OS controls: access control, audit logging, patching and privileged-account management. Because the OS sits under every application, these controls protect everything above it.

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at a pharmaceutical distributor compares twelve new database servers with the hardened baseline. Four still have the vendor's default administrator account enabled, unflagged because the configuration scanner covers only older server groups. She recommends scanning every server class and disabling default accounts before go-live. The infrastructure lead owns the fix.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Secure the base before the layers above it: harden from an approved baseline, watch for drift, and treat utilities as privileged tools. If full hardening breaks operations, set baselines per server class with formal exceptions backed by compensating controls; never roll back to defaults.

exam_traps.trap: Hardening caused outages, so roll the whole fleet back to vendor default settings.
exam_traps.why: That replaces one risk with a greater one. Tailor the baseline to each server class, and handle the rest through documented exceptions with compensating controls that management formally accepts.

exam_traps.trap: Developers need utilities on production for support, so logging their use is enough.
exam_traps.why: Logging finds misuse after data has changed. Utilities bypass application controls, so the main control is preventive: named administrators only, through approved requests.

key_terms.definition: The approved, documented secure settings that every system of one type must match.
Gradual, unapproved movement of live settings away from the approved baseline.
An account a vendor ships with a known name or password; it should be disabled or changed before use.

subtopics.name: Hardware Maintenance and End of Support
subtopics.definition: Hardware maintenance keeps equipment reliable through monitoring and planned repair; end of support (EOS) is the date a vendor stops providing fixes, parts and help.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Failing or unsupported hardware causes outages and leaves known security flaws open. Each month past end of support raises the risk, and only management can decide to accept it.
how_it_works: Telemetry, the health data devices report, is trended so failing parts are replaced in planned windows, not during an outage.
Maintenance contracts and warranties are tracked against each asset, and expiry dates feed the refresh plan.
Capacity forecasts and warranty dates feed one total cost of ownership (TCO) decision about when to refresh.
Hardware reviews give most attention to unsupported components that run critical services.
When replacement cannot finish before end of support, extended support or compensating controls cover the gap.
The accountable business owner formally accepts the residual risk, tied to a funded, dated replacement plan.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Removes the unsupported item
Keeps vendor fixes coming for a fee
Shrinks exposure with compensating controls

rows.label: Cost
cells: Highest up front
An ongoing premium
Lowest now, but the risk stays

rows.label: Fits when
cells: A successor is ready in time
Replacement is under way but late
The system is low risk or cannot be replaced yet

rows.label: Still needs
cells: Secure disposal of the old item
A dated exit plan
Formal risk acceptance by the business owner

subtopics.example: A port operator's crane-control servers run as redundant pairs, so the infrastructure manager has skipped preventive maintenance for two years. Both servers in one pair now show warnings from the same aging fan model. The IS auditor explains that redundancy limits the impact of one failure but does not slow wear, and recommends restoring planned maintenance. The operations director funds it.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Running unsupported hardware is a business risk decision, not an IT convenience. The IS auditor verifies that the owner formally accepted the risk, that interim controls exist and that a funded replacement date is set. A future plan does not reduce today's exposure.

exam_traps.trap: Servers are redundant, so preventive maintenance can wait.
exam_traps.why: Redundancy reduces the impact of a failure, not how often failures happen. Trend monitoring and planned replacement reduce the failure rate itself.

exam_traps.trap: A replacement project is approved, so the end-of-support risk is handled.
exam_traps.why: A plan lowers only future risk. Until the item is replaced, the exposure exists today and needs extended support or compensating controls plus formal acceptance.

key_terms.definition: Scheduled servicing and part replacement done before failure, based on age, usage or health data.
The risk that remains after controls are applied; above appetite, management must treat it or formally accept it.
The vendor's promise to repair or replace faulty equipment for a set period at no extra cost.

topics.overview: IT asset management keeps an accurate, owned record of every hardware, software and cloud asset from purchase to disposal. Without it, the organization cannot patch, license, recover or safely retire what it runs.
can_do: Explain why discovery and reconciliation, not purchase records, keep an inventory accurate
Test license compliance by comparing what is installed with what is owned
Choose clear, purge or destroy for a disposal scenario and name the evidence to expect

subtopics.name: Asset Inventory and the CMDB
subtopics.definition: An IT asset inventory lists every piece of hardware, software and cloud resource the organization relies on, each with a named owner, location and status.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An organization cannot protect, patch, license or recover assets it does not know it owns. Unknown assets miss patches and backups, and they give attackers an easy entry point.
how_it_works: The asset lifecycle runs from request and purchase through deployment, change and support to secure disposal.
Each record names an owner who is accountable for the asset's use, protection and retirement.
Automated discovery scans networks and cloud accounts, and the results are reconciled to the register, with every gap followed up.
Cloud resources appear and vanish in minutes, so discovery runs continuously through the provider's interfaces and enforces ownership tags.
A configuration management database (CMDB) also records how items connect, so a change or failure can be traced to every service it affects.
CMDB governance starts by defining which item classes are in scope and who owns them; discovery tools come after.

rows.label: Main question
cells: What do we own, where is it and who owns it?
How do the parts of each service connect?

rows.label: Focus
cells: Cost, contract, location and lifecycle status
Technical relationships and dependencies

rows.label: Main users
cells: Asset, finance and license managers
Change, incident and problem teams

rows.label: Kept accurate by
cells: Discovery reconciled to purchase and disposal records
Discovery plus updates from every approved change

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at a hospital network plans to test the medical-device inventory. Her program samples register entries and locates each device, which proves only that listed devices exist. She adds the reverse test, tracing devices found by a network scan back to the register. Twenty-two infusion pumps are unlisted, and she reports them to the clinical engineering manager.
subtopics.isaca_rule: An inventory is a control only while it matches reality. Test completeness from what actually runs back to the register, and expect defined scope, named owners and regular reconciliation before any tool.

exam_traps.trap: Purchase orders give a complete asset register.
exam_traps.why: Purchases miss transferred, self-provisioned and cloud assets, and keep listing retired ones. Only discovery reconciled to the register shows what is really running.

exam_traps.trap: To test completeness, trace each register entry to the equipment.
exam_traps.why: That proves listed items exist but can never find unlisted ones. Completeness is tested the other way, from discovered assets back to the register.

key_terms.definition: Any component under configuration control, such as a server, application, network device, document or service; the CMDB records it and its links.
Software that scans networks or cloud accounts to find connected assets and record their details.
A label on a cloud resource naming its owner; untagged resources are flagged or blocked.

subtopics.name: Software Licensing
subtopics.definition: Software license compliance means every installed or used copy of software is covered by an entitlement the organization holds and is used within that license's terms.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Over-deployment leads to vendor audit charges and legal claims, while unused licenses waste money. Open-source terms carry duties too, and breaking them can expose proprietary code.
how_it_works: Discovery finds what is installed or used, including cloud subscriptions and virtual machines.
Software asset management (SAM) reconciles those findings with purchased entitlements, counted by the license metric.
Gaps are confirmed before action, because some installs are unused or covered by other agreements.
New software passes an approval step that checks license terms, so gaps do not grow back.
Open-source components are inventoried, and their terms are reviewed before code is shipped to customers.

types.meaning: A one-time purchase to use a version indefinitely, limited by user, device or processor counts in the contract.
Paid access for a set period; use stops when payment stops. Common for software as a service (SaaS).
Free to use, change and share with few conditions beyond keeping notices, for example the MIT and Apache licenses.
Free to use, but distributed changes or derived products must carry the same terms, for example the GNU General Public License (GPL).

subtopics.example: A freight company moves its database software onto a larger virtual server cluster. The license counts processor cores, and the contract may count every core the software could run on. The IS auditor compares deployed cores with entitlements, finds a possible large shortfall, and recommends that the software asset manager confirm the counting rules before the vendor's annual review. The chief financial officer decides how to close any gap.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Compliance is proven by comparing what is installed or used with what is owned; purchase records show only one side. Confirm the true gap before spending, then fix the process that let it grow.

exam_traps.trap: Procurement records prove compliance ahead of a vendor audit.
exam_traps.why: Records show what was bought, not what is installed. Only reconciling discovered installs with entitlements shows over- or under-deployment.

exam_traps.trap: Open-source software is free, so it carries no license risk.
exam_traps.why: Copyleft licenses can require a distributed derived product to be released under the same terms. Free to use does not mean free of obligations.

key_terms.definition: The right to use software that a license grants, in a stated quantity.
The unit a license counts, such as named users, devices, processor cores or concurrent sessions.
A contract-based check by the vendor of installs against purchases, with charges for any shortfall.

subtopics.name: Secure Disposal and Media Sanitization
subtopics.definition: Media sanitization makes data on retired or reused storage unrecoverable by clearing, purging or destroying it, matched to the data's sensitivity and destination.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Retired laptops, disks, tapes and leased equipment leave with whatever data they held. Deleting files or formatting a drive leaves the data recoverable with ordinary tools.
how_it_works: NIST SP 800-88, guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, defines the clear, purge and destroy sanitization levels.
The level is chosen from two facts: how sensitive the data is and whether the media will leave the organization's control.
Media stay tracked from collection to sanitization, with a chain of custody (a signed record of each handover) when a vendor handles them.
In shared cloud storage, a customer cannot shred disks, so cryptographic erase is the practical method.
A designated person verifies that the method worked and records each item, method, date and operator; the asset record is then closed.

types.meaning: Overwrites data so ordinary tools cannot recover it. Fits media reused inside the organization.
Defeats even laboratory recovery, for example by secure-erase commands, degaussing magnetic media or cryptographic erase. Fits media leaving the organization's control.
Shreds, disintegrates or burns media so it can never be used again. Fits the most sensitive data and media that cannot be purged.

subtopics.example: A city council's IT team plans to degauss the solid-state drives of retired laptops that held resident tax records, then sell the laptops. The IS auditor notes that degaussing does not erase solid-state drives. She recommends a purge method suited to them, such as the drive's verified secure-erase command, with each serial number recorded on a sanitization certificate. The IT manager updates the procedure.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the method to the data's sensitivity and where the media is going, then verify and document. Evidence of sanitization, such as a certificate or a key-destruction log, matters as much as the act itself.

exam_traps.trap: Formatting a disk or deleting its files is enough before it is reused or returned.
exam_traps.why: Deletion and quick formats remove only the pointers to data. The content stays recoverable until it is overwritten, purged or destroyed.

exam_traps.trap: Ask the cloud provider to shred the disks that held the organization's data.
exam_traps.why: Cloud storage is shared and spread over many disks, so one customer cannot have them destroyed. Destroying the customer-managed keys makes the data unreadable, and the log proves it.

key_terms.definition: Destroying the keys of encrypted data so it can never be decrypted again.
Erasing magnetic media with a strong magnetic field; it does not work on solid-state drives.
A signed record of each item sanitized, the method used, the date and the person responsible.

topics.topic_name: Job Scheduling and Production Process Automation
topics.overview: Production work such as overnight batches, file transfers and software robots runs with no one watching each step. This topic covers how the schedule is authorized, how failed jobs are recovered without losing or doubling records, and how bots are controlled as both users and programs.
can_do: Explain why a job's success status does not prove correct processing
Choose restart or rerun for a failed batch and name the controls that prevent duplicates
Recommend identity, ownership and change controls for a software bot

subtopics.name: Job Scheduling Controls
subtopics.definition: A job scheduler is software that launches production jobs by time and dependency, holds each job until its inputs are ready, and records the outcome.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scheduling removes the keying errors of manual job submission. But an unauthorized or mis-sequenced job can post wrong data and still report success, so the schedule itself needs control.
how_it_works: The schedule lists approved jobs, their run times and dependencies, and who may change them.
Schedule changes go through change management, with an expedited emergency route for urgent business requests.
People who maintain schedules do not approve production schedule changes; independent approval enforces segregation of duties.
Record counts and control totals gate dependent jobs, so an empty or partial input stops the chain.
Dependency mapping shows which jobs sit on the critical path, so testing focuses on failures that cascade.
Production jobs run only through the scheduler; submissions outside it are blocked or tightly controlled.
subtopics.example: A sporting-goods retailer's job schedule still runs a nightly job that sends loyalty-card data to a marketing agency whose contract ended a year ago. The job never fails, so no one noticed it. The IS auditor finds no current business approval for the job, recommends suspending it at once, and reports the possible data exposure to the chief privacy officer, who decides on next steps.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Test the schedule against approved business requirements, not just failure logs. Urgency changes the route, never the need for authorization. When a bypass is active, close it first, then measure its impact.

exam_traps.trap: Reviewing the scheduler's failure log shows whether jobs ran as intended.
exam_traps.why: An unauthorized or wrongly sequenced job can run successfully and never appear as a failure. Compare the schedule with approved requirements and change records instead.

exam_traps.trap: The payroll job ended with a success status, so payroll processed correctly.
exam_traps.why: Status shows the job ran, not that it processed the right data. An empty input file can produce a clean success; counts and control totals prove completeness.

key_terms.definition: A rule that one job may start only after another finishes successfully.
A one-off job run outside the regular schedule; it needs the same authorization as any other.
The chain of dependent jobs whose delay or failure delays the business outcome.

subtopics.name: Batch Monitoring, Restart and Rerun
subtopics.definition: Restart and rerun procedures are documented steps for recovering a failed batch job so that no record is skipped and none is processed twice.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Batches often fail midway. A careless recovery can post the same transactions twice or silently drop some, and a slow batch can spill into business hours and delay customers.
how_it_works: Checkpoints record the last committed record, so a restart can resume from that point.
A rerun starts the job again from the beginning, but only after partial updates are reversed.
Control totals compared before and after recovery prove that nothing was lost or doubled.
Operators follow written runbooks and log every restart, rerun and manual step for supervisory review.
Deadline alerts warn when a batch has not finished on time, before it overruns into online hours.

rows.label: Starts from
cells: The last valid checkpoint
The beginning of the job

rows.label: Must happen first
cells: Confirm the checkpoint is valid
Reverse partial updates or restore the input

rows.label: Risk if done carelessly
cells: Skipping or repeating records if the wrong checkpoint is used
Posting the same records twice

rows.label: Best when
cells: Long jobs with reliable checkpoints
Short jobs, or when checkpoint data is doubtful

subtopics.example: An insurer's premium-billing batch fails at 3 a.m. The night operator restarts it from a checkpoint but cannot say which one, and no log records the manual step. Next morning, finance finds some policies billed twice and others not at all. The IS auditor recommends written runbooks, a log of every restart with supervisory review, and control totals reconciled before invoices go out. The operations manager owns the changes.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Recovery from a failed batch must protect completeness and accuracy. Restart from a valid checkpoint where possible, prove the result with reconciled totals, and log every manual step for independent review.

exam_traps.trap: Rerunning the whole job from the start is always the safest choice.
exam_traps.why: Unless partial updates are reversed first, a full rerun posts the same transactions twice. Restart from a checkpoint, or back out before rerunning.

exam_traps.trap: Customer complaints are an acceptable way to learn that a batch overran.
exam_traps.why: By then the damage is done. A deadline alert on each critical batch warns operators while there is still time to act.

key_terms.definition: A saved marker of the last committed record that lets a failed job resume without starting over.
Step-by-step operating instructions for running, restarting and recovering a job.
A warning raised when a batch has not finished by the time it must.

subtopics.name: Robotic Process Automation (RPA)
subtopics.definition: Robotic process automation (RPA) uses software robots, called bots, to perform rule-based screen tasks a person would do, such as keying data from one system into another.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Bots act fast and at scale, so a faulty rule or a stolen bot credential can post thousands of wrong entries unnoticed. A bot needs the controls of both a user and a program.
how_it_works: Each bot gets its own identity with least-privilege access, never a shared or personal human login.
A named business owner is accountable for what the bot does and approves its access.
Bot passwords are kept in a credential vault, not in scripts, and are changed regularly.
Bot logic is production code: changes are tested, approved and promoted through change management.
Bots log every action and send cases they cannot handle, such as an unreadable invoice, to a person.
Segregation of duties applies to bots too: one bot should not both create and approve the same payment.

types.meaning: Runs on a user's desktop when that person starts it, helping with part of a task.
Runs on a server on a schedule or trigger with no person present, so it needs the tightest control.

subtopics.example: At a property management firm, one unattended bot creates supplier payments and approves them, and its password sits in its script. The IS auditor recommends splitting creation and approval between separate identities, with a person approving payments above a set amount, and moving the password into a credential vault. The finance director, the bot's owner, sets the timeline.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat a bot as both a user and a program. As a user it needs its own identity, least privilege and an accountable owner; as a program its logic changes are tested and approved. Shared or personal logins break accountability.

exam_traps.trap: Running the bot under an employee's login is acceptable if that employee supervises it.
exam_traps.why: No one can then tell the bot's actions from the person's, and the bot inherits rights it does not need. Each bot needs its own traceable identity.

exam_traps.trap: Bot rules are business settings, so the owner may edit them directly in production.
exam_traps.why: Bot logic decides what gets posted and paid. Like any production code, its changes need testing, approval and controlled promotion.

key_terms.definition: A dedicated account used by one bot only, so every action traces back to it.
A secured store that holds and rotates passwords so scripts never contain them.
A list of cases a bot could not process, routed to a person to handle.

topics.overview: Interfaces move data between systems, often in bulk and with no one watching. This topic covers where data can be lost, changed or duplicated along the way, and which controls prove that what arrived matches what was sent.
can_do: Trace interface risk from the sender through transport and middleware to the receiver
Choose between control totals, sequence checks and unique identifiers for a given interface risk
Explain why a job's success status is not evidence of a complete transfer

subtopics.name: Where Interface Risk Sits
subtopics.definition: A system interface is an automated link that moves data from one application to another, either directly or through middleware that routes and reformats it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Interfaces carry payments, orders and journal entries with no human review. An error at any hop can silently lose, alter or duplicate records while both ends report success.
how_it_works: At the sender, the extract can be wrong or partial, for example a missed date range.
In transport, messages can be lost, delayed or intercepted between systems.
In middleware, mapping rules that convert formats can change values, such as cutting off amounts or swapping fields.
At the receiver, records can be rejected, loaded twice or only partly posted.
Data communications software manages delivery with acknowledgments and retries; its settings decide whether lost messages are resent.
An audit traces sample transactions through every hop, from source to final posting.

types.meaning: Files sent on a schedule, such as a nightly payment file. Risk: partial, late or duplicate files.
Real-time requests from one system to another. Risk: timeouts and duplicates when requests are retried.
Middleware that holds messages until the receiver takes them. Risk: lost or stuck messages.
Standard business documents, such as orders and invoices, exchanged with trading partners. Risk: rejected or misread documents when formats or mappings differ.

subtopics.example: A health insurer's claims interface sends files to a payment processor over an encrypted channel, and the interface owner cites the encryption as proof the data is complete. The IS auditor traces sample claims and finds that a middleware rule cuts amounts above 99,999 to five digits. She explains that encryption protects confidentiality, not accuracy, and reports the mapping error to the application owner.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Scope follows the data, end to end. An interface is only as reliable as its weakest hop, so test the sender, transport, middleware and receiver, not just the system that owns the data.

exam_traps.trap: Test the sending system, because it owns the data.
exam_traps.why: Many silent losses happen in middleware mapping or at the receiving end. Testing only the source misses them.

exam_traps.trap: Messages are encrypted in transit, so the interface is complete and accurate.
exam_traps.why: Encryption protects confidentiality on the way. It does nothing to prove every record was sent, mapped correctly and posted once.

key_terms.definition: Software between applications that routes, queues and converts messages.
The rules that convert each field from the sender's format into the receiver's.
A reply from the receiver confirming it got the data, so the sender knows whether to resend.

subtopics.name: Interface Controls
subtopics.definition: Interface controls are the checks that prove data arrived complete, accurate, once and on time, such as control totals, sequence checks and unique message identifiers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without them, an interface can drop or double records for days while every job reports success. On payment and posting interfaces, those errors turn straight into financial loss.
how_it_works: The sender produces control totals: record counts, amount totals and hash totals of key fields.
The receiver recalculates the totals and reconciles them with the sender's, and every difference is followed up.
Sequence numbers reveal missing or out-of-order batches and messages.
Interfaces that retry carry a unique identifier per message, so the receiver rejects repeats before posting.
Rejected records go to a suspense queue that is worked and cleared, not left to age.
Patches to connected systems include regression testing of dependent interfaces before they go live.

rows.label: Catches
cells: Missing, extra or changed records in a batch
Missing or out-of-order batches or messages
Duplicate messages from retries

rows.label: Type
cells: Detective: shows a difference to investigate
Detective: shows a gap to investigate
Preventive: rejects the repeat

rows.label: Fits best
cells: Nightly files, such as payments
Numbered message streams
Interfaces that resend on timeout

subtopics.example: A university's nightly student-fee file to its finance system has a rejected-records queue of 1,400 items, some eight months old. Control totals compare only the records that posted, so the gap never shows. The IS auditor recommends reconciling the sender's totals to posted plus rejected records, and naming an owner who clears the queue within set days. The bursar agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Reconcile at the receiving end and act on every exception. Prevent duplicates before posting with unique message identifiers, because reconciliation only finds them afterward; sequence checks reveal gaps. Job status is never proof of completeness.

exam_traps.trap: The interface job finished successfully, so all records arrived.
exam_traps.why: Job status shows the process ran, not what it carried. Only reconciled counts and totals at the receiver show completeness.

exam_traps.trap: Daily reconciliation is the best control against duplicate retried messages.
exam_traps.why: Reconciliation finds duplicates after they post, perhaps after goods ship or money moves. A unique identifier check rejects them before posting.

key_terms.definition: A sum of a non-money field, such as account numbers, used only to detect changed or missing records.
A holding area for rejected records that must be corrected and reprocessed.
Re-testing existing functions after a change to confirm that what worked before still works.

topics.overview: Business teams sign up for their own services and build their own tools, often faster than IT can deliver. That meets real needs, but those tools bypass IT's controls even when they hold client data or feed regulatory figures, so the IS auditor identifies them, ranks them by risk and expects controls in proportion.
can_do: Name the evidence that reveals shadow IT and explain why surveys miss it
Recommend a first step when staff use unapproved AI tools with company data
Recommend risk-tiered controls for spreadsheets and other user-built tools
Decide when a user-built tool should move to an IT-managed platform

subtopics.name: Shadow IT and Shadow AI
subtopics.definition: Shadow IT is hardware, software or cloud services used for business without the organization's approval; shadow AI is the same thing with artificial intelligence (AI) tools.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unapproved services can hold client data with no contract, security review, backup or exit plan. With public AI tools, staff may paste confidential data into a service that keeps it or learns from it.
how_it_works: Discovery relies on independent evidence, such as proxy logs, expense claims and a cloud access security broker (CASB), because surveys under-report.
Each service found is risk-ranked by the sensitivity of its data and its value to the business.
Each is then sanctioned and secured, migrated to an approved tool, or retired, highest risk first.
For shadow AI, the first step is an acceptable-use rule for data in AI tools, plus an approved tool that meets the need.
A quick, easy route to request new tools removes much of the reason to bypass IT.

rows.label: Who provides it
cells: A team, buying or signing up outside IT
Business users who build it themselves
IT or an approved supplier

rows.label: Does IT know about it?
cells: No, by definition
Sometimes; it should be in an inventory
Yes

rows.label: Typical example
cells: A team's own file-sharing or AI subscription
A spreadsheet that calculates loan loss reserves
The corporate email service

rows.label: Main control
cells: Discover, risk-rank, then sanction, migrate or retire
Owned inventory and risk-tiered controls
Standard IT controls and change management

subtopics.example: A design agency's approval process for new software takes eight weeks, so teams sign up for their own file-sharing and whiteboard tools, three of which hold client artwork. The IS auditor traces the cause to the slow approval route, not careless staff, and recommends a fast-track request process for low-risk tools with clear data rules. The chief operating officer owns the plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Find shadow IT through evidence, not by asking. Then manage it by risk: bring valuable tools under governance, and replace or retire risky ones. A ban with no approved alternative usually drives use further out of sight.

exam_traps.trap: Banning every unapproved cloud and AI tool is the strongest control.
exam_traps.why: If the tool meets a real need, a ban pushes its use out of sight. Risk-assess it, then sanction and secure it or replace it.

exam_traps.trap: A survey of department heads will show how much shadow IT exists.
exam_traps.why: People forget or choose not to report what they use. Proxy logs, CASB data and expense records show actual use independently.

key_terms.definition: A tool between users and cloud services that shows which services are used and can enforce data rules.
A record of web traffic through the company's proxy server, showing which sites and services staff used.
A policy stating what staff may and may not do with company data and tools.

subtopics.name: End-User Computing (EUC)
subtopics.definition: End-user computing (EUC) means applications that business staff build and run themselves, such as spreadsheets, desktop databases, macros and scripts, outside formal IT development.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some user-built tools quietly become critical, such as a spreadsheet that calculates regulatory figures. They often lack testing, version control, backup and a second person who understands them.
how_it_works: Control starts with an inventory of user-built tools, each with a named owner and a criticality rating.
Ratings follow defined criteria, such as financial or regulatory impact, and are checked independently rather than left to owners.
Controls scale with the rating: light for low-risk tools; for critical ones, independent review of logic changes, version control, restricted access and testing.
Logic written with an AI (artificial intelligence) assistant gets the same independent review and testing as logic written by hand.
A tool that becomes a system of record, or too critical for its controls, moves to an IT-managed platform.
subtopics.example: A home-care agency's nurse-scheduling spreadsheet, rated critical in the EUC inventory, is overwritten by a copy with broken formulas, and no earlier version exists. The IS auditor finds none of the tier's required controls in place and recommends version control, backup, restricted editing and review of logic changes. The director of nursing owns the actions, and the IS auditor follows up.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Control effort follows risk. Start with an owned, criticality-ranked inventory, rate tools against defined criteria with independent checking, then apply controls that match each tier. Migrate tools that outgrow their controls.

exam_traps.trap: Under the EUC policy, owners can rate the risk of their own spreadsheets.
exam_traps.why: Owners tend to rate their own tools low, even ones feeding financial statements. Tiering works only with defined criteria and independent checking of the ratings.

exam_traps.trap: Under a deadline, rebuild the broken spreadsheet properly before filing.
exam_traps.why: An untested rebuild adds risk at the worst time. Run the proven model with independent review, then fix the weakness after the deadline.

key_terms.definition: The authoritative source for a type of data, such as claims paid, whose values other systems trust.
A register of user-built tools, each with a named owner, purpose and risk tier, used to decide which controls apply.
Keeping each saved version of a file with who changed it and when, so changes can be reviewed and reversed.

topics.overview: Availability is whether users can actually use a service when they need it. Capacity management makes sure enough processing, storage and network exists before demand arrives. Both start from business need and are measured the way users experience the service.
can_do: Tell mean time between failures (MTBF) from mean time to repair (MTTR) in a scenario
Explain why availability is measured end to end over the hours the business needs
Recommend demand management and peak-based planning before buying capacity
Name the capacity limits that still apply in the cloud

subtopics.name: Availability and Its Measures
subtopics.definition: Availability is the share of agreed service time during which users can actually complete their work on a service, usually stated as a percentage.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Availability targets decide how much redundancy is bought. A figure that excludes business-hours maintenance, or measures only servers, can report the target as met while customers cannot finish a transaction.
how_it_works: Targets come from business impact and tolerance for downtime, so resilience spending matches need.
Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime sharply: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours a year, and 99.99% about 53 minutes.
Availability is measured end to end, for example with synthetic transactions that act like a real customer.
It is measured over the hours the business needs the service; exclusions such as planned maintenance are agreed and limited.
Availability equals MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), where MTBF is mean time between failures and MTTR is mean time to repair. Rarer failures or faster fixes both raise it.
Monitoring covers every critical component and network segment; an unmonitored segment is a blind spot.

rows.label: Stands for
cells: Mean time between failures
Mean time to repair, or to restore service

rows.label: Measures
cells: Reliability: how often things break
Recovery speed: how fast service returns

rows.label: Better when
cells: Higher
Lower

rows.label: Improved by
cells: Better components, preventive maintenance, removing causes
Monitoring, spare parts, clear procedures, automation

subtopics.example: A ticketing platform's monthly outages fell from six to two, but each now lasts five hours instead of one. The service owner calls the platform more available. The IS auditor shows that monthly downtime rose from six to ten hours: failures are rarer, but repairs are slower. She recommends tracking MTBF and MTTR together, and the operations director agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Availability is defined by the business and measured as users experience it, over the hours they need the service. When component dashboards report normal service but customers cannot complete transactions, trust the end-to-end measure.

exam_traps.trap: MTTR halved this year, so the system now fails less often.
exam_traps.why: MTTR measures how fast service returns. How often failures happen is MTBF, which did not change. Availability improved; reliability did not.

exam_traps.trap: IT should set the highest availability target it can afford.
exam_traps.why: Extra nines for a low-impact system waste money. Targets follow business impact and tolerance for downtime.

key_terms.definition: A scripted test that performs a real user action, such as placing an order, to measure service as users see it.
Agreed outage time for maintenance; it counts against availability unless the agreement excludes it.
The hours when the business needs the service, over which availability is measured.

subtopics.name: Capacity Management
subtopics.definition: Capacity management monitors, forecasts and plans processing, storage and network resources so performance targets are met at sensible cost, before demand arrives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A capacity shortfall causes slowdowns and outages just as a failure does. Buying and setting up resources takes time, so shortfalls have to be seen months ahead.
how_it_works: Monitoring compares use and spending with thresholds; alerts reach a staffed team queue with a named backup, so someone always reviews them and acts on trends.
Forecasts model peak demand, such as month-end batches, not averages that hide saturation.
Demand management comes first: moving or rescheduling workload, such as reports run off-peak, before buying more.
Plans add capacity early enough to cover purchase and setup lead times.
In the cloud, autoscaling stops at the provider's service quotas, so plans track those limits.
On shared platforms, limits per tenant (each customer sharing the platform) stop one customer's workload from using capacity sold to others.

illustration.caption: The capacity cycle: watch usage, forecast demand, then add capacity before it is needed, so a shortfall never turns into an outage.

subtopics.example: A streaming service's forecast shows storage running out in five months, and the infrastructure lead plans to order more in month four. Supplier delivery and setup take about ten weeks. The IS auditor recommends triggering orders from lead time plus a safety margin, with the forecast based on peak growth, not averages. The chief technology officer approves the purchase schedule.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Monitoring is a control only when someone reviews results against thresholds and acts on trends. Plan for peaks, not averages, try demand management before adding resources, and never assume the cloud is unlimited.

exam_traps.trap: Cloud autoscaling means capacity planning is no longer needed.
exam_traps.why: Autoscaling stops at the provider's quotas and costs more as it grows. Plans still track quotas, spending alerts and peak demand.

exam_traps.trap: Average utilization well below the limit shows the servers have plenty of headroom.
exam_traps.why: Averages hide peaks. If periodic workloads saturate the servers, plan from peak demand and its trend.

key_terms.definition: Spare capacity kept above normal peak use to absorb growth and spikes.
A cloud provider's limit on resources per account; a soft quota can be raised on request, a hard one cannot.
Shaping when and how much resource is used, for example by scheduling, so existing capacity goes further.
One tenant on shared infrastructure whose heavy use degrades service for the others.

topics.overview: Incident management restores normal service as fast as possible; problem management finds and removes the underlying cause so the same incident does not recur. The IS auditor verifies that both processes operate, that response steps happen in the right order, and that decision rights are clear under pressure.
can_do: Tell an incident, a problem and a known error apart
Put operational incident steps in order, restoring service before root cause analysis, and say how security incidents differ
Choose outcome measures that show whether the service desk is effective
Recommend who decides during a major incident

subtopics.name: Incident Management and the Service Desk
subtopics.definition: Incident management is the process of restoring normal service as quickly as possible after an unplanned interruption or drop in quality, limiting business impact.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every minute of outage costs the business. Without one consistent process, incidents get lost, wrongly prioritized or closed before users can work again.
how_it_works: The service desk is the single point of contact: it logs every incident, classifies it and sets its priority.
Priority combines business impact and urgency, so exposed customer data outranks a broken office printer.
Agents restore service first, using a workaround if needed, and raise a problem record when the cause is unknown.
Incidents beyond the desk's skill or authority are escalated, and calls that look like security incidents go to the response team.
An incident closes only after the user confirms that service works.
Effectiveness shows in outcome measures, such as first-contact resolution and reopen rates, not speed or volume alone.

rows.label: Moves the incident to
cells: A team with more skill, such as database support
A manager with more authority

rows.label: Triggered by
cells: The desk cannot fix it
A decision is needed: high impact, a missed target or an unhappy customer

rows.label: Example
cells: A failed disk passed to the storage team
A breached service target raised to the service manager

subtopics.example: A warehouse scanning outage at a logistics company has passed its four-hour resolution target, and the service desk agent keeps retrying fixes alone. The IS auditor finds no functional escalation to the network team and no hierarchical escalation to the service manager when the target was missed. She recommends defined escalation triggers, and the IT service manager updates the procedure.
subtopics.isaca_rule: For an ordinary outage, restore service first, even by workaround, then pursue the cause through problem management. When harm is still spreading, as in a security incident, contain before restoring. Judge the desk by outcomes such as reopen rates.

exam_traps.trap: Measure the service desk by average handling time and tickets closed.
exam_traps.why: Fast closure can hide unresolved issues. Reopen rates and first-contact resolution show whether problems are truly fixed.

exam_traps.trap: A caller who knows an executive's personal details may have that executive's multi-factor authentication reset.
exam_traps.why: Attackers gather such details easily. Resets of privileged credentials need out-of-band verification, such as a call back to a registered number.

key_terms.definition: A temporary way to restore service without fixing the underlying cause.
The share of incidents solved during the user's first contact with the service desk.
Confirming identity through a separate, trusted channel, such as a call back to the number on file.
Severity is a fault's technical size; priority is response speed, set by business impact and urgency.

subtopics.name: Handling Incidents in Sequence
subtopics.definition: The incident handling sequence is the order for an operational incident: detect and record, limit spreading damage, restore service, then review; root cause analysis belongs to problem management.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Under pressure, teams often chase the root cause while users stay down. The right order limits harm and restores service fast, and clear decision rights stop the response waiting on executives.
how_it_works: Detection: the event is logged with a timestamp, classified and prioritized.
Containment: if damage is still spreading, stop the spread, for example by taking a failing server out of service.
Restoration: service returns by fix or workaround and is checked with users; the root cause goes to problem management.
Security incidents differ: contain the attack and remove the attacker's foothold before restoring service, as 5B5.1 explains.
Review: a blameless post-incident review records what happened and why, before corrective actions are chosen.
An incident commander holds pre-delegated decisions; a liaison sends executives scheduled updates and users a status notice, so the desk is not flooded.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Operational incident handling: detect, contain spreading damage, restore service, close with the user, review lessons learned'><rect x='8' y='24' width='90' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='53' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Detection</text><rect x='120' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='172' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Containment</text><rect x='246' y='24' width='98' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='295' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Restoration</text><rect x='366' y='24' width='82' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='407' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Closure</text><rect x='470' y='24' width='102' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='521' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Lessons learned</text><line x1='100' y1='46' x2='111' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M111,42 L118,46 L111,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='226' y1='46' x2='237' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M237,42 L244,46 L237,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='346' y1='46' x2='357' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M357,42 L364,46 L357,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='450' y1='46' x2='461' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M461,42 L468,46 L461,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: An operational incident runs left to right: service is restored, by workaround if needed, before anyone hunts the root cause, which problem management takes over. Security incidents add eradication of the attacker's foothold before recovery (5B5.1).

subtopics.example: A ticket-sales website slows sharply, and the on-call engineer restarts the web servers as for a routine outage. Within an hour the slowdown returns: cryptocurrency-mining malware is still running. The IS auditor recommends that triage flag signs of compromise and route them to the security team, which contains and removes the foothold before restoring. The IT service manager updates the runbook.
subtopics.isaca_rule: For an operational incident, limit spreading damage, then restore service, by workaround if needed; root cause belongs to problem management. Security incidents contain and eradicate before restoring. Pre-delegate decisions to an incident commander, and prove the process with real incident records.

exam_traps.trap: Find the root cause before restoring service, so the fix is permanent.
exam_traps.why: Users stay down while the cause is investigated. Restore service first, by workaround if needed, and open a problem record for root cause analysis.

exam_traps.trap: Every major decision during an outage should wait for the executive team.
exam_traps.why: Waiting slows the response at the worst moment. Decisions are pre-delegated to the incident commander, and executives get scheduled updates.

key_terms.definition: The one person who directs a major incident response and its time-critical decisions.
An incident with high business impact that triggers a dedicated, coordinated response.
A fact-based look at what happened that seeks process weaknesses, not someone to blame.

subtopics.name: Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis
subtopics.definition: Problem management finds and removes the underlying causes of incidents so the same disruption stops recurring, and manages known errors until a permanent fix arrives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fixing each incident separately treats only symptoms. Recurring incidents waste effort and point to a weakness that may later cause a bigger outage.
how_it_works: Trend analysis spots recurring incidents that share a likely cause, and a problem record is opened.
Root cause analysis (RCA) works from facts, such as a timeline rebuilt from monitoring data, not from opinions.
Analysis looks past human error to the process, tool or procedure weakness that let the error happen.
If the cause is known but the fix is not ready, a known error is recorded with its workaround for the service desk.
Permanent fixes go through change management, and the problem closes once the fix is shown to work.
Management gets periodic reports of recurring problems weighted by business impact.

rows.label: What it is
cells: An unplanned interruption or drop in quality
The cause of one or more incidents
A problem with a known cause and a workaround

rows.label: Goal
cells: Restore service fast
Remove the cause for good
Resolve repeat incidents quickly until the fix

rows.label: Closed when
cells: The user confirms service works
The permanent fix is in place and proven
The underlying problem is resolved

rows.label: Example
cells: Email stops sending
A memory leak in the mail server
The leak is documented, with a nightly restart as the workaround

subtopics.example: A broadband provider's problem team closes a recurring router-crash problem as soon as a firmware fix is deployed. Two weeks later the crashes resume. The IS auditor recommends reopening the problem and closing problems only after monitoring shows the incidents have stopped for an agreed period. The service owner agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Recurring incidents signal a problem. Find the common root cause from facts before choosing a permanent fix, look past human error to the process that allowed it, and report trends by business impact so management can act.

exam_traps.trap: The analysis found operator error, so retraining the operator closes the problem.
exam_traps.why: Human error is a symptom. Good analysis asks why the process or tool allowed the error and fixes that, or the error will happen again.

exam_traps.trap: The main goal of problem management is to restore service as fast as possible.
exam_traps.why: That is incident management's goal. Problem management reduces how often and how badly incidents recur by finding and removing their root cause, even after service is back.

key_terms.definition: A structured, fact-based method for finding the underlying reason an incident happened.
A simple RCA technique that asks why repeatedly until it reaches a process cause.
The entry that tracks a problem from investigation through workaround to permanent fix.

topics.topic_name: IT Change, Configuration, and Patch Management
topics.overview: Most outages and many security gaps begin with a change. This topic covers how changes are authorized, how systems are kept at their approved settings, how patches are ranked by risk, and how groups of changes go live together, each with a tested backout plan.
can_do: Explain how emergency changes stay controlled
Detect unauthorized change by comparing actual settings with the approved baseline
Rank patches by risk and handle a deferral properly
Tell change management from release management in a scenario

subtopics.name: Change Management
subtopics.definition: Change management is the process that records, assesses, approves and reviews every change to production, so only authorized, tested changes go live.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unauthorized or untested changes are a leading cause of outages and security gaps. The process also shows auditors and regulators that production is controlled.
how_it_works: Each change is requested, assessed for risk and impact, approved by the change authority, tested and recorded.
Higher-risk changes go to the change advisory board (CAB) for review before the change authority approves them.
Developers have no standing production access; pipeline separation of authors and deployers is covered in 3B2.2.
Every change has a tested backout plan to restore the prior state.
Emergency changes take a faster route, with independent review and approval soon after implementation.
The IS auditor traces changes found in production back to approved requests, not only requests forward to production.

types.meaning: Low risk, pre-approved and repeatable under a documented procedure, such as applying a routine, pre-tested desktop patch.
Assessed and approved one by one, by the CAB when the risk is higher.
Needed at once to fix a serious fault or threat; approval may follow implementation, but review is never skipped.

subtopics.example: At an online travel agency, on-call engineers fix a night-time pricing outage through a shared administrator account, leaving no change record. The IS auditor recommends named firecall IDs that log every action and are disabled after use, with each emergency change recorded and reviewed by the change advisory board the next working day. The platform engineering head agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: No unauthorized change reaches production. Urgency changes the route, not the need for control: emergency changes still get independent review and approval soon after. When a release causes harm and a validated prior version exists, back out first, then investigate.

exam_traps.trap: The change was urgent, so no approval was needed.
exam_traps.why: Emergency changes may skip prior approval, but they still need documentation, independent review and approval soon after implementation.

exam_traps.trap: Send every routine, pre-tested desktop patch to the CAB for approval.
exam_traps.why: Standard changes are pre-approved under a documented procedure. Routing each to the CAB wastes its time; review the procedure and sample its results instead.

key_terms.definition: Tested steps that return a system to its state before a change.
The person or group allowed to approve a type of change.
ITIL 4's name for change management; ITIL is a widely used IT service management framework.
Any production change that cannot be traced to an approved request.
A temporary privileged account issued for an urgent fix, with every action logged and reviewed afterward, then disabled.

subtopics.name: Configuration Management
subtopics.definition: Configuration management records the approved settings and versions of each system, called the configuration baseline, and keeps checking that live systems still match it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Settings drift as people make quick fixes. A change nobody logged can create a security weakness or break recovery, and no change ticket will ever reveal it.
how_it_works: Each managed component, such as a server, network device or application, has an approved baseline of settings and versions.
Automated tools compare running configurations with the baseline and alert on any difference.
Every alert is traced to an approved change; unexplained differences are investigated and reversed.
Production source code lives in one access-controlled repository with full change history, not on developers' machines.
The main code line that releases are built from is protected: nothing merges into it without an independent, approved review.
For programs, code-comparison tools match production code with the last approved version in the repository; any difference without a change record is unauthorized.

rows.label: Shows
cells: Changes someone recorded and approved
Every difference between live settings and the approved state

rows.label: Misses
cells: Changes made without a ticket
Settings outside the tool's monitored scope

rows.label: Best for proving
cells: The approval process works
No unauthorized change happened

subtopics.example: An IS auditor at an online lender wants assurance that the loan-pricing program in production matches what was approved. She runs a code-comparison tool between the production version and the last approved version in the repository and finds a changed interest rule with no change record. She reports the unauthorized change to the chief technology officer and the head of credit risk.
subtopics.isaca_rule: To find unauthorized change, compare what is actually running with the approved baseline; ticket reviews cover only what someone recorded. Keep production code in one protected repository where nothing merges without independent review.

exam_traps.trap: Reviewing change tickets will reveal unauthorized changes.
exam_traps.why: Unauthorized changes have no ticket. Only comparing actual configurations with the baseline shows them.

exam_traps.trap: Backing up developers' laptops protects the production source code.
exam_traps.why: Backups protect availability only. Without one controlled repository, no one can prove which code is in production or who changed it.

key_terms.definition: Automatic comparison of live settings with the baseline that alerts on any difference.
A version-controlled store that keeps every change to code with its author and history.
Repository rules that block merges into key branches without approved, independent review.

subtopics.name: Patch Management
subtopics.definition: Patch management identifies, tests, approves, deploys and verifies vendor fixes for software flaws on a schedule set by risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each day a known flaw stays open gives attackers a chance, but a rushed patch can break production. The process balances both and makes someone accountable when a patch must wait.
how_it_works: Vendor notices and threat feeds identify new patches, which are matched against the asset inventory.
Patches are ranked by risk: flaws being actively exploited on exposed systems come first, ahead of raw severity scores.
Testing is shortened for urgent patches but never removed, and each deployment has a rollback plan.
Scans verify that each patch is actually installed.
When a patch must wait, compensating controls cover the gap and the business owner accepts the risk for a set period.
Internal risk acceptance cannot override an outside mandate, so a regulator's own exception process is used instead.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 524 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Patch management process: identify, test, approve, deploy, verify'><rect x='8' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='54' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Identify</text><rect x='122' y='24' width='70' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='157' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Test</text><rect x='214' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='260' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Approve</text><rect x='328' y='24' width='86' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='371' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Deploy</text><rect x='436' y='24' width='80' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='476' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Verify</text><line x1='102' y1='46' x2='113' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M113,42 L120,46 L113,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='194' y1='46' x2='205' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M205,42 L212,46 L205,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='308' y1='46' x2='319' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M319,42 L326,46 L319,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='416' y1='46' x2='427' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M427,42 L434,46 L427,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The patch cycle: identify, test, approve, deploy and verify. Testing protects production, but it must not become a reason to leave an exploitable flaw open.

subtopics.example: A school district's patch report shows a critical browser fix deployed to all 3,000 staff laptops. The IS auditor asks for verification scans and finds the fix installed on only 61 percent, because laptops kept off the network never received it. She recommends confirming installs by scan and following up every unpatched device. The IT director assigns an owner.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Patch by real risk, not by raw score or vendor order. Urgency shortens testing but never removes it. A patch that must wait needs compensating controls and documented, time-bound acceptance by the accountable owner.

exam_traps.trap: Patch strictly in order of severity score.
exam_traps.why: A high score on an internal, unexploited system can matter less than a medium flaw being actively exploited on an exposed server. Exposure and exploitation lead.

exam_traps.trap: Management accepted the risk, so a regulator's patch deadline can be missed.
exam_traps.why: Internal acceptance cannot waive an outside mandate. Use the regulator's formal exception process, with compensating controls.

key_terms.definition: A 0 to 10 scale rating how severe a flaw is in general, not how risky it is for one organization.
A flaw attackers are known to be using now, often listed in public catalogs of exploited flaws.
A documented decision to delay a patch, with compensating controls, an owner and an end date.

subtopics.name: Release Management
subtopics.definition: Release management plans, builds, tests and deploys a package of already-approved changes as one coordinated release, with a tested way to roll it back.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Changes that each work alone can clash when they go live together. Coordinating the release keeps partial, untested combinations out of production.
how_it_works: Approved changes are grouped into a release with one plan, schedule and owner.
The combined package is built once and tested as a whole, including links to connected systems.
It moves through environments, from development to test to staging to production, each acting as a checkpoint.
Staging mirrors production, so the final test is realistic.
A release goes live only after test or pilot results are reviewed and a tested rollback is ready; rollout methods such as canary releases are in 3B2.3.
Across platforms with different release cycles, one joint plan coordinates dates, testing and rollback.

rows.label: Unit of work
cells: One change
A package of approved changes

rows.label: Main question
cells: Should this change be allowed?
How do these changes go live together safely?

rows.label: Key output
cells: An approved, recorded change
A tested, deployed release with a rollback

rows.label: Typical failure
cells: An unauthorized change in production
Approved parts deployed separately and never tested together

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 496 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Release pipeline: development, test, staging, production environments'><rect x='8' y='24' width='116' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='66' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Development</text><rect x='146' y='24' width='90' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='191' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Test</text><rect x='258' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='308' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Staging</text><rect x='380' y='24' width='108' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='434' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Production</text><line x1='126' y1='46' x2='137' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M137,42 L144,46 L137,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='238' y1='46' x2='249' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M249,42 L256,46 L249,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='360' y1='46' x2='371' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M371,42 L378,46 L371,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Promotion through environments. A release moves from development to test to staging to production, and staging should look like production so the last check is realistic.

subtopics.example: A hotel chain's booking release passes every test in staging, then fails in production because staging runs an older database version. The IS auditor recommends keeping staging matched to production, checked before each release, and holding a release until its test results come from a matching environment. The head of digital platforms owns the fix.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Change management decides whether each change may happen; release management decides how approved changes reach production together. A release moves forward only on test or pilot evidence, with a tested rollback.

exam_traps.trap: Every change in the release was approved, so the release is under control.
exam_traps.why: Approving each part does not test how the parts work together. Release management packages, tests and rolls out the combination.

exam_traps.trap: The pilot is slow, so release to everyone now and fix issues as they appear.
exam_traps.why: Without reviewed pilot or test evidence, defects reach every user at once. Hold the release until the evidence is reviewed and the release is approved.

key_terms.definition: A pre-production copy of the live setup used for the final, realistic test.
A limited release to a small group to prove a change before full rollout.
The agreed time when a release may be deployed, chosen to limit business impact.

topics.overview: Logs record what happened on each system and who did it. They support troubleshooting, investigations and legal evidence, but only when every layer is covered, retention fits legal needs, records are protected from tampering, and someone actually reviews them.
can_do: Set log retention per log type from legal and business requirements
Recommend controls that keep logs complete, trustworthy and in time order
Explain why collecting logs is not the same as reviewing them
Preserve logs correctly when a regulator or court asks for them

subtopics.name: Log Coverage and Retention
subtopics.definition: Operational log management decides which events each system records, how long each type of log is kept, and how logs stay usable for operations and evidence.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A gap at any layer is a blind spot, and logs deleted too early cannot answer a regulator. Logs that capture too much can themselves leak personal data.
how_it_works: Every layer keeps its own logs, and all of them are in scope: network, operating system, database and application.
Privileged actions, such as commands run as administrator, are logged with the individual who ran them, not just the login.
All clocks synchronize to redundant, trusted time sources, with alerts on drift, so events from different systems line up.
Retention is set per log type from legal, regulatory and business requirements, not one uniform period or storage cost.
Personal and card data are masked or left out at the source, so logs keep what they need and nothing more.

types.meaning: Startups, logins, privilege use and service errors on a server.
User transactions, errors and business events inside an application.
Data changes, structure changes and administrator actions on a database.
Connections allowed or blocked, and setting changes, on firewalls, routers and switches.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 450 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Log management: collect logs, store them securely, monitor and analyze them'><rect x='8' y='24' width='84' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='50' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Collect</text><rect x='114' y='24' width='108' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='168' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Store securely</text><rect x='244' y='24' width='88' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='288' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Monitor</text><rect x='354' y='24' width='88' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='398' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Analyze</text><line x1='94' y1='46' x2='105' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M105,42 L112,46 L105,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='224' y1='46' x2='235' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M235,42 L242,46 L235,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='334' y1='46' x2='345' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M345,42 L352,46 L345,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The log pipeline: collect from every layer, store where they cannot be altered, then monitor and analyze. Skipping the last two steps means the logs detect nothing.

subtopics.example: A card issuer uses a software-as-a-service (SaaS) customer-service platform whose vendor keeps activity logs for seven days. The issuer's rules require one year for records of agent access to card data. The IS auditor recommends exporting those logs daily to the issuer's own log store and adding retention terms to the contract. The vendor manager arranges both.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Coverage first, then retention, then protection. Every layer logs, privileged actions tie to a named person, clocks agree, and each log type is kept as long as law and business require. Capture what is needed and mask what is sensitive.

exam_traps.trap: Logging every login gives full accountability for administrators.
exam_traps.why: Logins show who got in, not what they did. Privileged commands must be logged against the person who ran them.

exam_traps.trap: Set one retention period for all logs to keep things simple.
exam_traps.why: Legal and regulatory requirements differ by log type. Retention is mapped per type; storage cost and simplicity do not decide it.

key_terms.definition: How long a type of log is kept before deletion, set by legal, regulatory and business needs.
Keeping every system's clock aligned to a trusted source so event times can be compared.
Recording only the data the purpose needs, and masking or leaving out the rest.

subtopics.name: Protecting and Reviewing Logs
subtopics.definition: Log protection and review keep log records unaltered and flowing without gaps, and make sure named people examine them and act on what they find.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A log an attacker can edit proves nothing, and a log nobody reads detects nothing. Silent failures, such as a source that stops sending, can leave weeks of blind spots.
how_it_works: Hashing (storing a digital fingerprint of each file) or write-once storage makes any change to archived logs detectable; the protection is checked periodically.
Log administration sits with a role independent of the administrators whose actions are logged.
Named owners review logs at a frequency set by risk and follow up on what they find.
Source-health monitoring alerts when an expected log source goes quiet.
Storage thresholds trigger archiving before logs overwrite themselves, and changes to logging levels need approval and raise an alert.
When logs are requested for an inquiry or legal hold, scheduled deletion is suspended first, before retrieval.
subtopics.example: A pension administrator's log platform hashes each archived log file, but the hash values sit on the same server, where administrators could alter both, and no one has ever checked them. The IS auditor recommends storing the hashes in write-once storage outside the administrators' control and verifying a sample each quarter. The security operations manager owns the change.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Collection is not detection. Trust a log only when those it records have no control over it, a named owner reviews it, and gaps in flow or capacity raise alerts. When logs are requested, preserve first.

exam_traps.trap: Logs are collected centrally and stored, so the monitoring control works.
exam_traps.why: Storage alone detects nothing. The control needs assigned, risk-based review and follow-up, plus alerts when sources stop sending.

exam_traps.trap: When a regulator asks for older logs, update the retention policy first.
