exam_traps.why: Policy work takes time while scheduled deletion keeps running. Suspend deletion first to preserve what exists, then retrieve, then fix the policy.

key_terms.definition: Storage that accepts data once and then blocks any change or deletion.
An instruction to preserve records needed for litigation or an inquiry, overriding normal deletion.
Whether each expected system is still sending logs at its normal rate.

topics.overview: Service level management defines the service the business needs, records it in measurable terms and checks performance against it, for internal IT teams and outside suppliers alike. The IS auditor tests whether targets reflect business need, are measured accurately and hold end to end.
can_do: Tell a service level agreement (SLA) from an operational level agreement (OLA) and an underpinning contract
Spot a metric set that reports every target met while users are dissatisfied
Recommend independent measurement when payments depend on a provider's own figures
Explain why service credits do not transfer business impact

subtopics.name: Service Level Agreements and Metrics
subtopics.definition: A service level agreement (SLA) is a documented agreement between a service provider and its customer that sets measurable service targets, reporting and remedies.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An SLA turns good service into numbers both sides can check. Targets that cannot be measured, or that measure only speed, give false comfort and make penalties unenforceable.
how_it_works: A service catalog lists each service on offer, its owner and the service levels available.
The SLA defines each metric exactly: what counts, how it is measured, over which hours and what is excluded.
Metric sets balance speed with quality and satisfaction, such as resolution time, reopen rate and user surveys.
Internal operational level agreements (OLAs) and supplier contracts are set so that they support the SLA targets.
When a provider reports its own performance and money depends on it, the customer measures independently and reconciles the figures.
In a dispute, both sides start from the contract's definition of the metric.

rows.label: Between
cells: The service provider and its customer
Teams inside the provider
The provider and an outside supplier

rows.label: Purpose
cells: Sets the service the customer receives
Commits internal teams to support the SLA
Commits the supplier to support the SLA

rows.label: Example
cells: Payroll available 99.5% of business hours
Database team restores a failed database within 2 hours
Network carrier repairs a failed link within 4 hours

subtopics.example: A benefits agency's service level agreement (SLA) promises program managers that the benefits-payment system will be restored within four hours. The network carrier behind it is contracted to repair links within eight hours, and the database team has no agreed restore time. The IS auditor reports that the underpinning contract and the missing operational level agreement (OLA) cannot support the SLA. The service level manager renegotiates both.
subtopics.isaca_rule: An SLA works only if every target can be measured and reported. Balance speed with outcome measures, define each metric precisely, and measure independently when payments depend on the provider's own figures.

exam_traps.trap: All SLA targets are met, so the service is performing well.
exam_traps.why: If users are unhappy while speed targets are met, the metric set is incomplete. Add outcome and satisfaction measures.

exam_traps.trap: Penalty clauses are the most important part of an SLA.
exam_traps.why: Penalties mean nothing until performance can be measured. Numeric targets with agreed reporting come first.

key_terms.definition: A published list of IT services, their owners and the service levels each one offers.
A payment or discount the provider owes when it misses an agreed target.
The exact rule for calculating a measure, including what counts, the time window and exclusions.

subtopics.name: Service Levels, Architecture and Suppliers
subtopics.definition: End-to-end service level is the performance of the whole transaction path as the user experiences it, across every system, team and supplier involved.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A promise of 99.99% availability is empty if the systems behind it cannot deliver it. With several suppliers, each can meet its own target while the customer's service still fails.
how_it_works: Service tiers set by business need drive the architecture and the investment, not the other way around.
Architecture reviews check that redundancy and capacity can actually deliver each committed target.
When commitments exceed capability, the IS auditor quantifies the gap and the cost of options, and management decides.
End-to-end monitoring traces full transactions, so the failing link is found before blame is assigned.
Outsourcing transfers the work, not the accountability; service credits rarely cover the business impact of an outage.
A supplier's independent audit report, such as a System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 report, is relied on only after confirming its scope and period cover the services used.
subtopics.example: A courier company's board believes service credits protect it if its cloud tracking provider fails. The IS auditor compares a full-day outage's estimated lost revenue, about $2 million, with the contract's maximum credit of $40,000. She recommends planning resilience for the tracking service instead of relying on credits. The chief operating officer decides on the design.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Service levels shape design, and the organization stays accountable for end-to-end results even when suppliers deliver the parts. The IS auditor quantifies gaps and options; management makes the investment decision.

exam_traps.trap: Service credits protect the organization against supplier outages.
exam_traps.why: Credits are usually small next to lost revenue, fines and reputation damage. The organization keeps the business impact and must plan resilience accordingly.

exam_traps.trap: The supplier's SOC 2 report covers everything, so no further checks are needed.
exam_traps.why: First confirm that the report's scope and period match the services and period the organization relies on. A supplier's report also never covers the organization's own controls.

key_terms.definition: A class of service, such as gold or bronze, with its own targets and matching architecture.
A service level for one part, such as a network link, which can be met while the whole service fails.
The services, locations, controls and period that a supplier's assurance report covers.

topics.overview: Databases hold the organization's authoritative records. The IS auditor reviews how data is structured and kept consistent, who can change the data and its definitions, and whether every change is traceable and recoverable to the point the business needs.
can_do: Match a workload to a relational or NoSQL model and name where the IS auditor should look
Explain how keys, constraints and locking protect data integrity
Describe how rollback, roll-forward and restores recover a database
Recommend controls over powerful database administrator rights

subtopics.name: Database Models
subtopics.definition: A database model is the way a database organizes data and relationships: as trees, as networks, as related tables, or as flexible non-relational (NoSQL) structures such as documents.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The model decides where integrity is enforced. When the database does not enforce structure, validation moves into the application, and that is where the IS auditor must look.
how_it_works: Hierarchical databases store records in parent-child trees; network-model databases (nothing to do with computer networks) let a record have several parents.
Relational databases store data in tables of rows and columns, linked by keys and queried with Structured Query Language (SQL).
NoSQL (not only SQL) databases include document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores built for scale and changing structures.
Relational systems enforce a fixed schema and full transaction guarantees, which suits financial records.
Many NoSQL systems trade strict consistency for speed and scale, so the application must validate the data.

rows.label: Structure
cells: Records linked in trees or networks
Tables linked by keys
Documents, key-value pairs, wide columns or graphs

rows.label: Schema
cells: Fixed by the design
Fixed and enforced by the database
Flexible; may differ per record

rows.label: Best fit
cells: Older mainframe systems
Transactions, joins and reporting
Huge volumes and fast-changing data

rows.label: Audit focus
cells: Vendor support and scarce skills
Access, constraints and change control
Validation inside the application

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Relational databases store data in related tables; NoSQL databases handle flexible, unstructured data'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Relational</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Tables with set relationships</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>NoSQL</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Flexible, unstructured data</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Two families of databases. Relational stores data in linked tables with a fixed structure; NoSQL gives up some of that structure to handle flexible or unstructured data.

subtopics.example: A ride-hailing company plans to keep driver payout balances in a NoSQL key-value store with eventual consistency. The IS auditor notes that two copies could briefly show different balances, so a payout might be made twice. She asks the engineering lead to show how the design prevents this, such as a strongly consistent store for balances, before go-live.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the model by workload, then follow the controls. Where the database enforces structure, test its constraints and access; where it does not, test validation in the application. For legacy models, current risk comes from vendor support status and scarce skills.

exam_traps.trap: A planned replacement of the legacy hierarchical database lowers today's risk.
exam_traps.why: Today's exposure comes from vendor support status and scarce skills. A future migration changes nothing until it actually happens.

exam_traps.trap: A NoSQL store gives the same transaction and schema guarantees as a relational database, so the same controls apply.
exam_traps.why: Many NoSQL systems relax consistency and enforce no fixed schema. Integrity checks then move into the application, and that is where the IS auditor must test them.

key_terms.definition: The formal definition of a database's structure: its tables or collections, fields, data types and rules.
A NoSQL database that saves each item as a unique key paired with a value, built for very fast lookups.
Copies of data may briefly differ after an update but match again soon; common in NoSQL systems.

subtopics.name: DBMS Structure and the Data Dictionary
subtopics.definition: A database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores, retrieves and protects data; its data dictionary holds the definitions of every table, field and relationship.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Change one definition in the dictionary and every program that relies on it is affected. Uncontrolled changes can corrupt data silently or break reports across the business.
how_it_works: The DBMS controls storage, access, concurrent use, backup and logging for every program that uses the data.
The three-schema design separates what users see, how data is logically organized and how it is physically stored, so one can change without breaking the others.
The data dictionary records each data element's name, type, meaning, owner and relationships.
Schema and dictionary changes are limited to database administrators (DBAs) using logged, versioned scripts under change control.
Named data stewards own business definitions, so different units do not define the same field differently.

types.meaning: Commands that create or change structure, such as tables, fields and indexes.
Commands that read, add, change or delete the data itself.
Commands that grant or revoke access rights to data and objects.

subtopics.example: At a transit authority, analysts query the fares database with full table access, though they need only trip totals by route. The IS auditor recommends a database view that shows only those fields, granted by the database administrator (DBA) under change control. The data owner approves the view's contents and removes the table access.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Metadata is data that controls data, so guard it like production code. Changes are restricted, logged and versioned, and business definitions have named owners. Conflicting definitions are a governance gap, not a reporting bug.

exam_traps.trap: Conflicting field definitions across reports are a reporting tool problem.
exam_traps.why: They come from ungoverned metadata. The fix is ownership of definitions by data stewards and controlled approval of changes.

exam_traps.trap: Developers need direct dictionary access to keep projects moving.
exam_traps.why: Direct changes bypass review and logging and can break every dependent program. Schema changes go through DBAs using versioned scripts.

key_terms.definition: Data that describes other data, such as a field's name, type, format and meaning.
The business person responsible for the definition and quality of a set of data elements.
A stored query that shows users only the fields and rows they need.

subtopics.memory_aid: DDL Defines structure, DML Manipulates data, DCL Controls who gets access.

subtopics.name: Data Integrity and Simultaneous Updates
subtopics.definition: Database integrity controls keep stored data accurate and consistent, using normalized design, enforced keys and rules, and locking when many users change data at once.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without them, one fact is stored twice and the copies drift apart, records point to customers who no longer exist, and simultaneous updates overwrite each other.
how_it_works: Normalization splits data into tables so each fact is stored once and cannot drift between copies.
Entity integrity requires every row to have a unique, non-empty primary key.
Referential integrity requires every foreign key to match an existing primary key, so no orphan record points at a row that no longer exists.
Constraints such as allowed values and ranges are enforced in the database, where they apply to every program.
Every transaction, a group of steps that succeed or fail together, follows the four ACID properties below; locking provides the isolation.
Denormalization, storing data twice for speed, is a deliberate trade-off that needs checks to keep the copies consistent.

rows.label: Guarantees
cells: All steps happen, or none do
Data moves from one valid state to another
No one sees another's unfinished work
Committed work survives a crash

rows.label: Failure it prevents
cells: A debit with no matching credit
A record that breaks a key or rule
Two clerks overwriting each other's update
A confirmed payment lost in an outage

rows.label: Main mechanism
cells: Rollback of incomplete work
Keys and constraints
Locking
Log written before commit

subtopics.example: Two booking agents at a ferry operator sell the last cabin seconds apart, and both customers get confirmations. The IS auditor finds the reservation program reads availability, then writes the sale, without locking the record. She reports a missing isolation control and recommends locking within a transaction. The systems owner schedules the fix.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Enforce integrity as close to the data as possible: keys, constraints and transactions in the database rather than in each program. Where a design trades integrity for speed, expect compensating checks such as reconciliations.

exam_traps.trap: The data entry screens validate input, so database constraints are unnecessary.
exam_traps.why: Data also arrives through interfaces, scripts and utilities that skip the screens. Constraints in the database apply to every path.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting a customer is safe because payments are kept in a separate table.
exam_traps.why: Without referential integrity, those payments become orphans linked to no one. The database should block the delete or handle linked records by rule.

key_terms.definition: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability: the four properties of a reliable transaction.
A field, or set of fields, whose value uniquely identifies each row in a table.
A field that refers to the primary key of another table, linking the two.
Two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds; the database cancels one to break it.

subtopics.name: Database Recovery
subtopics.definition: Database recovery returns a database to a correct, consistent state after a failure, using backups plus a transaction log that records every change.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Crashes, corrupt storage and erroneous updates will happen. Backup and log-copy frequency decides how much work can be lost, which must stay within the recovery point objective (RPO).
how_it_works: Each change is written to the transaction log, with before-images and after-images, before it is committed.
Checkpoints periodically write changes to disk, so crash recovery starts from a known point.
After a crash, the database undoes uncommitted work from before-images and redoes committed work from after-images.
After media loss, the last backup is restored and the log is rolled forward to the latest or a chosen point.
Backups and log copies run at least as often as the RPO requires and are stored apart from the database.
Scheduled restore tests prove both the recovery time and the data recovered.

rows.label: Uses
cells: Before-images in the log
After-images in the log
A saved copy of the database

rows.label: Purpose
cells: Undo work that was never committed
Reapply committed work after a crash or restore
Replace damaged or lost data files

rows.label: Typical trigger
cells: A failed transaction or a crash mid-update
Recovery to the latest or a chosen point
Disk loss, corruption or ransomware

subtopics.example: At 2 p.m., a faulty script at an online grocer overwrites 40,000 delivery addresses. The last full backup is from midnight, and the transaction log is intact. The IS auditor confirms the database administrator's plan: restore the backup to a separate server, roll the log forward to 1:59 p.m., verify, then copy back the correct addresses. The operations director approves.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Backup and log-copy frequency must meet the RPO, or the possible loss exceeds what the business accepted. When recovery paths trade data loss against time, the IS auditor reports each path's impact and the business owner decides.

exam_traps.trap: Nightly full backups protect a database whose RPO is measured in minutes.
exam_traps.why: A failure just before the next backup loses almost a day of work. Only frequent log copies or replication keep loss within minutes.

exam_traps.trap: When the ledger is corrupt before a deadline, IT should pick the fastest restore.
exam_traps.why: The fastest path may lose more data or carry corruption forward. Present each path's data loss and timing; management, as risk owner, chooses.

key_terms.definition: The database's running record of every change, used to undo or redo work during recovery.
Copies of a record as it was before a change and as it became after it.
Restoring a database to its exact state at a chosen moment, such as just before a bad update.

subtopics.name: Database Controls and Administration
subtopics.definition: Database administrator (DBA) controls limit, separate and monitor the powerful rights needed to run databases, so every change to data or structure is authorized and traceable.
subtopics.why_it_matters: DBAs can read, change or delete any record. One misused DBA account can cause unnoticed fraud or data loss, so their power needs oversight from outside the team.
how_it_works: Each person, including analysts and DBAs, uses a named account with only the rights the role needs; shared accounts are removed.
DBA duties stay separate from development, from approving data changes, and from running the database audit trail.
If management accepts that DBAs need full rights, their activity is logged where they cannot alter it and reviewed by someone outside the team.
Direct fixes to production data go through approved requests, never ad hoc changes.
Trended performance metrics are compared with agreed thresholds, so slowdowns are found before users notice.
Sensitive fields are encrypted or masked, so database access does not expose everything in clear text.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Database controls: access controls, encryption, audit trails, backup and recovery'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Access controls</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Encryption</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Audit trails</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Backup and recovery</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Core database controls: access control decides who sees what, encryption protects the data itself, audit trails record changes, and backups make recovery possible.

subtopics.example: Billing staff at a telecom company email database administrators to correct customer balances, and the DBAs edit production tables directly. The IS auditor finds 300 such fixes in a quarter, none with an approved request or a record of the old value. She recommends approved data-fix requests, logged before and after values, and review outside the DBA team. The billing director owns it.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Where a role must hold broad power, control it through accountability: named accounts, separated duties, and independent review of activity the role cannot alter. Full DBA rights are acceptable only with that compensating oversight in place.

exam_traps.trap: A shared DBA account is acceptable if its password is strong and changed often.
exam_traps.why: Password strength does not show who acted. Shared accounts make every action untraceable, so each person needs a named account.

exam_traps.trap: DBAs should manage the database audit trail because they know the system best.
exam_traps.why: Then those being monitored could switch off or purge the record of their own actions. An independent role administers the audit trail.

key_terms.definition: Giving each account only the access its role needs, and nothing more.
A control that reduces a risk when the preferred control is not practical.
Hiding parts of sensitive values at display time, such as all but four card digits; stored data is unchanged.

topics.overview: The business impact analysis (BIA) is the foundation of all continuity work. It shows which business processes matter most and how fast harm grows when they stop. It also sets the recovery targets that every backup, site and plan must then meet.
can_do: Explain why a BIA starts from business processes and ignores likelihood
Tell the recovery point objective (RPO), recovery time objective (RTO), maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and minimum business continuity objective (MBCO) apart
Spot recovery targets that do not fit the MTD, the dependencies or the backups
Identify who supplies, validates, ranks and approves BIA results

subtopics.name: BIA Purpose, Scope and Ownership
subtopics.definition: A business impact analysis (BIA) is the study of how badly, and how quickly, a disruption to each business process would harm the organization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The BIA tells the organization what to recover first and how fast. Every later continuity choice, from backup frequency to recovery site, rests on it, so a BIA error spreads everywhere.
how_it_works: The unit of analysis is the business process, such as taking orders or paying staff; systems are identified afterward as dependencies.
Each process is scored for financial, customer, legal and regulatory, operational and reputational impact, using defined criteria.
Impact is measured over time, for example at one hour, one day and one week, because harm usually grows as an outage continues.
Scores use worst-case timing, such as month-end or a seasonal peak, not an average day.
The BIA records what each process depends on (systems, data, staff, sites and suppliers) and the minimum resources needed to resume it.
Impact is assessed regardless of likelihood; how probable an event is belongs in the risk assessment.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: If this process stops, how bad is it over time?
What could go wrong, and how likely is it?

rows.label: Starting point
cells: Business processes
Threats and vulnerabilities

rows.label: Considers likelihood
cells: No
Yes

rows.label: Main output
cells: Process priorities, dependencies and recovery objectives
Risks ranked for treatment

subtopics.example: A hospital's BIA gives the pharmacy dispensing process one 'high impact' score. The IS auditor recommends scoring each process at one hour, one day and one week, because harm grows as an outage continues and the steepest rise sets recovery priority. The continuity manager rescores them, and the executive committee approves the tiers.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Start from business processes, measure harm over time at worst-case timing, and set likelihood aside. Criticality is a business judgment: process owners and senior management decide it, and the IS auditor evaluates the method and advises.

exam_traps.trap: Start the BIA by listing the IT applications and rating each one's criticality.
exam_traps.why: The unit of analysis is the business process. Systems matter only as dependencies of processes, and an application list misses manual steps, staff and suppliers.

exam_traps.trap: Leave reputational or regulatory impact out because it cannot be priced exactly.
exam_traps.why: Both are real impacts. Assess them through measurable proxies such as customer attrition, fines, license action or regulator scrutiny.

key_terms.definition: How important a process is, judged by how fast and how severely its loss harms the organization.
Anything a process needs to run, such as a system, dataset, skilled person, site or supplier.
Agreed scales, used across the whole organization, for rating financial, customer, legal and reputational harm.

types.meaning: Cannot run without identical replacement capability and cannot be done manually; very low tolerance for interruption and very high downtime cost.
Can be done manually, but only for a short time; slightly higher tolerance for interruption.
Can be done manually at tolerable cost for a longer period, though with extra effort or staff.
Can stop for an extended period at little or no cost, with little catch-up work once restored.

subtopics.name: Recovery Objectives: RPO, RTO, MTD and MBCO
subtopics.definition: Recovery objectives are the business's limits for a disruption: the data it can lose, the downtime it can bear, and the minimum service it needs.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These numbers set backup frequency, the recovery site and the cost of continuity. If wrong or unapproved, a plan can pass every test and still fail the business.
how_it_works: The business impact analysis (BIA) shows how harm grows over time when each process stops.
Business owners set the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), also called the maximum tolerable period of disruption (MTPD), where harm becomes severe or lasting.
The recovery time objective (RTO) sits inside the MTD, leaving time to verify data and clear the backlog.
The recovery point objective (RPO) reflects how much recent work the business can lose.
Supporting systems and suppliers need targets at least as tight as the process.
Management sets targets where combined outage and recovery costs are lowest, within the MTD, approves them and accepts the residual risk.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: How much data can we lose?
How fast must service be back?
When does the outage become intolerable?

rows.label: Measured
cells: Backward from the disruption to the last good copy
Forward from the disruption to restored service
Forward from the disruption; the outer limit

rows.label: What meets it
cells: Backup frequency and replication
Recovery site, staff and procedures
Not met directly; RTO must fit inside it

rows.label: Smaller value means
cells: More frequent copies, higher cost
Faster site and more readiness, higher cost
A more critical process

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 148' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The data lost between the last backup and a disruption must not exceed the RPO; the downtime until service is restored must not exceed the RTO'><line x1='20' y1='80' x2='480' y2='80' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='250' y1='30' x2='250' y2='112' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='250' y='24' text-anchor='middle' font-family='JetBrains Mono, monospace' font-size='7.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--accent-fill)' letter-spacing='0.08em'>DISRUPTION</text><rect x='40' y='60' width='110' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='95' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Last backup</text><rect x='350' y='60' width='120' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='410' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Service restored</text><line x1='150' y1='116' x2='248' y2='116' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='252' y1='116' x2='350' y2='116' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='200' y='134' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Data lost ≤ RPO</text><text x='301' y='134' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Downtime ≤ RTO</text></svg>
illustration.caption: RPO and RTO on one timeline. The data written since the last good backup is lost, and that gap must not exceed the RPO; the time from the disruption until service is back must not exceed the RTO.

subtopics.example: A food distributor's BIA sets a 24-hour MTD for order picking and a 22-hour RTO. Staff need about six hours after systems return to verify stock data and clear the backlog. The IS auditor reports that the process would exceed its MTD; the operations director decides whether to tighten the RTO.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The business sets recovery targets through the BIA; IT designs solutions to meet them. The IS auditor verifies that targets are approved, consistent with each other and with dependencies, and proven by testing.

exam_traps.trap: A hot site will improve the RPO.
exam_traps.why: A hot site shortens downtime, which is RTO. Data loss depends on how recently data was copied, so only more frequent copies improve the RPO.

exam_traps.trap: IT should set the RTO to what the current infrastructure can achieve.
exam_traps.why: Targets come from business impact, not current capability. A target IT cannot meet is a gap to report, not one to loosen.

key_terms.definition: The reduced service level the business accepts until normal operations return.
ISACA's term for the service level required in alternate mode; close to the MBCO.
ISACA's term for how long the organization can wait for critical service before losses become unaffordable.
ISACA's term for the longest the organization can operate in alternate mode; not the MTD.

subtopics.memory_aid: RPO looks back at the Point you restore to; RTO looks ahead to the Time you are running again.

subtopics.name: Conducting, Validating and Approving the BIA
subtopics.definition: Conducting a business impact analysis (BIA) means gathering impact data from process owners, checking it, ranking processes on common criteria and getting senior management to approve the results.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unchecked or unapproved BIA results give every recovery plan a weak base. If each department rates itself critical, or nobody signs off, funding follows influence instead of the greatest impact.
how_it_works: The continuity team gathers data from process owners through questionnaires, interviews and workshops, and checks it against records such as revenue and transaction volumes.
Blank or vague questionnaire answers are followed up in interviews or workshops before anyone relies on them.
Processes are ranked against one enterprise-wide set of impact criteria, so departments cannot all rate themselves critical.
Processes with similar needs are grouped into recovery tiers that share the same targets.
Disputes between executives are settled by reconciling the evidence and letting the accountable executive committee decide.
Senior management approves the results before recovery strategies are chosen or funded.

types.meaning: Reaches many process owners quickly, but answers are often incomplete or inconsistent.
Clarifies impacts and dependencies in depth with one owner at a time; slower.
Brings owners together to agree on impacts and shared dependencies across processes.
Uses data such as revenue, volumes and contracts to test what owners claim.

subtopics.example: In a utility's BIA, the call-center manager reports that losing the outage-reporting line causes no harm for two days. Call records show storm-season peaks of 9,000 calls an hour and regulator penalties for unanswered reports. The IS auditor recommends a follow-up interview to reconcile the answer with the records before the tier is set. The executive committee approves the result.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The BIA is a business document. Owners supply the data, follow-up validates it, common criteria rank it, and senior management approves it. The IS auditor evaluates the method and the evidence and advises, but never sets criticality.

exam_traps.trap: Every department rated its processes critical, so fund fast recovery for all of them.
exam_traps.why: When everything is critical, nothing is prioritized. Rank processes against enterprise-wide impact criteria so recovery funding follows real impact.

exam_traps.trap: IT may start selecting recovery strategies from a finished BIA that management has not yet approved.
exam_traps.why: Unapproved results are not an agreed basis for priorities or spending. Obtain senior management approval first, then select strategies.

key_terms.definition: The manager accountable for a business process, who supplies and confirms its impact and dependency data.
A band of processes that share recovery targets, such as all tier 1 processes back within four hours.
Formal sign-off that confirms recovery priorities and makes them the basis for continuity funding.

topics.overview: Resilience means keeping services running through a failure, not only restoring them afterward. This topic covers the design choices that remove single points of failure, the redundancy techniques that put them into practice, and the fallbacks for people, suppliers and operational technology (OT).
can_do: Find single points of failure, including hidden shared dependencies such as one cable route
Match redundant array of independent disks (RAID), clustering and network diversity to the failure each one covers
Explain why mirrored disks and extra servers are not a backup
Recommend tested fallbacks for key people, critical suppliers and operational technology

subtopics.name: Resilient Technology Design
subtopics.definition: Resilient technology design builds systems that keep working, sometimes at reduced capacity, when a component fails, instead of relying only on recovery afterward.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Recovery always costs some downtime and often some data. Resilience prevents many outages altogether, which matters most for services with very short recovery time objectives (RTOs).
how_it_works: Designers trace each critical service end to end and list every single point of failure: one disk, server, network link, provider or site.
Each single point of failure gets a redundant partner, so the service continues when one fails.
Redundant parts must be truly independent, with different carriers, physical routes, power feeds and hazard zones.
Applications isolate a failing dependency with a circuit breaker and degrade gracefully, so core functions stay available.
If the backup path has failed or was never tested, deliberately run with reduced features rather than rushing to an untested environment.
Resilience is proven by controlled fault-injection tests, which break components on purpose, not by design documents.

rows.label: Goal
cells: Keep the service running through a failure
Restore the service after it stops

rows.label: Downtime
cells: None or very little
Up to the RTO

rows.label: Main tools
cells: Redundancy, failover, graceful degradation
Backups, alternate sites, recovery procedures

rows.label: Proven by
cells: Fault-injection and failover tests
Restore tests and disaster recovery tests

subtopics.example: A food processor runs its plant-scheduling system on two server clusters in separate buildings, and the IT manager reports no single point of failure. The IS auditor finds both buildings take power through one shared switchgear room. She reports the common-cause exposure and asks for a test with one power feed cut before accepting the claim. The plant director decides.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Redundancy counts only when it is independent and tested. The IS auditor looks for hidden shared dependencies, such as one cable route, power grid or provider, and asks for fault-injection or failover evidence before accepting a resilience claim.

exam_traps.trap: Two data centers mean the service has no single point of failure.
exam_traps.why: If both share a fiber route, power grid, flood zone or provider, one event can stop both. Independence matters more than the number of sites.

exam_traps.trap: An approved architecture diagram proves that failover will work.
exam_traps.why: Design documents show intent only. Controlled fault-injection or failover tests show the system really degrades gracefully when a part fails.

key_terms.definition: One event, such as a cable cut, that disables redundant parts together because they share a route, supply or site.
A software pattern that stops calls to a failing dependency, so its failure does not cascade.
Keeping core functions running, with reduced features or capacity, while some parts are unavailable.

subtopics.name: Redundancy Techniques: RAID, Clustering and Network Diversity
subtopics.definition: Redundancy techniques duplicate disks, servers and network links so one failure does not stop a service. Examples are RAID (redundant array of independent disks), clustering and diverse routing.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each technique protects against one kind of failure only. Spare disks or servers do nothing against deletion, corruption, ransomware or a shared cable route, so the IS auditor matches each technique to its risk.
how_it_works: Most RAID levels spread data across disks with mirror copies or parity, so the array survives one or two disk failures; RAID 0 survives none.
RAID applies every change across the array at once, so deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption are copied too.
Clustering links servers so another node takes over, or carries the load, when one server fails.

Diverse routing sends traffic over physically separate cables; alternative routing uses another carrier or medium, such as cellular or satellite; long-haul diversity uses separate long-distance carriers.
Last-mile circuit protection duplicates the local link between the building and the carrier's network, often the weakest point.

rows.label: How it runs
cells: All nodes serve users at the same time
One node serves; a standby node waits

rows.label: On failure
cells: Surviving nodes absorb the load, with little or no interruption
The standby takes over after a short failover

rows.label: Main risk
cells: Survivors overload if each node normally runs above half capacity
The standby falls out of sync with patches or configuration

rows.label: Typical use
cells: High-volume services that need near-zero downtime
Systems that can accept a brief pause

types.meaning: Striping across disks for speed, with no redundancy; one disk failure loses the whole array.
Mirroring: identical data on two disks; survives one disk failure at the cost of half the capacity.
Striping with parity spread across at least three disks; survives one disk failure.
Striping with double parity across at least four disks; survives two disk failures at once.
Mirrored pairs that are then striped; fast, and survives one failure in each pair.

subtopics.example: A call center buys internet circuits from two carriers, but both enter the building through one duct from the street. Roadworks cut the duct, and both circuits fail. The IS auditor reports the shared path and recommends last-mile protection, such as a second building entry or a wireless backup link. The facilities and network managers decide.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the failure first, then the control: RAID for disk failure, clustering for server failure, diverse routing for cable failure, a distant second site for site loss, and backups for lost or damaged data. High availability in one site is not disaster recovery. Untested redundancy proves nothing.

exam_traps.trap: RAID or disk mirroring means the data is backed up.
exam_traps.why: RAID applies every write, including deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption, across the array instantly. Getting data back needs separate point-in-time backups.

exam_traps.trap: An active-active cluster with both nodes at 70 percent load is fully protected.
exam_traps.why: If one node fails, the survivor must carry 140 percent of its capacity and may collapse. Each node needs headroom to absorb the other's load.

key_terms.definition: Calculated check data that lets a disk array rebuild the contents of a failed disk.
One server in a cluster.
Design that keeps a service running through component failures, usually within one site; it is not disaster recovery.

subtopics.name: People, Supplier and OT Resilience
subtopics.definition: Operational resilience is the ability to keep delivering critical services when any resource they rely on fails, including people, suppliers and operational technology (OT).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Plans often protect servers but forget that one expert can leave, a sole supplier can fail or a plant control system can stop, halting a critical process just as surely.
how_it_works: Plan for impacts, not causes: losing staff, a site, technology or a supplier is handled the same way, whatever triggered it.
Fix key-person dependency by cross-training a second person and rehearsing the task; documents alone do not create capability.
Capture leaving staff's knowledge in reviewed procedures before they go, as a bridge to successors.
Require critical suppliers to show evidence of tested recovery, or arrange an alternate source.
Include OT, such as SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) systems running production lines, in the enterprise plan with its own recovery and safety steps.
Give broad threats, such as a pandemic, one integrated plan under a cross-functional steering committee, because the workstreams depend on each other.

rows.label: Typical failure
cells: Only one person can do a critical task
A sole-source provider goes down
A control system stops or is attacked

rows.label: Fix
cells: Cross-train and rehearse a second person
Tested supplier recovery or an alternate source
OT recovery sequences inside the enterprise plan

rows.label: Evidence to ask for
cells: A rehearsal by the backup person
Supplier test results or a qualified alternate
Tested OT recovery and safety procedures

subtopics.example: A city government keeps separate continuity plans for floods, cyberattacks, strikes and pandemics, with conflicting contacts and steps. During a heatwave, none applies cleanly. The IS auditor recommends organizing plans around impacts, such as loss of staff, site, technology or a supplier, whatever the cause. The city manager assigns the rewrite to the continuity steering committee.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Every resource a critical service needs must have a tested fallback. Capability lives in trained people and proven arrangements, not in documents or contracts. In any OT incident, the safety of people and plant comes before production and before forensics.

exam_traps.trap: During an OT incident, keep production running or collect forensic evidence first.
exam_traps.why: Safety of people and the plant comes first. A controlled shutdown outranks output and investigation whenever safety margins are not assured.

exam_traps.trap: A detailed procedure document removes the risk of relying on one engineer.
exam_traps.why: Documents help, but capability is proven only when a second trained person has actually performed the task in a rehearsal.

key_terms.definition: Reliance on one person for a critical task or tool, so work stalls when they are absent.
The only provider of a product or service a process needs, with no qualified alternative.
Teaching a second person a critical task and proving it through practice.

topics.overview: Backups are the last line of defense against data loss. This topic covers how backups are taken and rotated, how network copying shrinks data loss, where copies are kept, and how test restores prove the data can really be recovered.
can_do: Tell full, incremental and differential backups apart and say what each restore needs
Match vaulting, journaling and replication to a recovery point objective
Evaluate offsite storage for distance, custody, inventory and key control
Choose the strongest evidence that backups can be restored

subtopics.name: Backup Schemes, Rotation and the 3-2-1 Rule
subtopics.definition: A backup scheme is the pattern of full, incremental and differential copies an organization takes; rotation is the schedule for reusing and retiring backup media.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The scheme sets how long backups take, how much storage they use and how long a restore will take. A poor choice can make restores miss the recovery time objective (RTO) or leave no clean copy.
how_it_works: Schemes are combined, such as a weekly full backup with daily incrementals, trading backup time against restore time.
Backups run at least as often as the recovery point objective (RPO) requires.
Grandfather-father-son rotation keeps daily, weekly and monthly sets, giving long retention without buying media for every backup.
The 3-2-1 rule keeps three copies of data, on two types of media, with one copy offsite; the newer 3-2-1-1-0 adds one immutable or offline copy and zero restore errors.
Fast disk backups serve everyday restores; at least one immutable or offline copy, managed with separate administrator credentials, stays out of ransomware's reach.
Retention must outlast the time it may take to notice silent corruption, or every remaining copy may already be bad.

rows.label: Copies
cells: All selected data
Changes since the last backup of any kind
Changes since the last full backup

rows.label: Backup time and storage
cells: Most
Least
Grows each day until the next full

rows.label: Restore needs
cells: The full backup only
The full plus every incremental since, in order
The full plus only the latest differential

rows.label: Restore speed
cells: Fastest
Slowest
In between

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 470 158' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Backup schemes: a full backup copies everything, incremental copies changes since the last backup, differential copies changes since the last full backup'><rect x='14' y='16' width='150' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='39' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Full</text><rect x='178' y='16' width='278' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='317' y='39' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Copies everything</text><rect x='14' y='60' width='150' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='83' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Incremental</text><rect x='178' y='60' width='278' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='317' y='83' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Changes since the last backup</text><rect x='14' y='104' width='150' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='127' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Differential</text><rect x='178' y='104' width='278' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='317' y='127' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Changes since the last full backup</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Three backup schemes side by side: full copies everything, incremental copies what changed since the last backup, differential copies what changed since the last full backup.

subtopics.example: A payroll bureau keeps 14 days of backups. Its incident records show corrupted tax codes usually go unnoticed for about five weeks, until employees query their pay. The IS auditor reports that a clean copy may no longer exist when corruption is found, and recommends retention longer than the usual detection time. The operations manager estimates the cost.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Backups are designed from business targets: frequency from the RPO, restore speed from the RTO, and retention from legal and corruption-detection needs. At least one copy must be offsite and one out of ransomware's reach.

exam_traps.trap: With daily differentials, a Thursday restore needs Monday's, Tuesday's and Wednesday's sets.
exam_traps.why: That describes incrementals. A differential holds every change since the full backup, so a restore needs the full plus only the latest differential.

exam_traps.trap: Several backup copies on different media, all kept in the same building, meet the 3-2-1 rule.
exam_traps.why: The rule needs one copy offsite. One fire or flood there could destroy every copy at once.

key_terms.definition: A media rotation that keeps daily (son), weekly (father) and monthly (grandfather) backup sets.
A backup copy that cannot be changed or deleted until its retention period ends, even by an administrator.

subtopics.name: Electronic Vaulting, Remote Journaling and Replication
subtopics.definition: Electronic vaulting, remote journaling and replication send copies of data to another site over a network, cutting data loss far below what shipping tapes allows.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When the recovery point objective (RPO) is minutes or near zero, nightly tapes cannot meet it. These techniques shrink data loss, each limited by distance, cost or corruption risk.
how_it_works: Electronic vaulting sends backup data over the network to an offsite vault in batches; loss reaches back to the last batch.
Remote journaling sends each transaction log entry to a remote site as it happens; replaying the journal onto the last backup rebuilds recent work.
Synchronous replication confirms each write only after both sites store it, so no committed data is lost, but distance is limited.
Asynchronous replication confirms writes locally and copies them moments later, allowing long distances but risking loss of the latest writes.
Replication copies deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption within moments, so point-in-time, immutable backups are still needed.

rows.label: What is sent
cells: Backup files, in scheduled batches
Database log entries, as they occur
Every write, moments after it is confirmed
Every write, before it is confirmed

rows.label: Data lost in a disaster
cells: Everything since the last batch, often hours
Log entries not yet sent, usually seconds
Writes still in transit, usually seconds
Near zero

rows.label: Ready to run after a disaster?
cells: No; restore the backups first
No; restore last backup, then replay log
Yes; the copy is nearly current
Yes; the copy is identical

rows.label: Cost and main limit
cells: Lowest cost; loss equals the batch interval
Moderate cost; restore plus replay takes time
Higher cost; a standby copy runs constantly
Highest cost; short distance, slower writes

subtopics.example: A logistics firm couriers backup tapes to a vault nightly, but its business impact analysis (BIA) now sets a one-hour RPO for bookings. The IS auditor reports that a site loss could destroy a day of bookings. The chief information officer prices vaulting, journaling and asynchronous replication, each with isolated backups. The operations director, as RPO owner, chooses.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Pick the technique from the RPO and the distance needed, not from what is newest. Every network copy also copies mistakes and attacks, so it never replaces isolated, point-in-time backups.

exam_traps.trap: Synchronous replication to a region 1,500 km away gives zero data loss with no side effects.
exam_traps.why: Every write waits for the distant site, slowing the application. Long distances usually need asynchronous replication and a small loss window.

exam_traps.trap: Real-time replication to a second region means separate backups are no longer needed.
exam_traps.why: Replication copies deletions, corruption and encryption within moments. Only point-in-time, immutable or offline copies restore a clean state.

key_terms.definition: A point-in-time image allowing fast rollback; it survives site loss only once copied to separate storage.
Travel delay between sites; it limits how far apart synchronous replication can run.
Backup that records every change, so data can be restored to almost any moment.
A remote duplicate database kept current by applying the primary's journal entries, ready to take over.

subtopics.name: Offsite Storage and Custody
subtopics.definition: Offsite storage keeps backup copies at a separate, secure location, far enough away that one event cannot destroy both the originals and the backups.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Backups beside the systems they protect can be lost in the same fire, flood or attack. Offsite copies help only if they are there, intact, findable and confidential.
how_it_works: The site must not share the primary site's regional hazards, such as a floodplain or power grid, yet stay close enough to retrieve media within the recovery time objective (RTO).
Every handover between operators, couriers and the vault is recorded on an itemized receipt signed by both parties.
The vault inventory is reconciled item by item against the backup catalog, proving the expected media is present.
A current backup catalog is kept offsite with the media, so the right tapes are found quickly.
Backups held by a vendor or cloud provider are encrypted with keys the organization controls.
Data residency rules are confirmed before choosing a cloud backup region; encryption does not change where data legally resides.
subtopics.example: A mining company sends backup tapes to a vault 600 km away to avoid shared hazards, but retrieval takes two days against a 12-hour RTO. The IS auditor reports the conflict and recommends a second copy closer by, still outside the hazard zone, or network vaulting. The chief information officer prices the options, and the business owner decides.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Offsite storage is a control only when distance, custody, inventory and security equal to the primary site are all proven. When a third party holds the data, the organization still controls the encryption keys and the legal location.

exam_traps.trap: Strong physical security at the vault proves the backups are safe.
exam_traps.why: Locks show the media is protected, not that it is there. Reconciling the vault inventory to the backup catalog proves the expected media is present.

exam_traps.trap: Encrypting cloud backups removes data residency concerns.
exam_traps.why: Encryption protects confidentiality, but the data still resides in the provider's region, so residency rules still apply.

key_terms.definition: An itemized, acknowledged record of every handover, so any loss can be traced to a point and a party.
The index of what each backup set holds and where its media is stored.
Legal rules on the country or region where data, including backup copies, may be stored.

subtopics.name: Restoration and Restore Testing
subtopics.definition: Restore testing means recovering data from real backup media into a test environment and checking that it is complete, correct and usable.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A backup job marked successful shows only that something was written. Without test restores, the organization may discover its backups are unusable in the middle of a disaster.
how_it_works: Restores are tested on a schedule, using samples drawn from the stored media, including offsite copies.
Restored data is checked with integrity checks such as checksums, record counts and reconciliation inside the application.
Tests are timed, so the organization knows whether a full restore fits within the recovery time objective (RTO).
Encryption keys and their escrow copies are tested too, because an encrypted backup without its key cannot be restored.
In cloud backup, the customer still owns restore testing; the provider's platform checks do not prove the customer's data restores.
After an attack, systems are restored into a clean environment from a copy confirmed to predate the compromise.

rows.label: What it proves
cells: A backup job ran and wrote data
The copy matched the source when written
The data can be recovered and used today

rows.label: What it misses
cells: Bad, partial or unreadable copies
Later damage, broken backup chains and missing keys
Little, if the sample and checks are sound

rows.label: Strength as evidence
cells: Weak
Moderate
Strong

subtopics.example: An online retailer restores a sample file each month and calls its backups tested. The IS auditor asks how long a full restore of the order database takes, and nobody knows. A timed test takes 31 hours against a 12-hour RTO. She reports the gap and recommends regular timed full restores. The IT operations manager decides how to speed recovery.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Recoverability is proven only by restoring data and checking it. Job logs, creation-time verification, contracts and provider assurances are weaker evidence. The IS auditor asks for recent, timed test restores with integrity checks.

exam_traps.trap: The backup job completed without errors, so the data can be restored.
exam_traps.why: Completion shows data was written, not that it is readable, complete or matched to its keys. Only a test restore with integrity checks proves recoverability.

exam_traps.trap: The cloud provider's platform health checks prove our backups will restore.
exam_traps.why: The provider runs the infrastructure; the customer owns its data and the proof that it restores.

key_terms.definition: A value calculated from data and compared before and after copying to detect any change.
A protected copy of encryption keys held by a trusted party, so backups can be decrypted if the original key is lost.
The most recent backup confirmed to predate an attack or corruption, used as the starting point for recovery.

topics.overview: The business continuity plan (BCP) keeps critical business processes running, or restores them, during and after a disruption. This topic covers how the continuity program is built, what a usable plan must contain, and how plans are kept current and audited.
can_do: Tell a BCP from a disaster recovery plan (DRP) and put the continuity lifecycle steps in order
Spot missing decision authority, activation criteria or crisis communications in a plan
Explain why insurance complements a BCP but never replaces it
Evaluate whether a plan is current, complete and understood by the people who run it

subtopics.name: BCP, DRP and the Planning Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: A business continuity plan (BCP) is the documented procedures for keeping or restoring critical business processes during and after a disruption, covering people, premises, suppliers and technology.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a program, departments act alone in a crisis and recover in the wrong order. The lifecycle grounds every plan, including the IT disaster recovery plan (DRP), in business priorities and keeps it tested and current.
how_it_works: Management issues a continuity policy setting mandate, scope, objectives and accountabilities; procedures belong in the plans beneath it.
A steering committee, assigned roles and regular management reviews turn the policy into a maintained program.
The business impact analysis (BIA) and risk assessment come next, followed by strategies for people, premises, suppliers and technology.
Plans are written to carry out the chosen strategies, and people are trained on their roles.
Plans are then tested, starting simply, and maintained as the business changes.
Continuity checks are built into project and change approvals, so new systems and processes are covered from the start.

rows.label: Scope
cells: The whole business: people, premises, suppliers, processes and technology
IT systems, data and infrastructure

rows.label: Goal
cells: Keep critical business processes running
Restore technology within its recovery time and point objectives

rows.label: Usually led by
cells: Business leadership and the continuity manager
IT leadership and technical recovery teams

rows.label: Relationship
cells: The umbrella plan
One component inside the BCP

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 118' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The business continuity plan is the umbrella; the disaster recovery plan sits inside it, focused on IT systems'><rect x='14' y='20' width='432' height='82' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent-fill)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><text x='230' y='38' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Business continuity plan (BCP)</text><rect x='70' y='52' width='320' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Disaster recovery plan (DRP)</text></svg>
illustration.caption: BCP and DRP. The business continuity plan is the umbrella for the whole business; the disaster recovery plan sits inside it and focuses on restoring IT.

subtopics.example: A fast-growing payments start-up hires a continuity manager, and the chief operating officer asks her to start BIA interviews next week. No continuity policy, scope or executive sponsor exists yet. The IS auditor advises first obtaining a management-approved policy that sets scope, objectives and accountabilities, so the BIA has an agreed boundary. The chief operating officer sponsors the policy.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Business continuity comes first; IT recovery follows from it. Senior management commitment and an approved policy start the program. Then the BIA comes first, strategy follows it, and people are trained before they are tested. Strategies cover every resource, not only IT.

exam_traps.trap: Choose the recovery site first, then run the BIA to confirm the choice.
exam_traps.why: The BIA sets the recovery objectives that justify a strategy. Choosing a site first risks paying for the wrong speed.

exam_traps.trap: Once management approves and publishes the plan, test it immediately.
exam_traps.why: Implementation comes before validation. Train people on their roles first; testing untrained staff only shows they have not read the plan.

key_terms.definition: Management's governance statement of the program's mandate, scope, objectives and accountabilities.
The chosen approach for meeting a process's recovery objectives, such as an alternate site or a manual workaround.
The international standard for business continuity management systems, used to structure and certify continuity programs.

subtopics.memory_aid: Order of the cycle: Policy, Analyze (BIA), Strategize, Plan, Train, Test, Maintain.

subtopics.name: Plan Contents and Decision Authority
subtopics.definition: Plan contents are the practical parts that let people act in a crisis: who decides, when the plan starts, how the organization communicates and what supplies it needs.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan with good procedures still fails if nobody knows who may declare a disruption or speak for the organization. Delays and mixed messages can cause more harm than the event itself.
how_it_works: Name a decision owner for each area, with clear limits and at least one trained alternate.
Set measurable activation criteria, so a named alternate can act without waiting for one unavailable executive.
Prepare crisis communications before any incident: named, trained spokespersons and pre-approved message templates.
Keep current call trees for staff, suppliers, regulators and customers, and plan copies offline and offsite, reachable when systems are down.
Hold reserves of critical supplies away from the main site, and qualify an alternate supplier.
Treat insurance as a complement that offsets financial loss, never as a substitute for recovery capability.
subtopics.example: Ransomware encrypts a regional insurer's file servers, including the only copy of its continuity plan and call tree. Managers spend the first hours rebuilding contact lists from memory. The IS auditor recommends current offline and printed copies of the plan and contacts with each team lead and at the alternate site. The continuity manager updates the distribution list.
subtopics.isaca_rule: People's safety always comes first. Crisis decisions never hinge on one person: the plan names who decides what, with alternates, limits and measurable triggers. Communications and critical supplies are prepared before the event.

exam_traps.trap: Comprehensive insurance coverage lets management reduce the continuity budget.
exam_traps.why: Insurance repays part of the financial loss but cannot restore operations, customers or reputation. It complements a continuity plan, never replaces it.

exam_traps.trap: Listing every senior executive as a decision maker gives the plan strong authority.
exam_traps.why: Without a named owner and limits for each decision area, decisions are delayed or contested. Specific, delegated authority lets people act.

key_terms.definition: The pre-agreed right of a named person or alternate to make continuity decisions within set limits.
Measurable triggers, such as expected outage length, for starting the plan.
A contact cascade in which each person notifies a few named others.
Coverage for lost profit and continuing costs during a disruption; it funds recovery but does not perform it.

subtopics.name: Maintaining and Auditing the BCP
subtopics.definition: Plan maintenance keeps the business continuity plan (BCP) current through scheduled and change-triggered updates; auditing checks that the plan is complete and people are ready.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Organizations change constantly through new systems, acquisitions, outsourcing and staff turnover. A plan that is not updated will try to recover a business that no longer exists.
how_it_works: Review the plan on a schedule and after significant changes, such as an acquisition; keep scheduled exercises running and add scenarios that probe the change.
When the plan is badly out of date, refresh the business impact analysis (BIA) first, then the strategies and procedures.
Test completeness by tracing each critical BIA process through a strategy to a working recovery procedure.
Test readiness by asking team members to describe their roles, triggers and contacts without the plan.
Report outcome metrics, such as recovery times achieved in exercises against each recovery time objective (RTO).
Track findings in one risk-ranked register, and close each only on evidence the fix works, such as a documented test.
subtopics.example: At a port authority, a call-tree test reaches only 60 percent of recovery team members because numbers changed in a reorganization, though the plan passed its scheduled review recently. The IS auditor recommends that joiners, leavers and role changes trigger updates to the affected plan sections, then a call-tree retest. The continuity manager agrees.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A plan is only as good as its last update and last test. The IS auditor traces coverage from the BIA, checks readiness through unaided interviews and test evidence, and closes findings only on proof the fix works.

exam_traps.trap: A guided walkthrough of the plan with each team member shows they are ready.
exam_traps.why: Guided walkthroughs mostly test agreement with the document. Unaided recall of duties, triggers and contacts reveals the real gaps.

exam_traps.trap: A remediation action can be closed once the plan document is revised.
exam_traps.why: A revised document shows intent, not capability. Close the action only when a documented test shows the control operates.

key_terms.definition: An update of affected plan sections prompted by a significant change, without waiting for the scheduled review.
A measure of results, such as recovery time achieved against the RTO, not activity such as meetings held.
One risk-ranked list of findings, each with an owner, a target date and retest status.

topics.overview: The disaster recovery plan (DRP) restores IT systems and data within the recovery time and point objectives set by the business impact analysis. This topic covers where to recover, what agreements secure that capacity, how recovery is invoked and run, and how tests prove it works.
can_do: Choose the alternate site that meets a given RTO and RPO at the lowest cost
Identify the main risks in shared, reciprocal and cloud recovery arrangements
Evaluate invocation criteria, delegated authority and restore order
Put plan test types in order and judge the evidence a test produces

subtopics.name: Recovery Strategies and Alternate Sites
subtopics.definition: An alternate processing site is a location prepared in advance to run critical systems when the primary site is unavailable, ranging from an empty room to a live copy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The site decides how fast systems return and how much data survives. A site that is too slow fails the business; one that is faster than needed wastes money.
how_it_works: The business impact analysis (BIA) sets the recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO); the strategy must meet both.
Management picks the least costly option that meets both targets; a mirrored site for a system that can wait days is also a finding.
Data at the site is only as current as its feed: restored backups lose everything since the last copy, while replication keeps data current.
Hardware needed to meet the RTO is pre-arranged with suppliers or held on standby, not ordered after the disaster.
The site must be far enough away to avoid shared hazards, and it must satisfy data residency rules.
The plan covers a range of scenarios, from one failed system to a cyberattack or the loss of the whole site.

rows.label: What is ready
cells: Space, power and cooling only
Some hardware and network links
Full equipment and connectivity
A live, continuously synchronized copy of production

rows.label: Typical recovery time
cells: Weeks
One to a few days
Hours
Minutes or less

rows.label: Data at the site
cells: Restored from backups after equipment arrives
Restored from backups at invocation
As current as the last copy or replication
Current to the last write

rows.label: Relative cost
cells: Lowest
Low to moderate
High
Highest

subtopics.example: A university pays for a mirrored site for its alumni-donation system, although the approved BIA allows a five-day recovery time objective (RTO) and a one-day recovery point objective (RPO). The IS auditor notes that a far cheaper site, restored from nightly offsite backups, would meet both targets, and reports the overspend. The vice president for advancement decides.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The site follows the targets: choose the cheapest option that meets both the RTO and the RPO from the approved BIA. Site readiness drives speed; copy frequency drives data loss.

exam_traps.trap: A hot site restored from last night's backup meets a near-zero RPO.
exam_traps.why: A hot site recovers quickly, but restoring a nightly backup loses everything since that copy. Near-zero data loss needs continuous replication or mirroring.

exam_traps.trap: The fastest site is always the safest recommendation.
exam_traps.why: Speed has a cost. When the BIA allows days for recovery, a slower, cheaper site that meets the RTO and RPO beats a hot or mirrored site.

key_terms.definition: A supplier's advance commitment to deliver replacement equipment within a set time after a disaster.
An area exposed to the same regional threat, such as a floodplain, power grid or earthquake fault.

subtopics.name: Recovery Site Agreements and Cloud Disaster Recovery
subtopics.definition: Recovery site agreements are the arrangements that secure a place to recover: commercial shared sites, reciprocal agreements, mobile units, duplicate sites or cloud services.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A recovery site helps only if it is available when needed. Contract terms, shared capacity and dependence on one provider decide whether the organization can recover.
how_it_works: Shared commercial sites serve many subscribers, so contracts need guaranteed capacity and priority rules for when several invoke at once.
Contracts also set test time, maximum use duration, notice periods, security standards and audit rights.
Relying on one shared facility is concentration risk no contract removes; when exiting a risky site, keep it until tested interim or replacement capacity exists.
In cloud recovery, the provider runs the platform; the customer still owns the plan, testing, keys, data residency and proof of meeting its recovery time objective (RTO).
The recovery region must be independent of the primary region, with capacity reserved, because many customers may fail over at once.

types.meaning: A provider's hot, warm or cold facility, shared by many subscribers under contract.
Two organizations agree to host each other's processing; cheap, but hard to enforce, test or size, and their systems may drift out of compatibility.
A transportable unit, such as an equipped trailer, delivered and set up near the damaged site; takes days.
A recovery site the organization owns and equips like the primary; costly but fully under its control.
A provider replicates the organization's systems to its cloud and runs them there when recovery is invoked.

subtopics.example: Two credit unions agree to host each other's core banking after a disaster. Each runs near full capacity, and one moves to a different banking platform next year. The IS auditor reports the pact is unlikely to work: no spare capacity, growing incompatibility and no agreed testing. Senior management weighs a commercial recovery site instead.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Judge a recovery arrangement by whether capacity will be there when many others need it too. Outsourcing the site or platform never outsources accountability: the organization must still prove, by testing, that it meets its own recovery targets.

exam_traps.trap: A reciprocal agreement with a peer firm is a low-cost way to meet a short RTO.
exam_traps.why: Peers rarely keep spare capacity, their systems may not be compatible, and the pact is hard to enforce or test. It suits only long recovery targets.

exam_traps.trap: The right to audit is the most important clause in a shared hot-site contract.
exam_traps.why: Audit rights help, but if several subscribers invoke together and capacity runs out, recovery fails. Capacity guarantees and priority rules matter most.

key_terms.definition: Dependence on one provider, facility or region, so a single failure removes many safeguards at once.
Selling the same recovery capacity to more customers than could use it at once.
A paid guarantee of cloud computing capacity in a region when the organization must fail over.

subtopics.name: Invocation and Recovery Procedures
subtopics.definition: Invocation is the formal decision to activate the disaster recovery plan (DRP); recovery procedures are the written steps teams then follow to restore systems in the right order.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every minute spent debating invocation comes out of the recovery time objective (RTO). Unclear procedures or a wrong restore order can turn a recoverable outage into a missed target.
how_it_works: Invocation uses measurable thresholds, such as an outage forecast to exceed the RTO, not vague triggers like "significant impact".
