When criteria are met, the named authority or delegated alternate invokes at once, without seeking consensus; anyone else escalates to them immediately instead of invoking alone.
Procedures are detailed enough for a qualified alternate to follow, because the usual experts may be unavailable.
Shared infrastructure, such as directory and network services, is restored first, then applications in business impact analysis (BIA) priority order.
Total recovery time follows the longest chain of dependent steps, given available staff, not the sum of every system's time.
Each workstream that must run in parallel has its own trained lead, so no one person becomes a bottleneck.

types.meaning: Acts first: protects people, contains the damage and alerts management.
Judges the extent of the damage and advises whether to invoke the plan.
Restore networks, platforms, databases and applications at the recovery site.
Recovers usable equipment and records from the damaged site and prepares the return.
Coordinates the move from the alternate site to a restored or new permanent site once recovery is complete.
Tracks progress across all teams and reports to management and stakeholders.

subtopics.example: A manufacturer has run from its hot site for five weeks after a warehouse fire, and the contract allows six. No one owns the move back to the rebuilt site. The IS auditor recommends assigning the relocation team now, with a tested cutover plan and data synchronization steps. The chief operating officer approves the return date.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Invoke fast, on measurable criteria, under authority named in advance. Then restore by business priority, adjusted for technical dependencies. The IS auditor evaluates triggers, delegation, procedure detail and team structure, because a weakness in any one can delay recovery beyond the RTO.

exam_traps.trap: An on-call director invoked the plan while the chief information officer was unreachable, so it needs approval afterward.
exam_traps.why: If documented criteria were met under delegated authority, the invocation is valid. Report it afterward, but do not make validity depend on ratification, which teaches people to wait.

exam_traps.trap: Total recovery time is the sum of every system's restore time.
exam_traps.why: Independent systems restore in parallel; total time follows the dependency critical path, given available staff.

key_terms.definition: The longest chain of dependent steps; it sets the shortest possible recovery time.
Services many applications need, such as directory, identity and network services.

subtopics.name: Testing the Recovery Plans
subtopics.definition: Plan testing exercises the continuity and disaster recovery plans, from desk reviews up to live failovers, to prove they work and to find gaps safely.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An untested plan is a guess. Tests expose wrong contacts, missing steps and unrealistic recovery times before a real disaster does, and give management and regulators evidence of readiness.
how_it_works: Before the test, define the scope, objectives, measurable pass or fail criteria, and stop conditions that protect production.
During the test, continue where safe, and have observers record every deviation, workaround and failure.
After the test, log each gap with its root cause, owner and due date, and confirm the fix in the next test.
Tests progress in realism and risk: discussion-based tests first, then live tests; the most critical systems need periodic parallel or full tests.
System-generated evidence, such as timestamped failover logs, is more reliable than recollection or management statements.
Tests committed to a regulator, or needed to prove a fix, stay on schedule; under resource pressure, narrow the scope rather than defer.

types.meaning: Team members check the plan's contents and contact details against current reality, without moving any resources.
The team talks through a scenario step by step to test roles and decisions; ISACA also calls this a paper or desk-based test.
A realistic scenario is played out with timed events, without moving live processing.
A localized live test of one part of the plan, such as one site or system, repeated over time; cost-effective evidence before a full test.
Recovery systems process real data at the alternate site while production keeps running.
Production is shut down and moved to the recovery site; the most realistic test and the riskiest.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 538 114' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='BCP test types by thoroughness: checklist is least thorough, full interruption is most thorough'><rect x='8' y='18' width='86' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='51' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Checklist</text><rect x='108' y='18' width='92' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='154' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Walkthrough</text><rect x='214' y='18' width='88' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='258' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Simulation</text><rect x='316' y='18' width='82' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='357' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Parallel</text><rect x='412' y='18' width='118' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='471' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Full interruption</text><line x1='8' y1='78' x2='521' y2='78' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M521,74 L528,78 L521,82 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><text x='40' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>least thorough</text><text x='490' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>most thorough</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Plan tests from least to most thorough: checklist, walkthrough, simulation, parallel and full interruption. Organizations progress through them in order; each step adds realism and risk.

subtopics.example: During a parallel test at a payments processor, transactions from the recovery site start posting to live customer accounts. The test plan has no stop conditions, so the team debates for 40 minutes. The IS auditor recommends defining stop conditions that protect production before any further test. The chief operating officer approves the retest plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A test is valuable for the honest evidence it produces, not for a clean pass. Define success in advance, progress from simpler tests to more realistic ones, record every failure, and track each gap to a verified fix.

exam_traps.trap: The full-interruption test is the best test, so schedule it first.
exam_traps.why: It is the most realistic but also the riskiest, because it stops production. It follows only after simpler tests succeed.

exam_traps.trap: When the test starts failing, stop it and reschedule to avoid a failed result.
exam_traps.why: Failures are the evidence a test exists to find. Continue where safe, record workarounds, and report each gap with an owner and date.

key_terms.definition: A predefined event, such as a threat to production or safety, that ends a test at once.
A person outside the recovery work who records times, deviations and results.
Measurable thresholds, agreed in advance, for judging whether each objective was met.

key_terminologies.Availability: The share of agreed service time during which users can actually use a service as required.
key_terminologies.Capacity management: Monitoring and forecasting resource use so enough processing, storage and network is in place before demand arrives.
key_terminologies.Single point of failure: One component whose failure stops a whole service because nothing else can take over.
key_terminologies.Redundancy: Extra components or paths that take over when one fails, reducing the impact of a failure.
key_terminologies.End of support (EOS): The date after which a vendor stops providing fixes, parts or help for a product.
key_terminologies.Media sanitization: Clearing, purging or destroying storage media so its data cannot be recovered.
key_terminologies.Job scheduler: Software that runs production jobs in order, by time and dependency, and records each outcome.
key_terminologies.Robotic process automation (RPA): Software bots that repeat rule-based screen tasks a person would otherwise do.
key_terminologies.System interface: An automated link that moves data from one application to another, directly or through middleware.
key_terminologies.Service desk: The single point of contact that logs, prioritizes and resolves or routes users' incidents and requests.
key_terminologies.Workaround: A temporary way to restore service without removing the underlying cause.
key_terminologies.Root cause analysis (RCA): A fact-based method for finding the underlying reason an incident happened, beyond its symptoms.
key_terminologies.Incident commander: The one person who directs a major incident response and makes its time-critical decisions.
key_terminologies.Emergency change: An urgent change made through a faster route, reviewed and approved independently soon afterward.
key_terminologies.Configuration baseline: The approved settings a system must match; live settings are compared with it to spot unauthorized change.
key_terminologies.Patch management: Finding, testing, approving, installing and verifying vendor fixes in order of risk.
key_terminologies.Log integrity: Assurance that log records have not been altered or deleted since they were written.
key_terminologies.Service catalog: A published list of IT services, their owners and the service levels each one offers.
key_terminologies.Data dictionary: The database's stored definitions of its tables, fields and relationships; its metadata.
key_terminologies.ACID: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability: the four properties of a reliable database transaction.
key_terminologies.Transaction log: A database's running record of every change, used to undo or redo work during recovery.
key_terminologies.Business resilience: The ability to keep critical services running through disruption and to recover quickly when they stop.
key_terminologies.Business impact analysis (BIA): A study of how harm grows over time when each business process stops, used to set recovery priorities and targets.
key_terminologies.Business continuity management (BCM): The ongoing program that plans, tests and maintains the organization's ability to keep working through disruption.
key_terminologies.Alternate processing site: A separate location, owned or contracted, where systems and staff can resume work when the main site is unusable.
key_terminologies.Invocation: The formal decision, by a named authority, to activate a continuity or disaster recovery plan.
key_terminologies.3-2-1 rule: Keep three copies of important data, on two kinds of media, with one copy stored offsite.
key_terminologies.Recovery point objective (RPO): The greatest data loss the business accepts, measured back in time from a disruption; it sets how often data is copied.
key_terminologies.Recovery time objective (RTO): The target time, set through the BIA, within which a process or system must be restored; it must fit inside the MTD.
key_terminologies.Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD): The longest a process can be unavailable before harm becomes severe or lasting; also called the maximum tolerable period of disruption.

domains.overview: This domain asks how an organization keeps its information safe and what an IS auditor should look for. Part A covers the protective layers: policies and classification, physical security, identity and access, networks and endpoints, data loss prevention, encryption and public key infrastructure (PKI), cloud and virtual platforms, and mobile, wireless and connected devices. Part B covers what happens when protection is tested: awareness, attack methods, security testing, monitoring, incident response and forensics. Throughout, the IS auditor evaluates whether controls fit the risk and operate effectively, then recommends improvements; management decides and owns the risk.
domains.analogy: Think of how a museum protects its collection. It decides which pieces matter most and how each must be handled (policy and classification). It locks galleries and controls who carries keys (physical and access control), seals valuable items in cases and records who opens them (encryption and logging), and trains staff to spot tricks (awareness). Guards watch cameras and alarms (monitoring), and a rehearsed plan covers a theft, including protecting the scene for the police (incident response and forensics). No single lock protects the collection; the layers working together do.

topics.topic_name: Information Asset Security Policies, Frameworks, Standards, and Guidelines
topics.overview: This topic covers the written rules and outside frameworks that steer an information security program, and the roles and classification that decide how much protection each asset gets. It also covers baselines that set minimum configurations, and the privacy and acceptable use rules that limit how data and systems may be used.
can_do: Place a security requirement in the right document: policy, standard, procedure or guideline
Tell when ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification or the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 fits an assurance need
Evaluate a baseline exception for an expiry date, owner approval and a working compensating control
Identify who decides classification and access, and who implements it

subtopics.name: Security Policy Set and Enforcement
subtopics.definition: An information security policy is management's approved statement of security objectives, scope and responsibilities, put into force through topic policies, standards, technical controls and monitoring.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The policy gives every security control its authority; without named duties and compliance checks, people ignore it. Document types are covered in 2A3.1.
how_it_works: Business objectives, risk assessment and legal duties shape it, with input from business, human resources and legal staff.
The board or senior management approves it, naming the security duties of data owners, administrators and users.
Technical settings enforce rules where possible, such as device management that blocks unencrypted laptops.
Compliance monitoring reports gaps to the policy owner, who reviews the policy on a set cycle and early after a major change, such as a new law.
Security spending is justified in business-risk terms, such as expected losses reduced, not by technical metrics or a quiet incident record.

rows.label: Covers
cells: Objectives, scope and responsibilities for the whole organization
Focused rules for one area, such as acceptable use or cryptography

rows.label: Audience
cells: Everyone
The people the topic affects

rows.label: Approved by
cells: Board or senior management
Management with authority over the topic, within the main policy

subtopics.example: A logistics firm's policy requires encryption on every laptop. The IS auditor samples 40 laptops and finds 9 unencrypted, because staff must switch encryption on themselves and nobody checks. The IS auditor recommends enforcing it through central device management, with monthly compliance reports to the policy owner, the chief information security officer (CISO).
subtopics.isaca_rule: A policy draws authority from top-level approval and drives action only when it names who is responsible. Build it from business risk and enforce it through technical controls and monitoring; a policy nobody monitors gives no assurance.

exam_traps.trap: The security policy only needs to name duties for the IT and security teams.
exam_traps.why: Protecting information is everyone's job, so the policy assigns duties to data owners, administrators and users.

exam_traps.trap: Buy and deploy the security tool now, and write the policy that governs it later.
exam_traps.why: Without an approved policy, the tool has no agreed rules, owners or authority. Policy and classification come first; technical controls then enforce them.

key_terms.definition: Using system settings to apply a rule automatically, so people cannot easily break it.
Regular, ideally continuous and automated, checks that people and systems follow the policy, catching failures early and evidencing the whole period.
Advisory direction teams may adapt; any mandatory rule belongs in a standard that draws authority from policy.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability; integrity means data stays accurate and unaltered without authorization, as with pay records.

subtopics.name: Running Security with ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF
subtopics.definition: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 sets certifiable requirements for an information security management system (ISMS); the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 lists voluntary outcomes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks give the program a tested structure and a shared language for the board and customers; used badly, they become a checklist that replaces risk decisions.
how_it_works: The ISMS runs as a cycle: scope, risk assessment, treatment, operation, measurement, internal audit, management review and improvement.
The Statement of Applicability (SoA) lists each Annex A control, whether it is implemented, and the risk-based reason for including or excluding it.
An accredited certification body certifies the ISMS only for the scope written on the certificate.
CSF 2.0 groups outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
Teams compare Current and Target Profiles; management ranks the gaps by business risk into a funded roadmap.
Framework choice starts from binding legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, then compares candidate frameworks against them.

rows.label: What it is
cells: Requirements for a management system
A voluntary set of security outcomes

rows.label: Key artifact to audit
cells: Statement of Applicability and risk treatment plan
Current and Target Profiles and the gap roadmap

rows.label: Independent certification
cells: Yes, by an accredited body, for a stated scope
No; alignment is self-declared

rows.label: Best fit when the scenario asks for
cells: Certifiable assurance to customers or partners
A flexible way to assess and communicate cyber risk

subtopics.example: A freight company has held ISO/IEC 27001 certification for three years. The IS auditor finds no management review in 18 months and audit findings without owners, though the chief information security officer calls the certificate valid. The IS auditor reports that the ISMS improvement cycle has stopped and recommends scheduled management reviews that assign every finding an owner and date.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Controls treat assessed risks; a framework is a reference, not a substitute for risk assessment. Choose frameworks after identifying binding legal and contractual requirements. ISO/IEC 27001 gives certifiable assurance; NIST CSF 2.0 is voluntary.

exam_traps.trap: A vendor's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers the service our company uses.
exam_traps.why: A certificate covers only its stated scope; the IS auditor verifies that the service's systems and sites fall inside it.

exam_traps.trap: Every Annex A control must be implemented before certification.
exam_traps.why: Exclusions are allowed when the SoA records a risk-based reason for each one.

key_terms.definition: The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 reference list of 93 controls in four themes: organizational, people, physical and technological.
Top management's scheduled check that the ISMS still fits the business, works and improves.
Guidance on implementing each Annex A control; certification is against ISO/IEC 27001, never 27002.
One control set mapped to every applicable standard and regulation, so each control is run and evidenced once.

subtopics.memory_aid: Govern steers; then know it, guard it, spot it, stop it, fix it (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover).

subtopics.name: Security Baselines and Exceptions
subtopics.definition: A security baseline is the minimum configuration every system of a given type must meet, such as patches applied, unneeded services turned off and logging on.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Baselines make protection consistent and testable across thousands of systems. Without them, or without a controlled way to depart from them, weak settings spread quietly and nobody can say which systems are exposed.
how_it_works: Teams build each baseline from a hardening guide, such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks, adjusted to the organization's risk.
New systems are built from an approved image or template, so they start compliant.
Automated configuration scans compare live systems with the baseline and flag configuration drift.
A system that cannot comply needs a formal exception: documented, risk-accepted by the asset owner, given an expiry date and backed by a compensating control.
Conformance reports are weighted by asset criticality and exposure, so failures on the riskiest systems do not hide in an average.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A security baseline: latest patches, antivirus active, unneeded services off, hardened configuration'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Latest patches</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Antivirus active</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Unneeded services off</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Hardened configuration</text></svg>
illustration.caption: A baseline lists the minimum settings every system of a given type must have. Systems may go further, never below it without an approved exception.

subtopics.example: A hospital's imaging server cannot take the latest operating system patch because its vendor has not certified it. The IT manager records an exception, the radiology director accepts the risk until June, and the server moves to an isolated segment. The IS auditor tests that the segment rules really block other traffic and confirms the exception carries an expiry date and a review.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A baseline is a floor, not a goal. Any gap needs a formal, time-limited exception owned by the business. Because the residual risk depends on the compensating control, the IS auditor verifies that control actually operates instead of accepting that it is recorded.

exam_traps.trap: An exception approved once can stay in place until the system is retired.
exam_traps.why: Risk acceptance holds only for the conditions assessed. Threats, data and systems change, so exceptions need expiry dates and reassessment.

exam_traps.trap: A high overall compliance rate shows the baseline is working.
exam_traps.why: An average can hide failures on the most critical or internet-facing systems. Weight results by criticality and exposure before drawing conclusions.

key_terms.definition: The gradual move of a system away from its approved settings through changes, fixes and workarounds.
An alternative control that reduces the risk when the required control cannot be applied.
A documented decision by an accountable owner to accept a known residual risk for a set period.

subtopics.name: Data Roles and Classification Handling
subtopics.definition: Data roles split security duties: the data owner classifies data and approves access, the data custodian applies the required controls, and users follow the handling rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Protection fits the data's value only when the person who understands that value decides; when administrators or the security team decide, controls drift from business need.
how_it_works: First inventory information assets and name an owner for each; the organization then approves one scheme, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted.
Each level has handling rules for storage, encryption, sharing, labeling, retention and disposal.
The data owner assigns the level and approves each access request against business need.
Data custodians, such as system and database administrators, configure access rights, encryption and backups to match the level.
The security function designs the scheme, advises and monitors compliance; it does not own business data.
Users handle data according to its label and report suspected misuse.
subtopics.example: A regional airline starts classifying its data, and the security team labels file shares by keyword search. The IS auditor finds no inventory of information assets and no named owner for loyalty-program member data, so nobody can approve its level or access. The IS auditor recommends that management first inventory the assets and name a business owner for each, who then assigns levels under one scheme.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The owner decides, the custodian implements, and the security function advises and monitors. Accountability stays with the business owner even when the work is delegated to IT or a provider. One organization-wide scheme, with handling rules per level, beats labels invented unit by unit.

exam_traps.trap: A user may lower a document's classification to share it more easily.
exam_traps.why: Only the data owner sets or changes the level. Users follow the label's handling rules and ask the owner when a label looks wrong.

exam_traps.trap: Database administrators should classify the data, because they know the systems best.
exam_traps.why: Custodians know systems, not the data's business value or legal duties. The data owner classifies and approves access; administrators apply the controls the owner specifies.

key_terms.definition: The business manager accountable for a data set's classification, access approvals and acceptable use.
The role, usually IT or a provider, that runs systems and applies the owner's protection requirements.
The required treatment for each classification level, from storage and sharing to disposal.

subtopics.name: Privacy Principles and Acceptable Use
subtopics.definition: Privacy principles limit why and how personal data may be collected and used; an acceptable use policy (AUP) states what every user may do with company systems.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security keeps data from the wrong people but cannot make a use lawful. Monitoring and data loss tools also process personal data and must follow the same principles.
how_it_works: Purpose limitation: data collected for one stated purpose is not reused for a new, incompatible one.
Minimization and storage limitation: collect only what a stated purpose needs, and keep it no longer than required.
Where consent is the lawful basis, it needs a clear affirmative act; pre-checked boxes and silence do not count.
Access and erasure requests are answered within one month under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), after identity checks; overdue backlogs are cleared first.
Transfers abroad need a lawful basis: an adequacy decision (such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework), standard contractual clauses or a narrow exception for legal claims; without one, they stop.
The AUP covers employees, contractors and temporary staff, and each user acknowledges it before getting access.
subtopics.example: A retailer's marketing team wants to train a sales model on customer support call recordings collected to resolve complaints. The recordings are well encrypted. The IS auditor notes that reuse for an incompatible purpose may breach the GDPR and recommends a documented compatibility assessment before any reuse.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Privacy limits the purpose, not just the access. Strong security does not make collection, reuse or transfer lawful; each needs its own lawful basis, and employee monitoring needs one in each country.

exam_traps.trap: Security monitoring and data loss prevention tools are exempt from privacy rules because they protect data.
exam_traps.why: They process personal data too, so each needs a documented purpose, a lawful basis and proportionate scope in every country.

exam_traps.trap: The acceptable use policy needs to cover only permanent employees.
exam_traps.why: Contractors and temporary staff use company systems too; without their acknowledgment, misuse cannot be enforced.

key_terms.definition: The legal ground for processing personal data, such as consent, a contract or a legal obligation.
Approved contract terms that let personal data leave the EU when no adequacy decision covers the destination.
A documented review, before new or changed processing, of its privacy risks and the controls that reduce them.

topics.overview: Logical controls mean little if someone can carry off a server or a burst pipe can flood it. This topic covers environmental hazards and power, the choice of fire suppression, and the physical barriers that keep unauthorized people away from equipment and media.
can_do: Match each environmental hazard to its detection, control and response
Choose fire suppression for an occupied server room and explain why
Evaluate physical access for least privilege, visitor control and timely removal
Pick the strongest preventive control against tailgating

subtopics.name: Environmental Hazards and Controls
subtopics.definition: Environmental controls protect equipment and data from heat, humidity, water, fire and power problems, each through detection, a protective measure and a response.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An overheated room or burst pipe can destroy the systems every logical control depends on. Damage can come in minutes, so an unanswered alarm is as bad as none.
how_it_works: Assessment comes first: list assets and hazards, review existing controls, then rate residual risk and plan fixes.
Cooling and humidity controls keep rooms in range; low humidity causes static discharge and high humidity causes condensation.
Water sensors under raised floors detect leaks, and pipes are routed away from the space above equipment.
An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) bridges short gaps and generator start-up; a fueled generator carries long outages.
Every alarm is routed, at all hours, to someone who can act before damage occurs.
When power loss is unavoidable, an orderly shutdown protects data integrity before failover.

rows.label: Protects against
cells: Short outages, dips and unstable power
Outages lasting hours or days
Sudden voltage spikes
Sags, brief spikes and electrical noise

rows.label: How long it lasts
cells: Minutes, limited by the batteries
As long as the fuel lasts
Not a power source
Not a power source

rows.label: Main weakness
cells: Batteries age and run out; needs testing
Takes seconds to start; needs fuel and load tests
No help in an outage
No help in an outage

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Environmental threats a data center must control: fire, flooding, power failure, temperature'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Fire</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Flooding</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Power failure</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Temperature</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Four hazards every data center must plan for. Each needs its own detection, its own control and a person who acts on the alarm.

subtopics.example: At a newspaper printing plant, file servers reboot several times a week when heavy presses start and the voltage briefly sags. The plant engineer proposes a larger generator. The IS auditor explains that a generator helps only in long outages, not momentary dips, and recommends a UPS or power line conditioner on the server circuits.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A sensor protects nothing unless its alert reaches someone able to act in time; monitoring and response are part of the control. For power, batteries bridge gaps and generators sustain operations, so critical sites need both, tested under load.

exam_traps.trap: A UPS alone can keep a data center running through a long outage.
exam_traps.why: Batteries last minutes. They bridge short gaps and generator start-up; only a fueled generator sustains power for hours.

exam_traps.trap: Installed sensors prove environmental risk is controlled.
exam_traps.why: Detection without response fails. The IS auditor verifies who receives alarms, at what hours, and whether they can act before damage occurs.

key_terms.definition: A review of the hazards facing a site, how well controls cover them, and the risk that remains.
A floor raised above the slab to route cables and cooling, often fitted with water sensors.
Stopping systems in a planned sequence so open transactions finish and data stays consistent.
Blackout is total loss; brownout is prolonged low voltage; sags, spikes and surges are brief drops or rises in voltage.

subtopics.name: Fire Suppression Systems
subtopics.definition: Fire suppression systems put out fires automatically; for computer rooms the choice is between water sprinkler designs and gas systems that leave equipment dry.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The wrong system can endanger staff or ruin the servers it should save; the choice balances safety, equipment damage, reliability and cost.
how_it_works: Smoke and heat detectors, with very early smoke detection in critical rooms, raise the alarm and trigger suppression.
Wet-pipe sprinklers hold water at all times and spray when heat opens a sprinkler head.
Dry-pipe sprinklers keep water out of the pipes until triggered; exam questions prefer them to wet pipe for computer rooms.
Pre-action sprinklers stay dry until the detection system opens a valve; a sprinkler head must then open too.
Clean-agent gas systems flood the room with a gas safe for people at the planned concentration, leaving no residue.
Carbon dioxide systems displace oxygen and can kill, so they suit only unoccupied spaces.

rows.label: Water in the pipes before a fire
cells: Always
No, until detection opens the valve
None used
None used

rows.label: Safe where people work
cells: Yes
Yes
Yes, at the planned amount
No; dangerous to people

rows.label: Risk to equipment
cells: High: leaks and water damage
Water damage once it discharges
Very low
Low

rows.label: Typical fit
cells: General office areas
Data centers that need a water system
Occupied server rooms
Unoccupied spaces only

subtopics.example: A logistics company's new data center must include a water-based system under the local fire code. The facilities manager proposes wet-pipe sprinklers as the cheapest option. The IS auditor notes that one leaking or knocked head would soak the racks, and recommends a pre-action design that stays dry until detectors confirm a fire, with very early smoke detection.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Protect people first, then equipment. Clean-agent gas with early detection fits occupied server rooms best. Among water systems, pipes that stay dry until a fire is detected (pre-action, often called dry-pipe in ISACA material) beat wet pipe. Carbon dioxide never belongs where people work.

exam_traps.trap: Pre-action sprinklers are the best choice because they keep water away from servers.
exam_traps.why: It prevents leaks and accidental discharge, but once it fires, water still damages equipment. Clean-agent gas is stronger for occupied server rooms.

exam_traps.trap: Carbon dioxide flooding is ideal for a staffed server room because it leaves no residue.
exam_traps.why: At extinguishing levels carbon dioxide can suffocate people, so it suits only unoccupied spaces.

key_terms.definition: Air-sampling detectors that sense smoke particles before a fire grows, giving staff time to act.
Pipes holding pressurized air that fill when a head opens, for freezing areas; ISACA also uses the term for alarm-triggered dry systems.
An older gas suppressant, banned from new production for ozone damage; clean agents such as FM-200 replaced it.

subtopics.name: Physical Access Controls
subtopics.definition: Physical access controls decide who can reach a site, building or room, using layered barriers that admit fewer people at each inner ring.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Someone who can touch a server, switch or backup tape can bypass most logical controls. Physical access must be as tightly limited, reviewed and traceable as system access.
how_it_works: Rings of protection run from the site perimeter to the building entrance to sensitive rooms such as server halls.
Badge systems tie each entry to one person, log it, and can be switched off quickly when someone leaves.
Each badge opens only the zones its holder's role needs, including badges for cleaning and maintenance crews.
Visitors need prior approval from a named host, identification, an escort, a distinct badge and a complete log entry.
A mantrap admits one person per authentication, which prevents tailgating.
Access lists are compared with current human resources (HR) and contractor records so leavers and movers lose access.

types.meaning: Discourage an attempt: warning signs, lighting, visible cameras.
Stop an entry: locks, badge readers, fences, mantraps.
Reveal an entry after it happens: alarms, camera review, access logs.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 352 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Layered physical security: perimeter, building entry, then the server room — control tightens at each layer'><rect x='8' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='54' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Perimeter</text><rect x='122' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='174' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Building entry</text><rect x='248' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='296' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Server room</text><line x1='102' y1='46' x2='113' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M113,42 L120,46 L113,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='228' y1='46' x2='239' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M239,42 L246,46 L239,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Control tightens as you move inward. Fewer people pass each ring, and the server room should admit only those whose job needs it.

subtopics.example: After someone forces a side gate at a telecom switching center, the site manager adds warning signs, brighter lights and more cameras. The IS auditor notes these only deter or detect, while the equipment hall door still opens with a keypad code shared by dozens of people. The IS auditor recommends an individual badge reader on that door, with entries reviewed monthly.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Physical access follows least privilege, just like system access. The strongest evidence compares all badge rights with an authoritative source such as HR records, and the best preventive control ties entry to one person and can be revoked quickly.

exam_traps.trap: Adding a guard or a warning sign is the best fix for tailgating.
exam_traps.why: A sign only deters, and a guard can be distracted. A mantrap that admits one person per badge enforces the rule; awareness training supports it.

exam_traps.trap: Camera footage is reliable evidence wherever it is stored.
exam_traps.why: If the people being watched can alter or delete recordings, the footage proves little, so recordings are protected from them.

key_terms.definition: Following an authorized person through a controlled door without authenticating.
Two interlocking doors, also called an access control vestibule or deadman door, that let one authenticated person through at a time.
A review of each site's physical controls and risks, done before setting a common standard, such as after a merger.

topics.overview: Identity and access management (IAM) makes sure each person or system is who it claims to be, can do only what it needs, and leaves a trail. This topic covers authentication and single sign-on, access control models, the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle, privileged access and zero trust.
can_do: Tell real multi-factor authentication from a multi-step login, and the false acceptance rate from the false rejection rate
Explain why disabling a user at the identity provider may not end their sessions
Recommend segregation of duties and least privilege over after-the-fact reviews
Evaluate privileged access for independent approval, time limits and recording

subtopics.name: Authentication, Authorization and Accountability
subtopics.definition: Authentication proves who a user is, authorization decides what that user may do, and accountability traces each action back to one person.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every access decision and every log entry depends on knowing exactly who acted. Weak authentication lets attackers in, and shared accounts leave investigators unable to name anyone.
how_it_works: Authentication factors fall into three categories: something the user knows, something the user has and something the user is.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines factors from different categories; two knowledge checks are still one factor.
Phishing-resistant authenticators, such as FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online) security keys and passkeys, are bound to the genuine website, so a fake page cannot relay them.
Authorization grants only the rights the role needs, after authentication succeeds.
Accountability needs a unique ID for each person and protected logs; shared accounts show the account, not the person.
Password rules follow National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-63B-4: length over composition rules, breached-password screening, and forced changes only on signs of compromise.

rows.label: What it measures
cells: Impostors wrongly accepted
Genuine users wrongly turned away
The setting where FAR equals FRR

rows.label: Why it matters
cells: Security failure: the impostor gets in
Inconvenience and lost time
Overall accuracy, for comparing products

rows.label: Exam cue
cells: The concern is impostors gaining access
The concern is user complaints
Choosing between biometric products; lower is better

rows.label: Also called
cells: Type II error
Type I error
Equal error rate (EER)

illustration.caption: The three As in order. Authorization only means something after authentication, and accountability only works when each action ties to one person.

subtopics.example: A pharmaceutical warehouse installs palm-vein readers on its controlled-drug cage. After night-shift complaints about rejections, the facilities supervisor lowers the match threshold. The IS auditor obtains the vendor's test results at the new setting, finds the false acceptance rate has risen sharply, and recommends restoring the threshold and improving enrollment quality instead.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Each action must trace to one identified person, so unique accounts come first. Real MFA mixes factor categories. When the risk is impostors, look at the false acceptance rate; when comparing biometric products overall, the lower crossover error rate wins.

exam_traps.trap: A password plus a security question is multi-factor authentication.
exam_traps.why: Both are knowledge factors, so the login is still single-factor. MFA needs factors from different categories.

exam_traps.trap: Any form of MFA stops phishing.
exam_traps.why: One-time codes and push approvals can be relayed through a fake site in real time. Only methods bound to the genuine site, such as FIDO2 keys, resist that relay.

key_terms.definition: Checking strong evidence, such as photo ID matched to the live applicant, before issuing credentials; knowledge-based questions give weak assurance.
One login used by several people, which breaks individual accountability.
Rules such as forcing a change of the initial password at first logon, favoring length, limiting failed attempts and blocking breached passwords.

subtopics.name: Single Sign-On and Federation
subtopics.definition: Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user authenticate once and reach many systems; federation extends that trust across organizations through a trusted identity provider.
subtopics.why_it_matters: SSO cuts password fatigue and lets access be removed in one place. It also concentrates risk: one stolen login or failed identity provider can expose or stop every connected system.
how_it_works: The identity provider (IdP) authenticates the user and issues a signed assertion or token that applications trust.
Inside many company networks, Kerberos has a key distribution center issue time-limited tickets; requests carry timestamps to stop replay, so clocks must agree within minutes.
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) passes signed identity assertions between an IdP and a web application, often across company boundaries.
OAuth 2.0 delegates limited access to an app through scoped tokens; OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds a login layer on top.
Applications keep their own sessions, so disabling a user at the IdP does not end them unless sessions and tokens are revoked.
The IdP needs strong multi-factor authentication (MFA) and high availability, as the single front door.

rows.label: Main job
cells: Sign-on inside one network
Web sign-on across organizations
Delegated access for an app
Login built on OAuth

rows.label: What it issues
cells: Time-limited tickets
Signed assertions
Scoped access tokens
ID tokens plus access tokens

rows.label: Typical risk
cells: Stolen or forged tickets
Forged or poorly validated assertions
Over-broad consent grants
Weak token validation by apps

subtopics.example: An online university moves 40 applications behind one cloud identity provider. The IS auditor finds the provider's administrator accounts use passwords only, and nobody has planned for online exams if the provider fails. The IS auditor recommends phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication for those administrators and a tested continuity plan for sign-in, agreed with the provost.
subtopics.isaca_rule: SSO moves the front door to one place, so that door needs the strongest authentication and monitoring. Disabling an identity is not the same as ending access: sessions and tokens must be revoked too.

exam_traps.trap: OAuth proves who the user is.
exam_traps.why: OAuth grants an app limited access to resources. Login identity comes from OpenID Connect, which adds an ID token on top of OAuth.

exam_traps.trap: Disabling a user at the identity provider immediately ends all their access.
exam_traps.why: Federated applications keep their own sessions and tokens. Unless revocation is handled, access can continue until those expire.

key_terms.definition: The trusted service that authenticates users and vouches for them to applications.
A user's approval letting an app reach their data through OAuth; it outlasts sign-in and bypasses MFA, so risky permissions need administrator approval.
The Kerberos server that authenticates users and issues the tickets they present to services.

subtopics.analogy: SSO is like a festival wristband: the gate checks a ticket once, then every stage lets the wearer in on sight. Canceling the ticket does not remove a wristband already on, just as disabling an account does not end open sessions.

subtopics.name: Access Control Models
subtopics.definition: An access control model is the rule system that decides access: by the owner's choice, by fixed security labels, by job role, or by attributes checked at each request.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The model decides how easily access can be reviewed, how well it follows job changes and whether users can give data away. The wrong model makes least privilege hard to keep.
how_it_works: Least privilege applies in every model: grant only the access a task needs, for only as long as it needs it.
Segregation of duties (SoD) splits sensitive processes so no one person can complete them alone.
Role-based access suits most businesses because rights are approved and reviewed per role, not per person.
Mandatory access suits highly classified data because users, including data owners, cannot change the labels.
Attribute-based access re-checks the user, the resource and the context at each request, so access follows changes automatically.

types.meaning: The resource owner grants access at will. Flexible, but hard to control.
The system enforces classification labels and clearances. Rigid, but strong.
Access comes from the job role. The common business model.
Each request is judged on subject, resource and environment attributes, such as time or location.

illustration.caption: Four access models, compared by what drives the decision: the owner, system labels, a job role, or attributes checked at request time.

subtopics.example: A hospital grants each nurse's system access one person at a time, and after 18 months of ward transfers nobody can say who should see which records. The IT manager suggests a yearly clean-up. The IS auditor recommends role-based access, with rights approved per ward role by the nursing director, so a transfer swaps one role for another instead of adding rights.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Prevention comes before detection. Build segregation of duties and least privilege into the model; detective reviews are a fallback, not a substitute. Under mandatory access control, the system enforces labels, and no user or data owner can override them.

exam_traps.trap: Under mandatory access control, the data owner can grant a colleague an exception.
exam_traps.why: The system enforces labels and clearances, and owners cannot override them. Owner discretion belongs to discretionary access control.

exam_traps.trap: Monthly log reviews are an acceptable substitute for segregation of duties.
exam_traps.why: Where the system can split the duties, reviews find misuse only after the damage. Independent log review compensates only when splitting is impractical, such as in very small teams.

key_terms.definition: Granting only the access a task needs, for only as long as it needs it.
Splitting a sensitive process so that no single person can complete it alone.

subtopics.name: Identity Lifecycle: Joiners, Movers and Leavers
subtopics.definition: The identity lifecycle manages each account from creation to removal, adjusting access as people join, change roles or leave, and confirming it through periodic recertification.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Access that is never removed piles up quietly. Movers who keep old rights and leavers whose accounts stay active are among the most common audit findings and a frequent route to fraud.
how_it_works: Joiners get access only after an approved request and completed security awareness training, triggered from human resources (HR) records.
Movers gain the new role's rights and lose the old ones in the same change.
Leavers lose access on their last day, or sooner for a risky exit; security learns of resignations as soon as notice is given.
Business owners recertify access on a risk-tiered cycle, with privileged access reviewed more often.
Every service account has a named owner who confirms its purpose, scope and continued need.
Reconciling accounts with HR records finds orphan accounts that no current employee owns.
subtopics.example: A credit union's IS auditor matches active core banking accounts against HR records. She finds 12 accounts of staff who left months ago and several tellers who kept branch manager rights after transfers. The IT manager traces the leavers to a manual HR email that IT often missed. The IS auditor recommends an automated HR-driven removal feed plus risk-tiered recertification by branch managers.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Access must follow the person's current role. Movers lose old rights, leavers lose all rights promptly, and business owners, not IT, confirm that the remaining access is still needed. Every account, including service accounts, needs an accountable owner.

exam_traps.trap: IT staff should run access recertification because they manage the accounts.
exam_traps.why: IT cannot assess business need. Owners or managers who understand the work confirm each right; IT carries out the removals.

exam_traps.trap: Adding the new rights when someone transfers is enough.
exam_traps.why: Without removing old rights, the mover collects access across roles, known as privilege creep, which breaks least privilege and can break segregation of duties.

key_terms.definition: The gradual build-up of excess access as people change roles without losing old rights.
A periodic review in which business owners confirm or remove each user's access.
An active account with no current, accountable owner, such as one left behind by a leaver.

subtopics.name: Privileged Access Management
subtopics.definition: Privileged access management (PAM) controls administrator-level accounts through vaulted credentials, approved and time-limited elevation, and recorded sessions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Administrator accounts can change, erase or copy almost anything, so attackers target them first. Standing, unmonitored admin rights turn one stolen password into a full compromise.
how_it_works: Administrators use separate privileged accounts for admin work, never their everyday accounts.
Just-in-time (JIT) access grants elevation on request, after independent approval, for a short period that then expires.
A vault stores and rotates privileged passwords, so people check them out instead of knowing them.
Session recording captures privileged work, and the recordings are stored where the administrators cannot alter them.
Privileged accounts sign in only to hardened admin workstations, so their credentials are not left on ordinary machines.
Secrets are kept out of source code and configuration files and stored in a managed vault.

illustration.caption: Just-in-time privilege. Admin rights are requested, approved by someone else, used in a recorded session and then expire on their own.

subtopics.example: A power utility keeps an emergency domain administrator account whose password sits in a sealed envelope in the control-room safe. The IS auditor finds the envelope was opened four times last year, with no record of who used the account or why, and the password never changed afterward. The IS auditor recommends logging every use, an independent review after each one and a password change once the emergency ends.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Remove standing privilege where possible, and make every elevation approved by someone else, time-limited and recorded. JIT without independent approval is just self-service. A leaked privileged credential is presumed compromised and is rotated at once.

exam_traps.trap: Time limits alone make just-in-time access safe.
exam_traps.why: If requesters approve their own elevation, nothing stops improper use. Independent approval is what gives JIT its control value.

exam_traps.trap: Resetting the password ends an active attacker's access.
exam_traps.why: Sessions and tokens already issued stay valid. Containment means disabling the account and revoking its sessions, then rotating the credential.

key_terms.definition: Admin rights that are always on, whether or not the person is doing admin work.
Capturing what a privileged user does during a session for later review and evidence.
A sealed high-privilege account for urgent fixes; each use is logged, independently reviewed afterward and its password then changed.
An account that can change systems, security settings or other users' access; as the highest-value target, it gets stronger controls first.

subtopics.name: Zero Trust Architecture
subtopics.definition: Zero trust is a security architecture that trusts no user, device or network location by default and authorizes every request by policy, using identity, device health and context.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Perimeter models trust anything inside the network, so one breach allows lateral movement from system to system. Zero trust limits the damage by checking each request at the resource itself.
how_it_works: A policy decision point weighs each request against identity, device health, data sensitivity and context.
A policy enforcement point in front of each resource allows, limits or blocks the request.
Access is granted per session with least privilege, not to whole network segments.
Trust is re-checked during the session and restricted when identity, device or context changes.
Calls between services are authorized by policy too, not just authenticated.

subtopics.example: A logistics firm's board is told the company now has zero trust after it bought a secure remote access product. The IS auditor finds the product brokers only remote connections, while office users and internal servers still trust anything on the local network. The IS auditor reports zero trust as partly implemented and recommends a roadmap covering users, devices, workloads and data, with senior management setting priorities.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Zero trust is an architecture of continuous, policy-based decisions, not a product. Proving identity is only the first step; a policy must still decide what that identity, on that device, may reach right now.

exam_traps.trap: Buying a zero trust product or turning on multi-factor authentication (MFA) delivers zero trust.
exam_traps.why: Zero trust is a design approach covering identity, devices, networks and data. MFA strengthens login but does not decide, request by request, what may be reached.

exam_traps.trap: Internal services that have authenticated each other can trust each other.
exam_traps.why: That is implicit trust moved to a new place. Each call still needs authorization by policy, or one compromised service reaches everything.

key_terms.definition: The component that evaluates a request against policy and decides whether to allow it.
The gateway in front of a resource that carries out the decision.
An attacker moving from one compromised system to others inside the network.

topics.overview: Networks carry data between systems, and endpoints are where people actually touch it. This topic covers filtering and segmenting traffic, secure remote access, detecting and blocking attacks, decoys that expose intruders, and hardening the laptops, servers and phones at the edges.
can_do: Explain why an intrusion prevention system on a mirrored port cannot block attacks
Recommend a screened subnet, and mapping data flows before any segmentation change
Compare signature and anomaly detection and the errors each tends to make
Evaluate endpoint and remote access controls by coverage and strong authentication, not dashboards

subtopics.name: Firewalls and Web Application Firewalls
subtopics.definition: A firewall enforces rules about which traffic may pass between network zones; a web application firewall (WAF) inspects web requests to block attacks on applications.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Firewalls are the main gate between trusted and untrusted networks. A weak rule set or an unmanaged change can expose sensitive systems as surely as no firewall.
how_it_works: Firewall types deepen in inspection: packet filters check addresses and ports, stateful firewalls track connections, application-level proxies inspect protocol content, and next-generation firewalls add application awareness.
Rule sets default to deny and allow only traffic with an approved business need.
Rule changes go through change management and peer review, and rules are reviewed periodically to remove stale entries.
A WAF sits in front of web applications and blocks attacks such as Structured Query Language (SQL) injection and cross-site scripting.
A WAF is tuned in monitoring mode, then switched to blocking, the only mode that prevents attacks.

rows.label: What it inspects
cells: Addresses, ports and connections; next-generation models add application awareness
The content of web requests and responses

rows.label: Typical attack stopped
cells: Unwanted connections to closed services
SQL injection and cross-site scripting

rows.label: Where it sits
cells: Between network zones
In front of web applications

rows.label: Its limit
cells: Cannot judge most web request content
A compensating layer; the code still needs fixing

subtopics.example: A regional insurer's firewall holds 2,300 rules, many for projects that ended years ago, and nobody knows who requested them. The network manager says rule count does not matter on a next-generation firewall. The IS auditor recommends a rule review with business owners to remove unused entries, a final deny-all rule, and peer-reviewed change tickets for new rules.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A firewall is only as good as its rule set and change control: default deny, approved changes and regular review. A WAF virtually patches web flaws while the code is fixed; it compensates for secure coding but does not replace it.

exam_traps.trap: The WAF is the fix for SQL injection.
exam_traps.why: It is a compensating layer. The real fix is in the code: queries that treat user input only as data, never as commands.

exam_traps.trap: When a WAF rule blocks legitimate traffic at peak, turn the WAF off.
exam_traps.why: Fix or relax only the faulty rule and keep the rest blocking; switching everything off creates far more exposure than the false positives.

key_terms.definition: A rule-set stance in which anything not explicitly allowed is blocked.
A proxy firewall that relays each session and inspects its content; the strongest traditional type, but slower.
A screened subnet filters both sides of a demilitarized zone and is stronger than a screened host (router plus bastion host) or a dual-homed host.

subtopics.name: Network Segmentation and the Screened Subnet
subtopics.definition: Network segmentation divides a network into zones with controlled paths between them, so one compromised system cannot reach everything; a screened subnet holds internet-facing systems.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers who breach one machine try to move sideways to valuable data. Segments limit that spread and shrink the scope of assessments such as payment card audits.
how_it_works: Internet-facing systems sit in a screened subnet, often called a demilitarized zone (DMZ), filtered from both the internet and the internal network.
Sensitive systems, such as payroll or payment systems, get their own segments with only approved connections.
Microsegmentation applies rules down to individual workloads, limiting east-west traffic between servers inside data centers and clouds.
Guest and other untrusted wireless users get a separate segment that reaches only the internet.
Data flows are mapped before zones are drawn, because sensible boundaries depend on where sensitive data travels.
Rule changes go through change control; one unapproved allow-any rule quietly undoes the segmentation.

subtopics.example: At a school district, the student information system shares one flat network with classroom tablets and visitor laptops. The IT director plans stronger antivirus on the servers. The IS auditor explains that a single infected classroom device could still reach student records, and recommends placing the system in its own segment that accepts only approved connections, with rule changes under change control.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Assume the most exposed system will be breached, and design so that a breach cannot spread. Put internet-facing systems in a screened subnet, keep sensitive zones separate and protect segmentation rules with change control. Map the data flows before drawing the zones.

exam_traps.trap: Hardening the public web server is enough, so it can stay on the internal network.
exam_traps.why: Hardening lowers the chance of compromise, but if the server is breached nothing stands between the attacker and internal data. Segmentation limits the damage.

exam_traps.trap: Changing the guest Wi-Fi password often keeps visitors away from corporate systems.
exam_traps.why: Every legitimate visitor still lands next to corporate assets. Only a separate segment that reaches just the internet removes the path.

key_terms.definition: A buffer zone for public-facing systems, filtered from both the internet and the internal network.
Fine-grained rules that control traffic between individual workloads, not just between large zones.
Traffic between systems inside the network, as opposed to traffic entering or leaving it.

subtopics.name: Secure Remote Access and VPNs
subtopics.definition: A virtual private network (VPN) creates an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network, letting remote users or sites reach internal systems as if connected locally.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Remote access faces the internet and accepts logins, so attackers target it often. A VPN protected only by a password gives anyone holding a stolen password direct access to the internal network.
how_it_works: Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) protects traffic at the network layer and suits fixed site-to-site links.

IPsec's Authentication Header (AH) authenticates packets without encrypting them; Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) adds encryption. Transport mode protects the payload; tunnel mode wraps the whole packet.
Transport Layer Security (TLS) VPNs run through a browser or light client and suit remote users.
Every remote login uses multi-factor authentication (MFA), and the device's health is checked before it connects.
Split tunneling sends non-company traffic straight to the internet, saving bandwidth but bypassing corporate filtering.
Retire TLS 1.0 and 1.1 after measuring who still depends on them; keep TLS 1.2 with strong cipher suites alongside TLS 1.3, which is preferred.

rows.label: What it protects
cells: All traffic between two networks or a device and a network
Sessions to specific applications or through a light client

rows.label: Best fit
cells: Site-to-site links and full network access
Remote users who need particular applications

rows.label: Setup
cells: Dedicated client and more complex configuration
Simpler for users; passes most firewalls

subtopics.example: A consulting firm lets remote laptops use split tunneling, so web browsing bypasses the corporate proxy. A consultant's laptop picks up malware on a hotel network and then connects to the firm's file servers through the VPN. The IS auditor recommends full tunneling, or equivalent cloud web filtering, for devices handling client data, and a device health check before each connection.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Encryption protects the tunnel, not the login. Remote access must require multi-factor authentication and a healthy device, and give only the access the user needs. Retire weak protocol versions on a plan, after measuring who still relies on them.

exam_traps.trap: Because the VPN is encrypted, remote access is secure.
exam_traps.why: Encryption hides traffic from eavesdroppers. It does nothing when an attacker logs in with a stolen password; MFA addresses that risk.

exam_traps.trap: Switch off old TLS versions overnight to meet the deadline.
exam_traps.why: First measure who still depends on them so the cutover can be staged. A blind switch-off can break critical customer or partner connections.

key_terms.definition: A permanent encrypted tunnel joining two offices' networks, as opposed to one remote user connecting.
Sending a connected device's non-company traffic straight to the internet instead of through the corporate tunnel.

subtopics.name: Intrusion Detection, Prevention and Network Access Control
subtopics.definition: An intrusion detection system (IDS) spots attacks and alerts, an intrusion prevention system (IPS) can also block them, and network access control (NAC) vets devices before they join the network.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Firewalls let approved traffic through, but attacks often ride inside it. Detection and prevention tools catch what gets past; NAC keeps unknown or unhealthy devices off the network.
how_it_works: A network-based sensor watches traffic on a segment; a host-based sensor watches activity on one server or endpoint.
An IPS must sit inline, in the traffic path, to block; on a mirrored port it can only alert.
Inline placement adds a point of failure, so the design sets whether the device fails open or closed.
NAC checks device posture, such as patches and endpoint protection, not just the user's credentials, and quarantines devices that fail.
Unified threat management (UTM) bundles several controls in one appliance, simplifying operation but creating a single point of failure.

rows.label: Placement
cells: Out of band, on a mirrored port or tap
Inline, in the traffic path

rows.label: Action
cells: Alerts only
Alerts and blocks

rows.label: Cost of a false positive
cells: Wasted analyst time
Legitimate traffic blocked

rows.label: If the device fails
cells: Monitoring stops; traffic still flows
Traffic stops (fail closed) or flows unchecked (fail open)

illustration.caption: A UTM appliance packs several security functions into one managed box. Simple to run, but one failure can take them all down together.

subtopics.example: An airline's inline intrusion prevention system in front of its check-in platform fails closed. When it crashed during an update, check-in stopped for 40 minutes. The network manager proposes moving it to a mirrored port. The IS auditor notes that this would end all blocking and recommends redundant inline units with tested failover, with the system owner deciding the failure mode on risk.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Evaluate a control against its purpose. An IPS that cannot block is only an IDS, and a NAC that checks only passwords lets infected devices in. Placement and configuration decide what a device can actually do.

exam_traps.trap: The main concern with a mirrored-port IPS is alert volume.
exam_traps.why: Alert volume is an operating issue; the design flaw is that the device cannot block attacks at all, so it fails management's objective.

exam_traps.trap: A UTM appliance removes the need for redundancy.
exam_traps.why: It concentrates several controls in one box; if it fails, they all fail, so critical sites need a resilient design.

key_terms.definition: A failed device blocks all traffic, protecting security at the cost of availability.
A failed device lets traffic pass unchecked, protecting availability at the cost of security.
A device's security health, such as patch level, encryption and running protection.
A switch port or hardware tap that copies traffic to a monitor, which sees attacks but cannot stop them.

subtopics.name: Intrusion Detection Methods
subtopics.definition: Intrusion detection methods are the ways an intrusion detection system (IDS) recognizes attacks: matching known signatures, spotting departures from normal behavior, or applying expert rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each method misses different attacks and raises different false alarms. Knowing the trade-off tells the IS auditor whether a sensor can catch new attacks and whether its alerts can be trusted.
how_it_works: Signature-based detection matches traffic against patterns of known attacks; it is precise but blind to new ones, such as zero-day attacks.
Anomaly-based detection learns a baseline of normal activity and flags departures, so it can catch new attacks but raises more false alarms.
Heuristic detection applies expert rules about suspicious behavior, such as one workstation scanning hundreds of ports.
Signatures need frequent updates, and anomaly baselines must be learned during clean periods, or the attack becomes normal.
Tuning removes false positives at the source while keeping coverage; switching rules off creates false negatives.

rows.label: Detects
cells: Known attacks with a defined pattern
Unusual activity, including new attacks
Behavior that matches expert rules

rows.label: Main weakness
cells: Misses new and altered attacks
More false positives; a baseline can learn an attack as normal
Rules need expert upkeep

rows.label: Stays effective through
cells: Regular signature updates
Re-learning when the business changes
Reviewing and refining rules

subtopics.example: A logistics company's IDS uses only signatures, updated monthly, and the security operations manager reports zero critical alerts for the quarter. The IS auditor notes that a signature-only sensor with stale updates would also stay quiet during a new attack. She recommends automatic signature updates and anomaly detection on the warehouse network, verified with simulated attacks.
subtopics.isaca_rule: For an IDS, a missed attack is worse than a false alarm. Signature detection catches the known; anomaly detection is needed for the new. Fix noise by tuning rules, not by disabling them, and prove detection works by testing it.

exam_traps.trap: Zero alerts means the network is safe.
exam_traps.why: A sensor with stale signatures, poor placement or rules switched off also shows zero alerts. The IS auditor tests detection instead of trusting a quiet console.

exam_traps.trap: Anomaly-based detection raises fewer false positives than signature-based detection.
exam_traps.why: The reverse is true. Signatures are precise but miss new attacks; anomaly detection catches new behavior but also flags harmless changes.

key_terms.definition: An alert raised on activity that is actually harmless.
A real attack that raises no alert; the more dangerous error for detection tools.
An attack on a flaw for which no patch or signature yet exists.

subtopics.name: Deception Tools: Honeypots and Honeytokens
subtopics.definition: Deception tools are decoy systems, networks or data with no business use, so any interaction with them signals an intruder.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers inside a network can hide among normal traffic. A decoy gives high-confidence alerts with few false alarms and shows how attackers work, but a badly isolated decoy can become a foothold.
how_it_works: Decoys are placed where an attacker would look, such as among real servers, in the directory or in a file share.
Because nobody legitimately uses them, any touch is a strong, low-noise alert.
Decoys are isolated and closely monitored, so attackers cannot use them to reach real systems.
Alerts flow to the security operations center like any other detection, with an owner and response steps.
Legal counsel reviews the design, because passively attracting intruders is acceptable but actively inducing a crime may be entrapment.

types.meaning: A single decoy system made to look valuable, such as a fake database server.
A network of honeypots used to study attacker behavior in more depth.
Decoy data, such as a fake account, credential or document, that raises an alert when used.

subtopics.example: A drug maker's security operations manager plants a fake research file share and a dummy administrator account in the directory. Three months later the dummy account is used from a finance workstation, revealing an intruder that other tools missed. Reviewing the program, the IS auditor confirms the decoy share cannot route to production systems and that legal counsel approved the design.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Deception adds detection, not prevention. Its value is high-confidence alerts, so decoys must be isolated, monitored and approved by legal counsel. A decoy nobody watches, or one that connects to production, adds risk instead of reducing it.

exam_traps.trap: A honeypot protects production systems by drawing attackers away.
exam_traps.why: It mainly detects and teaches. Attackers who find it can still attack real systems, and a poorly isolated honeypot can give them a launch point.

exam_traps.trap: Any decoy design is legally safe because the systems belong to us.
exam_traps.why: Enticement is generally acceptable, but entrapment, actively inducing someone to commit a crime, can undermine prosecution. Counsel should review the design.

key_terms.definition: Making a decoy available for an intruder to find, without encouraging a crime.
Inducing someone to commit a crime they would not otherwise commit, which is legally risky.

subtopics.name: Endpoint Protection and Hardening
subtopics.definition: Endpoint protection secures laptops, servers and phones through layered controls: hardened settings, patching, encryption, a host firewall and software that detects malicious behavior.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Endpoints are where people open email, browse the web and plug in drives, so most attacks land there. One unprotected device can be the way into the whole network.
how_it_works: Hardening applies a configuration baseline, such as a Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmark, and regular scans detect drift from it.
Endpoint detection and response (EDR) watches process behavior, catching attacks that misuse built-in tools and leave no malware file.
Application allowlisting and limits on scripting tools stop many fileless attacks before detection is needed.
Full-disk encryption protects lost devices; removable-media controls protect copies on portable drives.
Coverage reports compare the device inventory with the devices actually running the agent.
