illustration.caption: No single control secures an endpoint. Each layer closes a different gap, from malware and open ports to lost devices and missing patches.

subtopics.example: A casino's self-service kiosks run a full desktop operating system, and staff have installed games and remote-support tools on several of them. The IT manager plans weekly antivirus scans. The IS auditor notes that each kiosk has one fixed purpose and recommends application allowlisting so only the kiosk software can run, plus removing local administrator rights.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Coverage comes first: a device without the agent sends no data, so confirm the population before trusting results. Prevent misuse of powerful tools through least privilege instead of relying only on detection. Encryption must follow sensitive data onto every portable medium.

exam_traps.trap: Full-disk encryption on laptops protects data copied to portable drives.
exam_traps.why: It protects only the laptop's own disk. Copies on removable media need their own encryption, or the copying must be blocked.

exam_traps.trap: Antivirus or application allowlisting will stop attacks that run through administrators' own tools.
exam_traps.why: Those tools are legitimate and approved, so signatures miss them and allowlisting lets them run. EDR behavior monitoring detects misuse; least privilege removes the tools from accounts that never need them.

key_terms.definition: Letting only approved programs run on a device and blocking everything else by default.
An attack that runs in memory or through built-in tools, leaving no malicious file on disk.

topics.overview: Data loss prevention (DLP) tools look for sensitive data leaving where it should stay, whether by email, web upload, removable drive or cloud share, and then alert or block. This topic covers what DLP protects, how it recognizes sensitive data, and how the IS auditor tests whether it works.
can_do: Choose network, endpoint or discovery DLP for a given leak channel
Explain why data discovery and classification come before blocking rules
Decide when a DLP rule is ready to move from monitoring to blocking
Select the strongest evidence that DLP is effective

subtopics.name: DLP Coverage: Data States and Channels
subtopics.definition: Data loss prevention (DLP) is a set of tools that find sensitive data and alert on or block it when it moves through unapproved channels.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most leaks are ordinary: an email to the wrong person, an upload to personal cloud storage, a copy to a thumb drive. DLP catches them, but only for data and channels it can see.
how_it_works: Data exists in three states: at rest in storage, in motion across networks and in use on a device.
Discovery comes first: scan storage and have data owners classify what is found, because DLP cannot protect data nobody has identified.
Coverage follows the egress channels where data actually leaves, starting with the busiest.
Network DLP cannot read encrypted traffic, so uploads are decrypted and checked at the web proxy under an approved policy, called Transport Layer Security (TLS) inspection.
Endpoint DLP keeps working off the corporate network, covering removable media, printing and local copies.

types.meaning: Inspects traffic leaving the network, such as email and web uploads.
An agent on each device that controls copying, printing, uploads and removable media, on or off the network.
Scans file shares, databases and cloud storage to find where sensitive data sits.
Applies policy to data inside cloud services, often through a cloud access security broker.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 470 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='DLP protects data in three states: data at rest, data in motion, and data in use'><rect x='14' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='84' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>At rest</text><rect x='166' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='236' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>In motion</text><rect x='318' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='388' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>In use</text><text x='84' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>stored data</text><text x='236' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>data being transmitted</text><text x='388' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>data being processed</text></svg>
illustration.caption: DLP must cover data in all three states: stored, being sent, and being worked on.

subtopics.example: A biotech firm's network DLP inspects email and web uploads, yet lab managers often print formula sheets at home from laptops connected to personal printers. The IS auditor maps where research data really leaves and finds printing off the corporate network unmonitored. The IS auditor recommends endpoint DLP that covers printing and local copies wherever the laptop is.
subtopics.isaca_rule: DLP protects only identified data on channels it can see. Discovery and owner-led classification come before enforcement, and coverage should follow how data really leaves. An uninspected main channel is the largest blind spot.

exam_traps.trap: Network DLP on the email gateway also covers data leaving by web upload.
exam_traps.why: Each channel needs its own coverage. Encrypted web traffic is invisible to network DLP unless TLS inspection decrypts it at the proxy under an approved policy.

exam_traps.trap: Write blocking rules first and classify the data later.
exam_traps.why: Rules cannot protect data nobody has found or labeled. Discovery and owner classification come first.

key_terms.definition: Decrypting, checking and re-encrypting Transport Layer Security (TLS) web traffic at a proxy, under policy, so DLP can read it.
Any route by which data can leave, such as email, web, removable media, printing or cloud sync.

subtopics.name: DLP Detection Methods and Tuning
subtopics.definition: Data loss prevention (DLP) detection methods recognize sensitive content using patterns, fingerprints of real records or documents, and context such as sender, recipient and channel.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Detection that is too loose misses leaks; detection that is too strict blocks normal work until people bypass it or management demands it be switched off. Accuracy decides whether DLP can ever block.
how_it_works: Pattern matching looks for shapes such as card or national ID numbers; it is broad but noisy.
Exact data matching compares content with fingerprints of real records, cutting false alarms from look-alike numbers.
Document fingerprinting recognizes copies or parts of specific sensitive files, such as merger drafts.
Context rules weigh sender, recipient, channel and destination, so approved flows pass.
Rules start in monitor mode; once false-positive rates are measured and acceptable, they move to blocking.
Each rule has a named owner who reviews its alerts and false positives, so tuning has someone accountable.

rows.label: What happens
cells: The transfer goes through and an alert is logged
The transfer is stopped or quarantined

rows.label: Use it for
cells: Measuring accuracy before enforcement
Rules with proven accuracy on high-risk data

rows.label: Risk if misused
cells: Left on forever, it only records leaks
Switched on too early, it disrupts the business

subtopics.example: A brewing company's legal team fears leaks of a confidential acquisition plan, but its DLP rules look only for card and national ID numbers. The IS auditor notes that pattern rules cannot recognize deal documents and recommends registering the plan's drafts for document fingerprinting, so partial copies are caught, with the general counsel named as the rule's owner.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Combine content with context so legitimate work flows and leaks stop. Move rules from monitor to block only after measuring false positives, then block, not just alert, where the business case allows. Seniority does not create an exception when an approved channel exists.

exam_traps.trap: Turn on blocking on day one for the strongest protection.
exam_traps.why: Untested rules flood the business with false alarms, and pressure then builds to switch DLP off. Measure and tune in monitor mode first.

exam_traps.trap: Alerting is enough when classified data goes to unapproved destinations.
exam_traps.why: An alert records the leak after it happens. Where accuracy is proven and the business case allows, the rule should block.

key_terms.definition: Detection that compares content with hashed fingerprints of real records, such as rows from the customer database.
Detection that recognizes text taken from specific registered documents, even when partly copied.
Holding a blocked message or file for review instead of sending or deleting it.

subtopics.name: Auditing DLP Effectiveness
subtopics.definition: Auditing data loss prevention (DLP) effectiveness means testing whether it actually catches and stops sensitive data on each channel, instead of trusting dashboards or vendor claims.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A DLP console can look busy and still miss the leaks that matter. Only evidence that the control works on real channels supports relying on it.
how_it_works: Confirm scope: which channels, devices and data types the rules cover, compared with how data really leaves.
Send seeded test data, such as dummy card numbers, through each channel and check each record is caught and handled as designed.
Trace a sample of alerts through triage, escalation and closure.
Check rule changes and exceptions for approval, an owner and an expiry date.
When discovery finds sensitive data in the wrong place, verify that management restricted access first and that the data owner decided the remediation.
subtopics.example: A transit authority's DLP team cites 9,000 alerts last quarter as proof the control works. The IS auditor finds 30 rule exceptions added during the year with no approver or expiry, including one exempting the payroll team from every rule. The IS auditor recommends owner approval and an expiry date for each exception, and seeded test transfers through every channel as evidence of effectiveness.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Evidence the IS auditor generates by re-performance, such as seeded tests, outranks counts, claims and confirmations from the people who run the tool. Alert volume shows activity, not effectiveness. When sensitive data turns up in the wrong place, contain first, assess notification, and let the owner decide the fix.

exam_traps.trap: A growing number of DLP alerts proves the control is working.
exam_traps.why: Alert counts show activity, not whether leaks are caught on every channel. Seeded tests show effectiveness.

exam_traps.trap: Customer data in a test environment is a hygiene issue to fix later.
exam_traps.why: Exposure to people without a need to know may itself be a breach. Contain it and assess notification duties first.

key_terms.definition: An audit procedure in which the IS auditor independently executes a control, or a test of it, to confirm it works.
Dummy records that look sensitive, sent through a channel to check whether the control catches them.
Replacing real values with realistic fakes so test environments hold no live personal data.

topics.overview: Encryption turns readable data into scrambled data that only a key holder can restore. This topic covers symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing and tokenization, digital signatures, and the key management that decides whether any of it actually protects anything.
can_do: Choose symmetric or asymmetric cryptography for a scenario and explain the digital envelope
Name which key encrypts, decrypts, signs and verifies in each case
Tell hashing, encryption and tokenization apart by purpose
Evaluate key management for segregation of duties, dual control, rotation and retention

subtopics.name: Symmetric Encryption
subtopics.definition: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key both to encrypt and to decrypt data; the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is the common example.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is fast enough to protect whole disks, databases and network sessions. Its weakness is key sharing: both sides need the same secret, delivered safely, and every pair of parties needs its own.
how_it_works: The same key turns readable plaintext into ciphertext and back again.
AES with 128-bit or 256-bit keys is the current standard; older ciphers such as the Data Encryption Standard (DES) and Triple DES are retired.
A mode of operation is the recipe for encrypting data block by block; authenticated encryption modes, such as Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), also detect tampering.
Electronic codebook (ECB) mode encrypts identical blocks identically, so patterns leak and it should not be used.
Key numbers grow fast: n parties need n(n-1)/2 keys, so ten parties need 45.

subtopics.example: A hospital's legacy laboratory system still encrypts result files with Triple DES, and the vendor says the files are safe because nobody has complained. The IS auditor notes the cipher is retired and the key sits in the same folder as the files. The IS auditor recommends AES-256 in an authenticated mode on a dated plan approved by the lab director, with the key held in a separate key store.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The algorithm is rarely the weak point; the key and how it is used are. Strong encryption with a badly stored key or a weak mode gives little protection. Use symmetric encryption for bulk data, with keys delivered and stored separately from the data.

exam_traps.trap: AES-256 is secure in any mode.
exam_traps.why: ECB mode leaks patterns because identical blocks produce identical ciphertext. An authenticated mode such as GCM hides patterns and detects tampering.

exam_traps.trap: Symmetric encryption alone solves secure communication with many partners.
exam_traps.why: Every pair needs its own shared secret, delivered safely. Asymmetric methods are used to exchange those keys.

key_terms.definition: Readable data before encryption or after decryption.
Scrambled data produced by encryption, unreadable without the key.
Encryption that also detects whether the ciphertext was changed.

subtopics.name: Asymmetric Encryption and the Digital Envelope
subtopics.definition: Asymmetric encryption uses a linked key pair: a public key anyone may use and a private key only its owner holds; what one key locks, only the other unlocks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It solves key sharing: strangers can exchange secrets and verify each other without meeting first. It is slow, so it usually protects keys and signatures rather than bulk data.
how_it_works: To send a secret, encrypt with the recipient's public key; only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.
A digital envelope encrypts the message with a fresh symmetric key, then encrypts that key with the recipient's public key.
Common algorithms are RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), whose shorter keys suit mobile and low-power devices; key agreement often uses Diffie-Hellman.
Quantum computers threaten RSA and elliptic-curve methods, not AES-256; migration to the 2024 post-quantum standards (FIPS 203 to 205) starts with an inventory and builds crypto-agility.

rows.label: Keys
cells: One shared secret key
A public and private key pair per party

rows.label: Speed and use
cells: Fast; bulk data such as disks and sessions
Slow; key exchange and digital signatures

rows.label: Key distribution
cells: Hard: each pair needs a secret delivered safely
Easy: public keys can be shared openly

rows.label: Keys for n parties
cells: n key pairs

rows.label: Services
cells: Confidentiality; integrity through a MAC, but no non-repudiation
Confidentiality, authentication and non-repudiation

subtopics.example: A medical device maker's insulin pumps send readings to a phone app, and engineers plan RSA with 4,096-bit keys, which drains pump batteries. The IS auditor confirms that elliptic-curve cryptography gives comparable strength with shorter keys and less processing. The IS auditor recommends it, built so algorithms can later be swapped for post-quantum ones through configuration.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Use asymmetric cryptography to exchange keys and to sign, and symmetric for bulk data. Confidentiality uses the recipient's public key; proof of origin uses the sender's private key. Plan post-quantum migration from an inventory, long-lived secrets first, with swappable algorithms.

exam_traps.trap: To keep a message confidential, the sender encrypts it with the sender's own private key.
exam_traps.why: Anyone holding the sender's public key, which is everyone, could decrypt it. Confidentiality needs the recipient's public key; the sender's private key is for signing.

exam_traps.trap: Post-quantum migration can wait until quantum computers exist.
exam_traps.why: In a harvest now, decrypt later attack, traffic recorded today is broken once quantum computers can. Long-lived secrets sent now are already exposed, so inventory and planning start now.

key_terms.definition: Hybrid encryption: data travels under a symmetric key, and that key travels under the recipient's public key.
Recording encrypted data today in order to break it once quantum computers become capable.
Designing systems so algorithms and key sizes can be swapped through configuration, not code changes, making future cryptographic transitions fast and cheap.

subtopics.analogy: Asymmetric encryption is like handing out open padlocks. Anyone can snap one shut on a box meant for the owner, but only the owner's own key opens it.
subtopics.memory_aid: Secret for them: lock with their public key. Proof it's you: sign with your private key.

subtopics.name: Hashing, Salting and Tokenization
subtopics.definition: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed; changing even one character produces a completely different fingerprint.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hashes prove data has not changed and let systems check passwords without storing them. Salting protects stored passwords, and tokenization shrinks the number of systems that hold card numbers.
how_it_works: Integrity hashes must resist collisions, two inputs giving one output; Message Digest 5 (MD5) and Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA-1) fail, while SHA-256 passes.
Passwords are stored as salted, deliberately slow hashes, such as bcrypt or Argon2, so they can be checked but never recovered.
A unique random salt per password defeats precomputed rainbow tables and forces attackers to crack each hash separately.
Tokenization swaps a value, such as a card number, for a meaningless token and keeps the real value in a secured vault.
Systems holding only tokens fall outside much of the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) scope.

rows.label: Reversible?
cells: No; one-way
Yes, with the key
Only through the vault

rows.label: Main purpose
cells: Integrity checks and password storage
Confidentiality
Removing sensitive values from most systems

rows.label: Typical use
cells: File checksums, stored passwords
Disks, databases, network sessions
Card numbers in order and payment systems

subtopics.example: A loyalty program hashes customer phone numbers with SHA-256 and shares them with an advertising partner, describing the data as anonymous. The IS auditor notes that phone numbers have few possible values, so the partner could hash every number and match the list. The IS auditor recommends treating the data as personal, replacing the hashes with tokens, and obtaining a privacy review before sharing.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Hashing gives integrity, not confidentiality; encryption gives confidentiality; tokenization removes the sensitive value from most systems. Store passwords as salted, slow hashes so they can be verified but never recovered.

exam_traps.trap: A matching MD5 checksum proves a downloaded file is unaltered.
exam_traps.why: MD5 collisions can be manufactured, so a match is weak proof. Use a collision-resistant hash such as SHA-256, ideally with a digital signature.

exam_traps.trap: Encrypting card numbers shrinks compliance scope as much as tokenization.
exam_traps.why: Systems holding encrypted card data can stay in scope, because the data is recoverable with the key. Systems holding only tokens never see the real number.

key_terms.definition: A random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hashes.
A precomputed list of hashes for common passwords, used to crack unsalted hashes quickly.
Two different inputs producing the same hash, which destroys its value as proof of integrity.

subtopics.name: Digital Signatures
subtopics.definition: A digital signature is a hash of a message signed with the sender's private key, proving who sent it and that it was not changed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Signatures let software, documents and transactions be trusted at a distance, and they support non-repudiation. That proof is only as good as the custody of the signing key.
how_it_works: The sender hashes the message into a message digest and signs that digest with their private key.
The receiver checks the signature with the sender's public key and compares the result with a fresh hash of what arrived.
A match proves integrity and origin and, if only the signer controls the key, non-repudiation.
The message itself stays readable; confidentiality needs separate encryption.
A certificate from a trusted authority links the public key to the signer's identity.

illustration.caption: Signing and checking. The sender signs a hash with their private key; the receiver checks it with the sender's public key against a fresh hash. A match shows the message is genuine and unchanged.

subtopics.example: A city procurement office requires suppliers to email digitally signed bids and believes this keeps prices hidden from rival bidders. The IS auditor explains that a signature proves who sent a bid and that it was not changed, but leaves its content readable. The IS auditor recommends that suppliers also encrypt each bid with the office's public key until the deadline passes.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A signature gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, never confidentiality. The sender signs with its own private key; the receiver verifies with the sender's public key. A signature is only as trustworthy as the custody of the signing key, which must stay under the signer's sole control.

exam_traps.trap: A digitally signed email is also kept secret from others.
exam_traps.why: Signing does not hide content. Anyone can read a signed message unless it is also encrypted with the recipient's public key.

exam_traps.trap: The receiver verifies a signature with the receiver's own private key.
exam_traps.why: Verification uses the sender's public key. The receiver's private key only decrypts messages encrypted for them.

key_terms.definition: Proof strong enough that the signer cannot credibly deny having signed.
Signing software so users can confirm its publisher and that it has not been altered.
The fixed-length hash of a message, which is what actually gets signed.
A hash keyed with a shared secret; it proves integrity and origin between key holders but not non-repudiation.

subtopics.name: Cryptographic Key Management
subtopics.definition: Key management is the control of cryptographic keys through their whole life: generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, backup, revocation and destruction.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Encryption is only as strong as the protection of its keys. A stolen key reads everything, and a lost or destroyed key can make data permanently unrecoverable.
how_it_works: Keys are generated securely and kept in a hardware security module (HSM) or managed key service, never in code or configuration files.
Each key has a cryptoperiod, a set lifetime based on its type and use, after which it is replaced.
Control of keys is separated from control of data, so the people who run a database cannot also use its keys.
Critical key operations need dual control and split knowledge, so no single person can export or misuse a key.
Keys are destroyed only after the data they protect has passed its retention period.
Excess access to keys is fixed at the permission grant, not by rotating the key.

rows.label: Protection
cells: Tamper-resistant hardware; keys never leave in readable form
Keys protected by the operating system and file permissions

rows.label: Fit
cells: High-value and regulated keys, such as root certificate and payment keys
Lower-value keys

rows.label: If tampering is suspected
cells: Move work to a healthy module and preserve the suspect one
Assume the keys are exposed and replace them

subtopics.example: A broadcaster encrypts its film archive with keys held in a single hardware security module, with no backup. The IS auditor notes that losing that module would make decades of footage unreadable. The IS auditor recommends an encrypted backup of the keys held under dual control at a second site, tested by restoring a sample, and a key destruction rule tied to the archive's retention period.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Separate who holds the keys from who holds the data, and require dual control for the most sensitive key operations. Every key needs a cryptoperiod; secure storage does not remove the need to rotate. Never destroy a key before the data it protects is no longer needed.

exam_traps.trap: Rotate the key to remove users who have excess decrypt access.
exam_traps.why: If the same people keep the permission, they can decrypt with the new key too. Fix the permission grant; rotation does not remove access.

exam_traps.trap: Destroying old keys immediately is always the safest choice.
exam_traps.why: Data still inside its retention period becomes permanently unrecoverable. Key destruction must follow the data's retention needs.

key_terms.definition: The approved lifetime of a key, after which it is retired or replaced.
Requiring two people to act together to complete a sensitive operation.
Dividing a secret so no single person ever knows the whole of it.

topics.overview: Public-key encryption only helps if relying parties can trust that a public key really belongs to the person or system it names. Public key infrastructure (PKI) provides that trust through authorities, certificates and rules. This topic covers its parts, the certificate lifecycle and revocation, and the recovery of encryption keys.
can_do: Explain the roles of the root and intermediate certificate authorities and the registration authority
Decide what to do first when a certificate authority or signing key is compromised
Tell which keys may be escrowed and which never are

subtopics.name: PKI Components and the Chain of Trust
subtopics.definition: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the set of authorities, certificates and rules that binds public keys to verified identities so others can trust them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Asymmetric encryption and signatures help only if a public key really belongs to its claimed owner. PKI provides that assurance, and a weak link anywhere undermines every certificate it issues.
how_it_works: A certificate is a signed record linking a public key to a name, with validity dates and permitted uses.
The registration authority (RA) verifies the requester's identity before the certificate authority (CA) issues a certificate.
An offline root CA, its key in a hardware security module under dual control, signs intermediate CAs that handle daily issuance.
Software trusts a certificate by tracing its chain up to a root it already trusts.
The certification practice statement (CPS) explains how a CA proves identity, protects keys and handles revocation.

types.meaning: Top of the chain; self-signed, kept offline and used rarely.
Issues certificates day to day; can be revoked without replacing the root.
Used by a website, person or device; cannot issue other certificates.

subtopics.example: A parcel carrier's handheld scanners were set to accept any server certificate, because the vendor disabled chain checks to stop connection errors. The IS auditor notes that anyone could then impersonate the dispatch server. She finds the errors came from an expired intermediate certificate, and recommends renewing it and restoring chain validation to the company's root as trust anchor.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A certificate is only as trustworthy as the identity check behind it and the protection of the CA's keys. Keep the root offline, use intermediates for routine issuance, and review an outside CA's practice statement before relying on its certificates.

exam_traps.trap: Keep the root CA online so certificates can be issued faster.
exam_traps.why: An online root exposes the trust anchor. Online intermediate CAs handle routine issuance while the root stays offline in a hardware security module.

exam_traps.trap: Any certificate from a well-known CA proves the holder's identity was strongly checked.
exam_traps.why: Assurance depends on the identity proofing done for that certificate type. The CPS shows what was actually checked.

key_terms.definition: The function that verifies who a requester is before a certificate is issued.
A CA's published description of how it issues, protects and revokes certificates.
The root certificate a system trusts without further proof, from which chains are checked.

subtopics.analogy: PKI works like passports: an office checks the applicant's documents (the RA), the passport authority issues a hard-to-forge passport (the certificate), and border guards trust it because they trust that authority.

subtopics.name: Certificate Lifecycle and Revocation
subtopics.definition: The certificate lifecycle runs from request and identity check through issue, use, renewal and expiry, with revocation to withdraw trust early when a key is compromised.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Expired certificates cause outages; compromised ones let attackers impersonate sites or sign malware. Tracking every certificate and acting fast on compromise prevents both.
how_it_works: The organization keeps its own inventory of certificates, owners and expiry dates; public Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate lifetimes are shrinking toward 47 days, so renewal must be automated.
After a key compromise, the certificate authority (CA) revokes the certificate and publishes its status through a certificate revocation list (CRL) or the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP).
Revocation protects only if relying systems actually check status when they validate a certificate.
For a stolen code-signing key, revocation is backdated to when the theft began, so anything signed after that moment stops being trusted.
Certificate pinning lets an app reject unexpected certificates; Certificate Transparency logs reveal certificates issued by mistake.

subtopics.example: An online grocer's security team watches Certificate Transparency logs and spots a certificate for its checkout domain from an authority it has never used. The web operations manager suggests waiting to see whether it is misused. The IS auditor recommends asking that authority to revoke it now and investigating how the request passed validation.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The organization owns its certificate inventory instead of relying on reminders from a CA or vendor. A compromised CA or signing key must lose trust at once, even at heavy operational cost, and revocation works only where relying systems check it.

exam_traps.trap: Once a certificate is revoked, every system stops trusting it.
exam_traps.why: Systems that never check revocation status keep accepting it. Validation settings must enforce revocation checking.

exam_traps.trap: Finish the investigation before revoking the certificate of a possibly compromised CA.
exam_traps.why: A compromised CA key can sign trusted certificates for anything. Withdraw trust at once and investigate in parallel.

key_terms.definition: A signed list of certificates no longer trusted, published by a CA on a schedule.
A query asking whether one certificate is still valid; fresher than a CRL, though public web CAs may now offer CRLs only.
Public logs of issued certificates that let domain owners spot ones issued without their consent.

subtopics.name: Key Escrow and Recovery
subtopics.definition: Key escrow is keeping controlled copies of encryption keys with a trusted party so data can be recovered if the original key is lost.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without recovery, a lost key or a departed employee can lock the business out of its own data. A careless recovery process, though, can hand keys straight to an attacker.
how_it_works: Keys that encrypt stored data are escrowed so the organization can recover its information.
Signing keys are never escrowed, because a copy would let someone else sign as the owner.
Escrowed keys are held under dual control, apart from the systems they protect.
A key recovery agent releases a key only after verifying the requester's identity and getting documented approval.
Every release is logged and reviewed, and recovery is tested so it works when needed.

rows.label: Escrow it?
cells: Yes, so data can be recovered
No, never

rows.label: If the key is lost
cells: Data is unreadable without a copy
Issue a new key pair; past signatures stay valid

rows.label: If someone else holds a copy
cells: They can read the data
They can sign as the owner, so non-repudiation fails

subtopics.example: A law firm escrows the encryption keys for its document archive but has never tried a recovery. When the IS auditor asks for a test, the recovery fails, because the escrowed key belongs to an archive server retired last year. The IS auditor recommends scheduled recovery tests, updating escrow whenever keys change, and logging and reviewing every key release.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Escrow encryption keys for recovery; never escrow signing keys, or non-repudiation fails. Restricting who can release keys does not stop release to an impostor; verifying the requester's identity does.

exam_traps.trap: Escrow signing keys too, in case an employee leaves.
exam_traps.why: A copy of a signing key lets someone else sign as that person, so signatures prove nothing. If a signing key is lost, issue a new pair.

exam_traps.trap: Limiting release to two supervisors is enough to secure key recovery.
exam_traps.why: Trusted staff can still be fooled. The control that stops release to an impostor is verifying the requester's identity.

key_terms.definition: The authorized role that retrieves an escrowed key after approval.
Confirming a request through a separate, trusted channel, such as a call-back to a known number.

topics.overview: Virtual machines, containers and cloud services let many workloads share the same hardware and software layers. That sharing saves money but moves the risk: the layer that separates tenants becomes critical, and security duties split between provider and customer. This topic covers deployment models, shared responsibility, virtualization, containers and software-defined networks.
can_do: Tell cloud deployment models from service models and match each to its main risks
Assign a cloud control to the provider or the customer for infrastructure, platform and software services
Explain why the hypervisor, the container orchestrator and the network controller need the strongest protection
Determine whether a provider's assurance report covers the customer's own settings

subtopics.name: Cloud Deployment Models
subtopics.definition: A cloud deployment model describes who shares the cloud infrastructure: the public, one organization, a community of similar organizations, or a hybrid of these.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The model sets how much control, isolation and visibility the customer has, and so which risks and evidence apply. It is a separate question from the service model, which sets who manages which layers.
how_it_works: The choice follows data classification, legal duties such as data residency, and the risk appetite the board has approved.
Each provider's assurance reports are checked for scope against the services actually used.
Hybrid and multi-cloud designs need one identity, logging and configuration standard across every environment.
Exit and portability plans limit vendor lock-in and cover how data comes back if the provider fails or the contract ends.

types.meaning: A provider's shared infrastructure serving many customers; fast and scalable, with less direct control.
Cloud infrastructure for one organization, on premises or hosted; more control at higher cost.
Shared by organizations with common needs, such as government agencies or hospitals.
Private and public environments connected, so data and identities move between them.

subtopics.example: A regional health authority's finance director plans to move patient records to a public cloud to save costs. The IS auditor finds no assessment of data residency rules or of how the hybrid link to on-premises systems will be secured and logged. He recommends a documented risk assessment, approved by the data owner, before the move goes ahead.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the deployment model to fit data sensitivity, legal duties and risk appetite, not cost alone. Whatever the model, the customer stays accountable for its data and needs evidence that covers the services it actually uses.

exam_traps.trap: A private cloud is secure by nature, so it needs fewer controls.
exam_traps.why: A private cloud still needs patching, access control and monitoring. It removes co-tenant risk but not misconfiguration or insider misuse.

exam_traps.trap: Deployment model and service model mean the same thing.
exam_traps.why: The deployment model says who shares the infrastructure. The service model (infrastructure, platform or software as a service) says who manages which layers.

key_terms.definition: Using services from more than one cloud provider at the same time.
Legal or contractual rules on the country or region where data must be stored and processed.
Dependence on one provider that makes switching costly or slow.

subtopics.name: Shared Responsibility in the Cloud
subtopics.definition: The shared responsibility model splits cloud security duties between provider and customer; the split depends on the service model, but the customer always owns its data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many cloud breaches come from customer settings, not provider failures: open storage, missing multi-factor authentication, over-broad key permissions. Customers who assume the provider handles everything leave these gaps open.
how_it_works: In every service model the customer keeps responsibility for its data, its users' access and the settings it controls.
The provider's System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 Type 2 report tests its controls over a period; its complementary user entity controls list what the customer must run itself.

Continuous automated checks, such as cloud security posture management (CSPM), must cover every account, because settings change in minutes; unapproved changes that remove a security control are reverted at once.
Data-access logs, not only administrative logs, show who read sensitive records during an investigation.
Code running in the cloud uses a workload identity, issued automatically and short-lived, instead of long-lived stored keys.

rows.label: Provider manages
cells: Facilities, hardware, network and hypervisor
All of that plus operating system and runtime
All of that plus the application

rows.label: Customer manages
cells: Operating system, applications, data, identities, configuration
Applications, data, identities, configuration
Data, user access and the settings it controls

rows.label: Customer's audit focus
cells: Patching, hardening and network rules
Code security, secrets and platform settings
Access, sharing and data settings

subtopics.example: A marketing agency uses a cloud file-sharing service and assumes the provider decides who can see its files. The IS auditor finds 4,000 client files shared through public links that never expire. The IS auditor explains that in software as a service the customer still controls sharing settings, and recommends link expiry, a ban on public links for client work and regular reviews of shared files.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsourcing a service never outsources accountability. The customer remains responsible for its data, identities and the settings it chooses, and needs its own evidence for them. A provider's report covers only the provider's side.

exam_traps.trap: The provider's SOC 2 report proves our cloud configuration is secure.
exam_traps.why: It covers the provider's controls. Storage permissions, key access and login settings are the customer's to configure and evidence.

exam_traps.trap: Logging administrative actions is enough for cloud investigations.
exam_traps.why: Admin logs show who changed the environment. Only data-access logs show who read sensitive records, which breach scoping needs.

key_terms.definition: Tools that continuously compare cloud settings with approved baselines and flag drift.
A short-lived, automatically issued credential that lets cloud code reach resources without stored keys.

subtopics.name: Virtualization and the Hypervisor
subtopics.definition: A hypervisor is the software layer that runs many virtual machines (VMs) on one physical server and keeps each one isolated from the others.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Virtualization saves hardware and speeds delivery, but the hypervisor becomes the most important control on the host. Whoever controls it, or its management console, controls every virtual machine on it.
how_it_works: The management plane sits on a restricted, isolated network with strong authentication and least privilege.
Administrator activity is logged to a store the administrators cannot alter or delete.
Hypervisors are patched promptly, because an escape flaw lets one VM reach its neighbors.
An inventory with owners controls VM sprawl, so idle or forgotten VMs are patched or retired.
Snapshots and VM images are protected like the data they contain.

rows.label: Runs on
cells: The hardware directly (bare metal)
A host operating system

rows.label: Attack surface
cells: Smaller
Larger, because it includes the host operating system

rows.label: Typical use
cells: Data center and cloud servers
Desktops, testing and labs

illustration.caption: The virtualization stack. The hypervisor sits between the hardware and the virtual machines and keeps each guest operating system separate.

subtopics.example: At a regional newspaper, the IS auditor finds 140 virtual machines that nobody claims, several unpatched for two years, and copies of the subscriber database's VM snapshots on a share open to all IT staff. The infrastructure manager says the hypervisor itself is fully patched. The IS auditor recommends an owner for every VM, retiring unclaimed ones, and protecting snapshots like the data inside them.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Protect the hypervisor's management plane as the keys to every VM: isolated network, strong authentication and logs that administrators cannot alter. Direct testing of isolation is stronger evidence than vendor statements. Patching reduces escape risk; dedicated hosts remove co-tenant exposure.

exam_traps.trap: Patching the hypervisor eliminates VM escape risk.
exam_traps.why: Patches fix known flaws only. For the most sensitive workloads, dedicated hosts remove the exposure to other tenants.

exam_traps.trap: Hypervisor administrators can look after their own activity logs.
exam_traps.why: Administrators should never be able to edit the record of their own actions. Independent, tamper-resistant logging counters privileged misuse.

key_terms.definition: An attack in which code inside a virtual machine breaks out to the hypervisor or to other VMs.
Uncontrolled growth of virtual machines, leaving forgotten, unpatched systems running.
The consoles and interfaces used to create, configure and control virtual machines.

subtopics.name: Container Security
subtopics.definition: A container packages an application with everything it needs to run, while sharing the host's operating system kernel with other containers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Containers start fast and use little memory, so modern applications run thousands of them. Because they share one kernel, their separation is thinner than between virtual machines, and one flaw can reach the host.
how_it_works: Container images are built in a pipeline that scans them for known vulnerabilities and blocks those that fail.
Containers run without administrator rights and with only the host permissions they need, which closes the most common escape paths.
An orchestrator such as Kubernetes schedules containers; its control plane and stored secrets need strong access control.
Runtime monitoring adds detection of unusual container behavior as defense in depth.
A suspected escape is contained by isolating the affected containers and the server running them, which also preserves evidence.

subtopics.example: A food delivery platform's Kubernetes control plane is reachable from the internet with one shared administrator certificate, and application secrets are stored unencrypted in it. The platform lead points to clean image scans. The IS auditor recommends limiting control-plane access to the admin network with individual, strongly authenticated accounts, and moving secrets into an encrypted managed vault.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Prevent first: block vulnerable images in the pipeline and run containers unprivileged. Runtime scanning adds detection, not prevention. Treat the host and the orchestrator as high-value targets, because one escape reaches every container on that host.

exam_traps.trap: A container is as isolated as a virtual machine.
exam_traps.why: Containers share the host kernel. A privileged container or a kernel flaw can let an attacker escape to the host and its other containers.

exam_traps.trap: Runtime scanning is enough container security.
exam_traps.why: It detects problems after deployment. A pipeline gate that blocks vulnerable images is preventive and should come first.

key_terms.definition: The packaged template from which containers are started.
Software, such as Kubernetes, that deploys, scales and manages containers across many hosts.
A container given broad access to the host, which makes escape far easier.

subtopics.name: Software-Defined Networking
subtopics.definition: Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the control plane, which decides where traffic goes, from the data plane, which forwards it, and centralizes control in software.
subtopics.why_it_matters: SDN makes networks programmable and quick to change, which supports cloud services and microsegmentation. It also concentrates power: whoever controls the controller controls the whole network.
how_it_works: A central controller holds the control plane and pushes forwarding rules to the switches.
Switches keep only the data plane and forward traffic as instructed.
Applications ask the controller for network changes through programming interfaces, which need authentication and authorization.
Controller access is restricted, strongly authenticated, logged and placed under change control.
Controllers are made redundant, because their failure can stop network changes or traffic.

illustration.caption: SDN splits the network in two. A central controller holds the control plane and decides routes; the switches keep only the data plane and forward traffic.

subtopics.example: A university moves its campus network to software-defined networking to speed up changes. The IS auditor finds network engineers all use one login to the SDN controller, and automation scripts push changes without approval records. He recommends individual accounts with multi-factor authentication, change control for scripted changes, and logging of every controller action.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Centralizing control centralizes risk. Protect the SDN controller like any critical management system: restricted access, individual accounts with strong authentication, change control, logging and redundancy.

exam_traps.trap: Centralized control makes SDN automatically more secure.
exam_traps.why: It makes consistent management easier but concentrates risk in one place. A compromised controller can reroute or drop any traffic.

exam_traps.trap: The controller's programming interfaces are internal, so they need no access control.
exam_traps.why: Anyone who can call them can change the network. They need authentication, authorization and logging like any administrative channel.

key_terms.definition: The part of a network that decides how traffic should be routed.
The part of a network that actually forwards packets according to those decisions.
The central software that decides traffic paths and pushes rules to every switch; whoever controls it controls the network.

topics.overview: Phones, wireless networks and connected devices carry company data far beyond the office walls, often on hardware the company does not fully control. This topic covers mobile device management and bring your own device (BYOD), Wi-Fi security, wireless attacks, and the Internet of Things (IoT).
can_do: Explain why a mobile device management report is not a control unless non-compliant devices are blocked
Recommend enterprise wireless with server certificate validation over a shared passphrase
Identify rogue and look-alike access points and the controls that stop them
Choose proportionate containment for compromised connected devices

subtopics.name: Mobile Devices and BYOD
subtopics.definition: Mobile device security protects phones and tablets holding company data, whether company-owned or personal under bring your own device (BYOD), mainly through mobile device management (MDM).
subtopics.why_it_matters: The most common mobile threat is ordinary loss or theft. Phones also hold email, files and sign-in tokens that reach core systems, often on hardware the company does not fully control.
how_it_works: Loss and theft are the most common mobile threats, so baseline controls are device encryption, a screen lock and the ability to wipe remotely.
MDM enforces these settings and blocks non-compliant devices, such as jailbroken phones, from company resources.
On personal devices, mobile containerization keeps company data in a separate workspace that can be wiped on its own.
Only vetted apps are distributed, with app security testing matched to the sensitivity of the data each app handles.
A wipe counts only when the device confirms it has run, so evidence of completion is kept.
For a compromised device, sessions and tokens are revoked centrally, and evidence is captured before any wipe.

rows.label: Removes
cells: Everything on the device
Only company apps and data

rows.label: Fits
cells: Company-owned devices
Personal devices

rows.label: Privacy impact
cells: Erases personal photos and files
Leaves personal data untouched

subtopics.example: A property management firm lets agents read tenant files on personal phones, and its policy says any lost phone gets a full wipe. Several agents refuse to enroll because family photos would be erased. The IS auditor recommends a managed work container on personal phones, wiped selectively when a device is lost, so company data is protected without erasing personal content.
subtopics.isaca_rule: MDM protects data only when non-compliant devices are actually blocked; a non-compliance report is not a control. On personal devices, separate company data and wipe it selectively. Evidence that a wipe ran, not the command, closes a lost-device case.

exam_traps.trap: A remote wipe command that was sent proves the data is gone.
exam_traps.why: The wipe runs only when the device receives it. Until completion is confirmed, revoke access centrally and treat the data as exposed.

exam_traps.trap: Let staff install any app, because MDM will catch the problems.
exam_traps.why: That relies on user judgment. Distributing only vetted apps enforces the rule instead.

key_terms.definition: Keeping company apps and data in a separate, encrypted workspace on the device.
Removing a phone's built-in restrictions, which disables key security protections; called rooting on Android.

subtopics.name: Wireless Network Security
subtopics.definition: Wireless network security protects Wi-Fi networks, whose signals reach beyond the walls, through strong encryption and authentication of every user and device.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Anyone in range can try to connect or listen. A shared passphrase known to former staff, or laptops that trust any network with the right name, leave the network exposed.
how_it_works: Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) is the current standard and WPA2 remains acceptable; Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) and the original WPA are broken.
Personal mode uses one shared passphrase; enterprise mode authenticates each user through 802.1X and a central Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) server.
Enterprise mode lets access be revoked per person and ties activity to individuals.
Clients must validate the authentication server's certificate, or a look-alike access point can collect their credentials.
Guests are placed on a separate network that reaches only the internet.
Hiding the network name, or service set identifier (SSID), and filtering by hardware address add little, because both are easily bypassed.

rows.label: Authentication
cells: One shared passphrase
Individual credentials or certificates

rows.label: Removing one user
cells: Change the passphrase for everyone
Disable that user's account

rows.label: Accountability
cells: Users cannot be told apart
Activity traced to each user

rows.label: Fit
cells: Homes and very small offices
Organizations

subtopics.example: A boutique hotel chain's back-office Wi-Fi uses a WPA2 personal passphrase, a hidden network name and a list of approved device addresses, which the IT contractor calls three layers of protection. The IS auditor explains that hidden names and hardware addresses are easily discovered and copied, and recommends WPA3 enterprise authentication tied to each employee's own account.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Tie wireless access to individuals so it can be revoked and traced. Enterprise mode with server certificate validation is the standard for organizations; hiding the network name, address filtering and passphrase rotation are weak substitutes.

exam_traps.trap: Rotating the shared passphrase every quarter fixes the leaver problem.
exam_traps.why: Leavers keep access until the next change, and everyone still shares one secret. Individual authentication ends access when an account is disabled.

exam_traps.trap: Enterprise mode is safe even if laptops skip server certificate checks.
exam_traps.why: Without that check, laptops will sign in to any look-alike access point, which can capture staff credentials.

key_terms.definition: A network access standard that authenticates each user or device before it may connect.
The central server that checks each user's credentials for enterprise wireless.
The broadcast name of a wireless network.

subtopics.name: Wireless Attacks: Rogue Access Points and War Driving
subtopics.definition: Wireless attacks exploit radio signals: rogue and look-alike access points create unauthorized ways in, while war driving hunts for weak networks from outside.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One unauthorized access point plugged into an office port can bypass the firewall entirely. Fake networks trick staff into handing over credentials, and outsiders can probe Wi-Fi from a parking lot.
how_it_works: A wireless intrusion detection system (WIDS) watches the airwaves for unknown access points and attack patterns; a wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) can also block them.
Periodic site surveys walk the premises with radio tools to find unauthorized devices and signal leaking outside.
Port-based access control (802.1X) on wired ports stops unapproved access points from connecting at all.
Server certificate validation on laptops defeats evil twins that copy the company's network name.
WIDS alerts go to a named owner who reviews and acts on them.

types.meaning: An unapproved access point connected to the corporate network, often by a well-meaning employee.
An attacker's access point that copies a trusted network's name to capture logins and traffic.
Searching for wireless networks from a moving vehicle to map weak or open ones.
Forged messages that knock users off a network, often to push them onto an evil twin.

subtopics.example: A county library system has no wireless monitoring. During a site survey, the IS auditor finds a consumer router that a librarian plugged into a wired port to improve signal, broadcasting an open network that bridges to the staff network. The IS auditor recommends removing it, enabling 802.1X on wired ports and running periodic surveys or wireless detection with a named owner.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A detective control works only if its alerts are reviewed and acted on; unreviewed alerts give false assurance. Stop rogue devices at the wired port, and defeat look-alike networks through server certificate validation.

exam_traps.trap: Installing a WIDS controls the risk of rogue access points.
exam_traps.why: Detection without review and response protects nothing. The IS auditor verifies who receives the alerts and what happened to them.

exam_traps.trap: Rogue access points are always planted by outside attackers.
exam_traps.why: Many are plugged in by employees seeking convenience. The risk is the same: an unprotected bridge into the network.

key_terms.definition: A walk-through with radio tools to map coverage, signal leakage and unknown devices.
A wireless intrusion detection system that can also act, for example by blocking a rogue access point.

subtopics.name: Internet of Things Security
subtopics.definition: The Internet of Things (IoT) is the set of connected devices, such as cameras, sensors and building controls, that often cannot run security software or be easily patched.
subtopics.why_it_matters: IoT devices often ship with default credentials, get few updates and are invisible to IT, so attackers use them as footholds or botnet members. Some control physical processes, where a wrong move can harm people.
how_it_works: An inventory lists every connected device with its owner, location and support status.
Procurement requires unique credentials, supported updates and a vulnerability disclosure process before purchase.
Devices that cannot protect themselves are segmented and allowed only the traffic they need.
Monitoring watches device traffic for unusual destinations or volumes.
Containment is proportionate: cut the harmful traffic path while keeping essential operations running.
In operational technology, safety is checked before any controller is isolated.
subtopics.example: A grocery chain's refrigeration sensors report to the vendor's cloud service, and nobody watches their traffic. The IS auditor finds one sensor has sent data to an unfamiliar overseas address for weeks. The IS auditor recommends allowing the sensors to reach only the vendor's service, alerting on unusual destinations or volumes, and naming an owner for each device group.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Devices that nobody knows about cannot be protected, so inventory and ownership come first. Building security requirements into procurement is the strongest preventive control. Segment and monitor devices that cannot protect themselves, and contain proportionately, with safety first in operational technology.

exam_traps.trap: Shut down every affected device when IoT devices join a botnet.
exam_traps.why: Cutting the harmful traffic path stops the attack while essential services keep running. A blanket shutdown can cause more harm than the attack.

exam_traps.trap: Install endpoint protection on IoT devices as on any laptop.
exam_traps.why: Most cannot run security agents. Segmentation, allowing only needed traffic, and network monitoring protect them instead.

key_terms.definition: A network of compromised devices controlled remotely, often used for attacks or spam.
Systems that monitor and control physical processes, such as plant machinery or building systems.
Factory-set usernames and passwords, often public, that must be changed before use.

topics.overview: Many attacks succeed by fooling a person rather than breaking a machine. A security awareness program teaches each person to spot, resist and report attacks in their own role, and it proves its value through changed behavior. This topic covers how to design the program and how to tell whether it works.
can_do: Explain why awareness training is role-based and finished before system access is granted
Choose a technical control over more training when awareness has already failed
Evaluate awareness metrics by behavior, such as report rates and incidents, rather than completion
Spot simulation results that cannot be compared from one test to the next

subtopics.name: Role-Based Security Awareness Programs
subtopics.definition: A security awareness program is ongoing training that teaches every person to recognize, resist and report attacks, with deeper content for roles that carry more risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Staff are the easiest way in for attackers and the fastest sensors when something looks wrong. A program that ignores role or timing leaves the riskiest people least prepared.
how_it_works: Everyone gets a baseline: spotting phishing, protecting passwords, handling classified data and reporting anything suspicious.
High-risk roles, such as administrators, finance staff, developers and executives, get role-based training on the attacks aimed at them.
New staff finish training before they receive system access, not at the next scheduled session.
Content changes as threats change, with short reminders through the year.
Where training has visibly failed, a technical control closes the attack path.
subtopics.example: A construction firm's finance team paid a fraudster after a phone call that imitated the chief financial officer's voice. Their only training is a generic annual phishing module. The IS auditor recommends role-based training for finance staff on voice and video impersonation, refreshed as attack methods change, and confirms that a callback to a known number is required before any urgent payment.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Awareness is matched to risk: the more damage a role can do, the deeper its training, and nobody gets access untrained. Training supports controls but does not replace them. When people keep falling for an attack, add a preventive technical control.

exam_traps.trap: Staff keep plugging in drives they find, so the answer is another round of awareness training.
exam_traps.why: Training has already failed against this baiting attack. Device control that blocks unapproved drives on every endpoint stops it whatever people choose; training stays as support.

exam_traps.trap: Administrators can take the general staff course, as long as completion is 100 percent.
exam_traps.why: Completion shows attendance, not fitness for the role. Administrators can do the most damage, so they need training matched to their access.

key_terms.definition: Security training tailored to the attacks a specific job faces, added on top of the common baseline.
Software on laptops and desktops that allows only approved removable media and blocks everything else.

subtopics.name: Phishing Simulations and Awareness Metrics
subtopics.definition: A phishing simulation is a harmless fake phishing email sent to staff so they can practice spotting and reporting attacks, and so behavior change can be measured.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Senior management funds awareness based on its metrics. Metrics that count completions, or improve because tests got easier, can show success while real risk is unchanged.
how_it_works: Simulations run regularly, using phishing lures that resemble the attacks the organization actually receives.
Each lure gets a difficulty rating, so results compare fairly from one campaign to the next.
Click rate shows how many people fell for the lure; report rate shows how many actively warned the security team.
Results are broken down by group, such as department or role, because one average can hide a group that clicks far more.
People who click get immediate, supportive coaching, and people who report get thanks, which builds a reporting culture.
Success is checked against real outcomes, such as incidents caused by staff error.

rows.label: What it measures
cells: Attendance at training
Falling for a lure
Actively warning security

rows.label: Strength as evidence
cells: Weakest: shows exposure to content, not behavior
Useful, but depends on how hard the lure was
Strongest once clicks are already low

rows.label: Good direction
cells: Up, but proves little on its own
Down
Up, and faster

subtopics.example: A shipping line's phishing simulations use generic prize-draw lures, while real attacks against it impersonate port authorities and freight invoices. Click rates are low, and the awareness lead reports success to senior management. The IS auditor recommends lures modeled on the attacks the company actually receives, each rated for difficulty, so results reflect real risk.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Effectiveness is shown by changed behavior and fewer incidents, not by completion, satisfaction or quiz scores. Metrics count only when tests stay comparable, and reporting must be rewarded, never punished. Diagnose a stalled program before changing vendors or budgets.

exam_traps.trap: Simulation clicks dropped by two thirds this year, so the program is clearly working.
exam_traps.why: If this year's lures were easier, the drop may mean nothing. Rate each test's difficulty and compare like with like before reporting progress.

exam_traps.trap: Disciplining people who click will improve results fastest.
exam_traps.why: Punishment teaches people to hide mistakes. Clicks may fall, but reports of real phishing fall too, and reporting is how real attacks get caught early.

key_terms.definition: The fake message used in a simulation; its realism and difficulty decide what the result means.
A workplace where people quickly flag suspicious messages, and their own mistakes, because doing so is welcomed.
Evidence that people act differently at work, such as verifying unusual requests, not just that they know the right answer.

subtopics.memory_aid: Completion shows they came, clicks show they fell, reports show they fight back.

topics.topic_name: Information System Attack Methods and Techniques
topics.overview: The IS auditor cannot evaluate a control without knowing what it is meant to stop. This topic surveys how attackers get in, spread and cause harm: through malware, people, applications, networks, stolen credentials, patient advanced attackers and insider fraud. For each attack, the notes name the control that removes it at the source.
can_do: Name the attack from a short scenario description
Match each attack to the control that prevents it at the source, not just a detective layer
Explain why popular fixes, such as longer passwords or more training, fail against specific attacks
Decide when to act visibly and when to scope quietly against an advanced attacker

subtopics.name: Malware and Denial-of-Service Attacks
subtopics.definition: Malware is software written to harm a system or its owner; a denial-of-service (DoS) attack floods or breaks a service so legitimate users cannot reach it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Malware drives many breaches, including ransomware outages that halt operations. A denial-of-service attack targets availability directly, and a large distributed flood can overwhelm defenses inside the organization.
how_it_works: Malware types differ in how they spread and hide: some need a person to run them, others copy themselves across networks automatically.
Signature-based antivirus catches known malware; endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools catch new or disguised code by what it does.
A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack comes from many machines at once, often a botnet of hijacked devices, so blocking one source does not stop it.
Volumetric floods fill the internet link before traffic reaches the firewall, so mitigation must happen upstream, through a provider contracted in advance.
Egress filtering, which limits outbound traffic, stops malware reaching its command and control (C2) servers and keeps the organization's devices out of others' attacks.

types.meaning: Attaches to a file or program and spreads when a person runs or shares it.
Copies itself across networks on its own, exploiting flaws without any user action.
Poses as useful software so a user installs it, then works in secret, for example by opening a backdoor.
Hides itself and other malware deep in the operating system, often with administrator rights, so normal tools cannot see it.
Encrypts or steals data and demands payment to restore it or keep it private.
Quietly record activity, such as keystrokes and passwords, and send it to the attacker.

subtopics.example: A retailer's card payments fail when a huge flood fills its head office internet link. The network manager keeps adding firewall rules, but the link is already full. Afterward, the IS auditor finds no contracted upstream mitigation and no DDoS playbook, and recommends both for the operations director to approve.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the defense to where the attack works. Malware is stopped by layered prevention, such as patching, least privilege and allowlisting, backed by behavior detection. A flood that fills the internet link is stopped upstream, by mitigation arranged in advance.

exam_traps.trap: Up-to-date antivirus signatures protect against all malware.
exam_traps.why: Signatures match only code someone has already seen. New, custom and fileless malware slip past, so behavior detection and allowlisting, which runs only approved programs, are needed.

exam_traps.trap: A bigger firewall will stop a large DDoS attack.
exam_traps.why: A large flood fills the internet link before traffic reaches the firewall. Only upstream filtering by the provider or a scrubbing service can absorb it.

key_terms.definition: The hidden channel an attacker uses to send instructions to malware and receive stolen data.
A flood meant to exhaust bandwidth, so the internet link fills before any on-site defense can act.
A provider that diverts incoming traffic, filters out the attack and forwards only clean traffic.

subtopics.name: Social Engineering and Business Email Compromise
subtopics.definition: Social engineering is manipulating people, rather than technology, into giving away access, information or money, usually by faking urgency, authority or trust.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It works through people who already have access, so technical controls rarely see it. Business email compromise causes some of the largest cybercrime losses.
how_it_works: The attacker researches the target, then uses a pretext, such as an urgent executive request, to rush the victim.
Business email compromise (BEC) uses a spoofed, look-alike or hijacked mailbox to redirect payments or change supplier bank details.
Process controls defeat it: a callback control confirms payment changes through a number already on file, and changing bank details is split from releasing payments.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF), DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) and a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC) reject policy block mail faking the exact domain, not look-alikes.
When a fraudulent payment is spotted, stopping or recalling it comes first, because recovery chances fall every hour.

types.meaning: Mass fake messages that lure people to click a link, open a file or enter credentials.
Phishing tailored to one person or team with researched details; whaling targets senior executives.
Phishing by voice call or text message, such as a fake help desk asking for a sign-in code.
Inventing a believable story, such as posing as an auditor or new supplier, to justify an unusual request.
Leaving an infected drive or tempting download for a curious person to use.
Offering a small favor or reward, such as free technical support, in exchange for access or information.

subtopics.example: A caller posing as an external auditor phones a hospital's payroll office and asks for a staff salary list for sampling. The clerk emails it to the address the caller gives. The IS auditor recommends verifying every request for personal data through a known contact before release, and adding pretexting examples to payroll training.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Assume someone will be fooled, and design the process so one deceived person cannot cause the loss. Verify through a channel the attacker does not control, and segregate duties. If money is moving, stop the loss first.

exam_traps.trap: Training staff to spot spoofed sender addresses is the best defense against BEC.
exam_traps.why: Many BEC emails come from hijacked real mailboxes, so the address checks out. Callbacks and segregated duties stop the payment even when the email convinces.

exam_traps.trap: When a fraudulent wire is spotted, convene senior management and notify everyone before acting.
exam_traps.why: A settled wire is rarely recovered. Request a hold or recall through the banks at once, notifying affected parties and police in parallel.

key_terms.definition: Phoning the requester back on a number already held, never one given in the request, before acting on it.
A domain one character away from a real one, used to make fake email look genuine.
Watching someone enter secrets, or searching discarded paper and media, to collect information without any hacking.

subtopics.name: Web Application Attacks
subtopics.definition: Web application attacks abuse how a website or app handles input, sessions and permissions, to steal data, act as another user or run the attacker's code.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Internet-facing applications are open to anyone and sit in front of customer data; broken access control and injection are among the most common serious flaws.
how_it_works: Most of these attacks succeed because the application trusts input it should check, such as form fields, cookies or uploaded files.
Structured Query Language (SQL) injection slips commands into a database query; parameterized queries keep data and commands apart, removing the flaw.
Broken access control lets a signed-in user reach records or functions that are not theirs; the server must check permission on every request.
Input checks in the browser are a convenience only, because attackers send requests directly; input validation and authorization must run on the server.
A web application firewall (WAF) filters known attack patterns and buys time, but it does not fix the underlying flaw.

rows.label: What the attacker does
cells: Slips database commands into an input field
Plants a script that runs in other users' browsers
Tricks a signed-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request
Sends more data than a memory area can hold

rows.label: Typical harm
cells: Reads, changes or deletes database records
Steals sessions or changes what users see
Changes settings or moves money as the victim
Crashes the program or runs attacker code

rows.label: Root fix
cells: Parameterized queries
Encode output and validate input; a content security policy adds depth
A secret token on each form, so the site rejects requests it did not create
Check input length before storing it, and use safer programming languages

subtopics.example: A concert ticketing site limits each customer to four tickets through a check in the web page's script. Resellers send requests straight to the server and buy hundreds of seats. The IS auditor recommends enforcing the limit, and every input check that matters, on the server, with rejected requests logged for review.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Fix application flaws at the source, in the code and on the server. Filters in front of the application are compensating layers that buy time. When ranking web risks, letting users reach data they are not entitled to outranks cosmetic weaknesses.

exam_traps.trap: A web application firewall in front of the portal fixes SQL injection.
exam_traps.why: A WAF blocks known patterns, and attackers find ways around them; the flaw stays in the code until queries are parameterized.

exam_traps.trap: Validating input with browser scripts protects the application.
exam_traps.why: Attackers can send requests directly and skip the browser entirely. Every check that matters must run on the server.

key_terms.definition: A database query where user input is passed only as data, so it can never change the command itself.
A flaw that lets users act outside their permissions, such as viewing another customer's account by changing an identifier.
A managed entry point that authenticates, rate-limits and logs calls; every application programming interface (API) needs an owner and must pass through it.

subtopics.name: Network Attacks: Spoofing, Interception and Tunneling
subtopics.definition: Network attacks target traffic as it moves, by listening in, faking addresses to redirect it, or hiding stolen data inside traffic that looks normal.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An attacker who can read or redirect traffic can steal credentials and data without touching the systems that hold them, and hidden channels slip out through allowed routes.
how_it_works: Sniffing captures traffic passing a network point; encryption such as Transport Layer Security (TLS) makes the captured content unreadable.
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) spoofing sends forged replies on a local network, so a victim's traffic flows through the attacker's machine.
Dynamic ARP inspection on access switches checks replies against trusted address records and drops forged ones, preventing the spoofing.
Domain Name System (DNS) spoofing feeds false lookup answers that send users to fake sites; signed responses and trusted resolvers counter it.
DNS tunneling hides stolen data in lookups; it is found by analyzing requests for unusual length, volume and destinations.

rows.label: What the attacker does
cells: Watches or records traffic without changing it
Changes, redirects, injects or blocks traffic

rows.label: Examples
cells: Eavesdropping, sniffing, traffic analysis
Spoofing, man-in-the-middle, replay attacks, denial of service

rows.label: Detection
cells: Hard, because nothing changes
Easier, because it leaves traces

rows.label: Main defense
cells: Encryption, so captured data is useless
Authentication, integrity checks and network controls

subtopics.example: Staff at a law firm's branch land on a fake webmail page although they typed the correct address. The branch router was using an outside name server that returned forged answers.
