The IT manager proposes password resets only. The IS auditor recommends the resets plus forcing all lookups through internal resolvers that validate signed responses.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the control that works where the attack happens: stop local spoofing at the switch, defeat eavesdropping with encryption, and find hidden channels by analyzing permitted traffic. Prevention at the source beats an alert after the data has gone.

exam_traps.trap: Reviewing blocked firewall connections will reveal DNS tunneling.
exam_traps.why: Tunneled lookups are permitted, so they are never blocked; only analysis of the lookups themselves reveals the pattern.

exam_traps.trap: Once traffic is encrypted, passive attacks no longer matter.
exam_traps.why: Encryption hides content, not patterns: who talks to whom, when and how much can still reveal sensitive activity.

key_terms.definition: An attacker secretly sitting between two parties, reading or changing what they send.
A company-run DNS server all devices must use, giving one place to log and filter lookups.
Forging a packet's source address to pose as a trusted host; edge filters drop packets with impossible source addresses.
A response header telling browsers to use only HTTPS; browser preloading also protects the first visit, defeating protocol stripping.

subtopics.name: Credential and Endpoint Attacks
subtopics.definition: Credential attacks steal, guess or reuse sign-in secrets, and endpoint attacks abuse a compromised device, so attackers act as real users and spread further.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Activity under a valid account looks normal, so it slips past many defenses. One stolen administrator credential can open the whole network.
how_it_works: Attackers gain a first account through phishing, leaked passwords or guessing, then hunt for more powerful credentials.
Privilege escalation raises their rights on one system; lateral movement uses stolen credentials to hop between systems.
Administrators who sign in to ordinary workstations leave reusable credential material behind for an attacker on that machine.
Fileless attacks live off the land, running through built-in tools such as the PowerShell scripting tool; restricting those tools to people who need them removes the path.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) defeats most guessed and leaked passwords; phishing-resistant authentication, such as FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online) security keys, also defeats relayed sign-ins.

rows.label: What the attacker uses
cells: A few common passwords tried across many accounts
Username and password pairs leaked from other breaches
A stolen password hash, replayed without cracking
A stolen cookie or token from a signed-in session

rows.label: Why a common control fails
cells: Each account sees one failure, so lockout never triggers
The password is correct, so complexity rules do not help
Nothing is cracked, so password length is irrelevant
Password and MFA were already passed

rows.label: Best response
cells: Detection across accounts, plus MFA
MFA and checks against leaked password lists
Limit where privileged hashes are exposed and detect reuse
Revoke active sessions

subtopics.example: An online pharmacy sees thousands of successful customer logins from unusual locations, using correct passwords leaked from other websites. The product owner proposes stricter password complexity rules. The IS auditor explains that complexity cannot help when the password is already correct, and recommends multi-factor authentication for customers plus screening new passwords against lists of known breached passwords.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the control to how the attack works, not to the word password. Limit where powerful credentials are exposed, require MFA, and end active sessions when an account is compromised. Least privilege shrinks what any one stolen account can do.

exam_traps.trap: Tightening the account lockout threshold will stop password spraying.
exam_traps.why: Spraying tries one password per account, so no sensible threshold is ever reached. Detection across accounts and MFA close the gap.

exam_traps.trap: Typing a matching number into my sign-in app stops a fake login page from passing my sign-in on.
exam_traps.why: The fake page shows the user the real number and forwards the user's approval. Only keys bound to the genuine site, such as FIDO2 security keys, resist this relay.

key_terms.definition: Attacking with tools already built into the operating system, so the activity blends in with normal administration.
Sign-in methods, such as FIDO2 security keys, that check the real site's address, so a fake page cannot relay them.

subtopics.name: Advanced Persistent Threats and Zero-Day Exploits
subtopics.definition: An advanced persistent threat (APT) is a skilled, well-funded attacker that hides in a network for months; a zero-day exploit attacks a flaw that has no patch yet.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These attacks defeat routine defenses and target high-value data; a zero-day has no patch, so exposure must be cut in other ways.
how_it_works: Attacks follow a lifecycle: reconnaissance, initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement, command and control, then theft or damage.
MITRE ATT&CK is a public catalog of real attacker techniques; mapping detection rules to it shows which behaviors go unseen.
Against a stealthy attacker with unknown reach, the team quietly searches for indicators of compromise (IOCs), then removes every foothold in one coordinated step.
For a zero-day with public exploit code, apply a compensating control, such as a firewall rule, at once, or remove internet exposure.
Supply chain attacks hide in trusted updates: roll back the bad component first, then rebuild hosts from clean images and rotate secrets.

rows.label: Goal
cells: Quick gain from any vulnerable target
Specific high-value data or long-term access

rows.label: Time in the network
cells: Hours to days
Months, often unnoticed

rows.label: Typical tools
cells: Known exploits and off-the-shelf malware
Custom malware, zero-days and stolen credentials

rows.label: Response priority
cells: Contain and clean up quickly
Scope fully, then evict all footholds at once

subtopics.example: An aerospace supplier's analysts find a stealthy intruder, present for months, who since this morning has been sending engineering drawings to an outside server. The incident lead wants to keep watching quietly to map every foothold. The IS auditor points out that sensitive data is leaving now, so blocking the outbound channel comes first, with scoping continuing in parallel.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Act on real risk, not labels. With no patch, cut exposure now through a compensating control. Against a hidden, patient attacker, map the whole intrusion before visible action, unless sensitive data is actively leaving.

exam_traps.trap: Blocking the attacker's control server at once is always the right first move.
exam_traps.why: Visible action warns an advanced attacker, who shifts to footholds not yet found. Scope first and evict everything together, unless sensitive data is leaving now.

exam_traps.trap: Increase monitoring until the vendor's patch arrives for an actively exploited zero-day.
exam_traps.why: Monitoring shows the breach only after data is taken. A compensating control, or cutting exposure, closes the path until the patch arrives.

key_terms.definition: Techniques that keep an attacker's access after reboots or password changes, such as hidden accounts.
Evidence, such as a file fingerprint, domain or address, showing a system may have been attacked.
Compromising a trusted supplier's software or update so the malicious code reaches all of its customers.

subtopics.name: Classic Computer Fraud Techniques
subtopics.definition: Classic computer fraud techniques are long-known insider tricks, such as salami slicing, data diddling and logic bombs, that misuse normal systems from the inside.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Insiders with legitimate access can steal or sabotage without breaking in, so perimeter defenses never see them. Each named technique is paired with its own best control.
how_it_works: Each technique hides in a different place: in arithmetic, in input data or inside approved program code.
Because the fraud looks like normal processing, the control must work at the point where the fraud happens.
The check comes from independent people or data, since the fraudster controls their own part of the process.
Segregating who writes code, who approves changes and who runs production limits salami and logic bomb fraud; independent input checks limit data diddling.

rows.label: What it is
cells: Slicing or truncating tiny amounts from many transactions
Changing data before or while it is entered
Hidden code that runs when a condition is met, such as a date

rows.label: Why it goes unnoticed
cells: Each theft is too small to see
Stored records look legitimate
It runs with the program's own authority

rows.label: Best control
cells: Independent recalculation and reconciliation (detects)
Input controls with independent verification (prevents)
Independent code review within change control (prevents)

subtopics.example: At an insurer, a developer who can also move code into production adds a routine that would erase claims history if his user ID ever disappeared from the payroll file. A colleague spots it by chance. The IS auditor recommends independent code review within change control, and removing developers' ability to promote their own code to production.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Put the control where the fraud lives. Prevent bad input with independent verification, prevent malicious code with independent review before production, and detect skimming with independent recalculation. Checks after the fact only protect figures that are already false.

exam_traps.trap: Reviewing output reports is the best defense against data diddling.
exam_traps.why: By the time output is produced, the false data looks legitimate. Preventive input controls with independent verification stop it at entry.

exam_traps.trap: Disabling the developer's accounts on exit would have prevented the logic bomb.
exam_traps.why: The code was already inside approved software and fires whether or not the author's accounts work. Independent code review before production prevents it.

key_terms.definition: Comparing two independent records, such as recalculated interest and the ledger, and investigating every difference.
A check applied as data enters a system, such as matching it to a source document or an independent count.
A close cousin of salami that diverts the fractions of a cent dropped when amounts are rounded into the fraudster's account.

subtopics.memory_aid: Where it hides: salami in the arithmetic, diddling in the input, logic bomb in the code.

topics.overview: Security testing finds weaknesses before attackers do. This topic covers scanning for known flaws, testing designs, code and running applications, and simulated attacks by penetration testers, red teams and outside researchers. A test reduces risk only when its scope fits the risk and its findings are fixed and retested.
can_do: Choose the right test for each lifecycle point, such as static analysis at commit and signed-in dynamic scans before release
Tell black-box, gray-box and white-box tests apart, and blind tests from double-blind tests
Spot coverage gaps, such as missing assets, scans that never sign in or unscanned indirect libraries
Evaluate whether testing reduces risk by checking risk-based priorities, remediation and retesting

subtopics.name: Vulnerability Scanning and Prioritization
subtopics.definition: Vulnerability scanning is automated, scheduled checking of systems for known weaknesses, such as missing patches, weak settings and outdated software, without trying to exploit them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most breaches use known, fixable weaknesses. Scanning finds them cheaply and often, but only on assets it knows about, and only helps when findings are fixed in risk order.
how_it_works: The scanner compares each asset's software and settings with a database of known vulnerabilities and reports matches with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score.
Coverage depends on a complete asset list; automated asset discovery, such as cloud inventories and network sweeps, catches new servers as they appear.
Credentialed scans sign in to each host and see installed software; uncredentialed scans see only what the network exposes.
Findings are ranked by exploitability, such as presence on a known-exploited list, by exposure and by asset value, not by severity score alone.
Each finding gets an owner and a risk-based due date, and the next scan confirms the fix.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: Which known weaknesses exist?
Can weaknesses be exploited, and how far can an attacker get?

rows.label: Method
cells: Automated and broad
Skilled people, targeted and deep

rows.label: Frequency
cells: Often, such as weekly or monthly
Periodically, such as yearly or after major change

rows.label: Risk to systems
cells: Low
Higher; needs written authorization and an agreed scope

subtopics.example: A clinic network's quarterly scan report shows only a few low-risk issues across 300 servers. The IS auditor learns the scans run without credentials, so they see network services but not installed software. She recommends credentialed scans through a dedicated, monitored service account, with results ranked by exploitability and asset value.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A scan is only as good as its coverage, and a finding matters only once it is fixed. Prioritize by real exploitability, exposure and asset value, assign owners and deadlines, and verify fixes. Repeat findings point to a broken remediation process.

exam_traps.trap: An uncredentialed scan shows every missing patch on a host.
exam_traps.why: It sees only what the network exposes. A credentialed scan signs in and inspects installed software and settings, finding far more weaknesses.

exam_traps.trap: Scanning more often will fix a recurring list of critical findings.
exam_traps.why: More scans only report the same open flaws sooner. The gap is follow-through: each finding needs an owner, a deadline and a confirming rescan.

key_terms.definition: A scan that signs in to a host to inspect installed software and settings.
Automatically finding devices, servers and cloud resources as they appear, so none are left out of testing.
A standard 0-to-10 severity rating; its base score rates a flaw in general, without knowledge of the organization's environment.

subtopics.name: Application Security Testing Across the Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: Application security testing finds flaws in software at each stage: threat modeling checks the design, static analysis reads the code, and dynamic testing attacks the running application.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Flaws are cheapest to fix early. Each technique sees only part of the picture, so gaps in timing or coverage leave whole classes of flaws untested.
how_it_works: At design time, threat modeling maps data flows and trust boundaries to find missing controls before code exists.
Static application security testing (SAST) reads source code without running it, so it can flag flaws at every commit.
Dynamic application security testing (DAST) attacks the running application and must sign in to test functions behind the login.
Software composition analysis (SCA) checks open-source libraries, including indirect ones, against lists of known vulnerabilities.
Application programming interfaces (APIs) are tested by requesting another user's records while signed in as one user.
Dismissing a finding as a false alarm needs independent approval, not just the developer whose code was flagged.

rows.label: When it runs
cells: Design
Each commit, without running the code
On the running application, before release
Each build

rows.label: What it finds
cells: Missing design controls
Coding errors in source code
Flaws that show only when the app runs
Known flaws in third-party components

rows.label: Blind spot
cells: Coding mistakes
Runtime and configuration issues; many false alarms
Pages behind the login, if it never signs in
Flaws in the organization's own code

subtopics.example: A telehealth startup begins coding a video visit feature and plans security testing a week before launch. The IS auditor recommends threat modeling now, mapping where patient data crosses into the video vendor's service, because design gaps found at launch cost far more to fix, plus static analysis on every commit.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Test early and test where the value sits. Match each technique to its lifecycle point, make sure coverage includes signed-in functions and indirect components, and keep decisions to suppress findings independent of the people whose work is tested.

exam_traps.trap: Clean results from a DAST scan that never signs in show the application is secure.
exam_traps.why: Without signing in, the scanner sees only public pages. The functions behind the login, where money and customer data live, remain untested.

exam_traps.trap: SCA that covers the libraries developers declare is complete.
exam_traps.why: Many serious flaws, such as Log4Shell, sat in indirect libraries pulled in by other libraries, so coverage must include the full dependency tree.

key_terms.definition: A library the application uses only because another library it declared depends on it.
An API flaw where changing a record's identifier returns another user's data because ownership is never checked.
Letting a misfiring rule flag but not block while it is fixed, instead of removing it or allowing unrecorded bypasses.

subtopics.name: Penetration Test Types and Knowledge Levels
subtopics.definition: A penetration test is an authorized, simulated attack that tries to exploit weaknesses; its type depends on how much testers know and who is told.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Knowledge and notice decide what a test can prove. A test that cannot see internal paths, or that warns defenders in advance, gives different assurance from one that does neither.
how_it_works: Management gives written authorization and agrees on the scope and rules of engagement before any testing starts.
Testing moves through planning, discovery of targets, attack and reporting, and stops if testers find signs of a real intruder.
External tests attack from the internet; internal tests start inside the network, as an insider or an attacker with a foothold would.
Knowledge levels run from black box, with no inside information, to white box, with full details such as diagrams, code and accounts.
Notice levels decide who is told, so a test can check detection and response as well as defenses.

rows.label: What testers receive
cells: Little beyond the target's name
Some details, such as a user account
Full details: diagrams, source code, credentials

rows.label: Simulates
cells: An outside attacker
An insider or an attacker with a foothold
A thorough, fully informed review

rows.label: Strength
cells: Realistic outside view
Balances realism and depth
Deepest coverage for the time spent

rows.label: Limitation
cells: Budget spent on discovery; deep flaws may be missed
Results depend on which details are shared
Less realistic about what an outsider would find

types.meaning: Testers get little or no information about the target, but its security staff know a test is happening.
Testers get little information and the security staff are not told, so detection and response are tested too.
Testers and the target's staff both know the details and work together, often on one system.

subtopics.example: A hospital wants to know whether its new monitoring service would notice a real intrusion. The information security manager proposes a white-box test with the operations team warned in advance. The IS auditor notes that warned defenders cannot show whether detection works and recommends a double-blind test, authorized in writing by senior management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the test type from the question being asked. To test defenses deeply, share more knowledge; to test detection and response, tell defenders less. Every type needs written management authorization, an agreed scope and rules of engagement first.

exam_traps.trap: Black-box testing is always best because it is the most realistic.
exam_traps.why: Testers spend a fixed budget rediscovering what real attackers have unlimited time to find. Gray- or white-box tests usually find more weaknesses for the same cost.

exam_traps.trap: In a double-blind test, nobody in the organization knows it is happening.
exam_traps.why: Senior management must authorize it in writing, and a named contact must be able to confirm test activity, so a real attack is not mistaken for the test.

key_terms.definition: The written limits of a test: targets, timing, permitted techniques, contacts and when testers must stop.
Signed management approval to attack named systems, which separates a lawful test from a crime.

subtopics.name: Adversary Simulation, Bug Bounties and Remediation
subtopics.definition: Adversary simulation tests how well defenders detect and respond to a realistic attack, through red, blue and purple team exercises and invited outside researchers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Finding flaws is only half the value. Testing reduces risk only when defenders learn from it, findings are fixed in risk order and retests prove the fixes.
how_it_works: Red team exercises run for weeks toward a goal, such as reaching payment data, then share findings with defenders.
A covert exercise needs a trusted agent who can tell real incidents from test activity.
A bug bounty invites outside researchers to report flaws for a reward, under a published scope and coordinated disclosure rules.
Findings are ranked by exploitability and the value of exposed assets, each with an owner and a deadline.
A prompt retest confirms each critical fix; findings that return year after year show the remediation loop is broken.

types.meaning: Attackers who imitate a real adversary covertly to test detection and response.
The defenders who monitor, detect and respond, usually the security operations team.
Attackers and defenders working side by side, tuning detections and retesting during the exercise.

subtopics.example: A university security team runs a two-day purple team exercise: testers replay credential-theft techniques while analysts adjust detections in real time. Afterward, the IS auditor samples the new detection rules, confirms each has an owner and passed a retest, and recommends scheduling the techniques the exercise never reached for the next quarter.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A test reduces risk only when findings are fixed and a retest confirms the fix. Risk does not depend on how a flaw was found. Covert tests need authorization and a trusted agent, and bug bounties need a defined scope.

exam_traps.trap: Reject a critical finding because the tester went outside the agreed scope.
exam_traps.why: Scope controls what testers may do, not whether a flaw exists. Start fixing the flaw now, and pursue the contract question in parallel.

exam_traps.trap: Tell the incident response team the test window so they do not overreact to a covert red team.
exam_traps.why: That removes the danger but also destroys the test of detection. A trusted agent who can confirm test activity protects both goals.

key_terms.definition: A person told about a covert test who can confirm whether suspicious activity belongs to it.
A follow-up test that confirms a reported weakness has actually been fixed.
An agreed process and timeline for a researcher to report a flaw privately before it is made public.

topics.topic_name: Security Monitoring Logs, Tools, and Techniques
topics.overview: Prevention eventually fails, so organizations must notice attacks in progress. This topic covers collecting and protecting the right logs, turning them into tested detections, and running a security operations function that acts on real alerts instead of being overwhelmed by low-value alerts.
can_do: Explain why collecting logs is not the same as monitoring
Identify evidence that a detection works today, such as a simulated attack that raises the expected alert
Recommend fixes for alert fatigue, stale rules and missing internal visibility
Explain what can and cannot be handed to a managed security provider

subtopics.name: Security Log Management
subtopics.definition: Security log management is collecting, time-stamping, protecting and keeping records of who did what, when and from where, so attacks can be detected and investigated.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Logs feed detection and are the main evidence after an incident. Missing, mistimed or alterable logs leave attacks unseen and investigations unable to prove what happened.
how_it_works: Sources are chosen by risk: sign-ins, privileged actions, security alerts, network traffic and access to sensitive data.
In the cloud, administrative logs show who changed settings; separate data-access logs show who read sensitive records.
Logs flow to a central store that the administrators of the source systems cannot change or delete.
Time synchronization sets all clocks from a common, trusted source, so events from different systems line up in one timeline.
Recent logs stay in the security information and event management (SIEM) system; older logs move to cheaper, searchable storage.
When a monitoring gap over sensitive data is found, the gap period is reviewed for misuse, not just fixed going forward.

rows.label: Purpose
cells: Real-time detection and alerting
Investigations and legal retention

rows.label: Typical span
cells: Weeks to a few months
The full retention period, often a year or more

rows.label: Cost
cells: Higher
Lower

rows.label: Feeds live detection rules?
cells: Yes
No; it keeps history only

subtopics.example: A water utility's control-room servers log to local disks that their administrators can clear, and the server clocks differ by up to eleven minutes. After a suspicious configuration change, investigators cannot build a reliable timeline. The IS auditor recommends forwarding logs to a central store the administrators cannot alter, and setting every clock from one trusted time source.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Logs are evidence only if they are complete, consistently timed and out of reach of the people they record. Collection is not monitoring; someone must review and act. Fix gaps going forward, and look back over the gap for harm already done.

exam_traps.trap: Once a broken log feed is restored, the monitoring gap is closed.
exam_traps.why: Restoring the feed protects only the future. Review the source logs for the gap period to find misuse already done.

exam_traps.trap: Moving costly log sources to archive storage keeps detection intact.
exam_traps.why: Archives keep history for investigations but do not feed live rules. Check which detections depend on a source before moving or dropping it.

key_terms.definition: Setting every system clock from the same authoritative source, usually with the Network Time Protocol (NTP).
A record of who read or changed specific sensitive data, as opposed to who changed system settings.
How long logs must be kept, set by investigation needs, regulation and contracts.

subtopics.name: SIEM, Correlation and Detection Engineering
subtopics.definition: A security information and event management (SIEM) system gathers logs from many sources and applies rules that link related events into alerts about possible attacks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Single log entries rarely look dangerous. Without well-kept correlation rules, a multi-step attack passes unnoticed even though every step was logged.
how_it_works: Correlation rules connect events across systems, such as repeated failed sign-ins on one server followed by a large download on another.
Detection engineering treats rules like code: written, version-controlled, tested against known attack data and released through change control.
Every rule has a named owner and a review cycle, so stale rules are updated or retired as systems and threats change.
Simulated attacks in the live environment confirm each expected alert fires, which is stronger evidence than reading a rule's logic.
Two add-ons extend a SIEM: user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) flags unusual activity, and security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) runs scripted playbooks.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Collects logs and applies correlation rules
Learns normal behavior and flags departures
Runs automated playbooks on alerts

rows.label: Main strength
cells: Links events across many sources
Finds misuse that matches no known rule
Speeds up routine responses

rows.label: Key risk
cells: Untested rules silently stop working
A baseline learned during an attack treats it as normal
A faulty playbook can isolate critical systems

rows.label: Audit evidence
cells: Simulated attacks raise the expected alerts
Baseline built from clean, reviewed activity
Playbooks tested against simulated alerts before release

subtopics.example: A shipping company's SIEM team gives the IS auditor a document describing 300 correlation rules. Instead of reading the rule logic, the IS auditor asks for results of last quarter's simulated attacks and finds 45 rules never fired against their test data. She recommends regular attack simulations in production and repair or retirement of every rule that fails.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Detection decays unless someone owns it. Treat rules as code with owners, testing and change control, and prove they work with simulated attacks rather than design reviews. Test any automation before it can act on production systems.

exam_traps.trap: Delete the oldest rules to clear a backlog of unowned, stale detections.
exam_traps.why: Age is not relevance; some old rules guard critical systems. Assign owners and review every rule on a set cycle, retiring only those that no longer apply.

exam_traps.trap: Build behavior baselines now, while an intrusion investigation is still open.
exam_traps.why: A baseline learned while an intruder is active absorbs the attack as normal and then stays silent about it.

key_terms.definition: Logic that links several events, often from different systems, into one alert suggesting an attack.
The practice of designing, testing, versioning and maintaining detection rules the way software is maintained.

subtopics.name: Security Operations Center Models and Threat Hunting
subtopics.definition: A security operations center (SOC) is the team, in-house or outsourced, that watches security alerts, often around the clock, investigates them and starts the response.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Alerts protect nothing until a skilled person acts on them in time. An overloaded or blind operation misses real attacks even when the tools fire correctly.
how_it_works: Analysts triage alerts, investigate credible ones and pass confirmed incidents along an agreed escalation path to incident response.
Alert fatigue is fixed at the source by tuning noisy rules with analyst feedback, not by quotas, extra headcount or auto-closing alerts.
Threat hunting starts from a hypothesis about attacker behavior and searches for evidence that existing rules miss.
Network detection and response (NDR) tools watch internal traffic, where lateral movement happens, not only the internet boundary.
With a managed security service provider (MSSP), the organization keeps staff who oversee the provider and own incident decisions.
Before merging or replacing SOC platforms, inventory the existing detection rules so coverage is not silently lost.

rows.label: Round-the-clock coverage
cells: Costly to staff three shifts
Included in the service
Provider watches; in-house staff handle escalations

rows.label: Business context
cells: Strong
Weak unless shared deliberately
Kept in-house

rows.label: Good fit
cells: Large, high-risk organizations
Routine monitoring, with retained oversight
Small teams that need continuous coverage

rows.label: Who is accountable
cells: The organization
Still the organization
The organization

subtopics.example: A manufacturer outsources overnight monitoring to a managed provider that escalates only by email. A high-severity alert at 3 a.m. sat unread until morning while an attacker moved between plants. The IS auditor recommends a contracted escalation path with phone contact and acknowledgment times, and an in-house duty manager with authority to approve containment.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Monitoring can be outsourced; accountability cannot. Keep enough in-house capability to oversee the provider and make incident decisions. Fix alert fatigue by improving detection quality, and add hunting and internal visibility for attackers who avoid the perimeter.

exam_traps.trap: Release all in-house analysts once a managed provider takes over monitoring.
exam_traps.why: Without retained staff, nobody can challenge the provider's triage, add business context or decide on containment. Contract penalties compensate after a miss; they do not prevent one.

exam_traps.trap: Investigating every alert the monitoring system raises counts as threat hunting.
exam_traps.why: That is reactive triage. Hunting is proactive: it starts from a hypothesis and looks for attackers that current rules do not catch.

key_terms.definition: Quickly sorting alerts by urgency and credibility so analysts spend their time on the ones that matter.
Overload from too many low-value alerts, which makes analysts slower and likelier to dismiss real ones.
The agreed route by which a serious alert reaches the people who make decisions.

topics.overview: A security incident is an event that harms, or threatens, the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information. How fast and how well an organization responds decides how much damage it suffers and whether it meets its legal duties. This topic covers the response lifecycle, the plan and team behind it, and the notifications that follow.
can_do: Put response actions in the right order: contain, eradicate, recover, then learn
Evaluate an incident response plan, checking approval and alignment before its details
Decide who must be notified, by whom and when, including after a vendor breach
Recommend how to test a plan in stages and retest it after changes

subtopics.name: The Incident Response Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: The incident response lifecycle is the repeating cycle of preparing, detecting and analyzing, containing, eradicating and recovering, then learning lessons that strengthen the next response.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Order decides damage. Acting late lets an attack spread, restoring early brings the attacker back, and skipping the lessons step lets the same weakness cause the next incident.
how_it_works: Preparation puts the plan, team, tools, contacts, outside retainers and exercises in place before anything happens.
Detection and analysis confirm that a security event is an incident and assess its scope, severity and the data at risk.
Containment stops the harm proportionately, such as isolating a host; where systems control physical processes, operations staff first confirm isolation is safe.
Eradication removes the attacker's access and tools; recovery restores from backups proven clean, once the full scope is known.
A blameless review after the incident establishes the facts, and its lessons must change controls, playbooks and training.
Frameworks group these steps differently; National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-61 Rev. 3 maps them to Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions. Order matters, not phase count.

rows.label: Goal
cells: Stop the harm from spreading
Remove the attacker and their tools
Return to normal, safely

rows.label: Example action
cells: Isolate a host; disable an account and end its sessions
Remove persistence, close the entry point, rotate credentials
Restore from verified clean backups and watch closely

rows.label: Common mistake
cells: Pulling the power and losing memory evidence
Removing access piecemeal and alerting the attacker
Restoring before the scope is known

subtopics.example: During fieldwork at a credit union, the IS auditor sees a teller workstation encrypting shared files. She does not touch it; she alerts the incident manager at once, who isolates the host. Afterward, the IS auditor evaluates whether the response followed the plan's order and reports gaps to management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: When an incident is causing ongoing harm, contain first; only human safety comes before it. A hidden attacker causing no active harm is scoped quietly, then evicted. Recover only after eradication and clean backups. Lessons must change controls.

exam_traps.trap: The IS auditor who spots an active incident should isolate the affected systems right away.
exam_traps.why: Containment is the response team's job under management's authority. The IS auditor alerts the incident owner at once and later evaluates the response; acting directly would impair independence.

exam_traps.trap: A final incident report closes the lifecycle.
exam_traps.why: A report records what happened. Without a lessons-learned step that changes controls and playbooks, the same weakness causes the next incident.

key_terms.definition: Any observable occurrence, such as a failed sign-in; it becomes an incident only when analysis shows actual or likely harm.
A post-incident review that looks for process and control causes rather than people to blame, so the facts come out.

subtopics.memory_aid: Contain, then clean, then come back: containment, eradication, recovery.

subtopics.name: Incident Response Plan, Team and Escalation
subtopics.definition: An incident response plan is the management-approved document that sets who responds, how incidents are rated and escalated, and which outside help and messages are ready.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Decisions made under pressure without agreed roles are slow and inconsistent. An unapproved, untested or misaligned plan fails exactly when it is needed.
how_it_works: Management approves the plan and aligns it with the security policy and risk assessment before its procedures are refined.
A computer security incident response team (CSIRT) has an incident commander with decision authority, plus technical, legal, communications and business roles.
A severity matrix rates incidents by business impact and data classification, not just by the technical score of the exploited flaw.
Escalation has several triggers, such as missed containment targets or newly found sensitive data, so worsening incidents still reach senior management.
An incident response retainer guarantees outside forensic help within agreed times, and legal pre-approves message templates for each audience.
Tests build in stages, use current threats and rotate participants; the plan is retested after each revision.

types.meaning: Key people talk through a realistic scenario to test roles, decisions and plan logic, without touching systems.
Teams carry out specific procedures, such as isolating a host or restoring a system, with real tools.
A realistic, end-to-end simulation involving all teams and often outside partners.

subtopics.example: A port authority has run tabletop exercises for two years, and its incident plan reads well, but nobody has tried the isolation and restore steps with real tools. The IS auditor recommends a functional drill of those steps next, then a full-scale exercise with outside partners, and a retest after each plan revision.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Review the plan's authority before its details: management approval and alignment with policy and risk come first. Then check that roles, severity and escalation follow business impact, and that staged tests prove the plan after every change.

exam_traps.trap: Rank incident severity by the vulnerability score of the exploited flaw.
exam_traps.why: A low-scoring flaw exposing regulated personal data can matter far more than a critical flaw on an isolated test server; severity follows business impact.

exam_traps.trap: Run the same tabletop script every year so results can be compared.
exam_traps.why: A repeated script tests memory, not readiness. Scenarios should follow current threats, with fresh twists and rotating participants.

key_terms.definition: The person with authority to direct the response and make decisions, coordinating technical and business roles.
One organization-wide table rating incidents by business impact and data sensitivity to set priority, escalation and notification.
A contract signed before any incident that guarantees outside experts will respond within set times.

subtopics.name: Breach Notification, Legal Duties and Third Parties
subtopics.definition: Breach notification is the legal or contractual duty to tell regulators, customers or affected people about an incident within set deadlines, which usually run from discovery.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Missed deadlines bring penalties and leave people unable to protect themselves. Outsourcing or insurance never transfers these duties, so the organization acts on its own evidence.
how_it_works: Counsel maps every notification duty and deadline, by law, regulator, contract and country, and notices proceed in parallel.
Notices go out promptly with confirmed facts and are updated as the investigation continues.
After a vendor breach, the organization uses its own logs and the vendor's cooperation to establish its exposure and meet its own duties.
Strong encryption whose key was not exposed may remove a duty to notify, but that conclusion is assessed and documented.
Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial loss, not the duty to respond; containment continues while the insurer is notified.
Indicators shared with industry groups carry Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) labels, such as red or amber, and have personal data removed first.

rows.label: Who it is
cells: Decides why and how personal data is used
Handles personal data on the controller's behalf

rows.label: Breach duty
cells: Notifies the supervisory authority and, when risk is high, affected people
Tells the controller without undue delay

rows.label: Example
cells: A firm, for its own employees' records
A payroll or cloud vendor holding that firm's data

rows.label: Can it pass accountability on?
cells: No
No; it answers for its own failures

subtopics.example: A payroll software provider finds a faulty report emailed one client's salary file to another client. Its account manager plans to mention it at next month's review. The IS auditor explains that the provider, as processor, must tell the affected client without undue delay so the client, as controller, can meet its regulator deadline, and recommends notifying now.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsourcing processing does not outsource accountability. The organization establishes exposure with its own evidence, maps every deadline, and notifies on confirmed facts rather than waiting for certainty. Insurance and vendor promises never pause containment or its own legal duties.

exam_traps.trap: Wait for the full forensic investigation before notifying, even when the deadline is close.
exam_traps.why: Deadlines usually run from discovery, not from the end of the investigation. Notify with confirmed facts and add details as they emerge.

exam_traps.trap: Once a provider has notified its affected business clients, its notification duties are complete.
exam_traps.why: Not for data it controls, such as its own employee records; there it is the controller and files its own regulator notice.

key_terms.definition: The government regulator that oversees data protection in a jurisdiction and receives breach notices.
The deadline for telling regulators or affected people, counted from awareness; under the EU General Data Protection Regulation, 72 hours to the supervisory authority.

topics.overview: After an incident, an organization may need to prove what happened in a disciplinary hearing, a lawsuit or a criminal case. Digital forensics collects and examines evidence so its findings hold up under challenge. This topic covers preserving evidence, collecting it in the right order and keeping conclusions within what the evidence shows.
can_do: Explain why investigators image and hash evidence before any analysis
Put evidence collection in order of volatility, including cloud and mobile sources
Spot actions that destroy evidence, such as rebooting, reimaging or signing in to a suspect's account
Limit a finding to what the evidence supports, such as an account rather than a person

subtopics.name: Evidence Preservation and Chain of Custody
subtopics.definition: Evidence preservation keeps digital evidence exactly as found, using verified copies and a documented chain of custody, so findings stay trustworthy and admissible.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Digital evidence changes easily, even when a well-meaning technician opens a file or restarts a machine. Altered or poorly documented evidence can be excluded in court or successfully challenged in a dispute.
how_it_works: First responders isolate and document the system, but do not browse, scan, reboot or reimage it.
Investigators read the original drive through a write-blocker, so nothing can be written to it.
They create a bit-for-bit forensic image and record its hash value; matching hashes prove the copy equals the original.
Analysis uses working copies, while the master image stays sealed for later verification.
Tools are validated against known test data, and examiners are independent of any party whose actions are under review.

rows.label: What it copies
cells: Every bit, including deleted files and unused space
Selected live files and folders

rows.label: Effect on the original
cells: None, when a write-blocker is used
May update access times and other details

rows.label: Proof of integrity
cells: Hash values matched against the original
Usually none

rows.label: Main use
cells: Evidence for investigation and court
Restoring data after loss

subtopics.example: At a university, a laptop seized in a grade-tampering inquiry passed between a department head, IT staff and campus security over three days, with no record of who held it. The IS auditor reports that the gap weakens the evidence, and recommends a signed custody record from seizure onward, hashing at imaging, and training for staff who seize devices.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Preservation comes before analysis. Work only on verified copies and keep an unbroken chain of custody. When integrity is challenged, an independent hash comparison against the original answers it without replacing any evidence.

exam_traps.trap: An IT technician should take a quick look at the suspect laptop first.
exam_traps.why: Even opening files changes timestamps and can make evidence inadmissible. First responders must be trained to isolate and preserve, then hand over to trained examiners.

exam_traps.trap: When a custody gap is challenged, re-image the device with witnesses and discard the first image.
exam_traps.why: Discarding the image destroys the evidence under challenge. A neutral examiner comparing hashes of the image and the original shows it is unaltered.

key_terms.definition: A signed record of who held the evidence, when, where and why, from collection to court.
Hardware or software that lets investigators read a storage device while preventing any change to it.
A fixed-length fingerprint calculated from data; any change to the data produces a different value.
Whether a court will accept evidence, which depends on showing it is relevant, reliable and unaltered.

subtopics.name: Order of Volatility and Hard-to-Reach Evidence
subtopics.definition: Order of volatility is the rule of collecting the most short-lived evidence first, such as memory and live connections, before longer-lasting disk data and archives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some evidence vanishes fast: memory on shutdown, cloud resources on deletion and provider logs on expiry. Collecting in the wrong order can lose the evidence that explains the attack.
how_it_works: Capture a memory image, running processes and network connections first, then temporary files, then disk, then remote logs and archives.
To stop active data theft, isolate the device from the network but keep it powered, so memory can still be captured.
In the cloud, snapshot disks and preserve account audit logs before automatic scaling deletes the resource.
Ask vendors to preserve short-lived logs they hold, such as a smart lock's cloud events, before examining the device.
Preserve evidence in someone's personal cloud account through counsel and lawful process, never by signing in with their password.
Analyze custom malware in an isolated internal sandbox, never on a public service where embedded data could leak.

rows.label: When to use
cells: The device is running, especially if encrypted or if memory-only malware is suspected
The device is already off, or volatile data is not needed

rows.label: What it preserves
cells: Memory, encryption keys, processes and connections
A complete, stable copy of the disk

rows.label: Risk
cells: Capture tools make small, documented changes
Shutdown erases memory and may lock encrypted disks

subtopics.example: After a theft of design files at a logistics depot, investigators need to know which systems a contractor's laptop reached. The network engineer plans to restart the core switch tonight for an update. The forensic lead first exports the switch's short-lived connection tables, then the laptop's memory, then images its disk. The IS auditor confirms this order follows procedure.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Collect what will disappear first. Keep a running device on, cut its network connection and capture memory before any shutdown, reboot or reset. Preserve evidence held by others through formal requests and counsel, never by accessing it directly.

exam_traps.trap: Pull the power cord to stop data leaving an infected laptop at once.
exam_traps.why: Power loss stops the transfer but erases memory, which may hold the malware, keys and connections. Network isolation stops the transfer just as fast.

exam_traps.trap: Factory-reset a phone with suspected spyware to protect the user.
exam_traps.why: A reset permanently destroys the evidence. Give the user a clean device, isolate the old one and image it first.

key_terms.definition: A copy of a running computer's memory, holding processes, connections and keys that vanish on shutdown.
An isolated environment where suspicious code runs safely while analysts watch it.

subtopics.name: Forensic Readiness and the Limits of Findings
subtopics.definition: Forensic readiness is preparing, before any incident, to collect and keep the evidence investigations will need, and to report only what that evidence supports.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Evidence that was never kept cannot be recovered by any tool. Conclusions that go beyond the evidence collapse under challenge and can harm innocent people.
how_it_works: Log retention is set by how long intrusions take to detect and by legal needs, not by default storage settings.
When litigation is reasonably expected, a legal hold suspends routine deletion for the relevant people and systems.
Readiness plans name who may collect evidence, which tools they use and where copies are stored.
When an insider is suspected but no data is leaving, evidence is preserved quietly under legal direction before anyone is confronted.
Timestamps an attacker could alter are checked against independent sources, such as central logs and network records.
Cleared logs, a common anti-forensics step, are themselves a sign of attacker activity; events are rebuilt from copies held elsewhere.

columns: What it does not show alone

rows.label: Activity under a user account
cells: The account was used
Which person was at the keyboard

rows.label: Techniques matching a known group
cells: How the attack was carried out
Who the attacker is

rows.label: File timestamps on one host
cells: The times that host recorded
The true times, if the attacker could alter them

rows.label: No events in a log
cells: Nothing was recorded
Nothing happened

rows.label: Network flow records
cells: Who talked to whom, when and how much
What content actually left; only full packet capture shows that

subtopics.example: A retailer's investigator concludes that no data left the network during a five-week intrusion because the firewall logs show nothing. The IS auditor learns the firewall keeps logs for only ten days. He recommends reporting that data theft cannot be ruled out for most of the period, and setting log retention from typical detection times and legal needs.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Prepare to collect evidence before an incident, and report only what that evidence proves. Account activity shows which account acted, not who; naming a nation-state attacker is a judgment for government agencies. Corroborate anything an attacker could have altered.

exam_traps.trap: The incident report should say which foreign government is probably behind the attack.
exam_traps.why: Other actors can copy published techniques, and attribution needs intelligence the organization does not hold. State the technical indicators and leave attribution to government agencies.

exam_traps.trap: When a lawsuit looms, keep all company email forever to be safe.
exam_traps.why: A hold should cover the relevant people and systems. Keeping everything forever is disproportionate, costly and holds personal data far longer than needed.

key_terms.definition: An instruction to preserve information relevant to expected or actual litigation, overriding normal deletion schedules.
Confirming a fact with a second, independent source that the same party could not have altered.
Steps attackers take to hide or destroy evidence, such as clearing logs or changing timestamps.

key_terminologies.Information security management system (: A managed, repeating cycle of risk assessment, controls, monitoring and improvement; the subject of ISO/IEC 27001.
key_terminologies.Statement of Applicability (SoA): The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 record of which controls apply, which are excluded, and the risk-based reason for each.
key_terminologies.Security baseline: The minimum configuration every system of a given type must meet; a floor, not a target.
key_terminologies.Compensating control: An alternative control that reduces risk to an acceptable level when the required control cannot be applied.
key_terminologies.Data owner: The business manager accountable for a data set, who classifies it and approves access to it.
key_terminologies.Least privilege: Giving each person or process only the access its task needs, for only as long as it needs it.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties: Splitting a sensitive process so no single person can complete it alone.
key_terminologies.Defense in depth: Layering independent controls so that one failure does not expose the asset.
key_terminologies.Multi-factor authentication (MFA): Login that combines factors from different categories: something the user knows, has or is.
key_terminologies.Single sign-on (SSO): One authentication that gives access to many systems through a trusted identity provider.
key_terminologies.Privileged access management (PAM): Controls over administrator accounts, such as vaulted passwords, approved time-limited elevation and recorded sessions.
key_terminologies.Zero trust: A security approach that checks every request on identity, device and context instead of trusting network location.
key_terminologies.Screened subnet (demilitarized zone, DMZ: A buffer zone for internet-facing systems, filtered from both the internet and the internal network.
key_terminologies.Network access control (NAC): Checking a device's identity and security health before letting it join the network.
key_terminologies.Endpoint detection and response (EDR): Software on each device that watches process behavior to detect and help contain attacks.
key_terminologies.Data loss prevention (DLP): Tools that find sensitive data and alert on or block it leaving through unapproved channels.
key_terminologies.Symmetric encryption: Encryption in which one shared secret key both locks and unlocks the data.
key_terminologies.Asymmetric encryption: Encryption with a linked public and private key pair; what one key locks, only the other unlocks.
key_terminologies.Digital signature: A hash signed with the sender's private key, proving origin and integrity and supporting non-repudiation.
key_terminologies.Certificate authority (CA): The trusted party in a public key infrastructure that signs certificates binding public keys to identities.
key_terminologies.Certificate revocation: Withdrawing trust in a certificate before it expires, for example after its private key is compromised.
key_terminologies.Key escrow: Holding controlled copies of encryption keys so data can be recovered; never used for signing keys.
key_terminologies.Shared responsibility model: The split of security duties between a cloud provider and its customer, which varies by service model.
key_terminologies.Hypervisor: The software layer that runs virtual machines on shared hardware and keeps them isolated.
key_terminologies.Mobile device management (MDM): A system that enforces security settings on mobile devices and can block or wipe non-compliant ones.
key_terminologies.Security information and event managemen: Central log collection with correlation rules that turn events from many sources into attack detections.
key_terminologies.Chain of custody: The documented record of who held evidence, when and why, from collection to court.
key_terminologies.Order of volatility: Collecting the most short-lived evidence, such as memory, before more durable evidence, such as disk.
key_terminologies.Security incident: A security event that analysis shows has harmed, or is likely to harm, the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information.

cross_domain_connections.note: The same habit runs through all five domains: find what matters most and act on it first. Auditors plan by risk, governance sets risk appetite, operations recover the most critical services first, and security protects the most valuable assets most.

cross_domain_connections.connection: One control can be judged three ways
cross_domain_connections.note: A control can stop a problem, spot it, or fix it after the fact. Whatever the domain, ask which of those it does, and whether it addresses the cause or only the symptom.

cross_domain_connections.connection: Change control spans governance, development and operations
cross_domain_connections.note: Governance sets the change policy, projects build changes, and operations move them into live systems. The auditor checks that every change was approved, tested and traceable, including emergency changes reviewed afterward.

cross_domain_connections.connection: Continuity and security depend on each other
cross_domain_connections.note: A recovery site, backup or failover link is only useful if it is protected as well as the original. Continuity plans should assume an attacker may cause the outage.

cross_domain_connections.connection: Access principles repeat at every layer
cross_domain_connections.note: Least privilege, need to know and segregation of duties apply to applications, databases, networks, schedulers and cloud consoles alike. The layer changes; the principle does not.

exam_strategy_tips: Look for the priority word first: BEST, MOST, FIRST, PRIMARY or GREATEST. It decides which of several true answers wins.
Keep the roles straight: management owns and fixes controls, and the IS auditor assesses, reports and recommends.
When two answers both sound right, ask which must happen first. Understanding or assessing usually comes before acting, unless harm is spreading now; then contain first.
Prefer the answer that fixes the cause over one that treats a symptom or adds more checking.
Governance and process come before buying a tool. A technology answer rarely wins unless the gap is purely technical.
Stopping a problem usually beats finding it later, but a detective control is right when prevention is impractical.
Distrust absolute words such as always, never and all. ISACA answers are usually conditional on risk.
Base your answer on the facts in the question, not on what your own organization does.
